en: Preface to the Collated Readings of the Commentary on the *Awakening of Faith* (Qixin lun shuji).
The Tathāgata, in accordance with his nature, preached the sūtras, clarifying the one mind through the myriad dharmas; thus, the sūtras are already sublime.

The Bodhisattvas, relying upon these sūtras, composed treatises, opening forth the myriad dharmas from the one mind; how could the treatises not be profound? Those who wish to realize their own nature... [no more text provided]

If one wishes to thoroughly investigate the hundredfold scriptures and master their underlying meanings, there is nothing better than to specialize in the treatises of the Five Divisions (*pañcavastuka*).

In establishing its principles, it sets forth the Dharma of the One Mind, opens the gateway of the Two Truths, enumerates the significance of the Three Greats, and turns the vehicle of the Two Transmissions.
In its exposition of the teachings, True Suchness (*tathatā*) is expressed through words that transcend all words. It stands far beyond...

Beyond the four propositions and hundred negations, the storehouse mind is both non-awakened and awakened; it pervades throughout the three vehicles and the six realms of existence, whether expressed or unexpressed.
It is empty yet not empty—this is the ultimate convergence of the five teachings. It is both awakened and non-awakened;
it is undifferentiated yet differentiated—how could the distinct destinies of the ten realms be anything other than this? Thus, from the perspective of the true and the false...

Mutually perfuming, they are practiced until they form a nature; causes and conditions mutually complete one another, enabling the mind to be realized. Although the three subtleties and six coarsenesses arise according to defiled conditions, the source of the mind remains unmoved.
Through the four stages and six departures, one returns to cessation by relying on pure conditions; yet the nature is fundamentally quiescent.
In this state of quiescent nature, how could it obstruct the arousal of the ten wholesome actions and the three minds? It is like waves surging upon the ocean of wisdom.
When the mind is unmoving, there is no hindrance to shattering the five attachments and two views; it is like clouds dispersing across the sky of ultimate meaning.
If one does not realize the mutual interpenetration of phenomena and their convergence with reality, how could one manifest function from the essence? As for practicing these practices:

do not destroy faith in the Triple Gem within your own mind, but steadfastly cultivate the five practices within the dharma-realm. The two gates of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are both operated within the single-practice samādhi.

The two aspects of phenomena and principle interpenetrate the ten bodies of all Buddhas. As for the fruit of this cultivation: one now upholds the secret treasury and shall surely succeed to the lineage of the Buddhas.
Even if one were to take empty space as a mouth and the myriad phenomena as a tongue, one could not fully praise the merit of accord with nature nor the virtue of the transformative Way.
Thus established is the principle; the principle is already consummate. Thus expounded is the teaching; the teaching is already complete. Such is the case.
This is the practice of practices; the practice is now complete. Such is the cultivation of the fruit; the fruit is now perfected.
Without the Mahāyāna, there would be no means to give rise to faith; without giving rise to faith, there would be no means to expand the Vehicle.
If faith did not culminate here, it would not be ultimate faith. If greatness did not pervade this, it would not be true and genuine greatness. The preceding causes and conditions were the cause.
It is for this reason. The subsequent exhortations urge one to practice this. That which every Buddha has spoken is the teaching of this Dharma;
that which every sutra explains is the elucidation of this meaning. Thus we know that this treatise serves as the pointing finger of all Buddhas and the eye of all scriptures;
it is the path of the sages and saints, and the mirror for cause and effect. Therefore, our Master Xianshou—
He did not seek honor by being titled Imperial Preceptor; rather, he held the exegesis of the sutras as his primary pursuit.

Upon emerging from the translation hall, he reflected further upon this treatise and, with the mouth of the white curl, extensively elucidated the texts that transcend all marks. With the eloquence of a golden lion, he suspendedly expounded the meaning of words that leave nothing behind.
Vertically, based on the five kinds of *tathatā* (suchness), he established the doctrinal characteristics of the Initial, Final, Sudden, and Perfect teachings;

horizontally, relying on the five stages of birth and phenomena, he distinguished the sectarian vehicles of the Small and Great Vehicles regarding nature and characteristics. His capacity to define the essence of the teachings was as vast as the heavens, and his determination of the capacities of those to be converted was as firm as the kalpa-stone.
He analyzed the Dharma-treasure through four interpretations and distinguished the stages of realization through three types of awakening, all contained within these two gates.

It demonstrates non-duality; that is, by means of non-difference, it clarifies non-identity. The *dharmatā* encompasses the *buddhadhātu*. The wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*) is not external to the form-body (*rūpakāya*).

Initial awakening (*ādikṣānti-bodhi*) possesses four phases within a single thought-moment. Original awakening (*mūlabodhi*) possesses both the nature that accords with defilement and the nature that is pure.

It is eternally defiled even while being pure; though unchanging, it accords with conditions. It is eternally pure even while being defiled; though manifesting phenomena, its essence is empty. Or, one may be deluded.
Taking the real as the semblance, or grasping the semblance as the real, how could one know that the essence of phenomena has no beginning?

If the false defilements of birth and death contradict the principle, then there is an end but no beginning; yet the essence of phenomena is inexhaustible. If the true purity of nirvāṇa accords with the principle, then there is a beginning but no end.
This is like the contemplation of "arising is itself ceasing," which realizes true suchness within the process of arising and ceasing.
Thus, through contemplation, one comes to rest; one realizes the convergence of arising and ceasing within True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Spontaneously, immeasurable afflictions are transformed into sands-of-dust virtues, and the minds of sentient beings are transmuted into the Tathāgata-garbha. It is not merely the cessation of delusion, nor is it simply the departure from the Real;

both Real and delusive are simultaneously extinguished, leaving only the One Mind remaining. This is truly the emanation-body of the Lotus World; therefore, its wisdom and discernment are such as described. Since the Commentary [states]...
Vast and remote, it addresses only those of sharp faculties; were it not for the divine power of tranquil illumination, its profound source would be unfathomable.

Master Guishan, for the sake of those with middling or inferior capacities, further extracted the essential points and recorded them directly from the treatise. Dharma Master Shibie, based upon these concise and profound annotations, [compiled this work].

In the *Caiji* (Collection) section, the commentary is explained in detail. After Master Changshui awakened to the fundamentally pure nature, he verified the remaining traces of the Buddhas’ and Patriarchs’ minds and words.
He rejoiced in this treatise and commentary, deliberating upon the explanatory text and scrutinizing whether the phrasing was prolix or concise.
I have examined the merits and defects of the various compositions. Where details were excessive, I have abridged them so as not to trouble the divine mind;

where they were too concise, I have expanded them so that the source and its currents would not remain obscure. Having carefully reached a balanced compromise, I have revised the titles and made deletions.

Furthermore, these records were previously circulated separately and had never been compiled into a single volume. Master Fuzhai, pitying the difficulties faced by later students in understanding them, again requested that they be divided into sections.

Lacking wisdom (and continuing the Dharma), I have reflected upon the hardships endured by the hearts of former sages. How could I dare to oppose their noble intentions? Although I have not followed them slavishly, nor have I strayed from them;
though there is nothing subtracted and nothing added, I have succeeded in bringing the treatises and commentaries onto a single path.

I venture to compare this to the harmony of wind and string instruments, and the unifying thread of the sub-commentaries, which is like the blending of water and milk. Looking back from the present to the past, there is nothing that does not flow from this Dharma-realm.
The one becomes the immeasurable; viewing the past from the perspective of the present, there is nothing that does not return to this Dharma-realm. The immeasurable becomes the one;

thus, the beginning and the end are perfectly interfused, and opening and closing are non-dual. Were it not for one who has awakened to and entered the intent of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, who could believe and accept this Dharma?
Those who wish to exhaustively investigate its principles should devote their whole hearts to it.
Preface by the Initiation Practitioner (Xùfǎ), written in the chamber at Cíyún on the nineteenth day of the seventh month in the Gēngshēn year of the Kāngxī era.
*Commentary on the Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna: A Record of Revision*, Volume One, compiled by the Śramaṇa Fǎzàng of Tàiyuán in the Western Capital of the Tang Dynasty. Commentary.
Recorded and annotated by the Śramaṇa Zongmi of the Caotang Hermitage on Mount Zhongnan;
revised by the Śramaṇa Zixuan of Changshui in Xiuzhou during the Song Dynasty;
and compiled by the Śramaṇa Xufu of Ciyun Temple in Qiantang during the Qing Dynasty.
Reviewed and Verified by Dai Jingzeng, Vice Governor of Shuntian Prefecture.

[Commentary: First, the title of the commentary on the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* is presented. The title constitutes the general outline of the entire work; it is impossible not to know it beforehand.
Therefore, it is necessary to briefly explain the five characters in the title. These may be correlated with the Fivefold Profound Meaning (*wǔzhòng xuányì*) of the Tiantai school.
Whenever Tiantai masters interpret a sutra title, they invariably rely on these five meanings. Here, "Great" (*dà*) refers to the essence (*tǐ*); "Vehicle" (*chéng*) refers to the doctrine (*zōng*);

"Arousal of Faith" (*qǐxìn*) refers to the function (*yòng*); and "Treatise" (*lùn*) refers to the teaching (*jiào*). The single treatise expounds nothing other than essence, doctrine, and function; thus, these five characters are integrated.

Therefore, this is precisely what is meant by "name. Regarding the statement that "the Great [Vehicle] has the One Mind as its essence," there are both general and specific aspects. Generally, the One Mind constitutes the essence;
it is the fundamental substance of this treatise, for nothing transcends it.

This is because it is that which faith takes as its object, that which understanding realizes, that which practice pursues, that which realization enters, that which causes are induced by, and that which fruits manifest. Therefore, at the beginning of the treatise, it is designated as such.
It constitutes the essence of the Dharma. The text states: "The Mahāyāna consists of two aspects: first, the phenomena (dharma); second, their meaning (artha).
As for what is called 'phenomena,' it refers to the mind of sentient beings. This mind encompasses all mundane and supramundane phenomena.

Based upon this mind, the meaning of the Mahāyāna and so forth are revealed. This directly identifies the phenomenon itself and designates it as "Great" (Mahā), meaning that it vertically exhausts [all time].
Transversely pervasive, unimpeded, and perfectly interfused, it receives its name from its own essential nature rather than by depending on the small. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Because it does not depend on small emptiness, it is called great emptiness. Nirvāṇa is likewise: because it does not depend on small characteristics, it is called Great Nirvāṇa.

As for "distinctions," these are discussed in terms of their meanings, and there are three kinds: essence (*tǐ*), characteristic (*xiàng*), and function (*yòng*). These are simply the aforementioned single mind opened up into three meanings;
they are the three virtues (*triguṇa*) of the Great Nirvāṇa. As stated in the text below: "As for what is called 'meaning,' there are three kinds:
first, the greatness of essence (*tǐ-dà*), which refers to the fact that all phenomena are the equality of true suchness (*tathatā*), neither increasing nor decreasing."

Because it is diminished. Second is the greatness of its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-mahattva*): this refers to the *tathāgatagarbha*, because it is fully endowed with the qualities of untainted nature (*anāsrava-dharmatā-guṇa*).
Third is the greatness of its function (*vṛtti-mahattva*): it is able to produce all mundane and supramundane wholesome causes and effects.

Therefore, the single character "Great" (*mahā*) applies to all three. As for the vehicle (*yāna*), which is termed the "principle" (*mūla*), it is so called because it takes the essence [of the path] by proceeding from cause to fruit.

"Vehicle" (*yāna*) is a designation established through metaphor; its essential meaning is "conveying. It is like the boats and carts of the world, which can transport heavy loads over great distances.

This serves as a metaphor for the Bodhisattva, who, mounting this Great Dharma, crosses the wilderness of birth and death, traverses the river of afflictions, reaches the land of Bodhi, and ascends the shore of Nirvana.
Therefore, the subsequent text states: "Because it is that upon which all Buddhas have fundamentally mounted."

All Bodhisattvas ride upon this Dharma to reach the stage of the Tathāgata; herein, that which rides is initial enlightenment (*ādikṣaya-bodhi*), and that which is ridden is original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*).
When the subject and object merge in silent accord, such that the initial and the original are non-dual, it is called ultimate enlightenment (*niṣṭhā-bodhi*).
This is precisely the destination reached: a single characteristic and a single flavor, ultimately equal, with no further threefold distinctions. Within this one...
Within its essence, it is divided into the aspects of subject and object; thus, it is called the One Vehicle and also the Supreme Vehicle.

Regarding the term "arising" (*qi*) in the *Awakening of Faith*, it refers to this treatise’s ability to shatter doubt and attachment, thereby giving rise to correct faith; "arising" here signifies manifestation.
Faith means endurance and delight. This refers to manifesting a mind of endurance and delight toward the three meanings of the aforementioned Mahāyāna object;
this is called "arousing faith. Therefore, the Treatise says: "In order to cause sentient beings to eliminate doubt and abandon false attachments..."

One gives rise to right faith in the Mahāyāna so that the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed. When this faith arises, it necessarily has internal original enlightenment (*mūla-avabodha*) as its cause and external instruction from a teacher as its condition.
Through the conjunction of these causes and conditions, and through the mutual support of the internal and external, it is able to be manifested.
As the treatise below states: "The perfection of causes and conditions refers to having the power of one's own habitual permeation (*vāsanā*), and furthermore..."

Because all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas protect them through their compassionate vows, sentient beings are able to give rise to a mind of wearying detachment from suffering, believe in the existence of *nirvāṇa*, and cultivate roots of goodness and the like.
Yet, the single dharma of faith serves as the condition for all virtues and the beginning of the myriad practices;
understanding, conduct, cultivation, and realization all proceed from it. The ultimate state of realization is called the attainment of *nirvāṇa*. If this were not so...
Regarding this faith: how can one accomplish these matters? Thus, the *Avataṃsaka* says: "Faith is the source of the Way and the mother of merit;
it nurtures all wholesome dharmas. It cuts through the net of doubt and crosses the river of craving, revealing the unsurpassed path to Nirvāṇa."

However, this treatise does not merely give rise to faith; it also encompasses both understanding and practice. That is to say, of the five sections of the treatise, the second and third concern understanding, while the fourth and fifth concern practice.

Since it contains these manifold meanings and universally accords with the sentiments of the masses, and because it intends to lead one from the shallow to the profound, it is therefore titled simply "Awakening Faith.
As for what is called "teaching" (*jiao*) in the treatise, "teaching" refers to the words spoken by the Sages for the sake of those below them.
It is for the purpose of instructing the ignorant so they may become wise, and instructing the ordinary so they may become sages. "Treatise" (*lun*) refers to discursive discussion;

that is, the provisional establishment of proponent and opponent, wherein one asks and answers oneself, investigating and scrutinizing through a circular process to thoroughly elucidate the true principle. This means engaging in debate and deliberation regarding the aforementioned dharmas and meanings to instruct disciples.
However, there are differences between treatises of tenets (*zong*) and commentaries (*shi*); this is a treatise of tenets. [The text ends with] "by means of the horse..."

The Great Being Ming composed this work based on over one hundred treatises of the Mahāyāna of definitive meaning, such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Nirvāṇa*, the *Laṅkāvatāra*, and the *Saṃdhinirmocana*.
It can truly be said that its meaning is abundant while its phrasing is concise; there is no dharma it does not encompass.
Thus, the subsequent text states: "In this way, this treatise is intended to comprehensively subsume the boundless meanings of the Tathāgata’s vast, profound, and extensive Dharma."
One should explain this treatise. Furthermore, it says: "Thus, I have already expounded in summary the Mahāyāna, the secret treasury of all Buddhas.
It also says: "The profound and vast meaning of all Buddhas, I now explain in accordance with the *dhāraṇī*," and so forth.

However, this textual passage was composed by a Great Being who had realized the Truth (*tathatā*) during his subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*). Later generations failed to reflect upon this.
The rope is short, yet one claims the spring is dry; such people often slander it, saying it is not perfect or true. The subsequent passages exhorting faith are not lacking in earnestness;
the benefits of hearing, contemplating, and practicing are fully revealed as its merits. Those who do not believe and instead slander it will suffer for kalpas on end.

How could one not strive? These five characters mentioned above encompass the dharma and its metaphor, cause and effect, understanding and practice, principle and wisdom, the transformer and the transformed, and the signifier and the signified;
they are fully complete and exhaustively summarize the entire treatise, which is why this title was established.

The term *shu* (疏) means "to unravel" (*shū*) and "to decide" (*ketsu*). It refers to unraveling the principles, meanings, and purports of the Dharma, and deciding upon the phrasing and chapters of the text, so that they are all fully understood and unobstructed.
Now, regarding the six characters beginning with "Great" (*Dai*), they are analyzed according to the six types of grammatical interpretation (*ṣaḍ-vibhakti*) and collectively form five pairs:

First, the pair of the "vehicle" (*yāna*) and the "one who rides the vehicle" (*yāyin*). This means that "person" (*nin*) is the one who rides the vehicle, and "Great" (*Dai*) is the vehicle ridden. The vehicle ridden is...

1. "Great" refers to the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*). Because it is the vehicle of the Great, the three interpretations—*dharmadhāraya* (possessive), *tatpuruṣa* (dependent), and *bahuvrīhi* (possessive)—are all applicable.

2. This is the correspondence between the "ariser" and the "arisen. That is, the Great Vehicle is the ariser, and faith is the arisen. Thus, it is "the arising of faith in the Great Vehicle," explained by the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.
3. This is the correspondence between the "agent" and the "object of faith. That is, faith is the agent of faith, and the Great Vehicle is... [the object].

It is that which is to be believed. That which is to be believed is the Mahāyāna. Regarding the Mahāyāna as the object of belief, there are two interpretations: *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound) and *tatpuruṣa* (possessive compound).
Fourth, regarding the relationship between the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*): the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda* is the signified, and the treatise (*śāstra*) is the signifier. Fifth.
The "Explanatory and Explained" pair refers to the commentary as the "explanatory" and the aforementioned five [treatises] as the "explained";
both are *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compounds. — *Bishuoji*.
[Commentary] Next is the "Recorded Notes" (*Ji*). This is the title of the work. The composition of this text is based upon the *Shibei* [Lecture Record].

The *Shibei* is extremely detailed, proliferating into numerous phrases and sentences. Whenever a single point of doctrine is presented, it first begins with a question, followed by the citation of the *Śāstra* as the answer, and only then does it provide a comprehensive explanation.
Although it does not deviate from the essence of the original source, there are instances where it exceeds or falls short; thus, lecturers...
I have employed it, yet it has not yet reached a state of stability and fluency. Now, taking this text as my basis, I shall extract the essential and appropriate passages and record them in writing;
those that are redundant or prolix shall be excised. I will further add, delete, and revise them to achieve a balanced middle way, so that future students may...
It is not that his spiritual wisdom was exhausted in vain, for his illumination was never obscured. Thus it is said: "When to record, he recorded; when to excise, he excised.
It is for this reason that the title is given as "Pen and Erasure" (*Bi-xue*).
Composed by the Śramaṇa Fazang of Xitaiyuan Monastery.
[Commentary] Regarding the subsequent detailed explanation of the names of the commentators: first is the author of the sub-commentary (*shuji*).

As for "West Taishan Temple," this refers to Chongfu Temple in Chang’an. Since there were five temples throughout the realm all named Taishan, the term "West" is used to distinguish it from the other four.
East refers to Yangzhou; South refers to Jingnan Prefecture; West refers to Chang’an; and North refers to Tai... [text ends].
The original [temple] (also named Chongfu) was located in the Eastern Capital (the present-day Fuxian). Both were called "Taiyuan" because Empress Wu Zetian was born in Taiyuan.
Since these temples were both established using her former residences as a mark of respect for her birthplace, they were given this name.

"Śramaṇa" is a general title for the assembly of Śākyas; it is translated here as "diligent cessation," meaning to diligently cultivate precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom, thereby bringing them to rest and extinguishing [defilements].
Because he was free from delusion, karma, and suffering, he received this title. As for Dharmakara (Fazang), his secular surname was Kang;

he was the third patriarch of the Huayan school and was posthumously honored with the imperial title of Great Master Xianshou. His virtuous deeds were vast and flourishing, as detailed in his biographies and records.

The term "narrator" (*shu*) indicates that it was not a work of original composition. As Confucius said, "I transmit but do not create; I trust in and love antiquity," thereby clarifying his own humility and tireless devotion. Thus...
"Yun" means "to record.
"The Monk Zongmi of Caotang Records and Annotates" [Note]:
Next, "records" refers to the primary author. "Caotang" is the name of a monastery located on Mount Zhongnan. As for Zongmi, his secular surname was He.

He was posthumously titled Chan Master Dinghui (Master of Steadfast Wisdom). His learning exhausted both the internal and external traditions, and his realization of the Way outshone those of past and present.

His magnificent virtue and great achievements were fully known through what had been heard and seen. Regarding the recorded commentaries, previously the two versions—the treatise and the sub-commentary—had circulated separately, causing students to be unable to view them comprehensively;
thus, they were mutually deficient, making it difficult for their study to advance further. Now, the sub-commentary text is arranged here to complete the work.

Regarding this treatise: since there is a sub-commentary (*śāstra*) beneath the treatise and a topical outline (*kośa*) above it, the meaning of the text is clearly illuminated and its structural divisions are complete.
When scholars examine and unravel it, how could they fail to receive its generous bounty?
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zixuan of Changshui.
[The word] "compiled" (hui) indicates that he is the compiler. Changshui is the name of a place; Zixuan is his personal name (huì). As for "compiled," there are many types of ancient records.

It could not avoid the faults of being either too prolix or too concise; therefore, the Great Master re-edited and finalized it, titling it the *Pishuo Ji* (Record of Additions and Subtractions), so that it might attain the proper middle way.

△ Regarding the commentary on the treatise, it is divided into two main sections: first, a general exposition of the fundamental tenets; second, the opening of chapters and the explanation of the text.
First, a general statement of the fundamental purpose.
[Commentary: In the region of Central India, there was one named *Urumuṇḍi*, which in this land is translated as Aśvaghoṣa (Horse-Neck).

Within six hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he broke the banner of false views and erected the jewel-treasure of the True Dharma; taking all the teachings on reality as his school, he composed...
This single treatise is titled *The Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna*. It consists of five sections, which are broadly divided into three parts.

The first is the "Section on Causes and Conditions," which serves as the introduction; it clarifies that the composition of this treatise arose from eight causes and conditions, rather than being produced haphazardly or without purpose.
The final section encourages practice and its benefits, serving as the dissemination; it exhorts others to engage with this treatise.
By generating faith, contemplating, and practicing cultivation, one attains great benefit and joy that flows down to future generations to benefit sentient beings.
The middle three sections constitute the main body of the teaching (*śāstra-śarīra*): namely, the first part on establishing the thesis briefly outlines the essential framework;

it establishes the single dharma of the One Mind, enumerates the two types of gates, and presents the three great meanings. Cause and effect operate simultaneously, providing a brief overview for the subsequent sections.

Because this is the fundamental [text], I shall now provide an explanation of one portion. Since the meaning was not fully elaborated during the previous brief introduction, it is appropriate here to explain it extensively so that the meaning may become clear and understanding may arise.
Regarding the portion on faith, four kinds of faith and five kinds of practice are taught.
It causes all sentient beings to mature their faculty of faith and enter the stage of non-retrogression.

These three preceding sections arise from the aforementioned causes and conditions, while the final section is that which exhorts; for this reason, they are collectively termed the "True Doctrine" (Saddharma).

Having understood the major divisions of these three parts of the treatise, one should now understand how to interpret the commentary (*śāstra*). Since the commentary begins with a preface, it is treated as its own introduction.

The section beginning from the opening of the chapters constitutes the *zhengzongfen* (the main body of the teaching). Since the subsequent text lacks a restatement of the dedication (*huixiang*), it is deficient in the *liutongfen* (the section on dissemination).
As the three divisions are thus incomplete, the text is divided into two parts: first, a general exposition of the fundamental tenets;
second, the opening of the chapters and the explanation of the text. This is now the first part: the general exposition.
Preface [Commentary]: This was composed by the Master of the Commentary himself. The term "preface" (xu) carries two meanings. First, "xu" means "to narrate" (xu);
that is, to narrate the general purport of this treatise. Second, it is glossed as "thread" (xu), meaning the beginning thread of the undertaking when composing the commentary.
This is now the first meaning. △ The introduction is divided into two parts:
first, a summary of the general purport of the treatise; second, the reasons for composing the treatise. First, the summary of the general purport (four sections):
first, the exposition of the single mind-dharma; second, the revelation of the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*); third, the elucidation of the gate of arising and ceasing; fourth...
The two gates are non-dual.
[Commentary] The reason for listing these four is that they encompass the great purport of this treatise; nothing exceeds them.
From beginning to end, there is nothing that is not included within them.
△ First, the exposition of the Dharma of the One Mind.

[Commentary] Regarding the first section, the exposition of the Dharma of the One Mind: the text establishing the thesis states, "As for that which is called 'Dharma,' it refers to the mind of sentient beings."
This mind encompasses all mundane and supramundane dharmas. Based upon this mind, the meaning of the Mahāyāna is revealed.

The commentary on the text states: "To reveal the true meaning, based on the dharma of the one mind, there are two gates," and so forth, up to "the two gates are not mutually separated. Therefore, this is stated here.

Now, the true mind is vast and empty, transcending words and images beyond the reach of traps and nets; it is profound, silent, rarefied, and ineffable, forgetting the duality of object and subject within the realms of cognition.
[Commentary:
"Now" (*fu*) is a particle used to introduce a discourse, as in the saying: "Now, filial piety is the root of virtue and the source from which instruction proceeds."
[The Master] said: Furthermore, it is said that the *Yī* (the Book of Changes) is vast and great. In some instances, the characters "zhōng" (within) and "xià" (below) are merely auxiliary particles.
The two characters "zhēn xīn" (true mind) directly point to the essence of the Dharma. "Zhēn" means true, distinguishing it from the false or forgetful.
"Xīn" means spiritual discernment; it is the essential and profound reality. Generally, when speaking of the mind, there are four types. The first is the Sanskrit term *citta*.
*Hṛdaya*. This is translated as "flesh-ball heart," which is the heart-organ of humans. It is red in color and shaped like a lotus flower;
it has seven petals and is comprised within the category of form (*rūpa-dharma*). Second is *citta*, here translated as "accumulation-arising," which refers to the eighth *ālaya-vijñāna*.
This is because it can accumulate all seeds and give rise to active manifestations (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*). Third is "object-contemplation" (*ālambana-manasikāra*).
"Citta" (mind) refers here to the eight consciousnesses as the sovereign mind-kings (*cittarāja*), because each is capable of cognizing its own respective object.
Fourth is *kṣānti*, which is translated as "firm and solid mind. This refers to the Tathāgatagarbha, the mind that is intrinsically pure and neither arising nor ceasing.
What is clarified here is precisely this. The term "true" (*satya*) is used to distinguish it from other minds. If...

△ Second, revealing the gate of True Suchness (Tathatā).

[Commentary] The preceding section merely concerns the absolute (juedai), wherein all designations are extinguished and both nature and characteristics are transcended; thus it is described as "vast and empty," "profound and still," and so forth.

The present section, however, concerns the relative (dui) in contrast to arising and ceasing, thereby manifesting non-arising and non-ceasing; it establishes the True (zhen) in dependence upon the delusory.

Therefore, it is said that the "Gate of True Suchness" (zhēnrú mén)—as the text on the establishment of the doctrine below states: "This is the aspect of the mind as True Suchness, which demonstrates the essence of Mahāyāna."
The commentary on the text states: "The true suchness of mind is the essence of the great universal dharma-gate of the single dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).

It is what is called 'the nature of mind, which is neither born nor extinguished,' and so forth, up to: 'Because this realm free from thought can only be realized through direct correspondence with awakening.
The present sub-commentary (shū) now recounts that passage.
It is neither arising nor ceasing; it is not subject to the transformations of the four marks. It has no going and no coming; throughout the three periods of time, nothing can alter it.
[Commentary: "Non-" (fei) means "without" or "not. However, regarding arising and ceasing versus non-arising and non-ceasing, one must distinguish them by means of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
Furthermore, to speak in terms of the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the three natures: the falsely imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is exclusively subject to arising and ceasing;

the perfectly established nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is exclusively non-arising and non-ceasing; and the dependently originated, provisional nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) resembles the falsely imagined in that it appears to arise and appear to cease.
The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is unborn and unceasing. If one speaks according to reality, then all three natures are likewise without birth or cessation.

Nevertheless, for the time being, their meanings differ. Why is this? It is said that the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) involves no dharma that can arise and no dharma that can cease, like a snake [superimposed] upon a rope.
As for the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), it is such that arising is non-arising and ceasing is non-ceasing, as in the following example:

The rope upon the hemp is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). It is the middle [nature], devoid of the two aforementioned phenomena of arising and ceasing. It is like there being no rope and no snake upon the hemp; as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-kārikā* states:
"The first is the absence of nature in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*); the second is the absence of nature in terms of self-existence (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*);

the latter [the third] is due to being far removed from the nature of the self and dharmas as they are grasped. Thus, the perfected nature is precisely suchness (*tathatā*); therefore, it is said to be non-arising.

It is extinguished. However, this merely clarifies that the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is, in its very essence, neither arising nor ceasing; it does not involve the merging or the sublation of the phenomena of arising and ceasing.
Thus, the *Awakening of Mahāyāna* (or *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra*) states: "The Tathāgata’s nature of quiescent extinction has never had a beginning or an end."

Therefore, the subsequent text states: "That which is called the nature of the mind is neither born nor extinguished. It further says: "It is not born in the past limit, nor does it perish in the future limit;
it is ultimately and eternally constant," and so forth. This demonstrates that the true mind is unchanging.
Regarding the "four marks" (catur-lakṣaṇa), there are three types. First, the subtle four marks: this refers to the nine hundred births occurring within a single kṣaṇa.
Cessation (*nirodha*). These are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) subject to transformation; namely, arising, abiding, change, and cessation.

The Buddha praised him, saying, "Excellent! I speak of the four mountains; these are precisely birth, old age, sickness, and death, which constantly come to oppress sentient beings.

The characteristics of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing are collectively categorized as four: namely, there is one characteristic of arising, four characteristics of abiding, two characteristics of changing, and one characteristic of ceasing.

When reversing delusion through the process of severance, one begins from the first stage of faith by ceasing the characteristic of ceasing, and concludes at the tenth stage by severing the characteristic of arising, as will be explained in detail below.
What is now termed "non-transmigration" refers precisely to these subtle four characteristics.

This applies to the other two as well. Since the four characteristics merely cause conditioned phenomena to transition, and the mind is unconditioned and not of the nature of being produced, it cannot undergo such transition.
In the text, the beginning and the end are briefly cited to encompass the middle; therefore, it is said that it is neither arising nor ceasing.
Regarding "no going or coming," this means that this true mind does not go toward the prior limit, nor does it come from the subsequent limit.
It does not abide in the past, nor does it abide in the present. That which abides in the present consists of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that "abiding" indicates that a phenomenon possesses temporary utility; since the present case is not like that, it is said to be "non-existent.

Regarding the phrase "the three periods are equal," "period" (*ji*) refers to a temporal limit. "Mo" means "none. "Yi" refers to change or transformation. Although the three periods are capable of such change—
This is the Dharma. It can only transform and alter conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), causing them to change; however, the mind is not conditioned, and therefore it cannot be changed.
As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "It is merely by means of numerical designations that one speaks of the three periods of time; it does not mean that bodhi has past, future, or present."

[Commentary] Regarding the description of arising and ceasing, the text of the "Establishment of the Meaning" below states: "This is the characteristic of the causes and conditions for the arising and ceasing of the mind;

it is able to demonstrate the essence, characteristics, and functions of the Mahāyāna. The explanatory text states: "The arising and ceasing of the mind refers to that which relies upon the Suchness..."
The ālayavijñāna possesses a mind subject to arising and ceasing; that which is called "neither-arising-nor-ceasing" is conjoined with this arising and ceasing.

This state cannot be known through the conceptual discrimination of the ordinary mind, because it pertains to the meaning of the sovereign function of True Suchness (tathatā). I shall now describe it.

It takes non-abiding as its very nature; it branches out according to its various streams, rising or sinking in accordance with delusion or enlightenment, and arising or ceasing at the mercy of causes and conditions.

[Commentary] In this passage, the first sentence indicates the locus of arising and ceasing, while the subsequent sentences explain the characteristics of arising and ceasing. As for the word "but" (但):
"Yu" (語) means "speech"; "yi" (以) means "by means of"; "you" (由) means "due to.

Although this nature is tranquil and vast, profound and expansive, neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, it does not abide in this state of absolute quiescence devoid of defilement or purity.
Rather, following those perfuming agents, it gives rise to all phenomena. Following defilement, the nine aspects of arising and ceasing manifest; following purity, the three [aspects] manifest.

Those who ride upon the Noble Path all do so by means of True Suchness (tathatā), taking non-abiding as their seed-nature (gotra). Furthermore, because this nature itself is non-abiding, it is able to function in this way.
As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "From the root of non-abiding, all dharmas are established. And as the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* says:
Based on this non-abiding, the worlds and all sentient beings are established.

This is not the same as other schools which clarify that the essence of *tathatā* (suchness) is eternally firm and dense, like jade or stone, incapable of being perfumed and unable to respond to conditions;

they merely assert that the *ālayavijñāna* is the basis of both defilement and purity, being that which receives perfuming and maintains seeds. [This concludes] the section on following the school, the metaphors, and the clarifications. [The text now proceeds to] the division of waters.
A current is called a branch; a divided path is called a fork. Now, taking these forks and branches together as a single metaphor:
it is like water from a single source that, following whichever forked path, flows apart to form branches. True Mind is also like this:

according to whatever causes and conditions, it manifests as ordinary beings, sages, and so forth, as will be clarified below. From "following delusion" onwards, the text correctly distinguishes the characteristics of arising and ceasing.

"Chasing" means to follow or to allow things to take their course. In delusion, one turns away from awakening and unites with the sensory dust; in enlightenment, one turns away from the dust and unites with awakening.
Yet, both delusion and enlightenment each possess their own causes and conditions: in delusion, ignorance serves as the cause and objective realms serve as the condition;

in enlightenment, the internal permeation of original awakening serves as the cause and the external permeation of the teacher’s instruction serves as the condition. If one follows along within delusion...
If one follows the conditions of delusion, one sinks into birth and death;

consequently, all tainted, defiled dharmas arise, and all untainted, pure dharmas cease (cease meaning they become obscured). If one follows the conditions within awakening, one ascends the path of enlightenment;
consequently, all untainted, pure dharmas arise, and all tainted, defiled dharmas cease (cease meaning they vanish). As stated in the following text:

With ignorance as the cause, the three subtle states arise; with objective realms as the condition, the six coarse states arise. Thus one sinks and wanders through the five paths of existence; this is following delusion.
With original enlightenment internally perfuming as the cause and the teacher’s instruction externally perfuming as the condition, understanding is awakened and practice is initiated;
thus one transcends and ascends to the fruit of Buddhahood; this is following awakening. Both delusion and awakening are, in their entirety, the nature.
Although delusion and awakening differ, they are one in their inconceivability. Thus, the Sūtra says: "The nature from beginningless time is the support for all phenomena;

because of it, there are the various realms of existence, as well as the realization of the fruit of Nirvāṇa. This is precisely the meaning of the "Dharma-gate of the Arising of Nature" (*xingqi*) in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Buddha-nature follows the flow and becomes the various flavors," and so forth. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*... [text continues].
Yan said: "For example, it is like empty space. Its essence is not any of the manifold phenomena, yet it does not obstruct their manifestation.
When the sun shines, it is bright; when clouds gather, it is dark. All such instances reveal that True Suchness (Tathatā) does not abide in its own nature, but follows conditions to form phenomena."
△ Section Four: The Non-duality of the Two Gates.

[Commentary] The preceding discussion on True Suchness (*tathatā*) and arising-and-ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*) presents their meanings as distinct. Although their phenomenal aspects (*lakṣaṇa*) differ, their underlying principle ultimately converges upon a single path.
Because they are two yet non-dual, this section exists. As the explanatory text below states: "Furthermore, to reveal..."
This demonstrates how one enters the gate of True Suchness directly from the gate of birth and extinction.

That is to say, by investigating the five aggregates—the physical form and the mind—and the six objects of the sensory realms, one finds that they are ultimately devoid of thought. Furthermore, if one is able to observe and know that the mind is without thought...
One immediately attains entry into the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*) in accordance with it;

this is what is being described here. The section is divided into three parts: first, the principle (*dharma*); second, the analogy (*upamā*); third, the conclusion (*nigamana*). First, the principle (which has two sub-sections):
first, the direct clarification of non-duality; second, the explanation that establishes non-obstruction. First, the direct clarification of non-duality.

Although there is profuse arising and vigorous activity, it never stirs the source of the mind; although there is stillness, serenity, emptiness, and solidity, it has never deviated from the law of karmic cause and effect.
[Commentary] There are four phrases in this passage. The first two clarify that arising and ceasing do not obstruct True Suchness (*tathatā*); the latter two clarify...
Reality (*tathatā*) and arising-and-ceasing do not obstruct one another; since they do not mutually obstruct, this is the meaning of non-duality.

First, to clarify that arising-and-ceasing do not obstruct reality: although the phrase "furthermore" (*fu*) contains both concessive and restrictive implications, it governs the following two clauses. (This is detailed.)
"Many," "arising," "activating," "stirring," "leaping," and "bounding. When phenomena are manifold, the paths of defilement and purity are numerous;
when they arise, they emerge anew in every moment; when they activate, their substance is not permanent; when they leap, their characteristics do not remain for long.

Because the causes and conditions of defilement and purity are manifold, they arise, stir, and bound in leaping fashion, being produced and ceasing from moment to moment without ever abiding for even an instant. Although they do not abide for an instant, [they continue in this manner].
Yet its essence is unchanging. This unchanging nature is the source of the mind. Since the source of the mind has never known movement, the subsequent text states:
"When the awakened mind first arises, the mind has no initial characteristic. The *Awakening of Mahāyāna* (*Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda*) says:

"The awakened one is like empty space, equal, unmoving, and non-turning. Furthermore, the subsequent text states: "Although one contemplates the causes and conditions of good and evil and their resulting retributions..."

Furthermore, the nature of thought itself is ungraspable; hence it is said that "from the beginning... and so forth. Regarding the section "tranquil and still" (*jing-mi*) below, there are two points: first, it clarifies that True Suchness (*tathatā*) does not obstruct arising and ceasing;
second, it clarifies that True Suchness is inherently non-obstructive and perfectly penetrating. *Mi* (still) is also *jing* (calm). It is the calm within calm, and is thus called *mi*.

When it is *jing*, its characteristics are neither arising nor ceasing; when it is *mi*, its essence transcends existence and non-existence. *Xu* (void) refers to being non-obstructive and perfectly penetrating; *ning* (congealed) refers to being quiescent.

Yet it is constantly illuminating. Furthermore, the absence of the clamor and vexation of delusion is called "stillness" (*jing*); the absence of the shifting flow of karma is called "tranquility" (*mi*);
the departure from the obstructive nature of form is called "voidness" (*xu*); and that which is not the arising and ceasing of the mind is called "congealed" (*ning*).

Although the true essence is thus, its function always follows conditions. This function that follows conditions manifests as karma and its fruits—good and evil, pleasure and suffering—like a shadow following a form.
It is not so; therefore it is said, "never having been at variance," and so forth. "Tang" (甞) means "formerly" or "ever. "Guai" (乖) means "to deviate" or "to contradict.

The retribution of the causes and effects of karma encompasses both the wholesome and the unwholesome, as well as the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and the non-outflowing (*anāsrava*). This is precisely the establishment of all phenomena without ever departing from the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Thus, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* says: "There is no self, no agent, and no experiencer; yet the karma that has been performed does not perish. As the following text states: "Although..."

One contemplates that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is unborn, yet one simultaneously contemplates that the retributions of good and evil, suffering and pleasure, are neither lost nor destroyed.
△ Next, the unimpeded nature is explained and established.

Therefore, it causes the unchanging nature to arise through conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*), such that defilement and purity remain eternally distinct; yet, without abandoning conditions, it is identical with reality (*tathatā*), such that ordinary beings and sages reach unity.

[Commentary] Regarding the section beginning with "Therefore": first, this explains how True Suchness does not obstruct arising and ceasing. "Therefore" (*hugu*) indicates the causal relationship where the preceding gives rise to the subsequent.
The term "also" (*yi*) applies to the following two phrases as well. "Hence" (*gu*) has the meaning of "therefore. "To cause" (*shi*) means "to let.

Because True Suchness (*tathatā*) does not obstruct arising and ceasing, it causes its unchanging true essence to spontaneously follow conditions (*pratyaya*), giving rise to and forming both defilement and purity.
These two terms, "defilement" and "purity," encompass all phenomena; they have been thus from the beginning and are not merely the case now. Therefore, it is said:
They are eternally distinct. Nevertheless, this defilement and purity both arise entirely from the nature; therefore, the text below states:

"For example, various earthenware vessels all share the same nature and characteristics as fine dust; likewise, outflow-free phenomena and ignorance all share the same nature and characteristics as True Suchness."
"Not abandoning the inferior" [refers to] the second explanation: that arising and ceasing do not obstruct True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Because they are unobstructed, it causes one not to abandon the differentiated conditions of delusion; these are precisely the nature of the single True Suchness. Deluded conditions and their differentiations encompass all ordinary beings and sages.
Although ordinary beings and sages differ in appearance, their essence is one. Within this single essence, there are fundamentally no ordinary beings or sages; therefore, it is said:
To reach unity is to reach the fulfillment of the ultimate principle (*naya*). Therefore, the subsequent text states:

"All ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas are not born in the past limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) and do not perish in the future limit (*aparākoṭi*); they are ultimately and eternally so. The *Awakening of Mahāśrī* (*Mahāśrī-samādhi-sūtra*) says:
"Within the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), there are in reality no bodhisattvas nor any sentient beings. It further says: "Sentient beings and their lands..."
The same dharma-nature.
△ Second, the analogy:
It is like waves, which are no different from the movement of moisture; therefore, one distinguishes the waves by means of the water itself. Water is no different from the movement [of the waves].
"Wetness. Thus, one uses the waves to clarify the water.

[Commentary] Here, the preceding metaphor illustrates that True Suchness (tathatā) does not obstruct arising and ceasing. The word "its" (*ji*) is a term used to point to a phenomenon; "like" (*you*) means "as if.

The movement of the waves is a metaphor for the differences between arising and ceasing, defilement and purity. The wetness of the water is a metaphor for the single essence of True Suchness, which is without distinction.
Waves take movement as their characteristic; water takes moisture as its nature.

The first phrase uses a reductio ad absurdum to illustrate that within the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-dvāra*), there is no defiled or pure aspect that is distinct from True Suchness (*tathatā*). Therefore, it says "the waves have no [separate nature]," and so forth.

Consequently, the following section provides a direct analogy: because they are not distinct, one is able to discern arising and ceasing within a single mind; hence it says "it is precisely the water."

"Equality," etc., is a metaphor for the preceding text’s discussion of how the unchanging nature gives rise to dependent origination, wherein defilement and purity remain eternally distinct. "Water has no... and so forth:
the second set of metaphors illustrates that arising and ceasing do not obstruct True Suchness (*tathatā*).

The first phrase is a negative illustration (*pratiṣedha*), using a metaphor to show that within the gate of True Suchness, there is no separate mind of either defilement or purity. Therefore, it says "water has no," etc. The second phrase is a positive illustration (*anvaya*), because...
Because they are distinct, one is thus able to manifest true suchness (tathatā) through that very arising and ceasing; hence it is said, "identical with the waves," etc.
This metaphor illustrates how, as stated in the preceding text, one does not abandon conditions while being identical to the truth, whereby ordinary beings and sages reach a state of oneness.

△ Third, the Conclusion. Thus, movement and stillness penetrate one another; the ultimate and the conventional are fused as a pair; birth-and-death and nirvana are unified within a single thread, like the paths of Yi and Qi.

[Commentary] The two characters "Thus" (*shìyǐ*) are terms used to conclude the preceding discussion. Regarding the three pairs beginning with "movement and stillness," there are both general and specific explanations. Generally...

This does not go beyond the two meanings of *tathatā* (suchness) and arising-and-ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*). That is to say, movement within the conventional world of birth and death is precisely arising-and-ceasing;

all else is *tathatā*. To distinguish them further: movement and stillness refer to metaphors; the real and the conventional refer to the truths (*satya*); and birth-and-death and nirvāṇa refer to defilement and purity.
These various pairs of dharmas are fundamentally not identical; their characteristics are far apart.

Now, by means of a single nature, they are made to penetrate one another, so that movement and stillness are without distinction, the ultimate and the conventional are not different, and defilement and purity share the same essence, being entirely without disparity.

This is truly because the nature gives rise to phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*), such that object and wisdom are clearly distinct; yet when phenomena attain the nature, they merge, and body and mind become vast and open. Thus, the text below says:

It is like the waters of the great ocean, which, stirred by the wind, possess both the characteristics of the wind and the characteristics of the water, such that they are never separated from one another.
Furthermore, a sutra states: "The two truths are not dual; they are always in discord yet have never been separate. The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* also says:

"Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa—these two realms are equal; this is precisely the realm of the Buddha. Within this, there is mutual penetration and dual fusion, where [the extremes of] Yao and Qi are unified as one. This is precisely...
This reveals the words of non-duality regarding the preceding two dharmas; it is a thorough penetration, harmonization, leveling, equalization, and comprehensive integration.
This can be seen by comparing the texts. However, the purport of the above four gates is subtle and profound: the first establishes the root to manifest the branches.

It causes the myriad phenomena to be arrayed like stars across the sky of ultimate meaning (*yìtiān*). Subsequently, it gathers the derivative back to the fundamental, so that the multitude of forms is extinguished and unified within the ocean of nature (*xìnghǎi*).
Expanding and contracting, existing and perishing—the phenomena are simultaneous, and their meaning is without succession.
Thus, the environments and inhabitants of Avīci hell are entirely contained within the self-mind of the Ultimate Sage; the body and lands of Vairocana...
Transcending even a single thought of the ordinary person, the principle of perfect reality is manifested herein. Question: At the beginning, "one mind" is described;
at the end, the non-duality of the two gates is discerned, which is likewise one mind. What is the difference between the beginning and the end? Answer: Regarding the "one mind" at the beginning...

The mind should be able to give rise to the subsequent single mind; this mind is that to which all should return. Although the essence of the preceding and succeeding moments is identical, their meanings as "beginning" and "end" differ.
Since the original is but a single mind, free from names and beyond all marks, through delusion and awakening, the myriad dharmas arise accordingly.
The dharmas that arise are fundamentally empty; all are but consciousness. Consciousness is like an illusion or a dream, yet it is but the single mind. Thus...
The commentary explains according to the treatise, and this sub-commentary clarifies based on that commentary. These four successive sections do not overstep [the original intent];
the essential purport of the entire treatise resides herein.
△ Second, clarifying the causes and conditions for its composition (in two parts). First, the negative illustration; second, the positive clarification. First, the negative illustration:

It was simply because while the Tathāgata was in the world, those whose faculties were mature were easy to discipline; once they received the Honored One’s words, there was nothing that did not accord perfectly with reality.
[Commentary] Regarding "revealing by contrast": this intends to clarify that before the Bodhisattva composed this treatise, there was a time when it was unnecessary.
When the Tathāgata was in the world, the conditions were supreme and the faculties [of beings] were mature and easy to discipline; thus, both the faculties and the practice were supreme.

This refers to the period from the time the Muni Śākyamuni attained enlightenment until his parinirvāṇa, when the Dharma transformation was circulating, holy sages provided assistance, and the faculties of people [were such].

They have reached maturity; their nature and conduct are harmonious and gentle. They have planted various roots of goodness under many Buddhas, having long established the foundations of virtue over immeasurable eons.
Because they possess the superior characteristics of the faculties and practices of those who are "once-instructed," they do not need to hear [the teaching] again;

hence, it is called "once" (*eka*). Because they receive and comply with the holy intent, it is termed "instructed" (*śruta*). As for "the words of the Honored One," these refer to the eight tones and four types of eloquence, which were personally proclaimed from the golden mouth; thus, they are "heard."

Thus they obtain benefit and attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); hence it is said that this accords with the truth from afar. Furthermore, "from afar" (*xuán*) means distant.

It does not necessarily require hearing directly from the golden mouth of the Buddha; rather, it refers to successive oral transmission. For instance, Śāriputra heard the causal conditions from Aśvajit, and Maudgalyāyana received the teachings transmitted by Śāriputra.
Since these types of practitioners do not even rely on the sūtras compiled after the Buddha’s passing, how much less would they depend upon Bodhisattvas?

Therefore, the treatise below states: "If the Tathāgata were still in the world, and sentient beings possessed sharp faculties, and the person capable of expounding [the Dharma] possessed superior physical and mental karma, such that a single utterance of his perfect voice could be understood equally by all diverse classes of beings, then a treatise would not be necessary."
△ II. The Correct Exposition (II): First, the preface describing erroneous accounts and delusion; second, the arousal of compassion and the composition of the treatise.
First, the preface describing erroneous accounts and delusion (II): First, the general summary; second, the specific exposition. First, the general summary.
After the Great Master passed away, conflicting interpretations proliferated; some followed deviant paths, while others rushed down narrow byways.

[Commentary] As for the "Great Master," his virtue and achievements were lofty and preeminent, serving as a standard and model for all. He was one of the ten titles of the Buddha, specifically known as the "Teacher of Gods and Humans.
When his conditions ended and his transformative work ceased, the sun of the Buddha’s teachings withdrew its radiance; hence the phrase "after his passing. At that time, both conditions and...
"Inferior. At that time, the dark path loses its illumination; the world is entirely shrouded in gloom, and the True Dharma declines. Therefore, it is called "inferior.
Regarding "adhering to heterodox views," this clarifies that both faculties and practice are inferior. To hold perverted attachments is called "adhering to heterodox views.
Because they disrupt the correct principle, it is said they are "confused" (*fēnlún*). "Fēnlùn" means to confuse the underlying order. There are three categories of such adherent calculations.

They are the same; therefore, they are called "different. First, ordinary beings rely on dull afflictions to grasp at the five aggregates of form and mind, reckoning them as permanent, blissful, self, and pure.
Second, non-Buddhists rely on conceptual discrimination to reckon that there is a self within the five aggregates.
3. Some hold that the self is either identical to or distinct from the aggregates; they cling to annihilationism or eternalism, giving rise to the sixty-two views and so forth. 4.

Although the followers of the Lesser Vehicle have destroyed the grasping at a self, they still give rise to views regarding phenomena (*dharmadṛṣṭi*); not knowing true permanence, they calculate [reality] as impermanent and so forth.
Following their own respective understandings, each established its own school, dividing into more than twenty sects that mutually dispute right and wrong. This is the [first] category.
This refers to the attachment to different names, or to falling into lower realms; this clarifies their inferior characteristics. The word "or" (*vā*) is an indefinite term.

Since these types of faculties are inferior, they may, according to their sharpness or dullness, become ordinary worldlings or non-Buddhists; or, upon hearing provisional and shallow teachings, they may become followers of the Hīnayāna.

Ordinary worldlings and non-Buddhists do not follow the Buddha’s true Dharma, and are therefore called "erroneous paths. To take them as one's primary practice and orientation is what is meant by [this term].

As for the "small path": having already abandoned attachment to a self, it is not called "deviant"; yet, not having attained the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), it is not called the "Great Path.
Its approach to principle is biased, its mind weary of toil, and it ardently seeks the *parīttābha* (limited) city rather than seeking the place of jewels.
Craving only self-benefit, how could it transport others? Since it is not the great highway, it is called the "small path."
△ Second, the specific exposition (in two parts): first, delusion regarding principle; second, delusion regarding teaching. First, delusion regarding principle:

Consequently, the treasure storehouse within the house remains hidden, leaving those who are solitary and destitute in want; the bright pearl within the garment is not recognized, leaving one impoverished while performing menial labor.

[Commentary] "Consequently" refers to the phrase that follows upon what preceded it. Because the preceding faculties and conditions were inferior and divergent attachments remained manifold, sentient beings were consequently led to delude their fundamental true mind and pursue delusions in transmigration. Thus, the Dharma-jewel of merit, though inherently present, was of no use;
the divine pearl of perfect understanding, though covered by defilements, did not manifest. They wandered alone and destitute on the path of birth and death, laboring as hired hands in *nirvāṇa*.

The gate of the *pātra* has been traversed for kalpas as numerous as motes of dust; yet, with its traces drifting aimlessly, none have been able to enter the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa*).

Within this section, two metaphors are each drawn from a separate sutra. The first is the metaphor of the treasure storehouse of a poor householder, which is the fifth among the nine metaphors in the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*.
That text states: "For example, within a poor householder’s home, there is a treasury of rare jewels."
The treasure cannot speak; though I am within it, I do not know this myself, nor is there anyone to tell me. Thus, I am unable to open this precious treasury.
All sentient beings are likewise so: although the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision—the great Dharma-treasury—is within their own bodies, they neither hear of it nor know of it.
Deluded by the five desires, they wander through birth and death, undergoing suffering.

"Suffering is immeasurable," and so forth. "To hide and rescue" means to save those who are destitute and lacking. One who is young and without a father is called an orphan (*gu*). The ultimate state of having no wealth is called poverty (*qiong*).

The application of these terms can be understood accordingly. Second, the Parable of the Bright Pearl within the Garment. This refers to the passage in the *Lotus Sūtra* concerning the bestowal of predictions upon the five hundred disciples;
it is explained in detail therein. To hire one’s labor is called being a day-laborer (*yong*); to provide service is called working (*zuo*). The rest is as follows.
The text is intelligible.
△ Second, delusion regarding the teachings:

Furthermore, as for the profound purport of the Mahāyāna, it has lain submerged within the *palm-leaf* manuscripts without being sought; thus, the blind followers of various schools have galloped down divergent paths.
Do not turn back.
[Commentary] This section begins by clarifying that the framework of the Great Teaching has collapsed.

It states that although one does not personally receive the golden mouth [of the Buddha] after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, there are nevertheless compiled scriptural texts through which one may trace the words to perceive the meaning (the *tathatā*), and by tracing the meaning, one may realize the ultimate intent.
Although the faculties and natures of sentient beings are inferior and they frequently give rise to divergent views, were they able to hear the Great Dharma, they would naturally rectify themselves.
Now, however, they are unable to investigate it; its exposition has been abandoned. Since the Perfect Truth is no longer heard, false views remain uncorrected.
Now that the Sage has passed away, their faculties and practices remain feeble, and the teaching of the Perfect Reality is likewise suppressed and unheard.
Because it practices this, it is said to "additionally. Since its teaching is not a minor path but carries one to the Unsurpassed, it is called the Mahāyāna.

Because it reaches the ultimate, perfect, and true reality, distinguishing itself from that which is provisional and shallow, it is termed the "Profound Meaning. As for "palm leaves," these are the leaves of the *tāla* tree.
It is like the bamboo slips, silk scrolls, and wooden tablets of this region, which bear the expressive texts that can be consulted to perceive the principles they express;
yet, while one could practice according to what was taught and thus turn from delusion back to awakening, these are now hidden, discarded, and no longer practiced—hence the term "sunk."
"Multitudes of beings" (qún yǒu) refers to the preceding categories of ordinary people, non-Buddhists, and followers of the Hīnayāna, each of whom is numerous;
hence they are called "multitudes of beings. Lacking the eye of the True Dharma, they do not perceive Buddha-nature, and are thus termed "blind followers.
"Charging" (chí) means to rush toward. "Divergent paths" (yì lù) refers to heterodox ways and narrow byways. Since they cannot follow [the correct path], [they wander].
Regarding those on the Path, one should correct them with the Perfect Vehicle (Pūrṇayāna). Yet their delusions and errors grow deeper by the day, becoming habitual until they form their very nature.
If one takes medicine that does not cause dizziness and distress, how can the illness be cured? Since there is no means for them to return [to the truth], it is said that "they shall not turn back."
△ II. Arousing Compassion and Composing the Treatise (three parts): First, lamenting over persons and dharmas; second, stating the intent for composing the treatise;
third, formally composing the various treatises. First, lamenting over persons and dharmas.
There was a Great Being whose name was Aśvaghoṣa. He lamented this collapse of the guiding principles and grieved over this sinking into ruin.

[Commentary] The first two phrases express the capacity for lamentation. *Yuan* (爰) means "thereupon" or "thus. It refers to the fact that six hundred years had already passed since the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa;
although the faculties of human beings had become inferior, the True Dharma still remained. Thus, the Sage manifested his birth to establish my true teaching, which is why it says "there was."

"Mahāsattva" refers to the master of treatises, Aśvaghoṣa, who originally attained perfect enlightenment and was named Mahāprabha (Great Radiance). In his manifested traces, he dwells on the eighth stage as a Dharma-body Bodhisattva.

Having resolved upon the Great Mind, believed in the Great Dharma, understood the Great Meaning, cultivated the Great Practice, realized the Great Path, and proceeded toward the Great Fruit, he is not of the minor stream; therefore, he is called a "Mahāsattva. As for "Aśvaghoṣa," it refers to this Bodhisattva...
When Śākyamuni was born and when he preached the Dharma, the multitude of horses neighed mournfully; thus he received this title, as explained in detail below.
Regarding the two phrases following "慨此" (regretting this): the first phrase of the eulogy praises the Teaching. To sigh over that which is soundless is called "慨" (kai).

"The collapsing of the mainstay" (*tuīgāng*) is a metaphor. It means that the Perfect and True Teaching is rarely investigated and pursued, and having fallen into disuse, it is no longer practiced, like a great mainstay [of a net] that has sagged.
Once the net has collapsed, how can the lines and meshes be restored? If humans and devas have no means to scoop them out from the flood, by what path could they reach the other shore?
Wallowing in the ocean of suffering, there will be no time of escape. That the Way is not practiced is precisely due to this. To lament these words is to grieve for those who are deluded;
to lament and grieve is to mourn their sinking, drowning, and submersion. When the Great Being saw that the net and its lines had collapsed...
They do not lift [others up]. Knowing that those on the mistaken path are drowning and do not ascend, they sigh for them and grieve for them; how can they not think to rescue them?

Therefore, the Sūtra says: "With my Buddha-eye I observe the sentient beings of the six realms, impoverished and lacking in merit and wisdom, entering the perilous paths of birth and death, where suffering continues without interruption, such that they do not even seek the Buddha of Great Power, nor do they sever [their bonds]."
Regarding the Dharma of Suffering: for the sake of these sentient beings, he gives rise to the great compassionate mind and so forth.
△ Second, the statement of the intent for composing this treatise:
Desiring to reveal the wondrous purport of the profound sutras once more to illuminate the dark alleys, and to cast away the distorted vision of false views so that they may return [to the truth].
The correct path. To cause [beings] to return to the source is immediate;

to revert to the root is not remote. [Commentary: There are six phrases in this passage. The first two clarify the teaching and manifest the principle. "Jiang" (將) means "when," "about to," or "intending. "Qie" (且) means "provisionally" or "desiring."
This refers to the opening of aspirations; it refers to the revelation of the definitive meaning of the Mahāyāna, which is called the "profound sūtra.

Because it is the ultimate, perfect principle, it is termed the "sublime purport. When the Buddha personally taught it, those of sharp faculties were able to enter it, just as a person with eyes sees various forms when the sunlight shines upon them.
After his parinirvāṇa, those of dull and obtuse natures, hindered by their inherent obstructions—namely the icchantikas—[were unable to see it].
It is like a dark road. The nature of this dark road is what is called the two obstacles (*dvividhāvaraṇa*).

The Great Being (Bodhisattva), desiring to manifest the perfect and true meaning, seeks to cause those who are deluded to cast off the darkness of ignorance. The Buddha previously destroyed these [obstacles], and now he clarifies them once more;

therefore, it is said "shining again. The following two lines refute the heterodox and return to the orthodox. "To disparage" means to point out and destroy [the errors of] those whose mental activities lie outside of principle. In total...

This is called "false view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). It is not merely a matter of disbelieving in cause and effect; rather, both ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), and those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) are collectively termed "false.
Thus, Kāśyapa said: "From this point on, all of us were known as people of false views.
"Dian" (顛) means "summit" or "top"; because the head is turned downward, it is called "inverted" (*viparyāsa*). Alternatively, "dian" (顛) means "sickness. "Mou" (眸) refers to... [the pupil].
"The pupils of the eyes"—this is a metaphor. It is like when a person's eyes are diseased, they falsely perceive floating flowers, circling hairs, two moons, and so forth.
Furthermore, "insane" means a deranged mind; because of this mental derangement, whatever objects the eyes behold are all perceived incorrectly.
This refers to those who do not see their own relatives as such; that person of false views is just like this.
Within the state of intrinsic emptiness (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), they perceive birth-and-death and nirvāṇa; within wondrous clarity, they produce the delusion of discriminative seeing.

The "right path" is the true road to Bodhi. To go forth and then turn back is called "returning. Sentient beings, through deluded vision, do not rely on the correct path, but instead wander along the five [paths].
As for the realms: even if one were to transcend the three worlds, one would still fall into the pit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Now, I wish to cause them not to follow this divergent path, but to return to the direct road, free from all detours. The latter two lines conclude with the immediate benefit. First is the simile, followed by the application to the Dharma.
When water first emerges and can be contained in a ladle, it is called a "source. "That which is such" refers to the person. It is like a person tracing a river upstream to its source.

The source of that water is called "Returning to the Source" (*huányuán*), which serves as a metaphor for the practitioner reversing the flow of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) and returning to the fundamental limit (*pūrvakoṭi*).

One who attains this fundamental limit is said to have awakened to the source of the mind. Therefore, the subsequent text states: "One who awakens to the source of the mind is called one of ultimate awakening (*atyanta-bodhi*).
If one were to follow the teachings of other schools, it is only after three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) of cultivating vast practices and vows that one finally achieves [this state].
The Perfect Enlightenment is like drawing water from a stream to seek its source.

When it is said now that it is "attainable and not remote," it means that right at the place of arising and ceasing, one reveals that those causes and conditions have no inherent nature; that the locus where the four marks are fundamentally unborn is itself reality.

As the treatise states: "The four characteristics are fundamentally equal, for they are but a single awakening. It further states: "All dharmas are entirely true, for they are all identical to suchness (*tathatā*).
The *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*) says: "To know that it is an illusion is itself liberation; no expedient means need be employed."
To leave illusion is itself awakening; there is no gradual progression. Furthermore, Nanyue said: "The source of the Way is not far away; the ocean of nature is not distant.
Master Zhaoming also said: "Is the Way far? It is true in every encounter. Is the Sage far? Embodying it, one is divine.
These all express the meaning that [the goal] is not remote. It is like showing that the waters of the ten thousand streams are themselves [the ocean].
