First, the general characteristics of the causes and conditions: namely, for the sake of causing sentient beings to leave all suffering behind and attain ultimate bliss.
It is not for the sake of seeking worldly fame, profit, or honor.
[Commentary: This section serves as the general introduction to the entire treatise; therefore, it is called the "general characteristics of the causal conditions."
The former [teachings] encompass both the general and the specific; the latter seven are specifically intended for those who are suited to them. Regarding "suffering":

it refers to the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of birth and death through segmented transition (*paricchinna-bhava*), the suffering of birth and death through transformation (*pariṇāma-bhava*), and the two types of birth and death. Regarding "joy": it refers to the joy of awakening to the Dharma of unsurpassed Bodhi and the joy of the tranquility of unsurpassed Nirvana.
Regarding "not seeking": it means not desiring to cause others to seek the benefits of humans or devas in future lives.
Regarding "pleasure" and so forth, the Master himself may also state: "I have composed this treatise for the sake of benefiting others, not for the sake of fame, profit, or the like.
Therefore, it is called the "general characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "this section," etc.: the intent behind the composition of this entire treatise is solely for the sake of enabling sentient beings to leave suffering and attain happiness.
This constitutes the general explanation of causes and conditions. Furthermore, whatever actions all bodhisattvas undertake...

All of this is for the sake of sentient beings so that they may leave suffering behind and attain happiness. This is not merely the cause for the arising [of the teaching] within this single treatise;

rather, it serves as the cause for the arising of all treatises. Therefore, it is called the "general characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). Regarding the phrase "comprehensive, pervasive, and inclusive of both the primary and the secondary":

this is stated in reference to the capacities of those for whom the teaching is intended. It inclusively reaches those of fixed right and fixed wrong dispositions, while primarily benefiting those of indeterminate disposition. Now...

Since they are combined for discussion, it is said that they are "comprehensive" (*tong*). As for being "specific" (*bie*) for those who are appropriate vessels (*gengji*), first, the seven sections below consist of distinct capacities;
as within those seven, the second and third are for those of the fixed category (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*), while the others are for those of the indeterminate category (*aniyata-rāśi*).
Therefore, it is said that they are "treated separately. This means they are intended only for those belonging to the two [right] groups, and not for those of the fixed-in-deviation category;
hence, they are said to be treated separately. This is unlike the present section, which treats all beings collectively, seeking to cause them all to leave suffering behind and attain ultimate bliss.
Thus, in terms of the Dharma, this refers to the initiation of the entire treatise; in terms of the capacity of the recipients, it refers to the benefit and happiness of all.
The various classes of beings; for this reason, it is called the general characteristic of causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). Regarding "suffering of suffering" (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*):

the former refers to the body as the aggregate of retribution-suffering, while the latter refers to individual instances of suffering. Having already received a contaminated body (*sāsrava-kāya*), it is termed suffering;

when this is further subjected to various forms of oppression, it is therefore called the "suffering of suffering. These are the eight factors, such as birth and old age, which are added thereto. "Destruction" (*vipariṇāma*) refers to pleasure.

Once phenomena have ceased, their activity flows on from moment to moment; therefore, all are suffering. According to the *Ratnagotravibhāga*, one contemplates the three realms as the three types of suffering:

the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) is the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkha*); the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkha*); and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāraduḥkha*).
Among these, the realm of desire possesses all three; the realm of form possesses two; and the formless realm possesses only the suffering of formations. "Segmented" refers to the three realms.

The four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*). "Segmented existence" (*pindagraha-bhava*) refers to having physical form with distinct parts and a life span with fixed limits; when time reaches its ultimate end, one must perish.

"Transformative existence" (*pariṇāma-bhava*) refers to the two vehicles and bodhisattvas who have severed the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). Although they have departed from the coarse suffering of segmented existence, they still possess the *ālayavijñāna*’s transformative suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Because they are transmuted by the four characteristics (*catvāri lakṣaṇāni*) and undergo transformation and change, it is called "transformative. Furthermore, due to...

Because it shifts the fruit and changes [the basis], it is called "transformation" (*pariṇāma*). Regarding the phrase "unsurpassed," this refers to the transformation and cessation of afflictions and birth-and-death, thereby attaining this *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*.
Because it is attained once and attained forever, the treatise calls it "ultimate. Because there is nothing superior to it, the commentary calls it "unsurpassed.
Since its great suffering is eternally extinguished, one transcends the four flows, and karma and delusions are both eliminated. It is perfectly...
"Yet, to attain it for oneself—is this not joy? That which causes others above to leave suffering is the great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) of a Bodhisattva;

that which causes them to attain happiness is the great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) of a Bodhisattva. Thus, the mind of ultimate awakening is fully realized herein. It is not intended merely to cause those below to [attain it]."
These two points are explained in terms of both the transformed and the transformer, as can be seen in the text.
Second, it is for the purpose of explaining the fundamental meaning of the Tathāgata so that all sentient beings may attain correct understanding without error.

[Commentary: This serves as the causal condition for generating [the understanding] that displays the correct meaning and counteracts false attachments within the "Section on Establishing the Thesis" and the "Section on Explanation.
For it is stated in those texts that, based upon the single dharma of the One Mind, there are two gates, each encompassing all dharmas;
this is the very foundation of the Dharma-gates taught by the Tathāgata. Furthermore, within the gate of arising and ceasing...

Original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*) is called "Suchness" (*tathatā*); initial enlightenment (*ādi-awakening*) is called "coming" (*āgata*). The non-duality of the initial and the original is termed "Tathāgata.
Here, the fundamental truth of original enlightenment that is realized is called "Suchness," and the non-conceptual wisdom that realizes it is called "coming.
When sentient beings have not yet attained non-conceptual wisdom, this Suchness has no "coming. Now, the Tathāgata is established based upon this mind.
Therefore, this mind is named the "Tathāgata’s Fundamental Meaning.

To fully explain this meaning so that the bodhisattvas of the three stages of worthiness prior to the [ten] grounds may engage in corresponding inferential contemplation, it is called "correct understanding," which is to say, the manifestation of the correct principle.
Because inferential contemplation is free from inversion, it is called "unerring. Being unerring is precisely the antidote to false attachments.
[Commentary] The text of the sub-commentary has two parts. First, the explanation of the Tathāgata’s fundamental [nature]. Second, the first part: a general correlation with the subsequent sections.
From this point up to the end of this section of the treatise, all serves as the basis for what is to be produced.

However, if one were to correlate the text specifically within this section, it would extend only as far as the passage on the "three greatnesses. From the words "All Buddhas" downward, it clarifies the vehicle (*yāna*).
The meaning [of this] is that it arises from the third causal condition. As for why the *Sūtra* does not explicitly point this out, it is simply because it is abbreviated.
Regarding the phrase "to manifest," the initial text of this section states: "To manifest the correct principle means that based on the dharma of the One Mind, there are two gates," and so on, up to:
"If one can observe and know that the mind is without thought, one will immediately attain compliance and enter True Suchness (*tathatā*)."
Regarding the "antidotes" and so forth, the text states: "As for the antidote to false attachments, all false attachments depend upon the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
If one is free from the self, there are no false attachments.

Furthermore, it says that because recollecting all phenomena causes the mind to arise and cease, one does not enter into true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*). This clearly demonstrates that the second causal condition is that which initiates [the process].
This second causal condition (the present passage) is composed because the three preceding sections of the treatise have been cited as the basis for its initiation;
it seeks to explain the fundamental meaning of the Tathāgata so that all sentient beings may attain correct understanding without error.

The discourse concerning the "agent" and the "object" [of cognition] follows this same pattern in the subsequent six causal conditions. Among those, the latter two provide a specific explanation of the present meaning, while the former two [provide a general explanation].
The explanation of the Tathāgata’s fundamental basis according to the teaching of the Dharma is as follows:
these two gates are the fundamental basis of all dharmas, and the one mind is the fundamental basis of these two gates. Within that text, this meaning is precisely elucidated.
Although the Dharma-gates taught by the Buddha are immeasurable, when their fundamental basis is investigated, none transcend these. This is the explanation provided by the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa.
This is the profound, fundamental meaning within the Dharma-gates taught by the Transformation-body Śākyamuni Tathāgata.

Furthermore, it is explained below in two parts: first, explaining the Tathāgata’s fundamental nature in terms of the realized Dharma; second, the initial explanation of the Tathāgata in two sections. First, the formal explanation:
when deluded, one turns away from awakening and unites with the sensory dusts; this is "Thus Gone" (Tathāgata). Although it is called "going," its essential nature is immovable.

Therefore, "receiving as it is" (yathā-pratigraha) is identical to original enlightenment (mūla-awakening). At the time of awakening, one turns away from dust (phenomenal defilement) and unites with awakening; this is called the Tathāgata.

Because pure function arises within the essence of Suchness (tathatā), and because one returns to purity by reversing defilement, this is termed "coming" (āgama); this is the meaning of initial awakening (ādi-awakening).

Since the essence of True Suchness is one, yet "coming and going" occurs according to conditions, the original awakening is taken to be named "Suchness" (Tathā) and initial awakening is named "Coming" (Āgama). Thus, there is the distinction between initial and original [awakening].
Non-duality is ultimate enlightenment (*atyanta-bodhi*). Ultimate enlightenment is the union of *tathatā* (suchness) and the coming [of awakening];

because they were originally distinct from the beginningless past, it is called "Tathāgata. As stated in the following passage: "If one attains non-thought (*amanasikāra*), then one knows that the characteristics of the mind undergo arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing;
furthermore, there is no distinction between initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*) because the four characteristics exist simultaneously."
All are without independent existence; they are fundamentally equal because they share the same awakening. This concludes the preceding analysis of the text.

Thus, the *Tathāgatotpattisambhava-nirdeśa-śāstra* (The Treatise on the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma) states: "True reality (*tattva*) is called 'thus' (*tathā*); perfect awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is called 'come' (*āgata*). Perfect awakening of true reality is termed 'Tathāgata'.
This refers to the name "Tathāgata" applied to the self-enjoyment *saṃbhogakāya*. It is not the same as [the other interpretation].

The preceding passage was explained in terms of the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body). Within these two interpretations, the former—concerning the teaching—is a *tatpuruṣa* compound (*yathāsvāmika*) in which the Tathāgata is the primary element, because the speaker is preeminent.
This latter interpretation—concerning realization—is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, in which the mind is the primary element, as it is that which gives rise to the Tathāgata.
This can be understood through reflection. Following the phrase "all sentient beings," there is next an indirect clarification (*pratiṣedha*). By means of...
Although there is original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*), because there is no initial awakening (*ādi-awakening*), one cannot be called a Tathāgata.

Thus, the meaning of "Tathā" (Thus) is broad and pervasive, while the meaning of "Āgata" (Come) is narrow and restricted. Therefore, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "All sentient beings are thus;
all noble sages are also thus; even Maitreya is thus. Yet it does not mention "coming. Furthermore, although [the stage] prior to the [ten] stages possesses...

Initial awakening (*ādikṣaya-bodhi*) involves practicing through comparative contemplation; as it has not yet reached the ultimate truth and has not yet attained non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), it is not called "Tathāgata.

Although this wisdom exists on the stages (*bhūmi*), because obscurations and defilements have not been exhausted and contemplation of the mind remains intermittent, the two awakenings—the initial and the fundamental—have not yet attained ultimate, profound union;
thus, they likewise do not receive this title. By this reasoning, it is only the "wondrous awakening" (*sūkṣma-bodhi*) that does.
Only one [method] is permissible; all others are not. However, if one speaks in terms of inherent virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*), there is no such distinction. Thus, the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* says:
"Sentient beings are originally enlightened," and it also says: "All obstacles are ultimate awakening.

The present statement is made in reference to cultivation (*bhāvanā*); therefore, this distinction exists. From here below, the second section concludes the fundamental [principle], which refers to the aforementioned single mind (*ekacitta*).
This is the very root of the Dharma realized by the Tathāgata. It is because the Tathāgata achieves realization by relying upon this single mind.
Thus, faith, understanding, practice, and realization all rely upon this mind; from the subtle to the manifest, one never departs from it.
If one could attain Buddhahood apart from the mind, such a thing is impossible. Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "If a person..."
"To fully comprehend all Buddhas of the three periods of time, one should contemplate the nature of the dharma-realm: everything is created solely by the mind.

As for the meaning of "therefore called equal" (*samākhya*): thus, the Tathāgata is identical to the one mind, and the one mind is identical to the fundamental [nature]. These three meanings are a single essence.

This alone constitutes the ultimate teaching. It is simply that, based on the Dharma, it is called "mind"; in contrast to the derivative, it is termed the "root"; and according to how it is spoken of by people, it is designated as the "Tathāgata.
In its essential substance, it is one; yet when its meanings are enumerated, they form three. It is not three, yet it appears as three; it is not one, yet it is one.

The three [sections] constitute one body, which is the convergence of the Profound Text (Xuánwén). The second part provides a complete explanation of the correct understanding that is free from error.

"Complete explanation" refers to clarifying therein the two gates of True Suchness (tathatā) and Arising-and-Ceasing (utpāda-nirodha), the two types of awakening—the initial and the fundamental—and the two types of non-awakening—the fundamental and the derivative, the two bodies, the three greatnesses, and even the meaning of the non-duality of the two gates; all these meanings are entirely one.
This is the fundamental mode of activity of the mind. As for the "Three Worthies" (sādhakas): they are called so because they are adjacent to the Truth;

thus, they differ from ordinary beings before [the stages] and differ from sages after them. "Worthy" (sādhaka) means "good" or "conforming. These thirty individuals have all been accomplished through the accumulation of goodness.
Because one accords with the ultimate truth, one receives this designation. Regarding "inferential contemplation" (*anumāna*) and so forth:

since one has not yet personally realized *tathatā* (suchness), one can only rely on the teachings to engage in analogical observation. Because this conforms to and does not contradict [the truth], it is called "correspondence" (*yoga*).

This very contemplation through inference is termed "correct understanding" (*samyag-adhigama*), because it belongs to the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) prior to the [first] ground.

Because it gives rise to correct understanding, there are passages that reveal the correct meaning. As for "being free from error," it means being conjoined with correct understanding and accordant with the principle of *tathatā*, such that there is no deviation or perversity.
Because one is free from error, it is termed "non-erroneous. It does not, however, refer to...
"Correcting" refers to erroneous views, which are themselves false attachments.
These three are for the purpose of enabling sentient beings whose roots of goodness have matured to become capable of non-retrogressive faith in the Mahāyāna Dharma.
[Commentary]: This refers to the subsequent section on the characteristics of setting out upon the path (*pratipatti-lakṣaṇa*).

In that text, those of sharp faculties are directed to generate a resolute mind and advance toward the Great Vehicle, becoming capable of abiding in the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*). This corresponds to the final stage of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), where one’s own portion [of practice] is fulfilled;
thus it is called "maturation. One then enters the assembly of those fixed in rightness (*samyaktva-niyāma*) of the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*), thereby—
The preceding stage of faith is capable of withstanding non-retrogression.
[Commentary] Regarding "discrimination" and so forth, the text states:

"Discriminating the characteristics of setting out upon the path" means that it refers to the path realized by all Buddhas, because it has the sense of all Bodhisattvas generating the mind, practicing, and proceeding toward it, and so on, up to the mind...

If there are defilements, the Dharma-body does not manifest; therefore, this is precisely the assignment [of the stages]. The phrase "Because of that... below explains the reason for this, and all subsequent passages follow this pattern. That text states:
"Those who have thus perfected their faith and give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment enter the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), never again to regress.
They are said to dwell within the lineage of the Tathāgata because they are in accord with the primary cause (*pradhāna-hetu*). This refers to the final mind.

Regarding the stage of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), there are three types of mental states: namely, entering (*praveśa*), abiding (*sthiti*), and concluding (*niṣṭhā*). "Entering" refers to first departing from the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and entering the stage of the first faith.
"Concluding" refers to the fulfillment of the mind of faith, which is the tenth faith. "Abiding mind" refers to the intermediate eight faiths.

Since this is the case for the Ten Faiths, the same principle applies by analogy to the remaining stages of Abiding (*vihāra*), Practice (*caryā*), and Direction (*mukha*). As for "maturation," it is defined in relation to...
This is explained at the conclusion of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), where one is said to be "non-retrogressive" (*avaivartika*).

Looking toward the future entry into the ten stages of abiding (*daśa-vihāra*), it is taught that those whose faith is now matured receive the textual exposition on the characteristics of the path (*mārga-lakṣaṇa*) through discernment, thereby entering the state of non-retrogression.
Fourth, it is for the purpose of causing sentient beings with scanty roots of goodness to cultivate faith.
[Commentary: This refers to the four kinds of faith and the four kinds of practice at the beginning of the subsequent "Section on Cultivating Faith."

Because that text intends for those whose faith is not yet full to practice the mind of faith so as to bring it to fulfillment, this corresponds to the stage of abiding in the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).
Since the stage of faith is not yet complete, it is described as "slight"; because it causes one to advance toward completion, it is called "practicing the mind of faith."
[Commentary] Regarding the four kinds of faith: the subsequent text states, "Briefly stated, there are four kinds of faith. What are the four?
First, faith in the root, which means delighting in mindfulness of the *tathatā* (suchness) dharma. Second, faith in the Buddha, who possesses immeasurable merit;
it consists of constantly mindful proximity, making offerings, and showing reverence, thereby initiating roots of goodness and aspiring for [the state of] one..."
Third, faith in the Dharma, because it possesses great benefit and one constantly contemplates the practice of the various *pāramitās*.

Fourth, faith in the Saṃgha, because they are able to practice correctly for their own benefit and the benefit of others, and they always delight in drawing near to the assembly of Bodhisattvas to seek and learn the practice of true reality.
Regarding these four practices, the five practices are clearly explained in detail in the text below, namely:
Generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and tranquility and insight (śamatha-vipaśyanā). Therefore, the text states:

"There are five gates of practice that can bring this faith and so forth to completion. Since the single gate of tranquility and insight is specifically the sixth cause and condition arising from [the preceding], it says "four kinds" and so forth below.
This explains the reason for that; the text says: "In this context, based on those who have not yet entered the stage of the correctly determined group (*samyaktva-niyāma*)."

Because sentient beings [differ in capacity], it is said that they practice with the "mind of faith" and so forth. Although there are eight distinct types within the stage of abiding in the ten faiths, they will not be analyzed further here;
collectively, they constitute the "abiding mind. "Slight and small" refers to the fact that the mind of faith has not yet matured.
"Causing them to advance toward fulfillment" means causing them to receive this text, practice the preceding stage of faith and conduct (*śraddhācaryā*), and progress toward fulfillment. Fifth,
it is for the purpose of demonstrating the skillful means (*upāya*) to eliminate the obstacles of evil karma, to well-guard the mind, to remain far removed from delusion and pride,
and to escape the net of error.
[Commentary: From here below are four types of capacities (*indriya*). These correspond to the initial stage of the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*).

Because the first three faculties are superior and difficult to regress, they do not require many skillful means (*upāya*) to assist in perfecting the power of the Path; therefore, there is only one for each. Herein, the faculty is inferior and prone to regression;
it relies upon many skillful means, and thus there are four. Among these four, the first three represent the three types of persons—lower, middle, and upper—and the last one...
[The text] uses these [explanations] to encourage practice. [Commentary:

First, regarding the general classification of the latter four sections, the text has three parts; this is the first, the general judgment. "The four kinds" refers to the four sections of the treatise that follow.
"The initial mind" refers to the mind of entry (*praveśa-citta*). This is because the preceding and following [sections] address doubts in common. Alternatively...
An objection is raised: "The first three faculties each encompass a single section of the treatise; why then does the faculty of faith alone, at its initial stage, employ four texts?
This [passage] clarifies that point: as the preceding stages become progressively deeper when compared to the initial stage, they are therefore termed 'superior faculties' (*indriya-viśeṣa*)."
When the faculty of faith is about to be perfected, even if one encounters adverse conditions, there will be little retrogression or discouragement; hence it is said that "retrogression is difficult.

Nevertheless, this does not necessarily mean there is no retrogression at all, which is why it is said to be "difficult. For instance, Śāriputra entered the sixth stage (*ṣaṣṭha-vihāra*) yet still underwent retrogression.

How much more so for those of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*)? Regarding "those of inferior faculties": this refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who have first ascended to the stage of faith;
their roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) are so slight that they are no different from light feathers—difficult to advance when encountering the good, yet easily regressed when meeting evil.

Therefore, various expedient means are employed to assist the power of the Path, and it is for this reason that these four [qualities] are possessed. Within the four, the latter ones are distinguished separately. This refers specifically to this single class of inferior [faculties].

Furthermore, there are distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior faculties. Here, the fifth is taken as the inferior faculty, the sixth as the middling faculty, and the seventh as the superior faculty;
the eighth serves as a general exhortation. Question: According to the preceding sequence, all [stages] proceed from the superior to the inferior.
Why is it that hereafter, one instead proceeds from the inferior toward the superior? Answer: This is because Bodhisattvas of superior faculties are based upon their own dignity.

They are arranged in order of their lowliness. Those who have withdrawn from the state of sentient beings are placed last; because one first rescues those of inferior capacity out of compassion, they are listed in this sequence.
Thus, the former [sections] manifest the wisdom of the Bodhisattva, while the latter reveals the compassion of the Bodhisattva.

[Commentary] This is the first section, which corresponds to the "Lower Grade. It refers to the concluding passage of the fourth section, "The Section on Cultivating Faith," within the *Awakening of Faith*.

For that text instructs those sentient beings with heavy karma and many afflictions for whom it is difficult to give rise to roots of goodness, to eliminate their karmic obstructions through skillful means such as ritual prostrations and repentance.
Because these obstructions are lightened, they internally become free from stubbornness, stupidity, and delusion.
Pride. It is the snare and net of external demons.
[Commentary] Now, first, there are two parts. This is a detailed explanation of this single phrase. Regarding the concluding passage on practice, that text says:
"Furthermore, if a person, although practicing with faith, has from previous lives many heavy sins and evil karmas..."
Because of these hindrances, one may be troubled and disturbed by malevolent spirits and ghosts; or be entangled in various worldly affairs;

or be afflicted by the suffering of illness. Since there are many such obstacles as these, one should practice with courageous diligence, prostrating to the Buddhas during the six periods of day and night, repenting with a sincere heart, and making requests [for the turning of the wheel of Dharma].
Rejoice. Dedicate [the merit] toward Bodhi, never ceasing or abandoning it.

Because one will be freed from all hindrances and one's roots of goodness will increase, those with heavy karma—referring to the text’s mention of "heavy karmic obstacles"—and those with many afflictions—referring to the text’s mention of "numerous obstructions"—find it difficult for roots of goodness to arise.
Since these three obstacles are already heavy, goodness does not easily emerge; it is like drilling into damp wood: how could it [produce fire] immediately?

There is fire; it should be brought forth by exposing it to wind and sun, by drawing it out through soaking, and by employing a cord and a drill, guided by reeds and mugwort—then that fire may be nearly attained.
Thus, it is said: "through ritual repentance (*li-chān*) and so forth. Regarding "internally free from [afflictions]" and so on: because of ritual repentance, karma becomes light;
because karma is light, there is no delusion or distress within. Since one is internally free from delusion, external māras will naturally [be subdued].
"Eliminate. External demons are, in fact, obstacles to merit. Thus we know that external hindrances and afflictions all arise because of delusions and karma within.
That practitioners today encounter many obstructions in performing good deeds and find themselves unable to persevere on the Path is precisely what is induced by their internal minds.

Do not resent the crookedness of the shadow; merely reproach the concavity of the form. If one applies oneself diligently to cultivation and discipline, one will certainly be able to achieve transcendence. The *Zuozhuan* states:
"A mind that does not conform to the canons of virtue and righteousness is called obstinate; a mouth that does not speak words of loyalty and good faith is called insincere.
Here, we simply take the state of being uniformly deluded and dark, such that wisdom and understanding do not arise, to be what is meant by "obstinate and insincere."

Sixth: It is for the purpose of demonstrating the cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* as an antidote to the mental faults of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
[Commentary]: This corresponds to the middle section. That is, it refers to the fifth "Gate of Cultivating *Śamatha* and *Vipaśyanā*" below;
because that text elucidates both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* together to eliminate the dual attachments of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles, it is termed an "antidote."
[Commentary]: Regarding "calm abiding and insight" (śamatha-vipaśyanā), the text says: "How does one practice the gate of calm abiding and insight?
What is called 'calm abiding' refers to the cessation of all objective appearances, as it accords with the meaning of śamatha-contemplation.

What is called 'insight' refers to the discernment of the characteristics of arising and ceasing through causes and conditions, as it accords with the meaning of vipaśyanā-contemplation. And so on, up to: "If [one practices] calm abiding..."
If one lacks [the cultivation of] contemplation, one will be unable to enter the path to bodhi. Regarding the simultaneous clarification of both [calm abiding and insight], that text states:
"If one cultivates calm abiding (śamatha), it serves as the antidote to ordinary beings' dwelling in attachment to the mundane world, and enables one to abandon the timid views of the two vehicles."
If one practices contemplation, it serves as an antidote to the fault of the two vehicles’ failure to give rise to great compassion and their narrow-mindedness;
it distances one from the faults of ordinary beings who do not cultivate goodness and so forth.
Seventh, it is to demonstrate the skillful means of single-minded mindfulness, so that by being born before the Buddha, one’s faith will certainly never regress.

[Commentary] This refers to the "Superior Grade. It corresponds to the section at the end of the "Chapter on Cultivating Faith" (*Xinxin-fen*), specifically the passage beginning with "Furthermore, when sentient beings first study this Dharma," followed by the "Gate of Encouraging Rebirth in the Pure Land," and so forth.

Since that text presents superior skillful means to enable practitioners to attain partial correspondence through contemplative understanding, it instructs them to proceed [to the Pure Land], for sentient beings may fear that their future retribution will shift and they will encounter conditions leading to regression. Therefore, it directs them to go.
"Causing birth so as not to regress.
[Commentary] Regarding "encouraging birth" and so forth, the text says: "Furthermore, when sentient beings first study this Dharma and desire to seek correct faith..."
Their minds are timid and weak because they dwell in this Sahā world;
they fear that they will not always be able to encounter the Buddhas to personally receive their teachings and make offerings, and they dread that their faith may be difficult to perfect.

For those whose intentions are to retreat, even if they constantly and diligently practice, they will ultimately attain birth [in the Pure Land] because they abide in right concentration (*samyaktva-niyāma*). Regarding "superior skillful means," the text says: "One should..."
One should know that the Tathāgata possesses supreme skillful means to protect and sustain the mind;

that is to say, by means of the causal condition of single-minded mindfulness of the Buddha, one will be born in a buddha-land of another direction according to one’s vow, constantly behold all Buddhas, and forever leave the evil realms behind.

Regarding "contemplative understanding" (*guan-jie*), the text states: "If one contemplates that Buddha’s *dharmakāya* of *tathatā*, one will ultimately attain birth [there] and abide in right concentration."

Therefore, once one contemplates the Dharma-body, this constitutes the contemplation of True Suchness (*tathatā*). When the contemplation of the Buddha becomes mature, one partially attains correspondence with it.
Regarding the "subsequent retribution" and so forth: because the karmic legacy of sentient beings is immeasurable, even though they now resolve to practice, their power is weak and inferior;

it is difficult to withstand powerful evil. Fearing that when this [present] retribution is exhausted, they will again follow their old karma and be reborn according to the various realms of existence.
It is like a person burdened by debt; the stronger creditor drags them away first. When this retribution ends with life, one does not know where one will go.

One may pass through many kalpas, traversing the three miserable realms. Even if one obtains a human body, one remains constrained by karmic obstacles: perhaps taking birth among the barbarians, or dwelling in poverty;
perhaps being entangled by various illnesses, or lacking the six sense faculties; or perhaps being pressed by royal service and bound by the dust of worldly affairs.
In this life, some may have been ignorant during their youth, or fierce and violent in their prime, only realizing the joy of goodness when they have already reached old age.

Though they may have awakened to the impermanence of existence, it is difficult for them to persevere in spiritual progress. Furthermore, the True Dharma is rarely encountered, and virtuous friends are seldom met.

Even if such conditions are met, their faculties and natures are often dull. Only those of superior intelligence find it easy to awaken to the gates of the Dharma; even if they possess eloquence to proclaim it, they lack the skill...
It opens the minds of people. Intense evil habits arise spontaneously and in abundance; since accumulated merit is meager, powerful evils are difficult to avoid.
One consequently falls precipitously, and this is the cycle of saṃsāra—like ants circling in a loop. When will it ever be severed? The Bodhisattva contemplates this and is deeply moved by compassion.
If not through skillful means (upāya), there is no way to provide salvation. Thus the treatise says: "There is a superior method..."
Thus, one should restrain and protect the mind; hence it is said that one fears that after this life, when the retribution of karma shifts, one may encounter conditions that cause regression.

Regarding "rebirth" and so forth, the text states: "As it is taught in the Sūtras, if a person single-mindedly contemplates Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, and dedicates the roots of goodness they have cultivated with the vow to be born in that world, they shall immediately attain rebirth there."
Because one constantly sees the Buddha, there will ultimately be no regression or the like.

This intention is to cause sentient beings to focus their minds on the recollection of the Buddha, joyfully seeking and desiring to be born in that land. Whatever wholesome deeds they cultivate, they should all dedicate toward this goal.
Even if a person has committed every kind of evil, provided they can, at the time of death, achieve ten recitations with a sincere mind—or even a single recitation—they shall attain accomplishment.
One immediately attains rebirth there. Having been born in that land, one sees the Buddha and hears the Dharma, progressing spontaneously toward cultivation until directly achieving Bodhi.
Since there are no evil conditions to cause one to regress, it is said that "one is made non-regressive."
Eighth, it is for the purpose of demonstrating benefits and encouraging practice.
[Commentary]: This refers to the subsequent section on "Encouraging Practice and Benefits. Within that text, by citing those instances of loss and gain, it exhorts beings to practice relinquishment;
this serves as a general exhortation to bring the preceding practices to completion.

[Commentary] Regarding "Exhortation to Practice" and so forth: the text states, "The section on practicing with faith has already been explained; next is the section on the benefits of exhorting others to practice. It continues:
"Such is the secret treasury of all Buddhas, the Mahāyāna, which I have now explained in its entirety," and so on, until it says:
"Future bodhisattvas should rely upon this Dharma to achieve correct faith; therefore, sentient beings should diligently cultivate and study it."
Regarding those who bring benefit or harm, the text states:

"If there are sentient beings who wish to give rise to right faith in the profound realm of the Tathāgata, to remain free from slander, and to enter the path of the Mahāyāna, they should uphold this treatise, contemplate it, and practice it;
they will ultimately be able to reach the unsurpassed way. It continues, stating that the merit of such a person is boundless.
This undertaking is beneficial. Furthermore, it is said that there are sentient beings who, within this treatise, slander and do not believe;
the retribution they incur for such acts will cause them to undergo great suffering and distress for immeasurable kalpas. This undertaking is detrimental.

Those who practice should simply have faith from the depths of their hearts and act according to what is taught. Those who abandon it should not engage in disparagement, lest they invite great suffering. This is a general exhortation.

Regarding the term "and so forth" (*ādi*): according to the judgment in the aforementioned commentary, this refers only to the practices of the three faculties at the initial stage of the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*).

However, if one examines this further through principle, there is no contradiction in including those from the three stages of worthiness (*tri-pūrvayoga*) downward as well, so that the exhortation and encouragement apply to them collectively.
Thus, among the eight causal conditions, both the first and the eighth are general characteristics; the first generally benefits all classes of beings, and the eighth...
This concludes the general exhortation to practice. The six intermediate sections each address specific purposes, as previously assigned.
△ Fourth, the summary:
It is for such causes and conditions that this treatise was composed.
[Commentary] This is a summary; it may be understood.
△ Second, resolving the objection (in two parts): 1. The objection; 2. The resolution. 1. The objection: Question:
Since this teaching is already fully contained within the Sūtras, why is it necessary to state it again?
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "possessing [these]," the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* states: "The intrinsically pure mind is stained yet unstained—this is difficult to comprehend.
It is unstained yet stained—this is difficult to comprehend. Is this not precisely the meaning of the two gates of the one mind?
Furthermore, these two gates are none other than the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional. Which sūtra does not speak of these two truths?
How could it be initiated by relying on the second causal condition of the Master of Treatises? For instance, in the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, the four stages beginning with faith are taught;
is this not precisely the meaning of discerning the characteristics of the Path?

Moreover, the progression from cause to fruit through the various stages of practice for entering the Path is extensively taught in many sūtras; why then would it need to be produced by a third causal condition? As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
When a bodhisattva resolves their mind to seek awakening, it is not without cause or without conditions.
By giving rise to pure faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, they thereby give birth to the vast and great mind. Is this not precisely faith in the Three Jewels?

How much more so when one causes others to have faith in the Three Jewels—what sutra does not speak of this? Furthermore, as in the *Avataṃsaka*, the practices of the bodhisattvas of the ten stages are fully explained.
The practice of the ten pāramitās—how could it consist of only practices such as giving? Moreover, this sutra explains all of them, including giving, ethical discipline, and so forth;
how then could they be initiated solely by the fourth causal condition? Matters such as worship and repentance at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) are fully elucidated within the sutra.
Furthermore, within the *Samantabhadra-caryāpraṇidhāna*, ten types of vows for conduct are taught; are these not indeed skillful means for the elimination of hindrances?
Indeed, there is no need to rely on a fifth causal condition. Furthermore, as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

"For example, just as a powerful king is venerated by all the land, so too are concentration and wisdom (samādhi-prajñā) that upon which Bodhisattvas depend. Concentration and wisdom are precisely śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Moreover, in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*, it is taught that the Buddha’s Dharma-body arises from śamatha and vipaśyanā. What need is there for a sixth?

Is it not the case that [the mind] arises through conditions? As is fully explained in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha*, the *Amitāyus*, and other sūtras regarding the matter of rebirth in the Pure Land—let alone the many citations found throughout various scriptures—it does not depend on a seventh [consciousness] as the originator.

For instance, this sūtra speaks of exhorting and praising spiritual progress, and encouraging the indolent; why then would it require an eighth [consciousness]? (As for the refutation of the first [position], it is not difficult.)

Since these seven causes and conditions collectively refute the specific and thereby refute the general, it is thus: the Buddha’s sūtras are already complete; for the Bodhisattva to further clarify them—would this not be redundant?
The Bodhisattva acts upon seeing the meaning; if there is no benefit, one should desist. What purpose or advantage is there in reiterating the Buddha’s sūtras in such a manner? Is it for this reason?
△ II. The Twofold Penetration (2). First, the brief indication following the question; second, the detailed explanation according to the meaning. First, the brief indication following the question:

The answer states that although this Dharma exists within the Sūtras, because the faculties and practices of sentient beings are not equal, there are differing conditions for their reception and understanding.
"Distinct.

[Commentary: "Although there are [differences] within [the middle]" is a concessive statement regarding their inquiry. "The faculties are unequal" refers to the distinction between those who are sharp or dull, those who prefer extensive or concise [teachings], and those who rely on the *sūtras* or the *śāstras*.
"Differences in reception and understanding" refers to whether one encounters the Buddha or the teachings.

They are different. [Commentary] "Either sharp or dull" refers to the inequality of the faculties (*indriya*). "Faculties" means the spiritual capacities (*indriya-mūla*); they are so called because there are those that are sharp and those that are dull.

"Delighting in the extensive or the concise" refers to the inequality of practice (*caryā*). "Practice" means mental activity; it is so called because what is desired differs. "Pseudo-sūtras" refers to those for the sharp [faculties].

Regarding the faculties: those with sharp faculties understand the sūtras immediately without waiting for an explanation; thus, they rely on the sūtras. Those with dull faculties do not yet comprehend the sūtras and must wait for the exposition of the treatises;
thus, they rely on the treatises. As for those who prefer extensive or concise expressions, this applies to both sūtras and treatises:
there are those who attain understanding through extensive sūtras, and there are those who attain understanding through concise sūtras; it is the same regarding the treatises. This...
Thus, among those of sharp and dull faculties, there are differing preferences. However, because their faculties are unequal, they are restricted to specific matters within the sūtras and śāstras;
because their practices are unequal, they each prefer either the extensive or the concise versions throughout the sūtras and śāstras.

Nevertheless, this distinction between sharp and dull faculties is made solely based on whether one understands the Buddha’s intent or does not understand the Buddha’s intent; it need not [be applied otherwise].
Furthermore, one should explain the subtle distinctions between the retention of the text (*dhāraṇī*) and the retention of the meaning (*artha-dhāraṇī*) in terms of their sharpness or dullness;

the wise should reflect upon this. Regarding the distinction between "receiving" (*pratigraha*) and "understanding" (*avabodha*): "receiving" refers to the faithful acceptance of the teachings; "understanding" refers to the awakening to the Buddha’s intent.

One who encounters the Buddha’s teaching is said to have a karmic affinity with the Buddha; thus, through the Buddha they receive transformation and give rise to understanding. One who has an affinity with the teaching receives it upon encountering the teaching.

This refers to the understanding of "transformation-birth" (*upapāduka*). This [distinction] is made solely in terms of whether one gives rise to understanding through that [birth] or does not give rise to it, thereby explaining the presence or absence of conditions;
it is not based on whether one sees the Buddha and so forth. To discuss this in detail:

for instance, those such as the various Arhats of the Buddha’s era who personally heard the Dharma from the Buddha and realized the fruits of the Path—these are those who encountered the Buddha and possessed the necessary conditions. As for those such as Vasubandhu, however...
Encountering their teachings and thereby attaining awakening—this refers to those who possess the conditions for encountering the teachings; hence it is said that "conditions are distinct.
However, according to the intent of this treatise, one need only clarify the distinctions between the conditions for receiving and understanding based on the sūtras and śāstras;

there is no need to further discuss encounters with the Buddha and so forth. This is because the questions previously raised in the preceding treatise have already been addressed in the Buddhist sūtras; why then should they be discussed again here? Now...
The preceding passage provides a general response to the prior question, while the following section offers a detailed explanation. The intent of the treatise is as follows:

although the Sūtra has already explained this in full, sentient beings differ in the sharpness or dullness of their faculties (*indriya*), and their mental activities (*manas-kāra*) and inclinations (*ruci*) vary.
This is because the conditions for receiving the teachings with faith and awakening to the holy intent are distinct. Thus, if one possesses sharp faculties and, regarding the Buddha’s words...

Those who possess the necessary causes and conditions delight in the sūtras and, through faith and acceptance, attain realization of the holy intent; for them, there is no need for further discussion.

However, if one is of dull faculties and lacks a connection with the sūtras, but possesses a connection with the words of the Bodhisattva, they will delight in composing treatises to provide explanations, thereby finally understanding the Buddha’s meaning.
This is why it is called "distinct. Since the three—faculties, practices, and conditions—are thus established...
There is a difference. What prevents one from composing treatises separately outside of the sūtras? Is it not the case that this passage has already provided a general answer?

(In the commentary, "encountering the Buddha" refers to encountering the Buddha’s sūtras; "should correspond to the sūtras. "Encountering the teaching" refers to encountering the teachings of the bodhisattva treatises; "should correspond to the treatises. Those who read this must properly understand such an intention.)

△ Second, the detailed explanation by way of meaning (in two parts): First, clarifying that other types of practitioners do not require this treatise; second, clarifying that those who are the intended audience must have this treatise composed.
First, clarifying that other types of practitioners do not require this treatise (in three parts): First, superior practitioners who attain awakening upon encountering the Buddha;

second, those who attain awakening through their own power by hearing the sutras; third, inferior practitioners who attain awakening by searching through extensive treatises. First, the superior practitioner:
"Awakening upon encountering the Buddha.
[Commentary] Even during the time of the Buddha, there were no scriptures on paper or silk; how much less could there have been discourses?

[Sub-commentary] "Awakening upon encountering the Buddha without paper or ink" means that while the Buddha was in the world, he merely preached orally. After his parinirvāṇa, [the teachings were] compiled...

It was only after the assembly had gathered that the sūtras first came into existence. At that time, the conditions were so excellent that beings attained awakening upon hearing the teaching alone; they did not even require the sūtras, let alone the composition of treatises. As it is said:
"While the Tathāgata was in the world, sentient beings possessed sharp faculties, and the one who could speak—the Buddha—excelled in both form and mind; his voice was perfectly resonant."
First, regarding "exposition" (*vyākhyāna*): if there were uniform understanding among those of different dispositions, then a treatise would not be required.
[Commentary: In the world of the Tathāgata, the time is supreme; sentient beings have sharp faculties, which is supreme; the person who speaks and the karmic conditions are supreme.

"Complete exposition" (*pūrṇa-vyākhyāna*) reveals the supreme nature of the conditions; "uniform understanding" (*sama-adhimukti*) reveals the supreme nature of the faculties. "Not requiring a treatise" concludes that a treatise is unnecessary.
[Commentary] "First" refers to the general explanation of the phrases. "Tathāgata" refers to Śākyamuni, while also encompassing other Buddhas.
Regarding "superiority of time," since time has no fixed essence, it is called "superiority of time" simply by reference to the period when the Buddha was present there.

Regarding "superiority of faculties," this refers only to those of a certain class who, being in the world of the Buddha, have realized and understood through compliance with his teachings; it does not refer to those who merely encountered the Buddha [but did not practice].

They are the class of those who have attained realization. However, during the Buddha’s lifetime, there were many who realized awakening; since this discussion refers specifically to that period, it is said they are "superior.

They are superior because they surpass the other two vehicles and the bodhisattvas. Yet, when explaining the awakening and understanding of the faculties (*indriya*), one does not take the causal conditions for the arising of the teaching into account;
therefore, the Buddha is pointed out as the "superior condition" (*pratyaya*). As for "different types," these refer merely to the faculties of the three vehicles and five vehicles.
Their natures are different; therefore, they are called "different classes" (*nānājāti*). Alternatively, it may apply to other realms of existence (*gati*), though this is not the primary intention.

Regarding "equally producing understanding" (*samasamājñā*): "equal" (*sama*) means "identical. Because those various different classes equally produce understanding, this refers to the equality of the meaning of producing understanding.

This does not mean that their understanding is identical; rather, it refers to the comparison and differentiation between the superiority of the faculties (*indriya*) and the superiority of the time (*kāla*), which form four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
These are: first, superiority of time but inferiority of faculties, such as the six groups of monks during the Buddha’s lifetime;
second, superiority of faculties but inferiority of time, such as those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit during the final five hundred years; third, superiority of both, such as Śāriputra.

(3) Both are equally inferior. That is, those who do not produce understanding after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa (4). Since this does not depend on the treatise, it follows that the sūtra is likewise unnecessary.

However, according to what is questioned in the treatise, it merely holds that because [the meaning] has already been explained in the sūtra, the composition of the treatise is for the sake of emphasis;
it has absolutely no bearing on the period when the Buddha was still present. The intent of the current response is to demonstrate [the significance of] the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.

Subsequently, because faculties and practices differ, interpretations of the sūtras and śāstras vary accordingly. Therefore, we shall first clarify that when the Buddha was in the world, both faculties and conditions were superior;

even then, they did not rely on the sūtras, so why would it have been necessary to compose treatises to manifest [the truth]? This is because after his parinirvāṇa, both faculties and conditions became inferior;
thus, one must rely on the sūtras, and if one does not fully understand the sūtras, one must further rely on the śāstras. In this way, the superior is used to manifest the inferior.
Thus, the sūtras and śāstras each cater to a single faculty (*indriya*), unlike the perfect voice (*paripūrṇa-svara*) which universally accommodates many types of beings.
[Commentary: The "perfect voice" of form and mind refers precisely to the three karmas (*trividha-karman*).
[Commentary] Next is the separate explanation of the text. First, there is a brief correlation with the three types of karma, as in the text.
[Sub-commentary] Regarding "the single voice" and "the perfect voice," there are two parts. First, the Tathāgata’s single voice expounds all dharmas such that none are not clearly manifested;
therefore, it is called the "perfect voice. As the *Avataṃsaka* says: "Within a single utterance, the Tathāgata brings forth..."
The ocean of sūtras is boundless. Second, because the Tathāgata’s voice is identical to all sounds, it is called the "perfect sound" (*paripūrṇa-svara*). The *Avataṃsaka* states:
"All the languages and dharmas of all sentient beings are fully expounded in a single word without exception.

Because all sounds are identical to the one sound, it is called the "one sound" (*eka-svara*). Because the one sound is identical to all sounds, it is called the "perfect sound. Each and every word...
The sound pervades the entire realm of sentient beings, yet its melodic tones are never confused or disordered. If the sound did not pervade, it would not be perfect;
if the sound were to pervade equally while losing its melodic contours, it would not be a perfect sound.
Now, it pervades equally without destroying its melodic contours, and it varies in its tones without disturbing its pervasive nature. This is the Perfect Sound of the Tathāgata; it is not the mind.
"Consciousness is the realm of deliberation. [Commentary] "One sound," etc., has two parts.
Second, the extensive explanation of the perfect voice (paripūrṇa-svara) has two parts. First, the explanation of the meaning of the perfect voice. This also has two parts.

First, the correct elucidation according to the doctrinal meaning. First, the manifestation of the meaning of perfection through the distinctions of the Dharma taught. Regarding "the Tathāgata," etc., it means: [The text continues with the commentary on the Tathāgata's various modes of teaching.]
The Buddha’s voice has no distinction; therefore, it is called "one voice. Yet, the teachings it delivers differ; therefore, it is called the "perfect voice" (*paripūrṇa-svara*).

The supporting evidence can be understood from the scriptures. Regarding the second [point], there are two parts. This explains the meaning of perfection by way of the speech and sounds that accord with the various classes of beings.

As for "the Tathāgata," etc., it should be stated as: "The Tathāgata’s one voice is identical to all voices. The text omits the term "one voice" as an abbreviation. This means that the Buddha’s voice is singular.
It is called "one sound" (*ekasvara*). Because it accords with various different languages, it is called the "perfect sound" (*pariśuddhasvara*).
This can be understood from scriptural citations. Furthermore, the *Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna-sūtra* states:

"Whether they be devas, nāgas, yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, or even humans and non-humans—among all the languages of every sentient being, [the Buddha] preaches the Dharma using all those sounds. This is the Tathāgata’s single sound that accords with [all beings].
This refers to the differentiation of simultaneity; it is not like the differentiation of dharmas explained in the preceding section.
From "Because" (*yi*) downwards, [the text] next concludes the reason for obtaining these names: all sounds are precisely one sound, meaning that differentiation is precisely non-differentiation.
One sound is precisely all sounds, meaning that non-differentiation is precisely differentiation. The general purport takes non-differentiation as...
First: Difference is itself perfection; difference is itself non-difference; non-difference is itself difference. These two meanings exist simultaneously, without any sequence whatsoever.
Within both sections, this principle is present; only when they are perfectly interfused and unimpeded is it truly the Tathāgata’s secret of speech (*vāg-guhya*).
It is merely because the text does not repeat itself that these appear as preceding and following. [End of first section. Second: Manifestation.

The characteristics of the perfect sound (*pariṣphuṭa-svara*) are fourfold. First, the direct exposition: "Pervading and exhausting the realms of sentient beings" is the meaning of "perfect" (*pari*);

"ever without confusion" is the meaning of "sound" (*svara*). Furthermore, "pervading and exhausting" means that all six destinies hear it; "without confusion" means that the five types of vocal sounds are distinct from one another.

Moreover, "pervading and exhausting" means that those of the three vehicles listen together; "without confusion" means that their comprehension and understanding differ individually. Second, the indirect clarification (via contrast): if the sound were low... [and so forth].

Regarding "not being all-pervasive" and so forth: since there are places where it is not heard, how can it fulfill the meaning of being "perfect"? "Perfect" means "all-pervasive. Regarding "losing its quality of resonance" and so forth:
if there is nothing to be expressed, how can it fulfill the meaning of "sound"? For instance, the resonance of a bell or a drum pervades both the near and the far.
The sounds of strings and flutes are heard only at a distance of a few feet; this is the principle of the "mutually non-identical perfect sound" (*yuan-yin hu-fei*). Now, as for the third point:
"forming a completion without descending, being equal and pervasive while not destroying the melody"—this means that by means of the sound, one achieves the perfect circle.

"Remaining unmoving and pervasive yet possessing distinct tonal variations"—this means that by means of the perfect circle, one constitutes the sound. This is precisely the identity of the correct and the pervasive within the distinct, and the identity of the distinct within...

It is all-pervasive. Consequently, there is no sound that is not heard, and no meaning that is not correctly understood. This is the fourth [verse], expressing praise. As for the phrase "not the realm of consciousness, etc.":
the perfect voice manifested by the Buddha’s untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) cannot be fathomed by ordinary beings with tainted [minds] (*sāsrava*).

One may only believe in it with reverence; there is no need for analytical investigation, because it is not the domain of the mind and consciousness. That which is not the domain of consciousness means:
That which cannot be cognized by consciousness and is not an object of the mind cannot be known through wisdom or deliberation; for such deliberation is precisely the characteristic of consciousness.
Nevertheless, within the *Avataṃsaka*, ten metaphors are provided to manifest the characteristics of the Tathāgata’s perfect sound.
I cannot cite further examples at length.
△ Second, awakening through hearing the sutras by means of one's own power:
If, after the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, there are sentient beings who, by means of their own power, can hear extensively and thereby attain understanding; or...
There are sentient beings who, by their own power, understand much from hearing little. [Commentary]:
By their own power, they hear the extensive scriptural texts and attain understanding of the Buddha’s intent without requiring other treatises; hence it is called "by one's own power."

This [type of person] possesses both the retention of the text and the retention of the meaning; furthermore, by relying on their own power to investigate the abbreviated scriptural text, they are able to deeply understand the Buddha’s intent, and thus they do not require other treatises.
This [other type] possesses the retention of the meaning but lacks the retention of the text.
[Commentary] "Self-power" refers to those who do not rely on commentaries or sub-commentaries, but instead understand the meaning by themselves through the direct reading of the sūtra text alone.

Regarding "extensive sūtras," there are two senses: first, within the great collections of sūtras, one may extensively search through various sections to see the Buddha’s life from beginning to end and only then understand the broad paths of meaning; such individuals are of inferior faculties and practice.
Regarding those who have heard little but possess much understanding: there are two types. The first is like the commentary (*śāstra*), which maintains both the text and its meaning;

because they can understand every single passage as it occurs, their faculties are strong and superior to those who have heard little. Regarding those who [understand] the abbreviated sūtras: there are also two meanings.
The first is that, regarding the text of the abbreviated sūtras—whether it be a single phrase, a single verse, or the like—they immediately understand the profound [intent] of the Tathāgata.
Regarding the principles of the Dharma, there is no need for further elaboration. In the first case, both the faculties and the practice are superior;
in the second case, there is not sufficient mental power to engage in extensive study, so one attains understanding through only a small portion.

As for the distinction between "retention without textual basis" (*asūtra*) and "retention with doctrinal basis" (*sārtha*) mentioned in the commentary, according to the intent of the treatise, the former explanations are taken as correct for both the extensive and the abbreviated versions, because the treatise is concise.

The middle [version] says "many," while the extensive [version] does not include the word "many. Therefore, those who prefer the extensive are dull-witted, whereas those who prefer the concise are sharp-witted.

According to the intent of the commentary (*śāstra*), each should take the latter explanation as correct. Both interpretations are acceptable; one may choose between them according to one's own inclination.
△ Third, those of inferior capacity attain awakening through extensive treatises due to their seeking.
There may be sentient beings who lack the power of their own minds and attain understanding by means of extensive treatises.
[Commentary] They rely solely on the scriptural text and cannot comprehend its meaning; they attain full understanding only through the extensive treatises of others. Hence it is said.
They lack the power of their own minds; these possess the retention of the letter but lack the retention of the meaning.
[Commentary] Regarding "due to the extensive treatises," there are two intentions here. First, they do not understand the sūtras, but only understand them through the treatises (*śāstra*);
furthermore, they must rely upon extensive sections or search through various treatises before they can understand the Buddha’s intent. This is inferior.

The latter section contains few words yet encompasses many meanings; those capable of understanding it do so because, as explained in the Commentary, each point is interpreted according to its specific context, thereby enabling full comprehension.
Thus, this [latter] faculty is superior and more powerful than the subsequent text.
△ Second, explaining that those who are suitable vessels must compose this treatise (in two parts). First, the initial capacity; second, the conclusion. Regarding the initial capacity:

there are sentient beings who, moreover, find extensive texts cumbersome due to their great length, yet who delight in *dhāraṇī*—that is, those who can achieve understanding through concise text that encompasses many meanings.

[Commentary]: This person does not delight in prolixity; he relies solely on treatises that are concise in wording yet rich in meaning, thereby gaining a profound understanding of the essential purport of the Buddha’s sūtras.
Thus it is said that he "retains many meanings. There are two reasons why he need not be extensive: first, [the first reason].
[The faculties] are sharp and do not require [extensive teaching]. Second, the mind is vexed and lacks endurance. [Commentary]:
Regarding "the mind delights in *dhāraṇī*," there are also two meanings. First, because one hears little but understands much, one does not require prolix explanations.
Second, because one's spiritual faculties (*indriya*) are weak, one cannot sustain what is extensively taught. This is fully explained in the sub-commentary (*śū-wén*).
The purport of this treatise is as follows: regarding the extensive and concise versions [of the scriptures], one should take the former meaning as primary and the latter as secondary.
Thus, within the understanding derived from the extensive and concise expositions of the sūtras and śāstras, it serves both those of sharp and dull faculties.

Furthermore, among the four permutations of the two modes of retention—textual and doctrinal—one specifically attains the single permutation of "retaining the meaning without retaining the text. This is precisely the case of "retention of meaning without retention of text."
△ Second, the conclusion:
Thus, this treatise should be expounded in order to comprehensively encompass the boundless meanings of the Tathāgata’s vast and profound Dharma.

[Commentary: Although the words of this treatise are few, they comprehensively encompass the profound purport of all Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras. "Profound" refers to the objective realm of *jñāna* as it is (yathābhūta-jñāna);
"vast" refers to the objective realm of *jñāna* as it appears (yāvadbhāva-jñāna); and "boundless" means that these profundity and vastness are without limit.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "although the words and phrases are few," etc.: although the text consists of but a single fascicle, its meaning encompasses as many sands as the Ganges.

The sūtras that serve as our primary authority are all teachings of ultimate reality (*satya-dharma*). How could the principles they expound possibly be coarse or superficial? Even the essential doctrines of the perfect and real nature found in various treatises do not transcend these.
Therefore, it says "comprehensively subsumes," etc. The object of the wisdom of suchness (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) is precisely *tathatā* (suchness).
The "gate" refers to the fact that it is free from verbal expression while the mind takes such characteristics as its object; therefore, it is called "profound.

The realm of *yathāvad-jñāna* (wisdom as-it-is) is the gate of arising and ceasing; because it encompasses the myriad differences of defilement and purity, it is vast and extensive, and is thus called "broad.
"Boundless" means that the realm of *tathatā-jñāna* (wisdom of suchness) is profoundly deep and boundless, while the realm of *yathāvad-jñāna* is extensively manifold and boundless. Boundless.
The characteristics [of these two gates] have already been seen in the treatise. Nevertheless, these two gates encompass the entirety of the meaning of all sutras and śāstras.

Whether they speak of defilement or purity, ordinary beings or sages, delusion or awakening, cause and effect, good and evil, or any other phenomena distinguished by names and marks—all are fully subsumed within the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*).
If one speaks of that which is neither defiled nor pure, transcends ordinary beings and sages, and dispels both delusion and awakening, [it is subsumed within the gate of non-arising].
The meaning of the nature of detachment and so forth is entirely subsumed within the gate of True Suchness (tathatā). Thus, the Commentary from海东 (Haidong) states:

"Opening two gates within one mind, it comprehensively summarizes the extensive interrogations of Māra’s hundred and eight [verses] (Māra refers to the location where the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* was preached; with its hundred and eight phrases, it answers Mahāmati’s hundred and eight questions;

all have the lower phrase as the ultimate truth and the upper phrase as the conventional truth, which is identical to the meaning of these two gates). It demonstrates the purity of nature amidst the defilement of appearances, universally encompassing the *Udānavarga*."

The profound subtleties of the *Fifteen Chapters* (the place where the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* was preached in the country of Ayodhyā; it contains fifteen chapters whose great meaning all explain that which is defiled yet undefiled, identical to this principle of the *tathatā* of arising and ceasing);
up to the single-flavored school of the *Hèlín* (the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*) and the non-dual destination of the *Jiùshān* (the *Lotus Sūtra*).
The *Suvarṇabhāsa-sūtra* (Golden Drum), the *Mahāyāna-samatā-nirdeśa-sūtra* (Sameness of Nature), the ultimate fruit of the three bodies;
the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the profound cause of the four stages; the *Pañcaviṃśati-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* and the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, the most expansive of supreme paths;

the *Sūryagarbha* and *Candragarbha* [sections], the mysterious portals of the secret [teachings]: among all such works as these, that which penetrates them all with a single thread is... [the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*].
Is this merely a treatise? Since its fundamental tenets are profound and its principles are boundless, those of wisdom should study it with tireless diligence.

regarding the Mahāyāna, there are generally two types.
Second, listing the names by way of questions.
What are the two? First, the phenomenon (*dharma*); second, the meaning (*artha*). [Commentary:

As for "phenomenon," it refers to the essence of the Mahāyāna teachings. This is because it denotes its own nature, because it is contrasted with wisdom, and because it manifests the meaning; it is the fundamental doctrine itself.
Its "great" status resides in the causal stage, as it pervades both the defiled and the pure.
[Commentary] First, this explains the Dharma. Regarding "the essence of the Mahāyāna Dharma": the essence of the Mahāyāna is precisely the mind; thus, the mind is termed "Dharma.
Here, for the time being, the Dharma is explained as the essence of the Mahāyāna. The subsequent passage below then explains that the mind is the essence of the Dharma.
This is a progressive exposition of its essence. Now, it says: "to bring forth the Mahāyāna Dharma."

Regarding the term "essence" (*tǐ*): fearing that there may be many characters for the word *dharma*, let the wise examine it in detail. From this point downward, the three meanings explain the reason for naming it "Dharma.
Now, as for what is called "Dharma," it has two meanings: first, the meaning of maintaining its own essence; second, the meaning of serving as a guide that gives rise to understanding in beings.
Here, the first phrase refers to the first meaning. That is to say, the originally existing essence is truly [unfailing].
It is a transformation; it is not identical to the dependent nature (*paratantra*). It is provisionally established based on conditions and lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

However, because it has maintained its continuity without loss since beginningless time, the subsequent treatise states: "In reality, it is not empty, for it possesses its own essence and is fully endowed with immeasurable qualities of nature.
The latter two phrases refer to the meaning of "providing a standard that gives rise to understanding in beings. This means that "Dharma" is in relation to wisdom.

It is so named because this single mind is the principle of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), which can serve as a standard for wisdom, enabling it to become untainted (*anāsrava*) and non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*).

This is because it takes the signless object (*animitta-viṣaya*) as its counterpart to the signless wisdom (*animitta-jñāna*); thus, it is called "confronting wisdom. As the subsequent treatise states:

"Because it is exclusively in accord with realization. Furthermore, it is able to manifest the meaning of the three greatnesses (*trimahātmya*); there is not a single meaning that is not [contained therein].
Following Fa-xian, the subsequent passage states: "Based on this mind, the meaning of the Mahāyāna is revealed.

Since the principles and meanings have been made manifest, sentient beings then give rise to understanding; thus, these two phrases both pertain to the latter [the meaning]. Regarding "the school takes the fundamental [mind] as its basis" (*zong ben fa*):

this refers to that which is the primary tenet of the treatise, as it is the root of both defilement and purity. Alternatively, "school" (*zong*) may be synonymous with "fundamental" (*ben*), referring to the basis in terms of its underlying meaning.
"Relying upon" refers to the tenet (*siddhānta*). "Able to establish all phenomena" refers to the root. Thus, the sub-commentary below states:

"The distinct principles and meanings revealed by the tenet. Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "Based on the root of non-abiding, all phenomena are established. Moreover, the preceding treatise states:
