He asked, "If this is the meaning, how can sentient beings accord with it and thereby attain entry?"
[Commentary] "In accordance with" refers to the inquiry into skillful means (*upāya*) and the entry [into realization].

"The correct contemplation" (*samyag-darśana*) refers to the inquiry itself. [Record] "Such meanings" points to the aforementioned meaning of being ineffable and inconceivable. "Sentient beings, etc. refers to...

Since their speech already deviates from principle and their thoughts already diverge from the Truth, all sentient beings continue in a constant succession of moments, never free from discursive thought.
If they wish not to deviate, how should they accord with reality? If they wish to realize and witness it, how should they enter into it?
△ Second, the response by citing the truth to encourage practice.
The answer says: "If one knows that all phenomena, though spoken of, have neither speaker nor that which is spoken;
and though contemplated, have neither contemplator nor that which is contemplated—this is called 'conformity. If one is free from such contemplation, it is called 'attaining entry.'"

[Commentary] “If one knows” and below answers the question regarding the contemplation of skillful means. The statement that “mindfulness is entirely devoid of subject and object” clarifies that mindfulness is itself non-mindfulness;
it does not mean the extinction of mindfulness. Because mindfulness is not extinguished, although it is called “mindfulness,” it is free from the view of annihilationism.

Because it is precisely non-thought (*amanasikāra*), there is neither subject nor object; thus, one is free from the view of permanence. Within a single thought-moment, one is free from these two views.
Because these two do not exist, one is able to accord with the Middle Way and conform to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

Furthermore, although one may still abide within thoughts and the like, one contemplates these very thoughts as being eternally devoid of subject and object. Thus, even if one has not yet abandoned thought, [one remains in accordance with reality].
And because one accords with non-thought, it is called "conformity" (*anuloma*). [Commentary:
Although there is speaking and although there is thinking, this is correct speaking and correct mindfulness; that is, non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).

That which can be spoken and that which can be thought of are the object spoken of and the object thought of; this duality of subject and object is false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). As it says below: "All sentient beings, by means of..."
There is a deluded mind that discriminates from moment to moment; all such states are inconsistent [with reality]. Regarding "there being nothing": the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* says:
"At all times, do not give rise to deluded thoughts. When abiding in the realm of delusive thought, do not apply further cognition.
By not applying [cognition], there is no longer the discrimination of subject and object. This, moreover, serves as a skillful means within the skillful means of contemplation. The Commentary says:
"Mindfulness is itself non-mindfulness," and so forth, means that when one knows all phenomena while mindful, there is fundamentally no subject that minds nor object that is minded;

it does not mean that one must extinguish this mindfulness to make it non-existent. Because the essence of mindfulness is fundamentally transcendent, it is itself non-mindfulness. Thus, the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra* says:

"Regarding all deluded minds, do not even attempt to suppress or extinguish them. This explains both "mindfulness as non-mindfulness" and "non-mindfulness as mindfulness," thereby departing from duality.

If one extinguishes mindfulness so as to sever it, one falls into the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*). If one does not know that mindfulness is itself emptiness, one falls into the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*).
Now, since one neither extinguishes it nor fails to know that it is non-existent, one avoids these errors. This is thus the forgetting of words through words, yet it is not a total absence of speech;
it is the non-mindfulness of mindfulness, yet it is not a total absence of thought. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "There is no departing from the text."

One speaks of liberation through words; yet the nature of words is itself free from [duality], which is liberation. As the subsequent text states: "Because sentient beings are deluded, they take the mind to be thought.
In reality, the mind is unmoving. If one can observe and know that the mind is without thought, one immediately attains compliance and enters the gate of True Suchness.
This concludes the benefit: by means of this single thought being without thought, one has already transcended [delusion].
There are two errors. Since these two errors are absent, one accords with the *dharmatā* of the Middle Way; that is, one does not deviate from *tathatā*.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "also may": the former [approach] directly addresses the substance of the dharma (its nature), stating that mindfulness is itself non-mindfulness.

This [latter approach], however, involves the application of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) at the very moment a thought arises—cultivation through which both the subject who mindfully observes and the object being observed, whether already arisen or yet to arise, are realized to be utterly unobtainable.
The explanation is likewise. Therefore, it is said "and so forth. As for "not yet free from thought":
when observing in this manner, coarse thoughts do not arise, yet subtle thoughts still persist; hence, it is called "not yet free.
As for "conforming to non-thought": because one constantly observes that there is neither subject nor object, such observation is itself conformity with non-thought.
As the text below states: "If there are sentient beings who can contemplate non-thought, they are thereby heading toward Buddha-wisdom. [Commentary: The passage beginning with "If one is free from...

answers the question regarding correct contemplation (*samyak-darśana*). As explained above, by contemplating for a long time without ceasing, one is able to leave behind these deluded thoughts and accord with that truth of non-thought;
therefore, it is called "correct contemplation. Regarding the phrase "to be able to enter," it means that the wisdom of contemplation accords with and enters into [that truth].

The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Because it is the sphere of activity of wisdom. Furthermore, one may also correctly know that even the thought of non-existence of subject and object must be abandoned before entering true suchness (*tathatā*).
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "as stated above" and so forth: what was previously explained was merely a skillful means for entering into principle;
therefore, the preceding commentary states that it is the "response concerning skillful means contemplation. As for the phrase "is able to" and so forth:

through the prior mastery of observation, one is then able to depart from these notions of subject and object, thereby attaining accord with the truth of non-conceptualization (*amanasikāra*). Since there is truly no conceptualization of subject and object in this state, now that—

By departing from this, one is able to accord with the truth. As for "correct contemplation" (*samyag-darśana*), this contemplation corresponds precisely to *tathatā* (suchness), like a box and its lid fitting together.
Furthermore, "correct" (*samyak*) means "holy" (*ārya*). Those whose stage is at or above the first ground (*bhūmi*) are called holy persons who have entered into principle.

The preceding skillful means correspond to the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*). "Accordance and entry" has the meaning of realization (*sākṣātkriyā*). This is because one is free from subject and object.
Because of mindfulness, one attains the realization of *tathatā* (suchness); this is termed "entering into accord. Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"When, with respect to the object of cognition, wisdom perceives nothing at all, at that time one abides in *vijñaptimātra*, because one is free from the characteristics of the two graspings. However, regarding what was explained above:
Furthermore, if we consider one aspect, attaining untainted right knowledge (*anāsrava-samyagjñāna*) is called "entering by means of detachment from conceptual thought.

If we consider ultimate detachment, it applies to the Single One alone, namely the Subtle Enlightenment (*sūkṣma-bodhi*). As for the "sphere of activity of wisdom," True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the place traversed by right knowledge;
it is clarified as not being the sphere traversed by inverted delusions. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka* says: "The profound and true dharma-nature..."

"Wondrous wisdom enters in accordance [with reality]. Furthermore, 'also' means that while the previous explanation resolved that the object of contemplation is non-existent, the present explanation resolves that the subject of contemplation is also non-existent.
This mind of contemplative awareness is called the knowledge that there is no thought of subject or object."
If one merely maintains this thought, one will still not enter [the state], for the moment the mind is directed toward it, there is already a deviation.

Thus, the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*) says: "Leave behind that which is far removed from illusion; leave even that behind. When there is nothing further to be left behind, all illusions are eliminated.

Hézé said: "When delusion arises, one is immediately aware; when delusion ceases, awareness ceases. When both awareness and delusion have ceased, this is true suchness (*tathatā*). Thus, the essence of suchness is free from [conceptualization].

Thought: as soon as it moves, it deviates from the Truth. If one can know that thought is non-thought and observe without ceasing, following in this manner, there will still be a time of entry [into realization].

I hope that all practitioners will diligently cultivate sublime wisdom. Furthermore, according to the previous expedient means, one may also explain cultivation based on the former [section] and explain nature based on the latter.
When one correctly knows the state of detachment, wisdom has nothing at all to be attained. This is the fundamental [nature].
"Even the thought of neither subject nor object is transcended" means that both the perceived object and its conditions are quiescent.

This is the transcendence of the two grasps (*dvaya-grāha*), the pure Middle Way, the very nature of *tathatā*. What need is there to wait for it not to enter [the mind]? However, based on the preceding dialogue, both "speaking" and "thought" were clarified;

yet in the subsequent answer regarding correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*), "speaking" was not discussed. This is because the subtle is used as an illustration for the coarse; thus, it refers to mental thought (*citta-manasikāra*).
Even that which is subtle must still be left far behind; how could coarse and superficial speech possibly remain?
△ Second, distinguishing virtues based on words to clarify the realm for generating faith.
[Commentary] This explains the characteristic of *tathatā* (suchness) within the "Section on Establishing the Thesis" (*lìyìfēn*).

[Record] Regarding the characteristic of *tathatā*: previously it was stated, "This is the characteristic of the *tathatā* of the mind. Prior to this point, the two characters *zhēnrú* (suchness) had already been explained;
from here onward, the single character *xiàng* (characteristic) is finally explained. The topical outline (*kē*) designates this as "The Object for Generating Faith."
This is because the two types of meanings—the empty and the non-empty—admit of verbal expression; thus, those who hear it give rise to faith.
Therefore, the speaker also intends to inspire faith. As the treatise states:

"Based on verbal expression and conceptual differentiation, there are two kinds of meanings," and as the *Laṅkāvatāra* says: "Verbal expression is a distinct application... [The text continues with the analysis of these distinctions.]
This should be distinguished from the initial stage of practice.

△ Within this, there are three parts: first, stating the number to provide a general heading; second, opening the chapters for a brief discussion; third, providing a detailed explanation according to the chapters.
First, stating the number to provide a general heading.
Furthermore, regarding *tathatā* (suchness), there are two kinds of meanings based on verbal designations and conceptual discrimination.
[Commentary: To clarify these two meanings: if one were to depart from words, it would be of a single flavor; since we now rely upon words, it is said that there are two.
This demonstrates that one must not grasp at things according to words. It is merely for the purpose of generating faith and understanding in sentient beings.

This passage is stated for that reason. Thus, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* says: "Why is it not simply stated as 'beyond words'? It is to demonstrate that one seeks understanding by relying on words.

[Commentary] The treatise further states: "Next, regarding True Suchness (tathatā). Question: Since this already explains the characteristics of True Suchness, why does it not [explicitly] cite [the term]?
"Is it a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)? He replied: "Because characteristics are distinguished from within the signless (*animitta*), the characteristic is itself the signless.

This is because it is not different from the reality that transcends verbal expression. Furthermore, 'characteristic' is synonymous with 'meaning' (*artha*). Now, within the true essence (*dharmatā*), two meanings are disclosed;
therefore, it is said that there are two kinds of meaning. 'Meaning' is itself the characteristic. The Commentary states: "'Of one flavor' refers to the previously mentioned 'one mind.'"
Because it is the *dharmadhātu*. Nevertheless, from the perspective of ultimate principle (*tattva*), because it is free from all characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it is forcibly designated as "one.
Yet this single characteristic is itself unobtainable. As the *Dharmapada-sūtra* says: "The myriad phenomena and all forms are sealed by a single dharma;
yet even 'one' is not made one, for the purpose of destroying all numerical categories. This is what those of shallow wisdom hear: seeing 'one,' they take it to be one."

I pray that those of profound wisdom will set aside their preconceptions and realize this for themselves. Regarding the "existence of two": since it allows for verbal expression and conceptual differentiation, there is the appearance of duality.

One must not follow the words: although the preceding section revealed that the essence is beyond words, one must not cling to the idea that there is nothing to be said, because there are two meanings.
Although I have now differentiated these two meanings, they must not be grasped as such.

It is for the sake of having characteristics (*sanimitta*). Since characteristics are themselves non-characteristic (*animitta*), they are neither different nor beyond verbal expression; therefore, one must not grasp them according to words.
However, as for the phrase "but for the sake of [the inferior]," if there were no words at all, by what means could one rely upon faith and understanding? Thus, two meanings are taught.
This can be understood from the citation of the text following the section on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
△ Second, a brief exposition of the chapters.
What are the two? First is "emptiness as it truly is" (*yathābhūta-śūnyatā*), because it can ultimately manifest reality.
Second is "non-emptiness as it truly is" (*yathābhūta-aśūnyatā*), because it possesses its own essence and is fully endowed with the qualities of untainted nature (*anāsrava-dharmas*).

[Commentary] "How so? This is a question that raises the subject. Regarding "emptiness as it truly is" (*yathābhūta-śūnyatā*): this means that within the state of reality as it is, there is emptiness because of the absence of false defilements;
it does not mean that reality itself is empty. This is the emptiness of reality as it is. Because it is empty of falsehood, it is able to manifest true principle;
therefore, it is said that "manifesting reality as non-empty" has two meanings. First, that which possesses its own intrinsic nature is distinct [from the false].

Because delusion has no substantial nature. Second, regarding the possession of inherent virtuous qualities: this is because they differ from the *āsrava* afflictions, which are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Thus, a verse in the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra* says: "Because adventitious dust is empty, it is separated from the *dharmadhātu*; the unsurpassed Dharma is not empty."
It accords with the dharma-realm. [Commentary:
Regarding "that which is free from false defilement": within the reality-as-such (tathatā), it fundamentally does not correspond with the nine appearances or the six defilements.
Therefore, it is called "emptiness. This does not mean that the true essence itself is emptiness. As for "emptiness as suchness" (*yathābhūta-śūnyatā*):

"suchness" refers to the true nature, and "emptiness" refers to the absence of false defilements. "Emptiness as suchness" is thus a *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compound, just as one says "the emptiness of a jar."
This is because there is no object within the bottle; it does not mean that the substance of the bottle itself is empty.

This analogy is fully present in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. "Ultimate" (*jìngjiù*) means reaching the highest point. The intent clarifies that the statement establishing emptiness reaches its ultimate limit solely for the purpose of revealing the reality (*tattva*).
"Thus able to, etc. means taking illusory emptiness as the revealer (*nengxiǎn*) and reality as the revealed (*suǒxiǎn*). It is not...
Because that [delusion] is empty by nature, how could it know this reality? As for "different from delusion" and "without [delusion]," delusion gathers upon true existence;
true existence is inherently self-existent, and thus they are said to be "different. Regarding "the flow of existence": "existence" refers to the three existences or the twenty-five existences;
"flow" refers to the four flows or the nine flows. Because those various existences and afflictions can cause all beings to drift and drown, they are collectively termed "flows."
These are the root and derivative [afflictions], totaling twenty-six *anuśayas*. In this treatise, they are categorized as the three subtle and four coarse [afflictions].

Such afflictions are so numerous that they cannot be calculated; hence they are said to be "as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. If one follows what is taught in this treatise, they exceed the number of grains of sand in the Ganges;
in reality, they are immeasurable. How could they merely amount to the sands of a river? If there were a fixed number, it would likely not be of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Regarding what is called "difference": that [refers to] afflictions, while this is named merit; that is defiled while this is pure;

that is empty while this exists. Regarding "separation": the essence of delusion is fundamentally empty and has nothing with which it can be associated. Therefore, the subsequent text states: "All afflictions and defiled dharmas are merely falsely existent;
their nature is inherently non-existent from the beginning, and they have never been associated with the Tathāgatagarbha."
Because it is thus. The "unsurpassed Dharma" refers to the meaning of the light of great wisdom and so forth; it is the Dharma realized by the Buddha, and is therefore called "unsurpassed.
All of these are virtues of the very nature (dharmatā); the virtues are entirely the nature itself, and they are never separated from one another.
Therefore, it is said they "follow one another.
△ Third, the detailed explanation according to the chapters (in two parts): First, emptiness; second, non-emptiness. First, emptiness (in three parts): First, a brief clarification.
Second, the detailed explanation; third, the summary. First, the brief clarification:
that which is called "emptiness" is because, from the very beginning, it is not associated with any defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*).
This means it is free from the differentiated characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena, as it is devoid of false mental conceptions (*vitatha-citta-manasikāra*).

[Commentary] From "from the fundamental" (*ben*) downwards, this section generally enumerates both the subject and object of discrimination, showing that they are entirely non-corresponding. "That is to say, apart from" (*li*) below refers to the grasped characteristic (*grāhyalakṣaṇa*).

"Because there is no" (*yi wu*) below refers to the grasping view (*grāhakadṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, because false objects arise from deluded thoughts, it is explained to reveal their emptiness and non-existence.
This is truly because the inverted mind and false objects exist only in terms of conventional sentiment but lack reality; whereas the virtue of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is [the ultimate] principle.
Because sentient beings do not exist, they are not associated [with it].
[Commentary: "The distinction between subject and object" refers to mind and its objects (*viṣaya*). Although defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*) are many, they are all subsumed within these two;

therefore, while the treatise says "all," the commentary specifies "subject and object. As for the phrase "being apart from," etc., the preceding section provided a general explanation, whereas this [section] specifically...
This clarifies the distinction between the mind and its objects. That which is the "apprehended aspect" (grāhyalakṣaṇa) refers to the "aspect of the objective realm" (viṣayalakṣaṇa).

Within this, there are differences such as form, odor, taste, and tangibility; hence it is called "differentiated. That which is the "apprehending vision" (grāhakadṛṣṭi) refers to the "aspect of cognition" (jñānalakṣaṇa), "succession" (saṃtati), and so forth.

Within this, there are distinctions such as seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing; these are collectively termed the "apprehender," which corresponds to the "separating consciousnesses" (pravṛttivijñāna) mentioned below. This is...
The preceding section was explained by means of the simultaneous dismissal of both mind and object. What follows below is explained by means of dismissing only the objective realm.

The first two lines merely state that the object is non-existent; this [passage] explains the reason why the object is non-existent. That is to say, all objective realms arise from mental conceptions.
Since mental conceptions are absent, from where could objects exist? Therefore, the previous text states: "All objective realms are merely..."
Distinctions exist based on deluded thought; if one is free from thought, then no objective realms exist at all.

Based on this, it is the aspect of the "seer" within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*). This is because its function of producing objects and grasping objects differs from that of wisdom (*jñāna*).

The passage beginning with "It is truly because... provides a general explanation of the meaning of the text. Regarding the phrase "existent in deluded sentiment but non-existent in ultimate truth": it exists within deluded sentiment, yet is non-existent in ultimate truth.

In the ultimate principle (li), there is nothing; it is like a flower in the sky, seen only because of the eye-disease of cataracts. That while it exists for the emotional mind (qing), it is non-existent in principle, can be understood by reversing the previous case.
As for "non-correspondence," this concludes the discussion of the delusive dharmas: since they do not exist within the ultimate principle, with what could they be said to correspond?
This, rather, corresponds to the emotional mind, because they arise from deluded thought; once thought is transcended, all dharmas cease to exist.
△ Second, the detailed explanation.

One should know that the self-nature of *tathatā* (suchness) is not characterized by existence, nor is it characterized by non-existence; it is not characterized by neither existence nor non-existence, nor is it characterized by both existence and non-existence.
It is not characterized by unity, nor is it characterized by difference; it is not characterized by neither unity nor difference, nor is it characterized by both. It is not...
The characteristics of identity and difference. [Commentary:
"Neither existent" clarifies that the True [Nature] is free from delusory existence. Those who are confused say: "If it is not existent, then it must be non-existent.
Therefore, it is explained as "not non-existent. When those who are confused hear the aforementioned "neither existent nor non-existent," they take it to mean a double negation (ubhayābhāva).
"This is the dharma of *tathatā* (suchness). The commentary explains: "I do not say 'it exists' as you claim; I say it is 'not existent.

This does not mean that the essence of the dharma is non-existent. Nor do I say 'it is nonexistent' as you claim; I say it is 'not nonexistent. This does not mean that the essence of the dharma is nonexistent.

Therefore, it also negates the 'double negation' (*ubhayābhāva*). A deluded person says: "I previously established existence and established non-existence, while you establish double negation. Double negation..."
If [the self] exists, then existence and non-existence are simultaneously lost. Now, since both are negated, existence and non-existence are once again established.

The commentary states: "The 'self' is not your 'double negation'; therefore, it is called 'non-non'. It does not grant that both are affirmed; how then can you further cling to their mutual characteristics?"

[Commentary] First, this explains the four propositions of existence and non-existence. "To be free from false existence" means that because one clings to a person as existing, it is said to be "not existent.
If there were nothing to which one clings, with reference to what would one say "not"? The term "false existence" encompasses all phenomenal marks (*nimitta*).

Regarding the phrase "the deluded," those below [who do not understand] fail to comprehend the words "not existent"; they mistake the negation of emotional clinging for the existence of a dharma-substance (*dharmatā*).

"No. This current explanation states: The reason for the previous negation was not to negate your attachment to existence; it certainly does not mean that this dharma is simply non-existence. Therefore, it is said to be "not non-existent.
As for the statement that the double negation is *tathatā* (suchness), it is because one assumes that *tathatā* is a dharma that is neither existent nor non-existent;
thus, the treatise refutes this by stating: "It is not the case that it is not the characteristic of existence," and so forth.
"Non-characteristic. In both phrases, the upper character "non-" (fēi) is the medicine that serves as the remedy;

the lower three characters, "not" (fēi) and so forth, are the illness to be remedied. The commentary states: "The 'lower' refers to my initial [position] that it is not what you establish as 'existent';
therefore, it is said to be 'not existent. It does not mean that True Suchness itself is non-existent. Next, it is also not what you establish as 'non-existent'; therefore..."
It is said that it is "not non-existent. This does not mean that True Suchness (tathatā) is "not non-existent. It is neither existent nor non-existent; both are negated.
Therefore, it is also not the case that one removes this dual negation. This can be understood by examining it closely.

Regarding the four instances of the word "deemed" (wei) used here, in the first two, the former is the "deeming" of conceptualization, while the latter is the "deeming" of verbal expression. As for the latter...

"Second, to provide an analogy: regarding the passage 'The deluded person,' etc., the intended meaning is as follows: I first established existence, then I established non-existence; you, however, established the negation of both (the double negation).
If the characteristic of this double negation were to persist, then existence and non-existence would necessarily be lost.

When I established the third position—the double negation—you again negated that double negation. Now that the double negation has been negated, I shall re-establish existence and non-existence. 'Re-establishing' refers to clinging."
The first phrase is "existence" (you), and the second phrase is "non-existence" (wu). These two standing side-by-side constitute True Suchness (*tathatā*). The commentary below states:

the intention is that if I were to speak only of "neither existence nor non-existence" (referring to the third phrase of the treatise, which should be stated as "neither having the characteristic of existence nor having the characteristic of non-existence"), you would then cling to both characteristics of existence and non-existence simultaneously.
I now do not follow you by means of this "double negation" (also referring to the third phrase of the treatise, such as "neither [is it] not-...").

If there were a characteristic that is neither "not non-characteristic," then it would be neither a characteristic nor a non-characteristic; at once, both are negated. Since both negations are themselves negated, even the dual affirmation is not permitted.
Why, then, do you remain deluded and inverted, returning again to the dual grasping of both characteristics—existence and non-existence?

Therefore, the present treatise refutes this by stating: "It is neither the characteristic of existence nor the characteristic of non-existence. As for "the dual characteristic," this refers to existence and non-existence occurring simultaneously.
...and so forth. Now, all of these are likewise refuted. [Commentary:

"Identity" and "difference" may be understood by reference to the preceding four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). Although there are many ways of grasping [these concepts], they are all subsumed within these two sets of four propositions.
Thus, the *Śata-śāstra* states: "Furthermore, in order to demonstrate that all phenomena grasped by the world..."
It is not real. Furthermore, it reveals that the tenets held by non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) differ [from our own]. Thus, the verse says: "Existence, non-existence, both, and neither;
unity, plurality, and the sublation of both. These are assigned respectively. The wise understand these to be unreal.

That treatise extensively refutes the four schools of non-Buddhists in its sequential order; here, however, we address their successive conceptual attachments, which differs from the latter section of that treatise.
Refuting the assertions of the non-Buddhists. [Commentary] Two:

This explains the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) regarding identity and difference. Following the previous [section], the former was based on existence and non-existence, while this is based on identity and difference;

thus, the two types of grasping differ. All other aspects are no different, and may be understood by correlating and explaining them according to the previous commentary. However, as for the grasping...
Below, the general summary encompasses the specific details. That is to say, the immeasurable and boundless grasping of sentient beings arises fundamentally from these two sets of four propositions.
Therefore, the "hundred negations" (*śata-apavāda*) are explained solely in reference to this; the meaning is seen in the preceding text.

Thus, the extensive section below cites examples, all of which are not real, being false conceptual attachments that do not accord with the true principle—identical to this [discussion of] existence and non-existence as one.
This refers to the four alternative propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). Regarding the differences in their respective attachments, each of the four persons clings to one proposition:
"existence" is the first proposition, which is what is to be eliminated; "non-existence" is the second proposition, which is what is to be eliminated;
"both" is the fourth proposition (that of both existence and non-existence), which is what is to be eliminated; and "neither" is the negation of existence.
It is not the "non-existent" category; this is what is excluded by the third category. "One is not one," and so forth—apply the examples accordingly.
As for applying them in successive order, they are arranged as four categories as above; however, these are merely applied to those [external] positions and are not compatible with this treatise.
Since they are all false attachments, it is said that they are "not true. Regarding the four schools of non-Buddhists: first, the Sāṃkhya non-Buddhist...
The Master [Sthiramati] says: To hold that the nature of existence and so forth is one with all phenomena would fall under the category of "existence. Therefore, he refutes it, saying:
This attachment is not true. Why is this? If blue and other colors were one with the nature of color, they should be identical in essence, just like the nature of color.
If the five kinds of pleasant sounds and so forth were one with the nature of sound, they should be identical in essence, just like the nature of sound.
The various faculties, such as the eye, are one with the nature of being a faculty; thus, like the nature of being a faculty, their essence should all be identical.

Consequently, each individual faculty should perceive all objects, and each individual object should correspond to all faculties. Furthermore, all phenomena are one with the nature of existence (*sattā*);
thus, like the nature of existence, their essence should all be identical. Second, the Vaiśeṣika non-Buddhists assert the category of existence (*sattā*).
If [a phenomenon] were not identical with its nature (*dharmatā*), it would fall under the category of non-existence; yet this too is not true. Why?

If colors such as blue were different from the nature of form (*rūpa-svabhāva*), they should—like sound and so forth—not be the objects of the eye’s range (i.e., its cognitive domain). The same would apply to sound and the rest.
Furthermore, if all phenomena were different from their own nature, their essence would be fundamentally non-existent, like a rabbit's horn. Thus it is refuted at length.
Third, the shameless non-Buddhists (nirhrīka-tīrthika) maintain that the universal nature (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) and those various phenomena are both identical and different.

This should be categorized under the position of "both existent and non-existent. Yet this too is not true. Why? If the universal nature and form (*rūpa*), etc., were identical, it would share the same fault as the Sāṃkhya school;
if they were different, it would be the same as the Vaiśeṣika school. These two types—identity and difference—[are mutually exclusive].
The nature (*svabhāva*) and its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are mutually contradictory; therefore, to claim that their substance (*tattva*) is identical is logically untenable.

That which is one would necessarily not be one, because it is identical with difference; just as with difference. That which is different would necessarily not be different, because it is identical with oneness; just as with oneness. This refutation is extended at length.
Fourth, the Ājīvika heretics maintain that the universal existence (*sattā*) and those various phenomena are neither identical nor different. [This position] must be neither existent nor...
The statement "it is not existent" is likewise not true. Why is this? Regarding your claim that it is neither identical nor different:
does this consist solely of negation (*paryudāsa*), or does it partially involve affirmation (*vidhi*)? If it were to partially involve affirmation, it would not be a double negation.

If it consisted solely of negation, there would be no conceptual adherence (*abhiniveśa*). To have both negation and affirmation is logically contradictory; to have neither negation nor affirmation is [incoherent]. As for the word...
This constitutes conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). This is refuted at length, up to the point where it is shown that such a world gives rise to four kinds of denial (*apavāda*):

namely, existence, non-existence, affirming both, and negating both. These correspond respectively to the conceptual proliferations of superimposition (*samāropa*), deprecation (*apavāda*), contradiction (*virodha*), and proliferation itself.
Therefore, what is grasped by the world is not real. From here below, there is a distinction; regarding the latter section, we shall now take only the former section of that treatise.
The preceding passage clarifies that what is grasped is not true; it does not include the latter section of that treatise nor the subsequent passage that clarifies the non-Buddhists.
Within this, there are two distinctions: first, this [text] concerns a single person’s successive stages, whereas that [treatise] concerns four distinct schools;
second, this is intended to reveal the self-nature of *tathatā* (suchness), whereas that is solely for the purpose of refuting external heterodoxies.
[The opponent] maintains: "Therefore, they are not the same.
△ Third, the general conclusion.
Even when speaking generally: based on all sentient beings, because they possess a deluded mind that discriminates from moment to moment, none [of these states] are...
It is appropriate; therefore, it is said to be empty. If one is separated from the deluded mind, there is truly nothing that can be made empty.

[Commentary] "Having delusion" refers to the false conceptualizations regarding the sands of phenomena (*dharmas*), which are difficult to traverse exhaustively; therefore, they are now subsumed collectively to demonstrate their lack of correspondence.
This follows the conclusion. "Separation from delusion" is the reverse conclusion: because there is no defilement in contrast to it, the True is described as being empty.
It is not that emptiness exists by virtue of the absence of a true essence. Furthermore, this passage may serve as an explanation to dispel doubt.

Those who harbor such doubt, upon hearing of the aforementioned "true emptiness," might negate the existence of a true essence as well as the *saṃkhyeya* merits. Therefore, this explanation is provided;
thus, hearing of emptiness is no different from hearing of non-emptiness.

[Commentary] "The false conceptualization of [phenomena as numerous as] the sands of the Ganges" indicates the multiplicity of false attachments. Since these arise from discursive thought, how could they accord with the truth of non-thought?
Therefore, they are incompatible. However, in this passage, the connection is made only in terms of the mind and not in terms of the objects.
Since all objective realms arise from the mind, if one speaks only of the absence of mind, one knows that there are no objects;

therefore, they are not mentioned in detail. "In contrast to what follows" means that the essence of reality-as-it-is is called "emptiness" because it is devoid of delusion, not because the true essence itself is non-existent and thus called empty.
"Furthermore, below" refers generally to this concluding passage as a whole. All...

This is the resolution of doubts. Fearing that upon hearing the previous statement that the self-nature of True Suchness (tathatā) is neither existent nor non-existent and so forth, one might conclude that it lacks any intrinsic substance or qualities of merit, thereby falling into the view of nihilism (uccheda-dṛṣṭi), he now explains with the words "even unto" and so on.
Hearing of "emptiness" means that the false appearances are truly non-existent; hearing of "non-emptiness" means that its self-nature and merits are pure from the very beginning.
△ Second, the Non-Empty (2). First, the direct explanation; second, the resolution of doubts. First, the direct explanation:

That which is called "non-empty" refers to that which has already manifested the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Because it is empty of delusion, it is the true mind (*tathatā-citta*), eternally constant and unchanging.
When it is fully replete with pure phenomena (*viśuddha-dharma*), it is termed "non-empty."
[Commentary: "The essence of the Dharma is without delusion" reiterates what preceded to manifest what follows. "True Mind" refers to its entire substance:
it is eternal (nitya), blissful (sukha), unchanging (avikāra), and self (ātman), because it is free from the suffering of transformation and is not bound by karma, being sovereign.
"Pure phenomena" refers to its pure qualities; it is not empty—this is the conclusion.
[Commentary] "Citing and manifesting" means citing the preceding [point] that the essence is empty and without delusion, thereby manifesting the non-empty dharmas discussed below.

"Taking the essence as the basis" means that the essence is the foundation; all subsequent meanings such as permanence and so forth are explained based upon this. "Permanence" (nitya) means it cannot be altered by the three time periods or the four marks of existence.
"Bliss" (sukha) means it cannot be harmed by the three types of suffering or the eight types of suffering. This is assigned to the term "constant" (dhruva).
Regarding "delighting in virtue": it is called "constant" because it is free from birth, old age, sickness, and death;

since these—birth, old age, and so forth—are precisely the phenomena of suffering, they are now correlated with the preceding [analysis] based on afflictions and karma, and thus assigned to the four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*). Now, based on the retribution of the fruit, they are assigned to old age and the rest.
As for "self" (*ātman*), it carries the meaning of sovereignty (*vaśitva*); this is in contrast to the lack of sovereignty inherent in that which is bound, as one is liberated from karma.
Because it is free from the fetters of conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*), it is called "immutable. To be immutable is to be detached from activity.
Since activity is karma, being unbound by karma constitutes mastery; therefore, it is called "Self" (*ātman*). "Pure" means that although it is amidst defilement, it remains undefiled.
The term "fulfillment" serves as a general conclusion, signifying that apart from these four virtues, there are further qualities exceeding the sands of the Ganges.
All merits are contained therein; that is to say, it refers to what is described below as "the light of great wisdom universally illuminating the dharma-realm," and so forth.
Furthermore, the single character "dharma" (法) also applies both to the aforementioned "purity" and the subsequent "fulfillment. Reflect upon this.
It may also be described as the phrase "eternal and unchanging," which vertically reveals that the true essence is infinite across the three periods of time;

this explains the previous point regarding the existence of its own substance. It may also be described as the phrase "the fulfillment of pure dharmas," which horizontally reveals that pure virtues are inexhaustible throughout the ten directions;
this manifests the previous point regarding the possession of untainted [dharmas] and so forth. Since its own substance is both eternal and unchanging, it further possesses the untainted.
If the essence of the Dharma were thus, how could it be empty? Therefore, it is concluded that it is not empty.
△ Second, resolving doubts:
Furthermore, there are no marks to be grasped, because this realm beyond thought can only be realized through personal verification.

[Commentary]: Those who are deluded, hearing that pure dharmas are not empty, claim they are identical to the "existence" of emotional attachments. Therefore, this explanation states: "there are no marks to be grasped.
This means that while they are not empty, they do not differ from emptiness. The phrase "because it is free from... below explains the reason why there are no marks.
If something were an object of false conceptualization, it would possess marks; however, since these are solely the domain of true wisdom, they are without marks.
This clearly shows that there is no characteristic of false attachment.
[Commentary] "Attachment to existence" refers to the various phenomena, such as form (*rūpa*), which are conceptually constructed (*parikalpita*); they exist within the sphere of deluded sentiment.
"That is to say" means that although the true essence of phenomena, their self-nature, and their qualities are not lacking in the slightest, yet they... [are absent].

A single characteristic can be apprehended; therefore, it is not different from emptiness. To explain the "characteristicless" (*animitta*): that which possesses characteristics is an object of deluded thought.

Now, since one is in correspondence solely with realized wisdom (*pramāṇa-jñāna*), one knows it to be characteristicless. Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Verses on Representation-only) says:
"When, regarding the object of cognition, the intellect perceives nothing at all, at that time one abides in representation-only, free from the two graspings."
Because of their characteristics.
△ Second, the gate of arising and ceasing (in two parts): first, explaining the mind-dharmas of arising and ceasing; second, clarifying the meaning indicated.
First, explaining the mind-dharmas of arising and ceasing.

[Commentary] Regarding the explanation of arising and ceasing: since it was stated in the "Section on Establishing the Meaning" that "this is the characteristic of the causes and conditions for the arising and ceasing of the mind, which can demonstrate the essence, characteristics, and functions of the Mahāyāna," this section now provides the correct interpretation of the characteristic of the causes and conditions for arising and ceasing.

△ Within this, there are two parts: first, the arising and ceasing of defilement and purity; second, the mutual support of defilement and purity. First, the arising and ceasing of defilement and purity.

[Commentary] Defiled phenomena and pure phenomena each have their own arising and ceasing. Regarding defiled phenomena, flowing with the current constitutes "arising," while reversing the current constitutes "ceasing."
Purity takes the reversal of the current as its arising and the following of the current as its cessation. Furthermore, when defiled phenomena arise, it is the time when pure phenomena cease;
when pure phenomena arise, it is the time when defiled phenomena cease. Moreover, the arising of defiled phenomena is an arising of manifestation, while their cessation is a cessation of exhaustion;
the arising of pure phenomena is an arising of revelation, while their cessation is a cessation of concealment. Although both are generally termed "arising and ceasing," the meanings [are distinct].
There is this distinction. Within the middle section, there are again two parts: first, a general indication based on the essence; second, a detailed explanation according to the meaning.
First, the general indication based on the essence (three points): 1. Indicating the essence; 2. Discerning the characteristics; 3. Establishing the name. First, indicating the essence.
Regarding "the arising and ceasing of the mind": it is based upon the *tathāgatagarbha* that there is a mind subject to arising and ceasing.
[Commentary] "The arising and ceasing of the mind" is the restatement of the heading. "Based upon the *tathāgatagarbha* there is arising and ceasing" indicates its essential nature (*tattva*).

This means that the mind which is itself non-arising and non-ceasing, due to the wind of ignorance (*avidyā*), moves and functions through arising and ceasing; therefore, it is called the "mind of arising and ceasing. It is based upon the...
The mind of arising and ceasing. Yet these two minds ultimately possess no dual substance; they are merely described as being mutually dependent in terms of two distinct meanings.
It is like water that is inherently motionless, which becomes moving water when blown by the wind. Although movement and stillness differ, the substance of the water is one.
Thus, it can be said that there is moving water because of the still water. One should know that within this context...
The principle is likewise; it should be reflected upon. That which is called the *tathāgatagarbha* is the intrinsically pure mind.
Because it is moved by the winds of ignorance to give rise to arising and ceasing, it is said that "based on the *tathāgatagarbha*, there is the mind of arising and ceasing.

Both the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* and the *Śrīmālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* state this in common. This reveals that the true mind undergoes arising and ceasing by following movement; it does not mean [that the true mind itself arises and ceases].
It cites the basis and grasps that which depends upon it; because there are two meanings within this gate, it can demonstrate the three greatnesses.
Therefore, it comprehensively subsumes the basis, which also enters into this gate.

[Commentary] The treatise states that the *tathāgatagarbha* possesses three meanings: the meaning of being concealed (*gūḍha*), the meaning of containing (*garbha*), and the meaning of giving birth (*prasava*).
Within the sense of being concealed, there are further two meanings. First, because the *Tathāgata* is concealed within it, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Here, the afflictions (*kleśa*) act as the concealer, and the *Tathāgata* is that which is concealed; the *Tathāgata* is concealed therein, thus it is the "concealment of the *Tathāgata*" (*tathāgatasya garbhaḥ*). This is based on...
This is the primary interpretation. It is like a chest containing gold; it is called a "gold chest" because the chest itself is not gold.
The *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* states: "All sentient beings are the Tathāgatagarbha. This teaching is fully present in both the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* and the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*.
Second, the Tathāgata remains hidden and does not manifest; this is called the Tathāgatagarbha. The Dharmakāya is without marks (*animitta*).

It cannot be known by wisdom; it is known by consciousness—how much less so by the eye’s seeing? This is the Tathāgata as the *tathāgatagarbha* (the treasury), interpreted according to the *karmadhāraya* compound.
As stated in the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*, within this sense of "containing and encompassing," there are three further meanings. First, the essence contains its function.
First, within the Dharmakāya, there exist the aspects of body, land, and function; this is the "saint containing the ordinary.
Second, all sentient beings are contained within the wisdom of the Tathāgata, as stated in the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*; this is the "cause containing the fruit.

This means that the qualities of the resultant stage are already subsumed within the causal stage; thus, the cause acts as a "treasury" because it contains the resultant Buddha. The former two [meanings] constitute the "supporting" (dhāraṇa).

The analysis of the compound [tathāgata-garbha]: the latter part is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound. Regarding "birth" (*janman*): the realization of truth in the ten stages is called the "womb" (*garbha*);

being able to produce the fruit of Buddhahood is called the "Tathāgata. This is also a *karmadhāraya* (appositional determinative) compound. In this treatise, among the six meanings, four of the six are excluded.
The others all apply universally.
[Commentary] The sub-commentary contains two parts. First, the direct explanation. Regarding the designation of the essence (*tattva*): it is said that there are both specific and universal aspects.

The specific aspect takes only the basis as the essence; this is the *tathāgatagarbha*. The universal aspect includes both the basis and that which depends upon it; this refers to the *tathāgatagarbha* together with the sentient beings.
Cessation and mind together constitute its essence, because all phenomena subject to arising and ceasing depend upon this. Here, both perspectives are integrated.

However, what follows clarifies that while arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-non-ceasing are described in terms of the relationship between the dependent and the basis, in reality there is no duality of essence.
There is only the principle of mutual dependence, but no substantial entity that depends. This is illustrated by the analogy "as the unmoving [water]" below;

the application to the Dharma is indicated by "it should be known" below. Regarding the phrase "one who contemplates," the intention is to effect a subtle integration so that the Dharma conforms to the analogy, such that both lack two distinct entities.
Specifically, the two lines concerning self-nature correspond to the analogy of unmoving water; the two lines concerning ignorance as the cause... [and so forth].
The phrase: "It is like wind blowing upon water to produce movement. Although arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-non-ceasing are distinct, the substance of the mind is non-dual.

This combines the analogy of the difference between movement and stillness while the substance of the water remains one. This single phrase is what is missing from the commentary; therefore, it is said to consist of two phrases.
It combines the analogy that based on still water there is moving water. In the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, he cites scriptural evidence, where the sutra says:
The Tathāgatagarbha is the cause of the cycle of suffering and pleasure, which ignorant ordinary beings are unable to realize. The Śrīmālādevī-sūtra states:
"It is by depending on the Tathāgatagarbha that there is birth and cessation; it is by depending on the Tathāgatagarbha that one realizes nirvāṇa.
World-Honored One, if there were no Tathāgatagarbha, one would be unable to feel weary of the suffering of saṃsāra or seek the bliss of nirvāṇa. This reveals—

Below, second: distinguishing to avoid confusion. For example, when it is said that waves exist in dependence upon water, the intent is to reveal that the water, which serves as the basis (*āśraya*), arises in its entirety to become the waves, which are the dependent (*āśrita*).
This is a vertical discourse (*ūrdhva-vicāra*) citing a single phenomenon; it is not a horizontal discourse (*tiryak-vicāra*) concerning two distinct phenomena.
Regarding "the supported and the supporter": these refer to the distinct essences of two dharmas. It is not as when a mother has a son, nor is it that the mother entirely becomes the son;
for the subject and object are distinct. Thus it says, "it is not meant. The following section provides the reason for this in two points.
Based on awakening, there is non-awakening. Based on the three great [aspects], there are appearance and function. The essence of awakening is that which is relied upon;
non-awakening, along with appearance and function, are all that rely [upon it]. In terms of their meaning, they are said to be mutually dependent. Yet, in reality, not a single dharma exists. Why?
Because from this truth that is the basis, the delusion that relies upon it arises and is established; thus, the two meanings of awakening and non-awakening come to exist.
Because there are two meanings, one uses the delusive dharmas of non-awakening to reveal the three great aspects within the meaning of awakening.
It is like water that, having arisen as waves, possesses both motion and moisture in their entirety;

because motion and moisture coexist, one can use motion to manifest moisture. If one says that a child exists depending on a mother, yet the mother is not contained within the child, it is for this reason.
Because it does not abide within [the son], it cannot manifest the mother through the son. Therefore, the following concludes the preceding meaning:
that which is the basis is the *tathāgatagarbha*.
△ Second, the clarification of characteristics:
namely, non-arising and non-ceasing in conjunction with arising and ceasing.
[Commentary]: As for "non-arising and non-ceasing conjoining with arising and ceasing," this refers to the aforementioned Tathāgatagarbha, the intrinsically pure mind.
Because activity and arising-and-ceasing are not separate from one another, they are said to be "in harmony.

This does not mean that there is a distinct arising-and-ceasing that comes to unite with True Suchness (tathatā). Rather, it means that the mind of arising-and-ceasing and the arising-and-ceasing of the mind are without two distinct characteristics.

[Commentary] Regarding the explanation of this meaning of "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), there are three parts. First, a brief explanation: "It does not mean that... and so forth. The intended meaning is as follows:
the arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*) that originates within the realm of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is itself in conjunction with the True Suchness within the realm of arising and ceasing.
It does not mean that there is a separate segment of arising and ceasing coming from elsewhere to conjoin with True Suchness. As for "the mind of arising and ceasing," it is entirely delusory.

This is the reality of the mind. That which is the arising and ceasing of the mind is entirely the delusion within that reality. This clarifies that the fundamental and the derivative mutually encompass one another;
it is not merely the formation of the "dependent" (upādāya) sense within the six types of grammatical compounds (*ṣaḍ-vibhakti*). As for "the absence of dual characteristics":
The mind is the substance; arising and ceasing are its characteristics. Since these two are reciprocally identical, there is no duality between them.
[Commentary] The non-arising and non-ceasing of the mind is established due to ignorance, while the mind of arising and ceasing arises from original enlightenment.

Yet they do not possess two distinct substances and are never separated from one another. Therefore, the text below states: "It is like the water of the great ocean, which moves and waves because of the wind."
The characteristics of water and the characteristics of wind are not mutually separated; this is explained at length.

Herein, the movement of water is the characteristic of wind, and the moisture of that movement is the characteristic of water. Because the entire body of the water moves, water is not separate from the characteristic of wind.
There is no movement that is not moist; thus, movement does not depart from the characteristic of water. The mind is also like this:
because the mind that neither arises nor perishes moves throughout its entire substance, the mind does not depart from the characteristic of arising and perishing.

Since the characteristic of arising and perishing is nothing other than spiritual discernment, arising and perishing do not depart from the characteristic of the mind. Such non-departure is called "harmony" (saṃghāta).

"Within the *ālayavijñāna*, the seven consciousnesses, and within ignorance"—this explanation and its application should be understood by reflecting upon it oneself. First, it resolves the objection that the *tathāgatagarbha* is not contained within the seven consciousnesses. In the question, the commentary (*śūtra*) states: "Since movement and stillness are not identical, it is said that water does not exist within the waves.
Applying this analogy to the Dharma, one should say: [The *tathāgatagarbha* is not within the seven consciousnesses, just as water is not within the waves.]
It is said that arising and ceasing are not identical to non-arising and non-ceasing; thus, the Tathāgatagarbha does not reside within the seven consciousnesses.

For what reason, then, did the previously cited scripture state that the Tathāgatagarbha does not reside within the ālayavijñāna? Even if one were to claim that movement and stillness are not different, [the distinction remains].
One should also say that the Tathāgatagarbha exists within the seven consciousnesses; it should not be said to exist within the ālaya-vijñāna.
The meaning of the answer is that only when the true and the false are conjoined is it called the ālaya; as for this ālaya, it has no self-substance whatsoever.

Furthermore, speaking in terms of general principles, both the True and the False dharmas are contained therein. Consequently, the *ālaya-vijñāna* serves as the totality, while the True and the False serve as its particulars.
It would only be logical to say that [the movement] exists within the totality; it would not be logical to say it exists within the particulars.

Now, since movement and stillness have been distinguished, this renders the status of the *ālaya* as a totality untenable, such that there would be no locus for it to exist. Therefore, it is said that it does not reside in the *ālaya*.

In the commentary (*śūtra*), the two phrases concerning *ālaya* provide the reason; they also serve to resolve the objection that [the consciousness] resides within the *ālaya*. Now, with these three phrases, the difficulty is directly addressed.
That is to say, the direct explanation does not concern the doubt regarding its residence within the *ālaya*. If it were combined [with the *ālaya*], one should not say it resides elsewhere;
if it were separate, one should naturally say it does not reside within the totality (*samudāya*). [The text continues: "Question: Regarding 'within the *ālaya*'... and so forth.
Next, regarding the passage stating that the ālayavijñāna pervades [both states] but exists only within the gate of arising-and-ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*): the intent of the question is as follows.

Since the ālaya now pervades both movement and stillness, it should also exist within the gate of true suchness (*tathatā-mukha*). Why, then, does it exist exclusively within the gate of arising-and-ceasing? In the answer, first the reason why it exists only within the gate of arising-and-ceasing is explained;
finally, it is concluded that one should understand by analogy that it does not exist within the gate of true suchness.
This means that when the ālayavijñāna is said to pervade both movement and stillness within the process of arising and ceasing, it is because stillness gives rise to movement to constitute movement;
there is no separate essence of movement apart from stillness. Since they are not mutually separated, stillness likewise follows movement within this gate.
"Regarding 'not merely [the case of] equality,' etc.: it is not only that movement and stillness are both included herein; even if there were only stillness, it would also be included here.
If even non-movement remains within the category of movement, how much more so when movement and stillness are combined? Why is this? [The text] interrogates and explains the reason:
because apart from the *tathāgatagarbha*, there is no separate essence of arising and ceasing. 'One should reflect accordingly' concludes by instructing one to apply this principle."
For example, one should know with certainty that [the ālayavijñāna] does not reside within the gate of *tathatā*.

Although the *ālaya* possesses the quality of stillness, it does not reside within the gate of *tathatā* because this stillness is a stillness that follows movement; it is not the same as the stillness of non-arising found in the gate of *tathatā*.

While the substance of stillness is the same, the meaning of stillness differs. Furthermore, since the *ālaya* involves the coexistence of movement and stillness, [it cannot be equated with the gate of *tathatā*].

Therefore, it does not reside within the gate of *tathatā* (suchness), for that gate is exclusively quiescent. The sub-commentary (*shu*) omits this meaning and merely states, "Consider according to the principle. [Sub-commentary:

Furthermore, if they were one, then at the time when the characteristics of the consciousness of arising and ceasing are extinguished, the true mind would also have to be extinguished; thus, one would fall into [the error of nihilism].

To eliminate these faults: if they were different, then at the time the wind of ignorance stirs and perfumes [the mind], the essence of the tranquil mind would not follow conditions, and thus it would fall into the error of eternalism.
To avoid these two extremes, they are neither identical nor different. Furthermore, if they were identical, there would be no conjunction;
if they were different, there would likewise be no conjunction. Because they are neither identical nor different, conjunction is possible. As it is said:
The Sūtra says: "For example, a lump of clay and its subtle particles are neither different nor not different. It is the same with golden ornaments.
If the lump of clay were different from its subtle particles, it would not be composed of them; yet in reality it is so composed. Therefore, they are not different.

If they were not different, there would be no distinction between the lump of clay and its subtle particles. It is thus with the evolving consciousnesses and the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*)."

If the true nature (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*) were different from consciousness, the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) would not be its cause. If they were not different, then when the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) cease, the storehouse consciousness should also cease;
yet its own true nature does not actually cease. Therefore, it is not the true nature that ceases, but rather the karmic aspect (*karma-lakṣaṇa*) that ceases.

The explanation states: herein, "true nature" refers to the Tathāgatagarbha; "evolving consciousnesses" refers to the seven consciousnesses; and "storehouse consciousness" refers to the *ālayavijñāna*.
This is the *ālaya*.
[Commentary] Furthermore, below, there are two parts that together explain the two meanings. First, the refutation of identity and difference:

there are students of the schools of Characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and Non-characteristics (*alaksana*) who have lost their way; among these two, each incurs one fault. To distance oneself from such errors, it was previously said:
Based on the *tathāgatagarbha*, there arises the mind of birth and cessation. Later it says: "Because ignorance ceases, the nature of wisdom is not destroyed.

Furthermore, [the text] below has three parts: first, revealing their harmony; second, [revealing their] union; third, [revealing their] integration. First, the formal explanation: regarding the phrase "there is no integration," etc., if there were one, there would be no two.

Because if they were different, each would be separate. For example, as a verse in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* says: "If the defiled phenomenon and the defiler were one, how could a single phenomenon be joined?
If the defiled phenomenon and the defiler were different, how could different phenomena be joined? This establishes the meaning of conjunction through neither being identical nor being different.
As the Sūtra says below... Second, citing evidence. Third, first, the dual presentation of two metaphors, namely from the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*...
[This is] the *gāthā*. "If [it were] mud below" (line two): this explains "dust-mud" (*rajas-paṅka*) individually. "Not produced by that" means it is not produced by those atoms (*paramāṇu*).
"There should be no distinction" means that before the dust has been mixed with water, it should already be called a lump of mud; once it has become a lump of mud, it should be called atoms.
Thus, [the following three lines] apply the analogy to the Dharma in general. "The storehouse consciousness is not the cause" means it is not [the cause].
No; it does not exist. It is the cause; it is the true aspect (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*).

If they were established as distinct, then the store-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) would not be produced by the true aspect, just as the aforementioned lump of clay is not produced by atoms. How then can it be said that "the mind of birth and death arises based on the Tathāgatagarbha"?
For the store-consciousness would also have to be subject to cessation, because there would be no sense of integration (*saṃyoga*). Therefore, it is said below: "To destroy integration..."

Regarding the characteristics of the *ālayavijñāna*: what is here called "extinction" refers merely to the absence of even a single portion of arising and ceasing; therefore, it is not that the true characteristic itself is extinguished.

As stated below: "The deluded mind is extinguished, and the *dharmakāya* manifests. Furthermore, it says: "The characteristics of the mind are extinguished along with it, but the wisdom of the mind is not extinguished.

Regarding the phrase "the characteristic of karma is extinguished," this means that by citing the subtle, the coarse is subsumed. The commentary below provides three points explaining the intended meaning of the cited passage.
The text is easy to understand.
[Commentary: Now, this master of the treatise has synthesized the general meaning of the preceding and following passages of that *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* to establish this position;
therefore, he says it is "neither identical nor different."
[Commentary] From "Now, this... below, the three [sections] collectively conclude the formation [of the argument], which may be understood.
△ Third, the establishment of the name:
it is named *ālayavijñāna*.
[Commentary]: These two meanings—arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-non-ceasing—are one when integrated, yet distinct when analyzed.
The mind that perceives these two meanings as non-dual is called the *ālaya-vijñāna*. It is also referred to as *ālaya*; this is merely a difference in the dialects of the Sanskrit language.
The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of the Liang dynasty translated the name according to its meaning as "the consciousness that does not perish" (*wumoshishi*). In the present day...

Master Xuanzang translates *ālaya* according to its meaning as the "storehouse consciousness" (*cangshi*). "Storehouse" (*cang*) carries the sense of "storing away" (*she-cang*), while "without perishing" (*wumou*) carries the sense of "not being lost" (*bushi*).
Thus, the meaning is identical though the names differ. That which is stored within is called the "storehouse," because all sentient beings grasp it as their self.
The reason for this is that the true mind does not abide in its own nature; following the influence of perfuming (*vāsanā*), it enters into combination, appearing as if it were unitary and permanent.
Therefore, because the ignorant take what is similar to be real and grasp it as being within themselves, it is subsumed under the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*);
for this reason, it is called "store" (*ālaya*). By virtue of this meaning, when the two kinds of views of self never arise again, the name *ālayavijñāna* is lost.
Furthermore, it can store its own essence among all phenomena, and it can also store all phenomena within its own essence. As the treatise says:
This refers to that which can conceal, that which is concealed, and that which is clung to as "I" by self-love; this is what is meant. This name is established based on its meaning.

[Commentary] From here below is the first section: the formal explanation of the intended meaning of the name. Regarding "arising and ceasing," etc., this is stated by reiterating the meanings from the preceding text;

thus it says, "it is precisely the meaning of the treatise. While the characteristics of these meanings are not uniform and must be distinguished individually, the essence of the mind does not differ. This is the title.

From "This below" onward, the two meanings (the non-dual essence of the two aspects) are combined to conclude this name. Alternatively, from "Or below," there are two parts: first, a detailed explanation of the names and characteristics;

second, distinguishing the name by contrasting it with two masters. Regarding "Chu-xia" (South and North): this refers to how, just as in this land [China], the sounds and pronunciations have undergone corruption and change in regions such as Wu, Chu, and Hua-xia, so too is it in the Five Indias of the Western Regions;
therefore, those [Western terms] are pointed out as being the same as these [Chinese ones]. Furthermore, it says "A... [referring to *Ārya*].
Regarding terms such as *dhana* (giving/wealth), these differ only in degree of gravity. "Without perishing" (*amuta*) corresponds directly to the Sanskrit original.
"Ālaya-vijñāna" (storehouse consciousness) is a translation based on the meaning of the second character; "ālaya" means "to store.

Because it is stored by and comprised within the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), it causes the continuity [of existence] to proceed without interruption from beginningless time; thus it is said that it "stores and conceals."
[Omission]. Therefore, although the names above the meanings differ slightly, the meanings below the names are in fact no different.
For example, *buddhadhātu* (Buddha-nature) is [rendered as] "awakening," "knowledge," or "clearly discerning," and so forth.

Second, regarding the interpretation of the meaning based on the Tripiṭaka, there are therein the meanings of "that which is grasped and stored" (*ālaya*), "that which is stored in" (*ālīyate*), and "that which stores" (*ālayati*). These shall be explained and analyzed in their respective order, namely:

The section "All that is inferior" provides the heading; the section "Therefore" provides the explanation. Regarding "appearing as one": when the phase of karmic activity first arises, it has not yet differentiated between the sovereign mind and its objects;
thus, while in reality it is not one, it appears as one. Regarding "appearing as permanent":

because its arising and ceasing are so subtle, it appears to be permanent, though it is not. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Furthermore, that which is your brilliant clarity, profound and unmoving, is called 'permanent.'"

Within the body, there is nothing that does not arise from seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. If it were truly essential and authentic, it could not tolerate the cultivation of delusion; therefore, it is said to be "quasi-eternal.
Those who are ignorant—namely, all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who lack the wisdom of non-dual emptiness—take what is quasi-real to be real.

This is precisely the cognitive aspect of the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). To hold fast to this with absolute certainty and refuse to change is the function of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, which are the minds capable of such grasping.
"Internal self" refers to the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*), for it is the grasping that arises within one's own body.
Since grasping at other bodies and all phenomena as having their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is also termed "self," this [text] specifies "internal" to distinguish it from those.

Below the term "view of self" (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), it is concluded that this constitutes the meaning of "storehouse" (*ālaya*). "Appropriation" (*upādāna*) means grasping; because it is grasped by the view of self, it is called a "storehouse."

"Appropriation" (*upādāna*) is precisely "concealment" (*ālaya*). It is so called because it serves as the basis from which the two kinds of self-view—the views of a person (*pudgala*) and of phenomena (*dharma*)—arise.
The state in which these never again arise is the eighth stage (*bhūmi*). According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, this consciousness has three states:

first, the state of being appropriated through the attachment of self-love (*ātmasneha-upādāna*), which pertains to all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas in their stages of training (*śaikṣa*), and Bodhisattvas prior to the seventh stage.
All give rise to the grasping of a self (*ātma-grāha*). They grasp the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as the self;
therefore, the eighth consciousness is named *ālaya*. This is translated here as "that which is clung to and stored. Second, the stage of the fruits of good and evil karma:

this includes all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), up to the final mind of the tenth bhūmi, as well as the stages of the non-learners (*aśaikṣa*) of the two vehicles. Through the causes of good and evil, they bring about neutral (*avyākṛta*) fruits; thus, the fruits differ.

Regarding the cause, it is called the *vipāka-vijñāna*. Third, the stage of continuous maintenance (*saṃtati-parigraha*) encompasses all stages, both cause and fruit, because the eighth consciousness maintains the seeds of all phenomena, preventing them from being lost;
therefore, it is named *ādāna*. *Ādāna* is translated as "maintenance" (*zhíchí*). What is now called the "stage of non-arising" refers to the eighth bhūmi and beyond.
This is the highest [state]. Because it is free from the grasping of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), it is no longer called *ālaya*; thus, it loses this name.

Furthermore, it is said to be "permanent" because, when entering meditative observation at lower stages, there are times when it does not temporarily arise. However, since the substance of consciousness (*vijñāna-tattva*) is not lost, it is said that the name is lost.
Moreover, regarding the meaning of "storing" below: it means that the substance of this consciousness is stored within the sense organs (*indriya*), the body (*deha*), and the seeds (*bīja*).

Within the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) and the sensory faculties and body (*indriya-śarīra*), these are the objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) of this consciousness, just as a pearl exists within its image, rather than a body existing within a room.
If one seeks the *ālaya-vijñāna*, it is found only within form and mind;
if one seeks the *maṇi* jewel, it is found only within the blue and yellow [colors]. Furthermore, because it can store all phenomena, it possesses the meaning of "store" (*ālaya*).
This refers to the fact that dharmas such as the faculties and the physical body are all stored within the substance of consciousness, like images within a pearl.
If one wishes to seek all dharmas, they are entirely contained within the *ālaya-vijñāna*; if one wishes to seek all images, they are entirely contained within the *maṇi* jewel.

However, based on the preceding principle, these function mutually as subject and object. As for the passage "The treatise says, below," it cites the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* to establish this proof; thus it may be understood.

This is the basis for the term "sentence. There are three [types]. The establishment based on meaning refers to the fact that, between two names, it does not rely on ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) but is established according to the name;
rather, it was established by Master Xuanzang according to the meaning.
