This can be understood from this point. Therefore, it says again "somewhat" (*shāo*). "Somewhat" means "a little. "Comprehensively" (*kuò*) means "to examine. This refers to examining the preceding and succeeding parts of the treatise as a whole to explain this meaning.
However, this also only covers the single section on arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*).
[Commentary: Why is this so? It is because True Suchness (tathatā) possesses two meanings: first, the meaning of immutability; second, the meaning of conforming to conditions.

Ignorance (avidyā) likewise possesses two meanings: first, the meaning of being without substantiality and thus being empty; second, the meaning of having functional utility that accomplishes phenomena. Within these [categories of] the true and the deluded...
Each, by virtue of the former meaning, constitutes the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*); each, by virtue of the latter meaning, constitutes this gate of Arising and Ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*).

This True Suchness that accords with conditions (*anuparivartin-tathatā*), as well as the ignorance that accomplishes phenomena (*kṛtya-sampādaka-avidyā*), each likewise possesses two meanings. First:

The meaning of "contradicting oneself and complying with others" has two aspects; the meaning of "contradicting others and complying with oneself" [is likewise]. Within ignorance (*avidyā*), the first—contradicting oneself and complying with others—also has two meanings:

second, it is able to obstruct the pure function of knowing names and meanings. Contradicting others and complying with oneself also has two meanings: first, it conceals true reality (*tattva*); second, it brings about the deluded mind. True...
As in the middle [section], there are two meanings for "contrary to others and conforming to oneself": first, to reveal one's own true virtue by contrasting it with false defilement;
second, to internally permeate ignorance so as to give rise to pure function. There are also two meanings for "contrary to oneself and conforming to others":
first, the meaning of concealing one's own true essence; second, the meaning of manifesting false phenomena. Within these four meanings each for the True and the False above, by means of...
Within ignorance, there is the sense of opposing and negating [enlightened] expression; within True Suchness (tathatā), there is the sense of overturning delusion to reveal virtue.

From these two meanings, original enlightenment (mūla-awakening) is obtained. Furthermore, from the sense of being able to know names and meanings within ignorance, and the sense of internal perfuming within True Suchness, initial enlightenment (ādi-awakening) is obtained. Moreover, from the sense of obscuring the true within ignorance...
Furthermore, regarding the meaning of the hidden essence within True Suchness (*tathatā*), from these two meanings, there arises fundamental non-awakening (*mūla-abodhi*).

Moreover, due to the meaning of the formation of delusion within ignorance (*avidyā*) and the meaning of the manifestation of delusion within True Suchness, from these two meanings, there arises derivative non-awakening (*śākhā-pratyaya-abodhi*).
Within this gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-dvāra*), the true and the false are briefly opened into four meanings; extensively, they constitute eight.

Regarding the gates: if categorized by pairs of opposites that harmonize to form the characteristics of dependent origination, there are four gates, namely, the two types of awakening and the two types of non-awakening.
If the fundamental and the derivative are not separated, there are only two gates, namely, awakening and non-awakening.
If they are fused and subsumed as a whole, there is only one gate, namely, the gate of the single mind’s arising and ceasing.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "What are they? and below: there are two parts. The first explains the meaning by means of the full exposition of the three [categories]. First, the meaning is explained by way of the opening and closing of the True and the Delusory.
There are seven sections in the text. First, the opening of the True and the Delusory to form four meanings.

Now, both the True and the Delusory are spoken of in reliance upon the single *dharmadhātu-citta* (Dharma-realm mind). This is because this mind inherently possesses both essence (*tǐ*) and function (*yòng*). As for the essence that is itself the function...
Vastly empty and quiescent, it is the function of the very essence; thus, there is clear and lucid awareness.
Because one has been deluded since beginningless time, within this state of emptiness and quiescence, one stubbornly clings to the physical body and sensory objects;

and within the state of awareness, one is distracted by manifold discrimination and conceptualization. Therefore, Master Zhao said: "The Dharma-body is hidden within the shell of the physical form; true wisdom..."
It is hidden within the realm of conceptual thought (*ālambana-vicāra*). Yet its form is like an egg [unfolding from within]; its fundamental substance is empty.

This empty stillness of awareness has been immutable from the beginning. This truth of immutability has always conformed to conditions; this delusion of the empty substance has always manifested as phenomena.
It is not produced through artificial effort; it is simply so by the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). The body and mind of sentient beings are seen to be just like this now. Thus...
This meaning is established by way of these principles to clarify the significance of the defiled and pure dependent origination (*saṃkleśa-vyavadāna-pratītyasamutpāda*).

Now, the "One Mind" is not separately designated because it is subsumed within the character "True" (*zhen*), for there is no dualistic essence. As for "unchanging," it has never ceased to be empty and quiescent, nor has it ever ceased to be aware and cognizant.
Thus, the Treatise says: "That which is called the nature of the mind is neither born nor extinguished. It further says: "One..."

All methods of defilement are incompatible [with the nature of awakening]. Furthermore, it is said: "That which is called 'awakening' (bodhi) is the essence of mind free from thought, equal to the realm of empty space.
As for 'following conditions,' this refers to following defilement and flowing with the current to form the nine stages.

Thus the text says: 'Depending on the Tathāgatagarbha, there arises the mind of birth and death. Following purity and returning from the branches, one forms the four stages; thus it is said below: 'Awakening...'"
Knowing that a preceding thought has given rise to evil, one is able to restrain the subsequent thought so that it does not arise; this is what is meant by "the essence is empty.

This is because phenomena of the *parikalpita* (imagined) nature exist in the mind but lack objective reality. Thus, the Treatise states: "All dharmas exist only through the differentiation of deluded thoughts," and so forth.
Furthermore, as for phenomena of the *paratantra* (dependent) nature, their characteristics exist while their intrinsic nature is non-existent. Thus, the Treatise states: "Therefore..."

All phenomena are like images in a mirror; no substantial entity can be apprehended. As for the accomplishment of things: when it is the accomplishment of defiled things, it refers to the triple world of the environment and its inhabitants;
when it is the accomplishment of pure things, it refers to the causes and fruits of the three vehicles, such as the nine aspects and two bodies described below.

This is so. Herein, responding to conditions is like the dreaming; the manifestation of phenomena is like the dream-objects; their essence being empty is like the dream-objects being fundamentally void;
and their non-alteration is like the internal body being vividly present. From "This is truly" (*cizhen*) onwards, the second section binds these four meanings into two gates.

The first meaning refers to the unchanging nature within the True [Mind] and the emptiness of essence within the delusory [mind]. Based on these two meanings, it constitutes the Gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
When this gate subsumes the delusory, the essence of the delusory is empty; when it subsumes the True, the True does not change.

Thus, defilement and purity are equal, and there is a single characteristic that is without characteristic. Therefore, this gate exists. The latter meaning refers to following conditions within the True and the accomplishment of phenomena within the delusory. By means of...
These two meanings constitute the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*). When this gate encompasses the Real (*tathatā*), the Real follows conditions;

when it encompasses the delusory, the delusory constitutes phenomena. Thus, the various differentiated characteristics of defiled and pure dharmas are established. Therefore, there is this gate. This is explained in the following section.

Third: Opening up the aspect of arising and ceasing (shengmie) establishes four meanings. This is based on the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*), where the true and the false are contrasted;

by discussing them in terms of self and other, these four meanings are formed. Thus, that which in the true [aspect] opposes the other and accords with itself is precisely that which in the false [aspect] opposes itself and accords with the other.

That which in the true [aspect] opposes itself and accords with the other is precisely that which in the false [aspect] opposes the other and accords with itself. These are merely for the sake of the gate.

The phrasing differs, but the meaning is one and the same. The characteristics of the opposing and conforming modes of activity will be seen in the following text. Regarding "Ignorance" and below, there are four [sections].
Opening these four meanings results in eight meanings. First, the primary demonstration of the eight meanings; first, we shall clarify the four meanings within delusion.

Regarding "demonstrating the nature" (*prakṛti*) and so forth: this refers to the manifestation and revelation of the merit of true nature (*tathatā*) by means of counter-flowing and opposing defilement.
As it says below: "When non-awakening arises as thought and one perceives various objective realms, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
When the nature of the mind does not arise, this is the meaning of the radiance of great wisdom. Even if the mind were to move, it would possess delusions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."

Regarding the meaning of "defilement" (*rañjana*): when the nature of the mind is unmoving, there is the manifestation of the characteristics of all pure merits, numbering more than the sands of the Ganges.

Furthermore, it is said that the nature is fundamentally free from stinginess, and thus one practices in accordance with the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) and so forth. As for the phrase "knowing the meanings and so forth":
this refers to the time when the discriminative deluded mind accords with arising and ceasing; it belongs to ignorance and is termed the "function of defilement. If it accords with the Truth...
Thus, it is called the "pure function. Therefore, the subsequent passage states: "Because there is the deluded mind of non-awakening, one is able to know names and meanings;
for this reason, true awakening is taught. If one were apart from the mind of non-awakening, there would be no self-characteristic of true awakening to be taught.
It further states: "The defiled dharmas of ignorance truly possess no pure function; it is only because they are perfumed by True Suchness (tathatā) that [such a function appears]."
Thus, there is the function of obscuring purity. Regarding that which covers the truth: the principle of truth is equal, whereas the deluded mind is differentiated.

When the delusion of differentiation manifests, the truth of equality is immediately concealed. Therefore, it is said below: "The meaning of the defiled mind is termed the hindrance of affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*)."
Because it obstructs the fundamental wisdom of *tathatā* (suchness), the meaning of ignorance (*avidyā*) is termed "obstruction of wisdom.
Because it obstructs the spontaneous wisdom of worldly activity, it gives rise to the deluded mind; this is because the deluded mind is produced through the permeation of ignorance.
Therefore, the Treatise states: "Because there is the cause of defiled phenomena, namely ignorance (*avidyā*), it perfumes the *tathatā*.
Because of this perfuming, there arise the deluded mind and so forth. It further states: "The meaning of the perfuming of ignorance is twofold:
first, fundamental perfuming, because it can accomplish the sense-consciousness (*karmavijñāna*); second, the perfuming of views and craving that arises [from it]."

Because it can accomplish the meaning of the *vikaḷpa-vijñāna* (discriminative consciousness), the passage below clarifies the four meanings within True Suchness (*tathatā*). Regarding the manifestation of the virtues of the True [Suchness]:
by reversing the flow and overturning defilement, and by contrasting with deluded phenomena, these true virtues are revealed;

this refers to the "aspect of the purity of wisdom" within the "fundamental awakening that follows defilement" mentioned below. The text states: "That is to say, by relying on the power of the Dharma and through cultivation, one practices according to reality until fulfillment."

Because the skillful means are perfected, the characteristics of the synthetic consciousness are shattered and the characteristics of the continuous mind are extinguished, thereby manifesting the Dharma-body.
As for the arising of pure function because wisdom is pure and refined: ignorance is delusive and constantly gives rise to defiled function;

however, through the powerful permeation of the True, it causes that [ignorance] to flow back against the current and accord with the nature of True Suchness (Tathatā). Therefore, it is called "pure function. As stated below: "The permeation of its own essential nature."

As for "cultivation" (*vāsanā*): since beginningless time, it has possessed untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) and is fully endowed with inconceivable karma that constitutes the nature of the objective sphere.
Based on these two meanings, it constantly perfumes [the mind] and is able to cause sentient beings to undergo the suffering of birth and death.

They joyfully seek nirvāṇa. Furthermore, it is said: "Because the dharma of *tathatā* exists, it can permeate (*vāsanā*) ignorance, leading even to the attainment of nirvāṇa and the fulfillment of spontaneous activity (*anābhoga-karman*)," and so forth.
Regarding "the concealment of the true": this refers to what was previously explained—that *tathatā* follows conditions to become the *ālayavijñāna*.
Once it has become consciousness, it remains concealed within that consciousness. Because it is concealed therein, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*.
This has already been seen in the preceding text. Regarding "the manifestation of delusion": since the true essence is concealed, delusive appearances manifest;

this refers to what is called the "appearance of objective realms. As stated below: "Because one does not understand the dharma of True Suchness (tathatā), unawakened thought arises, and delusive objective realms manifest.
These two sections above and below correspond together to the four types of awakening. However, these awakenings and non-awakenings are merely presented in contrast to the true and the delusive.

Because the gates [of entry] differ, each possesses four meanings, thus opening them up to form eight. Now, as the true and the delusory are each divided into essence (*tī*) and function (*yòng*), they correspond in pairs;
consequently, there are only four. As in the four sections of the Commentary: the first two sections concern the pure portion (*śuddha-bhāga*) and its essence and function.
In the first section, the two are combined to accord with the essence and establish fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*). Next, from "Furthermore, by... onwards, the two are combined...

Following the application [of the principles], one achieves initial awakening (*abhisambodhi*). Subsequently, by means of the following two sections, one examines the essence and function of the defiled portion:

the first section combines the two [aspects] to accord with the essence, forming fundamental non-awakening; the next section, again by means of the following, combines the two to accord with the function, forming derivative non-awakening.
Thus, by discussing them in pairs, the defiled and the pure are established, each distinguished by its essence and function; therefore, they are combined.
The preceding eight sections constitute the four meanings. This section on "arising" follows below. Third, the conclusion points to the extensive and the abbreviated.

However, while the extensiveness of the eight gates has already reached its limit, the brevity of the four gates has not yet reached its limit, because there are subsequently further [combinations] of two and one.
Regarding the "four meanings," these refer to the aforementioned four categories of opposition and conformity, etc., rather than taking the four types of awakening mentioned here as the four.
This is because it serves to conclude and refer back to the preceding text. If one proceeds according to the subsequent section, the eight meanings are condensed into four gates.

As for the term "distinguishing characteristics" (*fenxiang*), it refers to the delimiting characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). This is because all pure conditions consist of delimiting characteristics of phenomena, which belong to the two [categories].
Awakening [discerns] the characteristics of all phenomena (dharmas) that constitute the boundaries of defiled conditions; these belong to the two types of non-awakening.
Furthermore, within this, the essence of pure dharmas belongs to original awakening (mūla-bodhi), while the function of pure dharmas belongs to initial awakening (ādi-bodhi).

The essence of defiled dharmas belongs to fundamental non-awakening (mūla-abodhi), and the characteristics of defiled dharmas belong to derivative non-awakening (śākhā-pratyaṅga-abodhi). Therefore, combining the preceding eight [categories], they form four.

Furthermore, if one takes the fundamental [nature] as primary, the six sections [of the text] group the four gates into two meanings. This means that initial awakening (*ādikṣaya-bodhi*) is the derivative;

it does not depart from the fundamental nature of original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*). Therefore, the subsequent text states: "Because initial awakening is identical to original awakening. It further says:
"In reality, there is no distinction of initial awakening, because they are equal and one in the same awakening. Thus, the non-awakening of the branches and the derivative is not [separate].

Because it is separate from fundamental non-awakening (*mūla-abodhi*), the subsequent text states: "One should know that ignorance (*avidyā*) can give rise to all defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*), for all defiled phenomena are the characteristics of non-awakening.
However, the two types of awakening—the fundamental and the initial—are merely a distinction between essence (*tattva*) and function (*vṛtti*);
the two types of non-awakening—the fundamental and the derivative—are merely a distinction between the coarse and the subtle. How could there be [non-awakening] apart from the essence?
As for "using": because there is the coarse apart from the subtle, there are only two.

If one merges the latter seven with the two meanings to form a single gate—namely, taking the fundamental [gate] to follow the one gate of arising-and-ceasing (shengmie men)—and thus unfolding it successively to form the meaning of eight gates, this is based on the fundamental to manifest the derivative.
Now, however, to condense these many meanings back into the one gate of arising-and-ceasing is precisely to subsume the derivative.
This is because they return to the source.

[Commentary: Furthermore, if one analyzes according to the "Gate of Distinguishing Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-vibhāga-mukha*) among the various consciousnesses, fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*) and fundamental non-enlightenment (*mūla-non-awakening*) reside within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), while the other two reside within the evolving phenomenal consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).
If one analyzes according to the "Gate of the Non-duality of Source and Branches" (*mūla-śākhā-advaya-mukha*), all are contained within the single fundamental consciousness.
Therefore, it is said that this consciousness has two meanings. [Commentary] Furthermore, from "If...

onwards, there are two points concerning the delimitation of the various consciousnesses, which serves as the conclusion. "The various consciousnesses" refers precisely to the two consciousnesses of the *Mūla-tantra*.
However, the delimitations and modes of activity (*ākāra*) of these two consciousnesses are each distinct and not identical; for the root consciousness (the *ālayavijñāna*) is...

The essence (*tattva*) and the phenomenal consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) belong to the functional aspect (*yong*). Now, since these two roots constitute the essence, they should be placed within the category of the essence.

Because the ālayavijñāna has continued in succession from beginningless time, possessing both awakening (*bodha*) and non-awakening (*abodha*), with their modes of activity (*ākāra*) following one another, therefore both of the two roots are contained therein.
Therefore, the subsequent text states: "Because the Tathāgatagarbha has no prior limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), the characteristic of ignorance (*avidyā*) likewise has no beginning.
As for the other two [categories], they exist only at the time of initial awakening (*ādikṣaya*). The six coarse [defilements] arise by depending on objects;

their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are coarse and superficial, and thus they properly belong to the coarse division. For this reason, these two are situated within the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*); this, then, subsumes the four."

"Awakening returns to the two consciousnesses. If we consider this in relation to the fundamental [consciousness], the phenomenal consciousness (*vṛtti-vijñāna*) is subsumed within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), because essence and function are non-dual, like waves and water. Therefore, these four meanings do not depart from the fundamental consciousness.

This is identical to what was previously stated regarding the gate of arising and ceasing; however, the former was explained in terms of gates, while the present discussion is in terms of consciousness. Thus, it says "below" to conclude.
Extended from this, they become eight; subsumed, they become two. Both meanings arise from within a single consciousness;
therefore, the present treatise states that this consciousness has two meanings.
[Commentary] Question: Within this context, a single consciousness possesses two meanings. How does this differ from the "one mind" having two gates mentioned above?

Answer: The aforementioned one mind contains these two meanings: namely, the meaning of not abiding in its own nature while following conditions (*anuparivartana*), and the meaning of the unchanging self-nature that transcends all marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
Here, however, we are dealing solely with the gate of following conditions; thus, regarding the defiled and pure aspects, as well as the principle and phenomena, there is no... [text continues].
The second [section] clarifies this consciousness (*vijñāna*). Thus, the meaning of the preceding "one mind" is broad, encompassing both gates;

whereas the meaning of this "one consciousness" is narrow, being restricted to a single gate. Question: What is the difference between the "original enlightenment" (*mūla-awakening*) herein and the "gate of suchness" (*tathatā-mukha*) mentioned above?
Answer: The gate of suchness is explained in terms of the essence that transcends all characteristics; original enlightenment is explained in terms of the qualities of its nature (*dharmatā-guṇa*).

That which refers to the meaning of the radiance of great wisdom and so forth is called the characteristic of original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*). "Original" (*mūla*) has the meaning of "nature" (*dhātu*); "enlightenment" (*awakening*) has the meaning of "wisdom" (*jñāna*).
Since these are all established by overturning delusive defilements to reveal [the true nature], they are subsumed within the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-dvāra*).
Because within the gate of True Suchness (tathatā), there is no sense of inversion or defilement and so forth, it differs from this [gate].

Therefore, both the essence and the characteristics of the two greats are termed original enlightenment (mūla-awakening); as they both reside within the gate of birth-and-death (utpāda-nirodha), they are able to possess the three greatnesses.
[Commentary] From "Question: Below this... onwards, there are three parts. First, regarding the question and answer that resolve objections to distinguish between two meanings:

first, the distinction between the two meanings. The intent of the question is clear. In the answer, first is the detailed analysis and direct response. First, the distinction between the two meanings within one mind:
namely, based on the dharma of one mind, there are two types of gates. Following conditions is the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*); remaining unchanging is *tathatā* (suchness).

From "Now, here below" onward, there are two sections that distinguish the two meanings of a single consciousness; this refers exclusively to the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*) and does not encompass the gate of suchness (*tathatā-mukha*).
Within this context, the purity of principle (*li-śuddhi*) is the meaning of awakening (*bodhi*); defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-vastu*) are the meaning of non-awakening (*abodhi*);

the equality of defilement and purity, etc., is the meaning of the aforementioned non-identity between arising and ceasing and non-arising/non-ceasing; and the absence of dual characteristics is the meaning of the aforementioned non-difference through their harmonious integration.

The details are as explained previously. "This then" [and so forth] below refers to the subsequent determination of the breadth and narrowness [of these categories], which may be understood accordingly. The section beginning with "Question: This below" consists of two parts that distinguish between the two types of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

The intent of the question is as follows: If they are said to be the same, then both should be designated by the single name "True Suchness," or else both should be designated by the single name "Original Enlightenment" (*mūla-awakening*).
Why, then, are their names established differently according to their sequence? If they are said to be different, on what basis is their distinction discussed?

In the response, regarding "the essence being devoid of characteristics," it is as stated previously: "The suchness of mind (*citta-tathatā*) is the very essence of the Dharma-gate of the Great Universal Characteristic of the Single Dharma-realm (*eka-dharmadhātu-mahā-sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-dharmamukha-svabhāva*)," up to "being free from the characteristics of verbal expression, names, mental objects, and so forth.

As for the phrase "that which is called 'Great' (*mahat*") and so on, this refers to the section on the "Greatness of Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-mahattva*) within the text. Below that, the reason is explained: namely, the "Original Nature" (*prakṛti*).
Virtue is itself awakening. Now, for the sake of brevity, it is given a name, called "original awakening" (benjue).

To manifest its characteristics through expansion, it is designated as "intrinsic virtue" (xing gongde). From this point downward, the text concludes by distinguishing what it differs from; namely, the name "original awakening."
The reason it is not explained within the gate of True Suchness (tathatā) but rather within the gate of arising and ceasing is that [the latter] is established by way of overturning delusion.
Therefore, what follows below cites the teachings shown to corroborate the preceding meaning.
It can encompass all dharmas and give rise to all dharmas. [Commentary:
In the previous two sections, it was stated that each [consciousness] "comprehensively encompasses" [all dharmas].

Here, the word "each" is not used because these two meanings are narrower than those two sections; therefore, only a single consciousness is clarified. Because it contains these two meanings, it encompasses everything. It is not...
It is said that each of these two meanings encompasses all things.

Furthermore, in the preceding text, it was stated only that they "encompass" and not that they "generate," because the *tathatā* gate lacks the capacity to generate. Within this consciousness, non-enlightenment perfumes the original enlightenment.
Thus, various defiled dharmas arise, causing one to circulate through birth and death. Because fundamental awakening (benjue) perfumes non-awakening, various pure dharmas arise;
this reverses the flow of the entanglements and brings about initial awakening (shijue). Based on these two meanings, all defiled and pure dharmas are universally produced;
therefore, it is said that [fundamental awakening] "is able to produce. This is extensively analyzed within the following four types of perfuming. It is not merely that they perfume one another...
All phenomena arise; moreover, having arisen, they do not depart from this mind, but are subsumed by it. Therefore, it is called "subsumption" (*saṃgraha*).
This is explained according to the two preceding gates, each subsuming its respective locus.

[Commentary] "Gathering sentient beings" (攝生) distinguishes its specific virtues. The sub-commentary (*shū*) divides this into three parts: first, confronting the preceding section to clarify each meaning;

second, restating the external objection and then correctly clarifying the narrow meaning with the words "By this... and below; third, simultaneously explaining the "gathering of dharmas" (攝法) with the words "Because it contains... and below.
Although all things are manifold, they do not transcend the categories of defilement and purity. Here, because there is the principle of awakening (*bodhi*), they are subsumed under purity;

because there is the principle of non-awakening (*abodhi*), they are subsumed under defilement. Therefore, it says "all dharmas. The phrase "not saying... below concludes by clarifying that these two gates are not identical.

It is only when the characteristics of defilement and purity are combined that they constitute "all" [dharmas]. Now, the principle of awakening subsumes purity but does not subsume defilement; as for the principle of non-awakening...
If it is said that the defiled is subsumed but the pure is not, then this would be acceptable if these two meanings together subsume everything;
however, it is unacceptable if each were to subsume everything individually. Within the context of one mind with its two gates, each gate already subsumes both the defiled and the pure on its own.

Because they differ in this way, the word "each" (*prati*) is not used. Furthermore, the two terms "above" and "below" distinguish themselves from the preceding text to explain the meaning of "arising.
First, the objection is restated. Then, starting with "By the True [Nature]," the explanation follows. Regarding the phrase "the sense of being able to produce does not exist," the text says:

"That which is called the nature of the mind is neither arising nor ceasing," and so forth. Starting with "By non-awakening," the explanation proceeds by means of the forward-flowing process to show how all defiled phenomena arise.

This refers to the three subtleties and six coarsenesses (*tri-sūkṣma-ṣaḍ-audārika*). Regarding the phrase "by means of fundamental awakening" (*mūla-bodhi*), this concerns the production of various pure dharmas through the reversal of the flow [of ignorance];

it refers to the four stages and two bodies (*catur-avasthā-dvi-kāya*), etc. Regarding the phrase "based on this," both [the preceding and following sections] are concluded. Regarding the phrase "the four below," this cites the source of the teaching. Question:

Since this section already contains the meaning of "arising," why was it not stated at the beginning of the two preceding sections? Answer: Because the preceding text dealt with birth-and-death (*saṃvarta-vivarta*).

It is designated as being co-extensive with the "True Suchness" (tathatā). Since it was not previously mentioned, it is clarified here alone; thus, one can say it is "produced. It is not merely a direct descent.
Third, by taking up the subsequent phrase, the meaning of inclusion is distinguished. This is like gold being able to form images, yet the images do not depart from the gold;
or water being able to produce waves, yet the waves do not depart from the water. This is precisely the meaning of the "container" (ālaya) within the Threefold Treasury (piṭaka).
*Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra-vyākhyā-pen-shuo-ji-hui-yue*, Fascicle Four,
Phonetic Glossary.
The sound "li" (驪) signifies separation; "li-long" (驪龍) refers to the black dragon.
The sound "yao" (耀) signifies manifestation; "guang-yao" (光耀) means radiance.
The sound "cang" (滄) signifies the blue-green; it refers to the sea.
Jù (pronounced jù): to squat; crouching and squatting.
Jiàn (pronounced jiàn): a wooden gong; a *khaṇḍa*.
Xuān (pronounced xuān): clamor; noisy bustle.
Guāi (乖): pronounced like "yin" and "guài"; it means to act contrary to or violate.
Sēn (森): pronounced like "shēng"; it denotes the appearance of many trees.
Píng (瓶): pronounced like "píng."
*Nì* (溺) means "to oppose" or "to submerge.
*Bō* (撥) means "to remove" or "to clear away. *Guì* (櫃) is pronounced like *kuì*;
it refers to a wooden chest.
"Tián" (田) refers to the sound of sweetness.
"Chóng" (蟲) refers to the sound of swarms. It describes the lush appearance of grasses and trees.
"Tǒng" (筩) is the same as "tǒng" (桶); the pronunciation is also the same. It refers to a bamboo tube.
"Cu" (醋) is pronounced "cuo" (措); it means sourness.
"Xian" (鹹) is the same as salt.
"Bi" (蔽) is pronounced "bi" (閉); it means to cover or conceal.
"Guàiyīn" (怪音) means strange and unusual; it denotes being startled by something extraordinary.
"Chǔ" (楚) is a state name pronounced with the third tone;
it is a corruption of the sound "hé" (禾). "Chuǎnmìu" (舛謬) means erroneous and mistaken.
*Yu* (pronounced *yù*) means "sphere" (*dhātu*), signifying a delimited boundary.
*Mi* (pronounced *miè*) means "to seek" (*mārga*).
*Maṇi* is translated here as "as one wishes"; it is the name for a jewel.
Guō (括): The pronunciation is guō. It means to examine; it means to encompass. Kèquè (穀):
The pronunciation is kèquè. It refers to the emptiness within a bird’s egg.
Qiān (慳): The pronunciation is qiān. It means to be stingy with what one possesses.

△ Second, the inquiry that enumerates the names.
What are the two? First, the meaning of awakening; second, the meaning of non-awakening.
[Commentary] "What" is the question. "First," and so on, is the enumeration.

△ Three: Explaining the Meaning Based on the Names (three parts). First, the meaning of awakening (*bodhi*). Second, the meaning of non-awakening (*abodhi*). Third, distinguishing their similarities and differences.
First, the meaning of awakening. [Commentary]:
This is because the arising and ceasing of the mind is elucidated in relation to pure dharmas.

[Commentary] Awakening is a pure dharma. Within it, there is both the beginning and the fundamental. When following the flow [of samsara], its essence (fundamental awakening) is concealed and its function (initial awakening) is suspended, which constitutes cessation.
When reversing the flow [toward nirvana], its essence is manifested and its function arises, which constitutes birth.

△ Section Two. First, a brief exposition of the two types of awakening—the fundamental and the initial. Second, an extensive clarification of the two types of awakening—the fundamental and the initial.

First, the brief exposition of the two types of awakening (II): first, fundamental awakening; second, initial awakening. First, fundamental awakening (II): 1. Revealing the essence of fundamental awakening;
2. Explaining the name of fundamental awakening. 1. Revealing the essence of fundamental awakening.
What is called the meaning of "awakening" (bodhi) refers to the essence of the mind being free from thought. This state of being free from thought is equal to the realm of empty space;

it is all-pervading and constitutes the single characteristic of the Dharma-realm. This is the Tathāgata’s equal Dharma-body. Based upon this Dharma-body, it is termed "original awakening" (mūla-bodhi).

[Commentary] The term "phrase" (*pada*) serves as a topical heading; "that which follows" refers to the explanation of its meaning. "Free from thought" (*vīta-kalpa*) means being free from deluded thoughts, thereby manifesting the absence of non-awakening (*abodha*).
As for "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*), it is not merely the absence of the darkness of non-awakening, but rather possesses the sense of the great light of wisdom and so forth.
Space has two meanings used as metaphors for fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*); hence the word "etc. First, it is all-pervasive...

The meaning of "pervasive" (vyāpti) means that it extends horizontally across the three periods of time and vertically through both the ordinary and the sagely; therefore, it is said to be "all-pervading.

Second, the meaning of "without differentiation" means that whether in bondage or free from obstructions, its nature is eternally non-dual; therefore, it is said that the *dharmadhātu* has a single characteristic, which is precisely the *dharmakāya*.
This is because one wishes to clarify the meaning of "awakening" (*bodhi*), as its characteristics become manifest upon emerging from bondage. As for the phrase "relying on these," since it is...
The awakening of the Dharma-body is not newly established by principle; therefore, it is called "original. The *Amala-vijñāna-śāstra* states:
"Stainless and unimpeded wisdom is termed the Dharma-body. The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* names the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom as the Dharma-body, and so forth—all of which share this same meaning.

[Commentary] The "Treatise" (lun) refers to the section following the "Mind" (xin). It is divided into three parts. First, the primary exposition of the essence of awakening (jue-ti). Second, the preliminary introduction. The Sub-commentary (shu) states: "As for 'detached from,' etc.:

the substance of the mind (xin-ti) is true reality, inherently and spontaneously lucid and discerning; whereas thought and conception (nian-xiang) are false and illusory, having been obscure and dull from the very beginning."
If the mind has thoughts, this is called obscurity and is termed non-awakening (*abodha*). Once the mind is free from thought, there is no longer obscurity;

there is only a single spiritual awareness (*jñāna*), which is termed awakening (*bodhi*). When the treatise speaks of the "essence being detached," one should know that it was originally non-existent.

Because it is fundamentally non-existent (*mūla-abhāva*), it is called "original enlightenment" (*mūla-awakening*, *mūla-bodhi*). The section beginning with "discarding the marks of thought" (*viveka-vikalpa-lakṣaṇa*) follows as the next explanation.

"Marks" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the characteristics of meaning; this corresponds to the two meanings explained extensively below. These two meanings are precisely the characteristics of original enlightenment, which is the "greatness of characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa-mahattva*).
"Equal" (*sama*) means being uniform; this is because the meaning of original enlightenment is equal to emptiness (*śūnyatā*). The commentary (*vyākhyā*) states: "Not only..."
The term "etc. (*ādi*) correctly explains the meaning of "equality" (*samatā*). Each individual meaning accords with the essence and is all-pervasive;
being neither different nor dual, they are all equal to empty space. This is the interpretation from the *Sūtra Commentary* (Sōgi) by Haidong, and is therefore cited here.

The two meanings are assigned as follows. Regarding the phrase "pervasively horizontal" (*hyangbyeon*): if one says "pervasive," it should refer to both ordinary beings and sages; if one says "penetrating," it should refer to...
Regarding the three periods of time (*trikāla*): what is distinct here is that the ordinary and the sage mutually interpenetrate throughout these three periods.

When one cites the three periods, within each individual period both the ordinary and the sage are necessarily present; since both the ordinary and the sage are *tathatā* (suchness), it is said that they "pervade horizontally across the three periods.

When one cites the ordinary and the sage, each individual ordinary being and sage necessarily possesses the three periods; since this is so from beginning to end, it is said that they "penetrate vertically through the three periods."

The terms "ordinary" and "sage" are intended to differ from conventional explanations; because they do not encompass the horizontal nor the vertical, these words were used to manifest that there is nothing to which they do not pervade.
Regarding the phrase "remaining in bondage," etc.: although this is explained vertically in terms of time, the phrasing seems incomplete, yet in principle it does indeed include everything.

This means that "remaining in bondage" necessarily refers to both sentient beings and their environments, while "emerging from obstacles" necessarily includes both the bodies and the lands; in both cases, there is no duality.
Furthermore, "treatise" (*lun*) is synonymous with "phrase" (*ju*). Second, the essence is identical to the body. The Tathāgata is the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*);

the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is the true body. Regarding the term "Tathāgata’s Dharma-body," it follows the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) analysis. This intends to clarify that the essence of the mind and the Dharma-body are non-dual;

therefore, it says "is identical to" (*ji shi*). Moreover, apart from the true there is no response; the response is itself the true. Therefore, it says "identical. Furthermore, as for the Tathāgata...
The Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is identical to the True Body (*satyakāya*); it is only because the Dharma is designated in relation to the person that it is called the "Tathāgata’s Dharma-body.
This is also a sense of identity (*tādātmya*). The three preceding [terms] are all *dharmadhāraya* (possessive) compounds. Thus, the word "identity" (*ji*) applies to these three functions.

However, the first one is primary, while the other two are secondary. As for "equality," it means that the mental states of the noble and the ordinary, as well as their environments, are non-dual and perfect.

"Because it is full. The Commentary states: "Wishing to clarify [the nature of] etc. means that, desiring to reveal the fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) while still enmeshed in afflictions (*saṃkleśa*), it cites the *dharmakāya* as having emerged from those entanglements.
This is an illustration of the cause by means of the fruit. Although their names differ as cause and fruit, their true essence is non-dual;
therefore, the Treatise says, "it is precisely this. Regarding the phrase "The Treatise relies on these etc.," it refers to relying on the essence [subsequently].
This is the establishment of the name. It means that the essence of the mind is quiescent and extinguished, without change or alteration.

Because it has been so from the very beginning and is worthy of being followed as a norm, it is called "Dharma" (the Law). Because this essence is a collection of supports, it is called "Kāya" (body).

Now, the name "Awakening" is established based on this essence in order to manifest the Dharmakāya; it is not unilaterally a state of rigid stillness, extinction, lack of cognition, or lack of activity.
It is awakening (*bodhi*). Furthermore, to reveal that this awakening is not a conditioned phenomenon subject to arising and ceasing, it is established by way of the *dharmakāya*.
Thus, within this single essence: because it is quiescent, it is called the *dharmakāya*; because it is illuminating, it is called original awakening (*mūlabodhi*).

What is termed "relying" (*āśraya*) merely carries the sense of "depending upon" or "referring to"; it is not like grass or trees, which depend on roots for their sprouts and possess a distinction between subject and object.
Furthermore, it is not the case that there is a distinction between the *tathāgatagarbha* as the basis for the arising and ceasing of the mind, or between the true and the false.
This is a single, true essence; however, when one speaks of the meaning of its luminous illumination from within this very essence, it is termed "original enlightenment" (*mūla-awakening*).

Regarding the phrase in the Commentary, "Since it is... and so forth: the principle of the *dharmakāya* is universally admitted in the teachings of the Three Vehicles to be neither born nor extinguished. This is...
Regarding the "primordially existing dharma": since this dharma is designated as "awakening" (bodhi), it can serve as the fundamental basis.

From the passage "lack of intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*) onwards, the text cites scriptural evidence for "original awakening" (*mūla-bodhi*), which is synonymous with the *dharmakāya*. In this school, there is no distinction between principle (*li*) and wisdom (*zhi*);

that is, wisdom that is identical to principle is called original awakening, and principle that is identical to wisdom is called the *dharmakāya*. It is like a jewel and its luminosity—they are non-dual.
There is no distinction. This is not like the provisional schools, which differentiate between the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
△ Second, explaining the name "original enlightenment" (*mūla-awakening*):

Why is this so? The meaning of original enlightenment is spoken of in contrast to the meaning of initial enlightenment (*ādi-awakening*). For initial enlightenment is identical to original enlightenment.

[Commentary]: "Why is this? asks for the justification of the name established. There are two intentions behind this inquiry: first, in the preceding opening chapter, it simply spoke of the meaning of "awakening" (*jue*);
why, then, in this concluding summary, is it named "original awakening" (*benjue*)?
Second, since it is already called "original awakening" here, why did the preceding text merely speak of "awakening"?
[Commentary] Regarding the two ways of censuring the intention: these are merely repeated formulations of an objection; in reality, there are not two. Therefore, the Original Commentary states:
"Whether one advances or retreats, an objection is established."
[Commentary]: Regarding "original enlightenment" (*benjue*): it is called "original" because it is contrasted with "initial" [enlightenment]. This answers the first point of inquiry.

Furthermore, because original enlightenment follows along with defilement to give rise to initial enlightenment, it is only in relation to this initial enlightenment that it is designated as "original enlightenment."

[Commentary] Part 1, Lower Section. First, there are two parts: the formal explanation and the clarification of the underlying intent. Regarding the first, the purpose of distinguishing the name "Original Enlightenment" (*mūla-awakening*) is as follows:
one should know that defiled phenomena and pure phenomena all exist in mutual dependence (*pratītya*). Here, for the time being, we shall consider this in relation to newly arisen [phenomena].

It is established as "original existence" (benyou). This is because initial awakening (shijue) arises anew through cultivation, whereas the nature of original awakening (benjue) has existed from the very beginning.

For this reason, the original is established in contrast to the initial. Furthermore, the following section provides an explanation based on a distinct meaning; previously, it was termed "original" in contrast to the "initial."
Now, "original" (ben) is designated in reference to the beginning of arising. When one traces back its initial awakening (shijue), it is that which is produced by the original.

Through internal causal perfuming and external reliance on the power of conditions, it first comes into being; thus it is called "initial. Because it arises from the original, it is called the "original."
If there is nothing produced, it cannot even be called the "original" (ben). It is like a woman who only receives the title of "mother" after she gives birth to a child. [Commentary:
"That which is identical to the original" refers to the time when one reaches the source of the mind; at that point, the beginning and the original are without two distinct characteristics.

Therefore, the preceding passage speaks only of "enlightenment" (jue) to answer the latter part of the question. Furthermore, this initial enlightenment (shijue) is accomplished by the original; it returns to accord with it.
The source of the mind is fused into a single essence;

only then is it called "initial awakening" (*ādikṣaya*). [Commentary] This refers to what follows below. Next, the reason why it is merely designated as "awakening" is explained: since the initial and the fundamental have already merged, there are no two distinct characteristics.
Because there are no two distinct characteristics, it is simply a single awakening. Therefore, the text below states: "Furthermore, there is no distinction between initial awakening."
Because the four marks are fundamentally equal and identical to one awakening. Furthermore, from here on, the explanation is given according to a specific meaning.

The preceding section distinguished the reason for "one awakening" (ekabodhi); this section, however, distinguishes the reason for "initial awakening" (ādikṣānti-bodhi). The intended meaning is that this initial awakening...
Because it relies on the original awakening (*mūla-awakening*), the initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) returns to be identical with that original; thus it is called "initial awakening" (*ādi-bodhi*).

Because one attains through this initial stage the awakening that is free from thought (*amanasikāra*), it is termed "true initial awakening. Although what preceded this was also called "initial awakening," because it had not yet abandoned thought, it was still termed "non-awakening" (*abodha*), or designated by such names as "resemblance" or "partial.
Now that thought has been exhausted and the initial phase has already been realized, [it is truly the initial awakening].

This is called initial awakening (*ādikṣaya-bodha*). It is known that one must wait until [the initial awakening] merges with the fundamental source of original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) to be termed ultimate awakening (*niṣṭhā-bodha*).
The "purity of wisdom" (*jñānaviśuddhi*) and other such characteristics are all likewise instances of initial awakening.

[Commentary] Question: If initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) were different from the fundamental [awakening], it would not constitute "initial" awakening; if initial awakening were identical to the fundamental, there would be no distinction of "initial awakening.
How, then, can one speak of the fundamental in contrast to the initial? Answer:

At present, within the gate of birth-and-death (*utpāda-nirodha-dvāra*), we speak of "initial awakening" by way of its conforming to defilement (*saṃkleśa-artha*), in contrast to the fundamental non-awakening. However, when actual initial awakening reaches the source of the mind, defilement...
When conditions are exhausted, the beginning and the fundamental are not distinct; this state of equality beyond words is subsumed within the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Therefore, the name "original enlightenment" (*mūla-awakening*) resides within the gate of birth-and-death (*utpāda-nirodha*), and does not belong to the gate of True Suchness.
[Commentary] Question: Next, the question-and-answer section resolves the objections. Regarding "the distinct [aspect] not constituting the initial awakening":

this is because the preceding text states that since this is what is accomplished by the fundamental [nature], it is only when it merges and becomes identical with the fundamental essence that it is called "initial awakening. Regarding "the identical [aspect] not constituting the initial awakening":

this is because the preceding text stated that upon reaching the source of the mind, the initial and the fundamental are non-dual, being a single mark of equality with nothing upon which to depend. Since this is so...

although there was no awakening in the past, there is now awakening for the first time. If one exhaustively investigates its essence, it is not different from the original;
