△ Next is initial enlightenment (*ādikṣaya*).

Regarding the meaning of initial enlightenment: because there is non-enlightenment based upon original enlightenment (*mūlapratyavekṣa*), initial enlightenment is said to exist based upon that non-enlightenment.
[Commentary] The phrase "initial awakening" (shijue) cites the name. "Based on the following" clarifies the origin of initial awakening.
"Based on fundamental awakening (benjue), there is non-awakening" means that this very essence of mind, following the conditions of ignorance (avidyā), gives rise to deluded thoughts.

"Based on non-awakening, there is initial awakening" means that due to the power of the internal permeation of fundamental awakening, there gradually arises a subtle awakening characterized by weariness with and seeking for [enlightenment]. Then...
Upon reaching ultimate perfection, it returns to identity with original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*). Therefore, the subsequent passage states:

"When original enlightenment follows defilement, the characteristic of the purity of wisdom arises"—this refers precisely to initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*). The meaning of this text clarifies that original enlightenment becomes non-enlightenment, non-enlightenment becomes initial enlightenment, and initial enlightenment becomes identical to original enlightenment.
Because it is identical to original enlightenment, there is no non-enlightenment; because there is no non-enlightenment...
Thus, there is no initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*). Because there is no initial enlightenment, there is no fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*).

Because there is no fundamental enlightenment, all is equal and equal—beyond words and transcending thought. Therefore, the fruit of Buddhahood is perfectly integrated and spontaneously free from dependence;

it does not even distinguish between the "initial" and the "fundamental," much less differentiate the three bodies (*trikāya*). It merely manifests according to the minds of sentient beings; thus, one speaks of the functions of the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*.

The following passage clarifies this. [Commentary] Regarding the initial section: first, the text provides a detailed explanation of the meaning of the words. As for the phrase "clarifying the arising," etc., this correctly explains *shijiao* (initial awakening).

Although the text places this later, by tracing back to its source, it is fundamentally due to *benjue* (original awakening). It is because of delusion regarding non-awakening that false thoughts (*wangnian*) arise; these false thoughts...

This is precisely non-awakening (*abodha*). As stated previously: "Based on the *tathāgatagarbha*, there is the mind of birth-and-death. And as stated later: "Because of awakening, there is delusion," and so forth.

This is like having a sleeping person based upon a person who is not sleeping; there is initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) based upon non-awakening, just as there is a person who awakens only in relation to a person who is asleep.
Regarding "the innate permeation of original awakening" (*mūla-bodhi-adhyātma-vāsana*), it is said below: "Because True Suchness exists..."

Because of the Dharma, it is able to permeate ignorance; by virtue of this permeation, it causes the deluded mind to grow weary of the suffering of birth and death and to joyfully seek nirvana and so forth.
Regarding "ultimately identical to the source," the text below states: "In reality, there is no difference in initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*);
they are originally equal, being one and the same awakening. Therefore, the subsequent passage cites evidence, namely: "it follows the defiled source."

The text states: "Awakening within the Innate. This means that when the Innate Awakening (benjue) is free from defilement and becomes initially pure, it is then termed Initial Awakening (shijue). In the passage below this, there are two points that collectively clarify the intent of the treatise:
first, it is like a good person becoming a sleeping person, a sleeping person becoming an awakened person, and an awakened person becoming a good person;

this demonstrates their mutual establishment through transformation. Second, by using the same [analogy] as below, it clarifies their mutual dissolution and cessation. As for the phrase "as with": [End of excerpt]
Because the awakened person is identical to the good person, there is no sleeping person. Because there is no sleeping person, there is no awakened person.
Because there is no awakened person, there is no good person. Because there is no good person, all is equal and equal, such that it cannot even be described.
Regarding "equality": because there is no beginning and they are fundamentally non-different, it is stated twice, which also carries two meanings.

First, initial awakening (*ādikṣānti*) is equal to original awakening (*mūlajñāna*), for the initial is itself the original; original awakening is equal to non-awakening (*avidyā*), for non-awakening is itself original awakening.
Second, the initial, the original, and non-awakening are ultimately without distinction, being inherently equal from the very beginning. Furthermore...

The distinction between them is itself equal. Furthermore, it is "beyond words" (*niṣprapañca*): if one wishes to speak of "initial awakening" (*ādikṣānti*), its essence is identical to that of original awakening;
if one wishes to speak of "original awakening," it has nothing with which to be contrasted; if one wishes to speak of "non-awakening," its essence is precisely awakening.

Because words cannot reach it, it is said to be "beyond words. Because it is beyond words, no characteristics can be apprehended, and the sphere of mental activity ceases; therefore, it is so described.
"Cutting off deliberation": this refers to the gate of merging into identity with True Suchness (*tathatā*). "Therefore, below" indicates the conclusion.

"Perfectly interfused" (*yuanrong*) means that both the defiled and pure aspects of awakening and non-awakening are perfectly subsumed and fused into a single essence; being pure, void, and free from entanglement, it is called "transcendent" (*xiaoran*).

Because one does not dwell or cling to either delusion, awakening, or the Middle Way, it is named "non-reliance" (*wujì*). How much more so when there are no distinctions among the three bodies (*trikāya*)?

Since the three bodies are established based on their primordial source (*ādi-mūla*), and that source is not itself established as a fixed entity, how could there be a distinction between the three bodies?

This passage distinguishes [the present teaching] from the provisional teachings (*neyārtha*) which definitively explain the differences among the three bodies, further dividing them into the distinction of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and the variations of the three types of permanence.
The subsequent section merely follows [this principle] to resolve doubts. Someone may say: "The following explains the inconceivable karma."
The marks [of the Buddha] are the mirror of the perfuming of conditions; they are the reward body (saṃbhogakāya) and the response body (nirmāṇakāya). Furthermore, it is said:

"When ignorance is exhausted, there is inconceivable karma that can manifest throughout the ten directions to benefit sentient beings. Is this not the function of the reward and transformation bodies? Why, then, do you say there are no three bodies? Therefore, this is explained:
it is only with respect to the differences in the perceptions of those with the capacity for enlightenment (*yogyatā*) that they are designated as the reward and transformation bodies. If...

Regarding the ocean of fruition, in reality there is no body to be spoken of. As for what is revealed in the subsequent text, it refers to the "Great Function" of True Suchness (*tathatā*). The text states:

"The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess only the body of the Dharma-body and the aspect of wisdom. In the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), there are no phenomena of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) that can be perceived.
It is only because they bring benefit to sentient beings according to their seeing and hearing that this is called 'function.'"

△ Second, a detailed explanation of the two types of awakening: original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) and initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*). (2) First, initial awakening; second, original awakening. Initial awakening (3):

First, a general presentation of the two awakenings of cause and fruit; second, a detailed explanation established by relying on the four phases (*catur-lakṣaṇa*); third, a concluding clarification that the initial is not different from the original.
[Commentary] Regarding "initial awakening" (*ādikṣaya-bodhi*): previously, the essence of initial awakening was briefly explained; now, its characteristics are explained in detail.
The subsequent statement that "the initial is not different from the fundamental" concludes that their characteristics are identical in essence.
△ First, a general presentation of the two types of awakening regarding cause and effect:
Furthermore, because one awakens to the source of the mind, it is called ultimate awakening; because one does not awaken to the source of the mind, it is not ultimate awakening.

[Commentary]: "The source of the mind" refers to the source of the defiled mind, which is its intrinsically pure nature (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*). Furthermore, it refers to the source of coarse characteristics, which is the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*).
"Ultimate" means that the path of initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*) is perfected and becomes identical with original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*); this occurs at the stage of Buddhahood.
That which is not ultimate does not comprehend its source, because the beginning and the end share the same fundamental nature. This refers to the stages from the *Vajra-samādhi* downwards.

[Commentary] "Defiled mind" refers to the six defiled minds; "inherently pure" refers to the *Tathāgatagarbha*. It is by means of these two—defilement and purity—that [the distinction is] established.
Because it is defiled, purity is said to be the source of defilement. Thus, the subsequent text states: "This mind has been intrinsically pure from the very beginning, yet there is ignorance;

being defiled by ignorance, there arises a defiled mind. As for its coarse aspects, these are the two aspects of the evolving [consciousness] and the manifesting [consciousness], as well as the six coarse [defilements].
The evolving and manifesting consciousnesses are also coarse within the subtle, and are thus categorized as coarse.

The characteristic of appearance (*lakṣaṇa*) and the characteristic of birth (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*) are identical to the characteristic of karma (*karma-lakṣaṇa*), which is the most subtle among the delusions.

Because the coarse arises from the subtle, the subtle is said to be the source of the coarse. Therefore, the subsequent text states: "The subtle within the coarse, and the coarse within the subtle—this is the realm of the Bodhisattvas."
The subtlest within the subtle is the realm of the Buddhas. Regarding the term "source of the mind" (*xinyuan*), there are two interpretations in the commentary (*shu*).

The first interpretation follows the *yishi* (dependent) analysis; the second interpretation allows for both the *yishi* and the *chizhiye* (appositional/possessive) analyses. Alternatively, it may be that the pure mind is itself the source.
This is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. This interpretation and the initial interpretation in the Commentary both refer to the ultimate limit of that which is realized.

The second interpretation in the Commentary refers to the ultimate limit of that which is severed. Thus, the two characters "mind-source" (*xinyuan*) apply to both the true and the deluded; the character "awakening" (*jue*) is precisely "initial awakening" (*shijue*).
Initial awakening reaches the stage of the "characteristic of arising" (*shengxiang*), at which point the characteristic of arising is fully severed. This is initial awakening.

As for the purity of nature (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*), its purity is sufficient for profound union. Thus the following passage states: "Awakening (*ādi-bodha*)—the mind of the purity of nature—first arises (the *utpatti-lakṣaṇa*).

The mind [in its state of] profound union has no initial characteristic (having severed it). Because one is far removed from subtle thoughts (those previously severed), one attains the vision of the mind-nature;

the mind is then eternally abiding (that which can unite). This is called ultimate awakening (*atyanta-bodha*). This refers to the path of initial awakening (*ādi-bodha-mārga*) after the subject and object have been unified.
"Perfect" (*yuan*) refers to the Path, which carries the meaning of "cause. Upon reaching this stage, the cause is fulfilled and the fruit is realized;

because it is fundamentally different from the beginningless [state of ignorance], it is called "Ultimate Enlightenment," which is the stage of Buddhahood (*buddhabhūmi*). Regarding the phrase "not understanding," etc., it means being separated by such factors as the marks of birth and so forth.
Regarding "the vajra-like and so forth": this refers to those from the state immediately following the vajra-like samādhi down to all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
This corresponds, in part, to what follows in the text concerning "similarity" and "non-awakening," and so on. These, then, are ultimately results;
they are not ultimately causes.
△ Second, the detailed explanation through the four characteristics.
[Commentary]: The first three characteristics explain the aforementioned non-perfect awakening; the final characteristic explains the aforementioned perfect awakening.

[Commentary] The first three are the characteristics of cessation (*nirodha*), change (*anyathātva*), and duration (*sthiti*). Having realized these three characteristics, one returns [to the source], which is called "not ultimate.

The last one is the characteristic of arising (*utpāda*). Because this single characteristic is exhausted, it is called "ultimate. This is based on the perspective of reversing the flow [of saṃsāra]; therefore, the characteristic of arising is placed at the end.
If based on the perspective of following the flow [of saṃsāra], then the characteristic of cessation would be at the end.
△ The text has two parts: first, the direct reliance on the four marks to reveal the four stages; second, the citation of sutras to establish that the source of the mind is non-thought.
First, the direct reliance on the four marks to reveal the four stages.

[Commentary] The meaning of this passage is as follows: by means of the coarse and subtle aspects of the four marks (*lakṣaṇa*), it provisionally reveals the four stages of the reversal of the flow [of consciousness], thereby clarifying the boundaries of initial enlightenment (*ādikṣaya*).

[Record] From here below, the Commentary provides a general summary of the intent, which is divided into seven parts. This is the first: a brief indication of the general significance. As for "coarse":
The characteristic of cessation; the subtle is the characteristic of arising. When viewed from the perspective of the intermediate stage, the coarse and the subtle mutually interpenetrate.

Regarding "relying on [the four types] to manifest": this means relying upon the four kinds of *rajas* (defilements) to clearly reveal the scope and limits of the power of initial awakening (*ādikṣaya-bodhi*).

This, then, is a differentiation of the depth of the subject that awakens based on the coarseness or subtlety of the object being awakened. As for the "four stages," these are the same as those in the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*).
These are the four: the stage of the worthy (śaikṣa), the stage of the noble (ārya), the stage of the fruit (phala), and the stage of the result. Alternatively, they may be expanded into five stages:

namely, the stage of equipment (sambhāra), the stage of application (prayoga), the stage of penetration (prativedha), the stage of cultivation (bhāvanā), and the ultimate stage (nisthā). Or, they may be condensed into three: namely, the stage of practice through faith (śraddhācaryā), the stage of pure mind (śuddhacitta), and the ultimate stage. In its most extensive form, there are fifty-two stages.
[Commentary: However, these four characteristics are posited as four by way of the coarse and subtle distinctions of the true mind as it follows along with perfuming;
they do not clarify the four characteristics in reference to a single moment of mind.

[Commentary] "However," and so forth. These two [sections] distinguish the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) in order to reveal that the True Mind, following the perfuming of ignorance, proceeds from the subtle to the coarse and from affliction (*kleśa*) to karma (*karman*).
It is upon these afflictions and karma that the four meanings are provisionally established; these are the four characteristics pertaining to a single lifetime (*ekakāla*).

This is not to be confused with [the four characteristics of] a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), for although those four characteristics are present within a single moment, they are not what is intended here.
[The text] distinguishes [them]; therefore, they are selected. [Commentary (Sū):
Now, they are briefly distinguished by means of two gates: first, a general explanation; second, a specific exposition. [Record (Jì):
From "Now" onwards, there are three parts. Third, the correct explanation of the original meaning, which has two sections. First, the heading and enumeration, as in the text.

[Commentary] Regarding the general [principle]: To trace the origin of the nature of mind, it is free from thought, neither arising nor ceasing. Yet, through ignorance (*avidyā*), one becomes deluded regarding the essence of one's own mind, contravening its quiescent nature.
This causes the stirring up of thoughts, giving rise to the four marks of birth and cessation.

Therefore, by the power of the wind of ignorance, it is able to cause the essence of the mind to undergo birth, abiding, change, and extinction, proceeding from the subtle to the coarse. As the Sūtra says: "Buddha-nature..."
It follows the stream and forms various flavors and so forth. Furthermore, a sutra states:
"This very dharmakāya, when tossed about by afflictions and wandering through birth and death, is called a sentient being. The following passage says: "The intrinsically pure mind..."
Regarding the passage beginning with "moved by the wind of ignorance," we shall now clarify the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) based on this meaning.

Since the quiescent is stirred into motion, there arises a distinction between the subtle and the manifest, as well as a difference between the prior and posterior limits. That which is most subtle at the prior limit is termed the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*);
continuing thus until that which is most coarse at the posterior limit is termed the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*). Therefore, the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra* states: "All that exists..."

Regarding phenomena (*dharma*): in relation to the prior limit, they are associated with the characteristic of arising; in relation to the posterior limit, they are associated with the characteristic of cessation;
and in relation to the intermediate limit, they are associated with the characteristics of abiding and change.

[Commentary] From "In total" below, there are two parts: first, a general summary; second, a detailed explanation. Within the first (the general summary), there are three sections. First, a general account of the arising of delusion, which has two parts. First, the actual account.

"Yuan" (originally) and "juqiong" (exhaustively investigating) are terms denoting the meaning of thorough inquiry. Specifically, they refer to investigating the source of these four characteristics, which are fundamentally produced by the deluded mind.

Alternatively, both characters may serve as introductory particles for the discourse. From the phrase "the nature of the mind" (*xìngxìng*) downward, the text describes the essence of the deluded mind.

This is the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā-mukha*). As stated in the preceding text: "That which is called the nature of the mind is neither born nor extinguished," and so forth, up to "being free from mental objects and signs.
Below this, it clarifies how delusion results in birth and extinction; this is the gate of Birth and Extinction (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*). As stated previously:
"Because of the *tathāgatagarbha*, there arise the mind subject to birth and death, and so forth. The passage beginning with "The sutra says... below consists of two parts:
first, citing scriptural evidence, which refers to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*; and second, another sutra, namely the *Dharmakāyānadhikānyūna-sūtra*. That text states:
"This very *dharmakāya* is enshrouded by boundless afflictions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and from time immemorial, it has conformed to the world."

Wandering like waves upon the current, coming and going through birth and death, they are called "sentient beings. This "lower-lower" [category] corresponds to the text within the "Inherently Pure Original Enlightenment Subjected to Defilement.

Now, for the second [point], it is applied to the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) as per the text. Regarding "Buddha-nature," thirdly, this cites a treatise to provide an explanation and establish the point.
That treatise states that every single conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) is without exception subject to transformation by the four characteristics, thereby serving as proof.
Now, this treatise discusses the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of a single period [of existence].

[The Commentary] states: "To explain them individually, according to the subsequent passage which distinguishes them by stage: the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) has one; the characteristic of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*) has four;
the characteristic of change (*anyathātva-lakṣaṇa*) has two; and the characteristic of cessation (*bhaṅga-lakṣaṇa*) has one."

[Commentary] Separate lower section. Two parts. Separate two. First: Brief correlation. Regarding the phrase "the subsequent sections concerning the stages," etc., this refers to correlating these four phases of awakening specifically with the text on the six underlying defilements;
from this, one will know how each of these four is separately divided into varying degrees of detail, as the subsequent text states:
"First is the defilement associated with attachment, which relies upon the liberation of the two vehicles and faith..."

"Appropriate detachment" refers to this very point. It is like the contemplative wisdom of the two vehicles, or that of bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds, who perceive the difference in thoughts and realize that thoughts lack characteristics such as difference and so forth. Furthermore, the text below states:
"Second is the defilement of continuous attachment; by relying on the stage of faith and practicing skillful means, one gradually abandons it and attains the stage of the pure mind."

Because they are ultimately detached. Up to the fifth [category], one is able to see the defilements dissociated from the mind; because one can detach from them by relying on the stage of mastery over the mind.

These four types of defilements above are what is meant here by "the Bodhisattva of the Dharma-body awakens to the application of mindfulness, realizing that mindfulness has no abiding characteristic," and so forth.
Furthermore, the text below states: "The sixth is the fundamental karma dissociated [from the mind]."
Regarding "defilement": because one relies on the Bodhisattva stages to their completion, one is able to enter the Tathāgata stage and thereby become free from it.

This is precisely what is meant here by the passage: "When the Bodhisattva stage is exhausted, skillful means are fulfilled; in a single thought-moment of correspondence, one awakens to the initial arising of the mind, yet the mind has no characteristic of an initial state," and so forth.
By comparing this with that [passage], the meaning of the distinct division of the four characteristics becomes fully evident. However, that [passage] is based on the perspective of purity.

The *Jizhi* (Commentary on Wisdom) reverses [the order] and discusses it solely from the perspective of the path of afflictions (*kleśa-mārga*); therefore, it does not mention the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*).

The present text, however, treats the beginning and end of awakening (*bodhi*) comprehensively; thus, it explains all four characteristics. According to the commentary by the Master of Haidong, the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*) has three aspects, which are the three subtle states (*san xi*).

The characteristic of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*) has four aspects, which are the four delusions of the seven consciousnesses. The characteristic of change (*anyathātva-lakṣaṇa*) has six aspects, which are the fundamental [delusions].
There are six afflictions. There are seven aspects of cessation, namely: three of the body and four of the mouth. However, what they teach is identical in its essential nature;

it is only in their classification and synthesis that there is a difference. Here, this commentary follows the distinctions made in the present treatise, as it is necessary to accord with our own school.
Do not abandon what is near to pursue what is distant.
[Commentary] "The single characteristic of arising" is called the characteristic of karma (*karmalakṣaṇa*). This means that due to ignorance (*avidyā*), the mind moves without awakening;
although there is arising and ceasing, the characteristics and the seeing have not yet been differentiated. By the power of ignorance, that pure mind is transformed, reaching this ultimate [state].
"Subtle" refers to the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*). It is profoundly deep and extremely subtle; only a Buddha can know it. As the subsequent text states:
"The consciousness that arises based on ignorance... [is such that] only a Buddha can know it. This refers to the first of the three subtleties (*tri-sūkṣma*) mentioned in the following section.
And the last of the six defilements, and the first of the five mental consciousnesses—these are all likewise subsumed under this characteristic of arising.

[Commentary] "Arising" follows. There are two parts: a broad explanation of four, the first of which is arising. Regarding the "characteristic of activity": the title is stated; "due to" below explains its characteristic.

"By means of ignorance" and below conclude [the section], indicating that this [ignorance] was previously absent; therefore, it is called the "characteristic of arising. "Profoundly deep" and below provide a specific eulogy.

"The following text" and below cite scriptural evidence, which refers to the passage concerning the four conditions for arising and ceasing. "That is, the following text" and below categorize [the characteristics] by analogy:
the first is the characteristic of karma; the latter is the fundamental karmic non-associated defilement. The first [of these] is the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*).
The phrase "these and so forth" below constitutes the general conclusion. Although they differ in that the gates through which they are explained vary, the essence of the Dharma (*dharmatā*) is one;

therefore, all are subsumed here. As for the difference in their gates: the nine characteristics clarify non-awakening (*abodhi*), while the five meanings and the six defilements clarify the causes and conditions of birth-and-death (*utpāda-vyaya*).
Specifically, the five meanings are the causes of birth, and the six defilements are the conditions of death.
Because their meanings differ, their names are distinct and the contexts in which they are taught are also separate; yet because their essence is the same, they are collectively subsumed.
The headings, explanations, conclusions, and subsumptions in all subsequent sections follow this pattern.
[Commentary] Regarding the four aspects of the abiding phase (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*): first is the aspect of transformation (*pariṇāma-lakṣaṇa*).

This means that by the power of ignorance (*avidyā*), one fails to realize that the preceding aspect of movement is itself non-moving, and thus it transforms into the faculty of seeing. Second is the aspect of manifestation (*pratibhāsa-lakṣaṇa*).

This means that by virtue of ignorance, based upon the aforementioned faculty of seeing, one fails to comprehend its lack of characteristics (*animitta*), whereby objects falsely manifest. These two, together with the first [aspect], all reside within the ālayavijñāna.
Within these stages, it belongs to the category of non-associated mental factors (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*). Third is the characteristic of cognition (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*):

this means that due to ignorance (*avidyā*), one is deluded regarding the objects manifested by one's own mind and falsely gives rise to the conceptualization of the characteristics of defilement and purity; therefore, it is called "cognition. Fourth is the characteristic of continuity (*saṃtati-lakṣaṇa*):
this means that due to ignorance, one fails to understand that what was previously conceptualized is empty and non-existent, and thus once again gives rise to...

"Mindfulness" and "continuity without interruption"—these two both belong to the stage of the *vikaḷpa-vastu-vijñāna* (discriminative consciousness of objects) and are associated with the mind (*citta*).
Here, ignorance merges with the preceding *janman-lakṣaṇa* (characteristic of birth), transforming that pure mind.

Up to this stage, the modes of activity (*ākāra*) remain subtle, and the attachment to dharmas (*dharma-grāha*) remains firmly established; this is termed the "characteristic of abiding. This corresponds to the latter two among the three subtleties discussed in the following text.
The first two among the six gross [defilements], the latter four among the five types of mind, and likewise the middle four among the six defiled [states]—
all these are equally subsumed within this stage.
[Commentary] "Abiding in the lower" refers to the second [level of] abiding. These two types [of consciousness] mentioned above are the three subtle [consciousnesses];
these three are non-associated mental factors that belong to the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*). "These two both abide in the same" refers to the subtle within the coarse;

this belongs to the phenomenal consciousness (*saviṣayavijñāna*). "Ignorance," etc., serves as the conclusion. Because it remains firm and unchanging, it is called "firmly abiding. The latter two are...

The transformational aspect (*pariṇāma-lakṣaṇa*), the manifesting aspect (*pratibhāsa-lakṣaṇa*), and the first two [aspects] are the cognitive aspect (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*) and the continuous aspect (*anubandha-lakṣaṇa*).

The latter four are the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), the manifesting consciousness (*pratibhāsa-vijñāna*), the cognitive consciousness (*jñāna-vijñāna*), and the continuous consciousness (*anubandha-vijñāna*).

The middle four are the defilement dissociated from the mind that is the perceiver, the defilement dissociated from the forms that are manifested, the defilement associated with discriminative cognition (*vikalpa-jñāna*), and the defilement associated with non-interruption (*asaṃucchinna*).
[Commentary: There are two aspects of the characteristic of differentiation: first, the characteristic of grasping; second, the characteristic of calculating names.

This refers to this ignorance (*avidyā*), which, being deluded regarding the aforementioned phenomena of defilement and purity, or opposition and compliance, further gives rise to greed, anger, the view of self and person, and craving; it grasps at characteristics and calculates names.

Attachment becomes increasingly deep. This occurs at the stage of the coarse division of the phenomenal consciousness (*saviṣaya-vijñāna*). Here, ignorance (*avidyā*) first merges with the characteristic of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*), transforming that pure mind and causing it to reach this state.
Its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is somewhat coarse; it mobilizes body and speech, causing them to perform karma. This is termed "differentiation" (*nānātva*).
It corresponds to the middle two of the six coarsenesses (*ṣaḍ-audārikatā*) mentioned below, as well as the first of the six defilements (*ṣaḍ-kleśa*).
Together with the last of the five mental consciousnesses (*manovijñāna*), these are all likewise subsumed under this category of "differentiation" (*viśeṣa*).

[Commentary] Regarding "differentiation" (*viśeṣa*) below: there are three types of differentiation. This refers to those that are the coarsest among the coarse; they belong to the *vastu-vijñāna* (phenomenal consciousness). As for "ignorance" (*avidyā*) and so forth:
delusive afflictions are grossly manifest, capable of giving rise to the distinctions of body and speech, such as greed, hatred, and the like; therefore, it is so named.

Regarding the two among the three distinct characteristics: these are grasping and calculating names. The first corresponds to the defilement of association with grasping (*saṃprayoga-kleśa*), because these two characteristics are combined into a single defilement.
"Mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*) refers to the consciousness of the mind (*manas*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the first, the characteristic of cessation, it is called the "characteristic of initiating karma. This refers to this ignorance (*avidyā*), which does not understand that good and evil karmas inevitably bring about the two retributions of suffering and pleasure;
therefore, in response to various conditions, it extensively creates and accumulates all karmas, and based on these karmas, one receives their fruits.
It extinguishes the preceding divergent mind and causes one to fall into the various realms of existence. By the power of ignorance, it turns that pure mind toward this subsequent limit;
its mode of activity is most coarse, reaching its ultimate extent and completing its final cycle—this is what is called the "characteristic of extinction.

This is precisely the fifth characteristic among the six coarse characteristics discussed in the following text. Because the fruit of retribution cannot be severed, the sixth characteristic is not considered here.

[This is] the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*). [Commentary: Regarding "Cessation" below, there are four points. "Cessation of the preceding divergent mind" means that when the afflictions reach their ultimate limit, they enter into the path of action (*karmapatha*).
This is like the characteristic of cessation in the Hīnayāna, which causes the present mind to cease and enter the past by means of ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth.
This refers to the process from the subtle to the manifest, wherein delusion arises and karma is created. Once the causes of karma are established, they inevitably summon future results.
When the affairs of a single lifetime are concluded, it is termed "complete exhaustion" (*parikṣaya*). Because they are completely exhausted, it is called the "characteristic of cessation.

This does not mean that afflictions will never arise again from this point forward. It is like a person planning an undertaking: when the conditions are prepared and the task is accomplished, it is called "complete exhaustion. Fifth, [the characteristic of] arising...

The characteristic of karma (*karmalakṣaṇa*). [This is] explained by means of the result (*phala*). Someone may ask: "Among the nine characteristics, the four characteristics such as birth (*jāti*) already subsume the first eight;
why then does it not subsume the suffering bound to karma (*karmabandha-duḥkha*)? Therefore, this is explained. The intended meaning is:

as for the cause (*hetu*), that which has not yet been produced is not produced, and that which has already been produced undergoes transformation and cessation; thus, there is the sense of being capable of abandonment (*prahātavya*). If, however, one reaches the stage of the resultant retribution (*vipākaphala*)...
When one is in the state of experiencing [retribution], it cannot be severed; it is like having already arrived in hell—one must necessarily undergo it.

Therefore, the Buddha taught that one should know suffering and sever the origin of suffering, rather than teaching the severance of suffering itself; this is the intended meaning. Thus, in the present text, it is set aside and not discussed.
The sixth [point] refers to the very last of the six coarse characteristics.
[Commentary: Therefore, the three realms and the four phases are but a single dreaming mind. All are due to the power of fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*). Thus, the Sūtra says:
"The stage of abiding ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) possesses the greatest power. One should understand this ignorance from the later sections of this treatise.
This refers to that which is able to give rise to all defiled phenomena.

[Commentary] "This below" refers to the fourth section, which summarizes what was previously stated. "The single dreaming mind" is the metaphor; it is like a certain person (who represents *tathatā*).
Suddenly falling asleep (ignorance), one dreams (the aspect of karma); seeing various things (the aspect of transformation), one gives rise to mental discrimination (the aspect of cognition).
From moment to moment, without interruption, they deeply give rise to grasping and attachment toward what is favorable or unfavorable.

They calculate whether something is good or evil, or whether someone is a relative or a stranger. Toward what is good and those who are close, they provide various benefits; toward what is evil and those who are distant, they inflict various injuries.
Thus, through the bonds of karma, they either receive happiness as a reward for kindness or suffer pain as retribution for resentment. Suddenly—

However, upon awakening, all the aforementioned matters are dispelled; one should know that this matter is solely the mind of a dream. Regarding the phrase "all are due to [this]," it refers to the *dharmas*.
The arising of the nine stages of meditative visualization (*navasaṃjñā*) all relies upon this power, just as various dream-events exist in reliance upon sleep.
The passage from the sutra below cites scriptural evidence from the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*. It says: "In this way, by the power of the ground of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*), within existence..."
Among the four *āśraya-bhūmis* (dwelling grounds), the *avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi* (ground of ignorance) possesses the greatest power. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"For example, because the great earth possesses superior power, it sustains four heavy burdens; therefore, it is called an 'āśraya-bhūmi. First, the great ocean; second, the various mountains."

Third, grasses and trees; fourth, sentient beings. Ignorance is likewise: among the five stages of abiding (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*), it is the most difficult to eliminate, and thus one knows its power is great.
The following passage is the concluding summary at the end of the section on the nine contemplations.

[Commentary: Although one distinguishes the sequential gradations of the four characteristics from their subtle beginnings to their manifest ends, in their beginning and end, there is ultimately no before or after.
Taken together as a single moment of thought (*ekakṣaṇa*), the coarse and the subtle are fused into a single mind;
therefore, it is said that they exist simultaneously, for none of them possesses independent self-existence.

[Commentary]: Although the subsequent five [stages] are presented according to the principle of harmonious inclusion, they first follow the preceding text by stating that the subtle is not the coarse, afflictions are not karma, the clinging to dharmas is not the clinging to a self, and the fundamental consciousness is not the phenomenal consciousness;

because the prior stage differs from the subsequent stage, they are called "gradations. Nevertheless, the subsequent [stage] subsumes those distinctions of coarse and subtle into a single thought-moment (ekakṣaṇa). This is what is meant by "one."
There are two aspects to the characteristic of mindfulness (*smṛti-lakṣaṇa*): first, it is simply the mindfulness of ignorance;
second, it is the mindfulness of a single moment (*kṣaṇa*). For example, suppose a person suddenly encounters an enemy and proceeds to kill them (the karma of mindfulness).

If one then designates [the victim] as "King Zhang" or "Person Wang" (conceptualizing names), one definitively asserts, "He is my enemy" (grasping). This malicious mind is uninterrupted (continuity), and one discriminates [him] as an enemy.

That which is not a relative (the characteristic of wisdom) becomes that which is seen (the characteristic of manifestation); having become that which sees (the characteristic of transformation), the mind’s thought arises (the characteristic of karma).
Thus, within a single moment of thought, the eight characteristics are fully present. However, between these two meanings, the former meaning alone is correct.
Furthermore, "a single moment" refers to the one mind; therefore, the subsequent text states: "Correspondence with a single moment is precisely non-thought."
This refers to a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*). It is called "coarse and inferior" to explain the reason for its arising. Someone may ask:

"Since there are distinctions such as coarse and subtle, or prior and subsequent, how can it be called a single thought-moment? This is the explanation for that: although there are distinctions such as coarse and subtle, [it is still a single moment].
It is created solely by this single mind. How could there be a mind existing within the characteristic of cessation, while there is no mind within the characteristic of arising?
If one says there is no [mind], upon what would arising depend? Nor can this single mind be divided to correspond to the four characteristics.
Since the mind cannot be divided and possesses neither prior nor posterior, how could the four characteristics have a sequence of before and after? It is like a person...
This is one. Although one dreams of various things, and though the dream-events are many, they have no sequence of before or after;
therefore, it is said below, citing proof, in the concluding passage on initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*):

"In reality, there is no differentiation of initial awakening, because the four marks exist simultaneously, none of which has independent establishment, being originally equal and identical with awakening."
[Commentary]: However, for those who have not yet fathomed the source, awakening occurs sequentially according to the depth of their respective stages.

For those who have reached the source of the mind, the four phases [of arising] are known simultaneously in a single thought-moment. As the Sūtra says: "Bodhisattvas know the end but do not know the beginning;
only the Buddha-Tathāgata knows both the beginning and the end. "Beginning" refers to the phase of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*); "end" refers to the remaining phases up to cessation (*nirodha*).

[This is] the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). [Commentary: Now, the following six sections resolve and clarify potential difficulties. Someone might ask: "Since the four characteristics occur simultaneously, why is it that for the awakened one there is a sequence of before and after?
Therefore, this is explained: "The mind that realizes... and so forth; this means that the realization of the four characteristics is based entirely upon the mind.
Only then can they be known simultaneously. It is like a person recounting a dream within a dream; one comes to know it gradually, until finally, upon waking, one can realize it all at once.
This depends on whether one gains or loses [insight], and one should not harbor doubts regarding the Dharma. As the Sūtra says below:
Citing Evidence. From "At first" onwards, the subsequent explanations of what was cited can all be understood.
[Commentary] That is to say, due to the power of ignorance and non-awakening, various dream-like thoughts such as the phase of arising and so forth are produced, which stir the source of the mind.
This continues until the phase of cessation, where one slumbers long within the three realms and wanders through the six destinies. Now, because of fundamental awakening...

Through the power of contemplative perfuming (*cintā-vāsanā*), one gives rise to a mind of weary detachment and seeking. Furthermore, by means of the teachings of hearing-perfuming (*śruta-vāsanā*) that flow from True Suchness (*tathatā*), one perfumes the Original Enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*).
Because essence and function are mutually integrated, one receives that perfuming of hearing, which increases the power of innate understanding and diminishes the capacity of ignorance.

Thus, one gradually moves toward the source of the mind, first ceasing the aspect of extinction and finally ceasing the aspect of arising. Thereupon, one attains a brilliant and great awakening, fully realizing.
The source of the mind is fundamentally unmoving; it is primordially quiescent and perfectly equal, without any distinction between beginningless awakening and non-awakening.
This is the general meaning of such passages as the simile of crossing a great river in a dream, as taught in the sutras.

[Commentary] "Since it has descended," etc. (7). This concludes the section on the initial awakening (ādi-bodhi) in two parts. First, the explanation of that which is awakened to, following the flow [of delusion].

That which is awakened to is precisely non-awakening (a-bodha). The various dream-like thoughts are the afflictive hindrance (kleśāvaraṇa). Their transition toward the state of cessation is the karmic hindrance (karmāvaraṇa).

"Deep sleep" and so forth refer to the retributive hindrance (vipākāvaraṇa). Since one is thus shrouded by these three hindrances, one is utterly unaware; from beginningless time until now, one has never [awakened].

Because they have awakened, it is said that [sentient beings] were in a state of "long sleep. The "three realms" refer to the *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment as retribution), while the "six destinies" refer to the *samyak-vipāka* (the primary body as retribution).

Because one repeatedly returns to and proceeds through these six, they are called "destinies" (*gati*). Regarding the passage beginning with "Now, because of... and continuing for two sections, this explains the "capacity to awaken" by reversing the flow [of samsara].

This "capacity to awaken" refers to the *ādi-bodhi* (initial awakening). First, it clarifies the causes and conditions for the arising of awakening. "The permeation of original awakening" refers to internal causal permeation.

The power of awakening’s subtle permeation is profound and unfathomable; it is called "inconceivable. Fundamental awakening is the essence (*tattva*), while its permeation that incites wearying detachment and seeking is the function (*vṛtti*).
This is the internal cause as essence and function. Furthermore, from the passage below, the power of external conditions is clarified:

True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the essence, and the teachings that flow forth from it are the function. This is the external condition as essence and function. (From the *Liang She lun* [She dasheng lun]).

It is said: from the pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) flows forth the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*); from the fundamental wisdom flows forth the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*);
from the subsequently attained wisdom flows forth the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-citta*); and from the mind of great compassion flow forth the twelvefold teaching (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*).

The pure dharma-realm is precisely suchness (*tathatā*). Regarding "perfuming through hearing" and so forth, it means that by means of the wisdom of hearing, one perfumes and attains that which flows from the true [dharma-realm].

The teaching reverses the conditions that obstruct the nature of awakening, enabling it to become powerful. Thus, the teachings that flow from original awakening (benjue) in turn permeate that very original awakening.

[The phrase] "because their substance is identical" (ti xia) clarifies that awakening gives rise to its functional activity; this refers to the aforementioned internal and external permeating forces, which are able to initiate initial awakening (shijue).
"Substance is identical" means that the substance of the external conditions and the substance of the internal cause are non-dual.
Because they share the same characteristic, they are identical to True Suchness and original enlightenment.

As for their "integration through function," it means that the external conditions of the teachings and the internal aspiration for liberation are harmonized in their characteristics, such that there is no conflict or rejection between them.

"Receiving these" precisely manifests the characteristic of identical integration; if they were not integrated, they would not be received. Because they are received, they are subsequently able to provide benefit and serve as internal perfuming.

The nature of awakening (*bodhicitta*) begins with the understanding of initial awakening (*ādikṣānti*). Once the power of this understanding has increased, the power of ignorance (*avidyā*) becomes weakened;

thus, one is able to flow against the current and gradually turn toward the source of the mind. The passage beginning with "initially ceasing" clarifies the meaning of this gradual turning. From the stage of Initial Faith (*prathama-śraddhā*), one stops committing evil deeds;

next, one realizes the emptiness of the person (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and gradually severs attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*). When awakening reaches the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), one thoroughly exhausts the characteristics of birth (*utpatti-lakṣaṇa*).

Since all subtle dust has been exhausted, enlightened illumination alone remains; hence it is called "luminous awakening. This means that the dream of ignorance has ended, and one has attained ultimate enlightenment (*atyanta-bodhi*).
Regarding "awakening to equality," the source of the mind is eternally tranquil and fundamentally unmoving. Since the characteristic of movement does not exist, [there is no arising].

Regarding "to whom does one speak of a face," the text below states: "When the mind first arises, the mind has no initial characteristic. It further says: "For example, it is like a person who mistakes east for west;
while the directions do not actually change, [the mind is deluded]. As for "equality," it means that the mind has no dualistic characteristics.

To speak further: it is because the characteristic of equality is itself equal. Alternatively, it is because the fundamental and the derivative are equal, the subject and the object are equal, and self and other are equal;
in short, because all phenomena that exist in relation to one another are entirely equal.

As stated below, the following scriptural citations are provided as evidence. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "For example, suppose there is a person who, in a dream, sees his own body falling into a great river.
Desiring to cross it, he exerts great courage and employs great skillful means.
Because of that great courage and the employment of skillful means, he immediately awakens from the dream. Once awakened, all that he was doing ceases. It is the same for the Bodhisattva."
Seeing sentient beings within the four currents, he gives rise to great courage and exerts great diligence for their sake of deliverance.
By means of this courageous diligence, he reaches the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*). Having reached this stage, all [disturbances] are completely stilled.

The two modes of activity do not manifest at all. The intent of that sutra is to say that this bodhisattva, having moved from the state of having signs and effort toward this stage of signlessness and effortless spontaneity, attains the forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Because they no longer perceive a self or sentient beings, nor awakening, nirvana, birth-and-death, or afflictions, both modes of activity are stilled; for they have attained the non-existence of dharmas.

Because of [prior] conceptualization, this present [discussion] refers to the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*). At this point, initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*) is identical to the fundamental [enlightenment];

there is no characteristic to be awakened to, and they are equal and equal. Although the stages differ, the general meaning is no different; therefore, it is said that "the general meaning is also thus.
(Furthermore, this single phrase "general meaning" also serves as a comprehensive summary of the preceding intent, distinguishing it from the subsequent explanatory text. Examine this carefully.)
△ This section is further divided into two parts: first, a general inquiry; second, a detailed explanation. First, the general inquiry:
"What is the meaning of this?
[Commentary] This inquiry is raised as a preliminary summary of the overall inclusion.
[Commentary] The question concerns whether awakening is ultimate or non-ultimate, both in terms of persons and dharmas. What is the meaning of this?
This constitutes a formal inquiry based upon the preceding general heading.
△ Next, the individual explanation.
[Commentary] This is the formal explanation of the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Within this, each is divided into four sections: first, the person who contemplates;

second, the characteristic that is contemplated; third, the discernment of the benefits of contemplation; and fourth, the conclusion regarding the limits of contemplation. These should be examined in detail according to the text.
△ There are four explanations: first, cessation; second, change; third, abiding; and fourth, arising. First, cessation:
as with ordinary persons, because they perceive that a preceding thought has given rise to evil, they are able to restrain the subsequent thought so that it does not arise.
Although this is called "awakening," it is in fact non-awakening.

[Commentary]: Regarding "ordinary persons" (*pṛthagjana*): first, there is the person who observes, whose stage is that of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*). "Awakened knowledge" (*jñāna*) refers to the following.

Second, there is the object of observation, which refers to the period prior to entering the ten stages of faith, during which one extensively committed evil karma of body and speech without awakened knowledge.

Now, having entered the stages of faith, one is able to know that evil karma will certainly bring about the retribution of suffering; hence it is called "awakened knowledge. This clarifies awakening to cessation (*nirodha*).

This is the meaning of the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Therefore, one is able to descend [from it]. Third, distinguishing the benefits of contemplation: since one has now awakened, one is able to refrain from creating evil; this is the cessation of the characteristic.
Although [the text says] "even though" (referring to point four), it concludes the limits of the contemplation:

because one knows that the characteristic of cessation is truly unwholesome (*akuśala*), one does not create evil; this is called "having awakened. Yet, one still does not know that the characteristic of cessation is a dream; therefore, it is said:
"Not awakened. This refers only to the cessation of evil karma; therefore it is said "though awakened. Since they have not yet awakened from the afflictions (*kleśa*), it is said "not awakened.

[Commentary] First: the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) are the ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) outside the kalpa. Generally speaking, the term "ordinary person" extends up to the stage prior to the *bhūmi*. Now...
Since this is capable of ceasing evil, it is not of the class of deluded beings who have not yet awakened from their afflictions; nor is it the stage of those above the Ten Abodes.
It is precisely within the "indeterminate group" (aniyata-rāśi), and is therefore called the "Ten Faiths. Regarding the phrase "second, below," and "not yet entered," etc.:

this clarifies that at the time when one has not yet entered the stage of faith while still in a state of delusion, the conduct one performs is exclusively evil. This refers to the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) that is being awakened to.
This is because the body has three evils—namely, killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—and the mouth has four evils—namely, false speech, frivolous speech, harsh speech, and divisive speech.
Failing to understand that these karmas will certainly bring about bitter fruits, one creates them fervently out of ignorance.
This is to be unaware of cause and effect, and to remain oblivious to the nature of sin and merit. Now, as for those who enter into equality... [the text continues].

"Clear awareness" refers to the function of awakening. It means having faith that the karmic conditions of good and evil deeds result in retributions of beauty or ugliness, which—like echoes and shadows—are invariably without error.
Therefore, one who awakens to the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) only then realizes that the faults of this characteristic are as described.

Although the treatise merely states that "awakening to arising" involves knowing evil, it lacks the phrase regarding the "characteristic of cessation"; thus, the commentary addresses this point. (Section 3, Part B)

Regarding "not creating evil": although a preceding thought may have arisen, it belongs merely to the gateway of affliction (*kleśa*); by ceasing it so that it does not arise again, it ultimately does not constitute a path of karma (*karmapatha*).
Once the mental ground has ceased, the body and speech do not act accordingly. Regarding "the four lower [stages] can know," etc.:
they merely know that the karma of good and evil does not perish, but they do not know there is no self and no creator. For this reason, although it is called "awakening" (*bodhi*), it is—
This is non-awakening (*abodha*). This [explanation] is interpreted according to its own stage. "This merely," and so forth, is interpreted in relation to the subsequent stage;

for in that subsequent stage, delusions have already been awakened from. In this present stage, one awakens only to karma. Delusion and awakening are diametrically opposed in meaning, whereas karma and initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) are not yet direct opposites;
therefore, it is merely termed "nominal awakening" (*nāmamātra-bodhi*). Although it is termed nominal awakening, it is nonetheless...
They do not realize it.
△ Second, the difference:

such as the contemplative wisdom of the two vehicles and bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds, they perceive that thoughts are different; yet thoughts possess no characteristic of difference. Because...
Because one abandons the coarse conceptualization and attachment to signs, it is called "similar awakening" (*sādṛśa-bodha*).

[Commentary: Those such as the "first resolve" refer to the Bodhisattvas of the Three Stages of Worthiness (*tri-kalyāṇaka*). The initial mind of the ten stages of understanding (*daśa-adhimukti*) is named the "Abiding in the Resolve" (*cittotpāda-vihāra*).

By mentioning the first, the subsequent stages are implied. Although these Bodhisattvas do not realize the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) because they intentionally retain their afflictions (*kleśa*), nevertheless, regarding the emptiness of persons—
Having truly attained mastery, they are discussed as being on the same level as the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*). Regarding "awakening to the difference in mindfulness":

this refers to the two kinds of differing characteristics mentioned above—namely, making distinctions between internal and external, reckoning in terms of self and what belongs to the self, and [the presence of] greed, hatred, views, attachment, and so forth.

Because these two types of persons understand this together, it is clarified that the fundamentally pure mind is asleep due to ignorance, dreaming of diverse characteristics and giving rise to various afflictions.
Now, gradually becoming conjoined with wisdom, one attains a slight awakening from the dream of diverse characteristics;
therefore, it is said that "one awakens to the diversity. As for "mindfulness of the absence of diverse characteristics," since one is already able to awaken to the diversity of characteristics—
The various signs in that dream are, in reality, eternally non-existent. "By abandoning attachment" explains the aforementioned point to establish the benefit of contemplation.
The arising of greed, hatred, and so forth is called coarse discrimination; being attached to favorable or unfavorable objects is called the mark of clinging.
Because one awakens from the dream of various signs, one is able to abandon them; yet, one still remains asleep within the dream of abiding marks.

Therefore, it is called "similar awakening. Because in this stage, the Bodhisattvas have not yet reached the stage of realization, and the followers of the Two Vehicles do not understand the emptiness of phenomena, it is called "similar awakening.
Question: Since they awaken to the marks of difference and so forth, yet do not awaken to the subsequent stages, why is the name "non-awakening" not also established for them?
Answer: Based on the principle that one awakens to what precedes but does not awaken to what follows, they may indeed be designated as "non-awakened. Therefore...

From the following passage down to the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), all are termed "non-awakening" (*abodhi*). If one distinguishes between awakening as activity and non-awakening as delusion, it is designated simply as "non-awakening.
This is because, within this specific text, awakening is used to directly counteract delusion; thus, it does not refer to the same thing as [karmic] activity.

[Commentary] First, the lower section. One is the "capable observer. Question: Why does the treatise not speak directly of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), but instead refers to them as "observers with wisdom" (*jñānadarśin*)?
What is meant by this? Answer: The two vehicles observe only the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), whereas Bodhisattvas observe both types of emptiness (*ubhaya-śūnyatā*);

thus, a distinction is made between the Great and Small Vehicles. Here, however, we speak only in terms of their shared use of the observation of the emptiness of persons; therefore, [the term is applied].
Commentary: This [classification] merely distinguishes [the practitioner] as being equal to a bodhisattva based on the functional application of their contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*);

it does not mean they are entirely identical. Since there is the principle of being "different yet the same," one must specifically mention "contemplative wisdom. If one were to speak directly of them as "those of the two vehicles" (*dvayayānika*), there would be the danger of confusion and error.

"Ten Understandings" (*daśa-adhimukti*) is a synonym for the "Ten Abodes" (*daśa-vihāra*). That [text] calls them "arousing the mind" (*cittotpāda*), while this [text] calls them "arousing the intention" (*cittotpādana*).
The name and its meaning are identical. The character "equal" (等) intends to include the nine stages (*navabhūmi*) as well as the paths of practice and convergence;

therefore, it is called "subsequent. Regarding "retaining delusions": this means they are suppressed but not yet severed. Regarding "not realizing [nirvana]": this is intended for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.

It means that this Bodhisattva realizes that the true is inherently existent and understands that the false is inherently empty; they accord with True Suchness (*tathatā*) and cultivate the contemplation of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*), [attaining] both...

The two obstacles are subdued; they do not arise as active manifestations, but their seeds remain. According to the teachings of the Dharmalakṣaṇa school, because the power of śamatha and vipaśyanā is weak, these [seeds] follow along with the eyes and are not severed.
According to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, however, Bodhisattvas prior to the stages (bhūmi) act in accordance with the teachings in an inconceivable manner;
while the afflictive obstacles do not arise, through the power of their compassion and vows, they assist the afflictions to moisten karma and thereby undergo rebirth.
The "dead body" refers to the teaching and transformation through the Six Paramitas; it is precisely according to this meaning.

In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, the principle of "retaining delusions" (*kleśa-avasthāna*) applies only to Bodhisattvas from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward whose compassion has increased. Now, in this commentary, the discussion of retaining delusions occurs at the stage of the Three Sages (*trayaḥ kalyāṇamitra-sthānāni*);
this is because these are Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-nature school’s definitive teaching, whose faculties and nature are sharp and keen, and who have just begun their resolve.
At the stage of the mind (citta-kṣaṇa), one is suddenly able to realize the fundamental nature and penetrate the emptiness of the essence of delusion.

By practicing the various *pāramitās* in accordance with this nature, one proceeds toward the principle with great speed and attains mastery over the afflictions (*kleśa*). Therefore, it is said that at the three stages of the *śaikṣas* (the three levels of the *sambhāra-mārga*), one "remains" [in this state].
Those who have attained mastery are able to enter this contemplation and subdue these afflictions; since their application of contemplation is equal, they are placed in the same stage.
"Awakening to the lower" refers to two things. Regarding the "two objects of observation," first, we shall harmonize this with the previous explanation.

The two differences are the two aspects of grasping and conceptualizing names (*nāma*). As for "discrimination" and so forth, one conceives of a self within the body and conceives of "mine" externally;
because these encompass both discriminative and innate [afflictions], they are called "view and craving. However, among the six fundamental [afflictions], "self" is excluded.

This "view" refers to the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-moha*); all others are craving (*tṛṣṇā*), as is commonly discussed. Regarding these two types [of practitioners], they refer to those of the Two Vehicles and the Three Stages of Worthies (*tri-śaikṣa*).

They are alike in awakening to this characteristic, for both are able to fully comprehend this grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*). Below the section on "Clarifying the Root," the text next provides the correct interpretation of the main body of the work.

First, it clarifies the distinct characteristics of that which is awakened to and the causal conditions that give rise to it; that is to say, prior to the arising of contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*).
The thought of ignorance combines with diverse characteristics to give rise to various afflictions that burn incessantly, yet one remains utterly unaware of this.
From here below, the text next clarifies the functional power of the contemplative observation that can awaken to these diverse characteristics;

that is, within the thought of ignorance, one illuminates and examines the principles regarding the existence or non-existence of the self, others, craving, and views, thereby knowing that these afflictions arise from ignorance.

"Clarity arises. This refers to the initial realization of coarse thoughts; hence it is called "subtle awareness. This is a distinct meaning within the context of awakened thought. Regarding "thoughts are without [distinction]," there are three points of benefit.
Since one is able to "equally" [observe], one examines the essence of the person and the self within ignorance according to the principle of reality and realizes that nothing is to be found.
Hence it is said, "thoughts have no differentiating marks. This is the meaning of the emptiness of the self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). By means of this...

"Abandoning the lower [levels], four. This concludes the contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Regarding "the mind abandons and so forth": first, this explains the distinct characteristics of the two preceding [states];

second, it concludes the contemplation. It should be understood by analogy. Regarding "because of [realizing] equality and so forth": because one awakens to the emptiness of the self (*ātman-śūnyatā*), the afflictions of self-clinging (*ātma-grāha-kleśa*) do not arise;

therefore, it is said that "coarse discrimination is abandoned," and so on. As for "yet still, below," it explains the similarity. Regarding "sleep abides in the state of equilibrium and so forth": because...

Because they have not yet awakened to the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), this refers generally to both the Two Vehicles and the three stages of the *śaikṣa* (the Three Sages), all of whom are termed "semblance awakening" (*sajñāna*).
From here below, the reason for this is explained. For the Bodhisattvas, not having yet realized their own fundamental portion is "semblance";

although the followers of the Two Vehicles are said to have "entered realization" within their own vehicles, when compared to the Mahāyāna, they have only attained the emptiness of the self (*pudgalanairātmya*) and have not yet realized the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), and thus they are likewise termed [semblance awakening].

Because it has not yet been realized, it is similar to a semblance of awakening (*sādṛśa-bodha*). Thus, in comparison to the realization of truth at the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), this is called "semblance.

Regarding the first, the cause: *The provided text consists of a structural outline (Sanskrit: *uddāna* or *vibhāga*) for a commentary on Buddhist doctrine, specifically concerning the "characteristic of purity" (*viśuddha-lakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the characteristic of the purity of wisdom (*jñāna-viśuddhi-lakṣaṇa*): it refers to practicing according to reality and fulfilling the skillful means by relying on the power of the Dharma’s permeation (*vāsanā*).

[Commentary] The term "wisdom" introduces the section. Regarding "the power of the Dharma’s permeation": this consists of the internal permeating power of True Suchness (*tathatā*) and the external permeating power of the taught Dharma that flows from it.
This occurs prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), wherein one cultivates the provisions (*sambhāra*) and the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) based upon these permeating powers.
These are the roots of goodness. One who practices according to reality has ascended to the stages (bhūmis) and above, such that their conduct accords with True Suchness (*tathatā*).
"Fulfillment" refers to the conclusion of the practices of the ten stages; this marks the ultimate limit of the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*) of the Vajra.

[Commentary] Regarding "True Suchness" (*tathatā*) and so forth: when internal, it is the Dharma as principle (*li*); when external, it is the Dharma as teaching (*jiao*). Although they differ between internal and external, both are termed "Dharma.
For this reason, the treatise refers to them collectively as "Dharma. Regarding "this [state] and so forth":

it is solely by the power of perfuming (*vāsanā*) that one takes the teaching as an object and practices, beginning from the stage of Initial Faith (*ādikṣānti*) and continuing until the tenth stage of Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).

The "provisions" (*sambhāra*) refer to the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) and the three stages of worthiness (*tri-kṣānti*), wherein one fully cultivates merit and wisdom as the provisions for attaining Buddhahood;

they are also termed the "wholesome roots conducive to liberation" (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*). The "preparatory practices" (*prayoga*) consist of the four types of preparatory stages: Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Supreme Worldly Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).
These occur after the stage of the three worthies and before the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*), where one applies effort and practice in order to seek the vision [of reality].

Because they accord with the Path, they are also called the "wholesome factors conducive to penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*). These four stages of preparatory application (*prayoga*) rely upon the four types of investigation (*vitarka*) and analysis (*vicāra*), as well as the four types of correct observation (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*):
observing names, objects, the intrinsic nature of names and objects, and the distinctions between names and objects; they observe that these are conventionally existent but ultimately non-existent.

As in the two stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and Summits (*mūrdhan*), one cultivates the four types of investigation and analysis; in the stages of Patience (*kṣānti*) and the Supreme Worldly Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*), one likewise cultivates the four types of correct observation.

At the stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*), one cultivates the concentration of "attainment of light" (*ālokalabdha-samādhi*) and gives rise to inferior vitarka and vicāra, contemplating that there is nothing to be grasped (*anupalambha*).

At the stage of Summits (*mūrdhan*), one cultivates the concentration of "increase of light" (*vṛddhāloka-samādhi*) and gives rise to superior vitarka and vicāra, again contemplating that there is nothing to be grasped.

At the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*), one cultivates the concentration of "sealing and conforming" (*anulomikī-mudrā-samādhi*), which seals what precedes and conforms to what follows, giving rise to inferior knowledge of reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).
