In this passage, both the true and the false aspects of the mind are encompassed; this is easily seen upon close examination. "Not as below" refers to the subsequent section on distinguishing the associated mental factors (*caitta*).

Since there is no external object to serve as a counterpart, by what means can their association be clarified? "This is not so," etc., constitutes the second [point]: pointing out the contradiction and the obstacle.

This is because the School of Characteristics (*lakṣaṇavāda*) asserts that this eighth consciousness possesses the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga-caitta*), and furthermore, it is associated with the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).
It corresponds to objects outside the realm (*dhātu*), yet it does not state that there is the meaning of "cognition" (*vijñapti*).

Regarding the various treatises such as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Yogācārabhūmi*, as for their reconciliation as explained elsewhere, I have not yet found where they are set forth. For now, I shall briefly reconcile what is taught by the two schools.
For instance, according to the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school (Faxiangzong), they assert that the eighth consciousness can take three types of objects as its cognitive domain (*ālambana*), based solely on...

In the present section on the stage of accomplishment (*niṣpanna-avasthā*), the eight consciousnesses are explained transversally (*tiryak*). This does not clarify the fundamental cause of their initial arising;
rather, it simply states that all sentient beings inherently possess these eight kinds of consciousness, which arise from their own seeds and are all capable of cognizing their respective objects.
Because they share the common meaning of "consciousness" as discernment (*vijñapti*), they are able to take objects as their conditions. Furthermore, it says:
This consciousness arises from its own seeds; yet, although it arises from its own seeds, it can only come into being by taking a provisional object as its objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

Therefore, it must depend upon an object. Although it is able to take an object, it is subtle and difficult to perceive, unlike the first seven consciousnesses which grasp at a self and grasp at phenomena.
In this treatise, the various consciousnesses are explained in their vertical progression, showing how they are formed through delusion regarding the Truth, proceeding from the subtle to the coarse.

[The *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*] states: "It is coarse; it does not speak of birth from seeds. Therefore, the eighth consciousness possesses only the function of producing objects, but lacks the sense of perceiving objects.

Because it arises from the internal perfuming of ignorance and is not produced by the牵引 (attraction) of external objects, the sūtras describe it as 'flowing and ceasing' (*pravāha-utpāda-nirodha*). This refers to its internal arising. For this reason, it does not perceive objects."

Regarding this meaning: if one were now to synthesize that [other] system with the present treatise, since that school asserts that this consciousness perceives objects in a manner so subtle as to be difficult to know, it should be understood that they are secretly in agreement with the intent of the present treatise; for that school maintains that [consciousness] arises from seeds.
Since they are both portions of consciousness (*vijñāna*), one cannot help but speak of their taking objects as conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

Furthermore, if one understands this in the same way as that [previous] explanation, the objects of the first six consciousnesses clarified in this treatise are precisely the coarse functional aspects of the eighth consciousness.

Because of these objects, they infuse (*vāsana*) the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), giving rise to this discrimination. Thus, the fundamental consciousness possesses the sense of taking objects as conditions. This is because...
Because it is coarse, it is separated [from the subtle] and termed the "active consciousness" (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*); it is not called the eighth.
Furthermore, according to that school’s doctrine, the eighth mind-king (*citta-rāja*) is associated with the five universal mental factors (*caitta*).

Since this consciousness is said to be able to take objects as its cognitive domain, there must be an association between the king and its attendants. For instance, when correctly taking an object, there must be attention (*manasikāra*) capable of alerting the mind and drawing it toward the object.

The mind moves toward the object. Because it moves toward the object, the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness undergoes differentiation and transformation, causing the mind to come into contact with that object.
Because it contacts the object, the four factors come together, experiencing what is favorable or unfavorable.

Because of this experience, one grasps the image of the object and establishes various matters of names and speech. Because of this grasping of the image, the mind subsequently engages in volitional construction.

The five [mental factors] such as *pradhāna* (dominance) and so forth are all obtained by virtue of having an object (*ālambana*). Therefore, the eighth [consciousness] possesses five associated mental factors.
Since this treatise does not state that this [eighth consciousness] has an object, nor are there any mental factors associated with it, it is not the same as those [other consciousnesses].

Furthermore, within that school, they do not explain the eighth consciousness as the originating cause from which the false arises from the true; rather, they speak only according to its state of actualization in the present.

Therefore, it lacks the meaning of "Awakening" (*bodhi*). Nevertheless, they also maintain that there exists the beginningless, primordially inherent seed of *bodhi*, yet this is not identical to the true suchness of original awakening (*mūlabodhi-tathatā*), because it has not yet been realized. Thus, for the time being, it is taught in a concealed manner. Now...
As clarified in the treatise: based upon the *tathāgatagarbha*, there arises the mind of birth and death; because it is deluded regarding awakening, it constitutes non-awakening (*abodhi*).

Although non-awakening is established, the nature of awakening remains unchanging; therefore, the principle of awakening exists. Because this is explained through the explicit characteristics of the definitive teaching (*nītārtha*), it is not the same as that [other teaching].
If that [teaching] had already stated the existence of the principle of awakening, how could these two teachings be distinguished?

[Regarding] the degrees of depth: [one] knows this (Cui’s biography states: "The original commentary consists of two fascicles and a separate record of one fascicle; the *Huìtōng* is detailed therein").
△ Third, citing the aforementioned defiled mind and ignorance, it establishes the meaning of the two obstructions (*āvaraṇa*) in relation to their objects.
[Commentary] This passage cites the aforementioned six defiled minds along with ignorance; regarding the objects that obstruct them, these are bound together as two types of hindrances.
This is because all obstructive defilements do not transcend these two kinds: namely, afflictions (*kleśa*) and the cognizable (*jñeya*).
Now, regarding this defiled mind and ignorance, how are these two obstacles to be subsumed within the categories of discrimination?

This is clarified here. △ This section also has two parts: first, the initial presentation; second, the detailed explanation. First, the initial presentation (which has two parts): first, the obstacle of affliction; second, [the obstacle of knowledge].
The obstacle of ignorance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). First, the obstacle of affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Furthermore, the meaning of "defiled mind" is termed the "hindrance of affliction" (*kleśāvaraṇa*), because it can obstruct the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) of *tathatā*.

[Commentary] "Defiled mind" refers to the six types of defiled minds. "Can obstruct," etc., clarifies its meaning as a hindrance; that is to say, it obstructs the wondrous [wisdom] that illuminates quiescence.
Wisdom that accords with reality is called fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*); this is precisely what was referred to above as the "characteristic of purity of wisdom.
Because the defiled mind is agitated and thus opposes this tranquility, the defiled mind is termed the "hindrance of afflictions" (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

Since it is the afflictions that cause movement, here, for the time being, we rely on the gate of the mutual dependence between the root and its branches, designating the defiled mind arising from ignorance as the hindrance of afflictions.

The ignorance that is able to give rise to defiled minds is called "obstruction to knowledge" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). This does not define the two obstructions by way of the two attachments to persons and phenomena.
[Commentary] The first two phrases indicate the names of the dharmas. Regarding the "six defiled minds," each takes one portion from among them.
Because it has the sense of continuity, and because this portion is clamorous, agitated, and not tranquil, it is called "affliction" (*kleśa*).

The phrase "capable of obstructing" (*āvaraṇa*) explains the meaning as being a hindrance. First, regarding the explanation of the text: below the section on "illumination and tranquility," the names of the wisdom that is obstructed are explained.

It is further called "true wisdom" (*tattvajñāna*), "wisdom that realizes the essence," "real wisdom" (*bhūtajñāna*), and so forth; it is so named because it is capable of realizing the principle of suchness (*tathatā*) as it truly is.
Because it is like the wisdom of suchness (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) and can give rise to subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), it is called fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

The phrase "the aforementioned text" below refers to the manifestation of the essence of the wisdom that is obstructed. The phrase "defiled mind" below explains the characteristics of the obstruction; this may be understood. Now, the phrase "herein" below next addresses a potential objection. Someone might ask:
"As stated in various places, the two obstructions arise based on the two attachments (*dvaya-grāha*); how does this differ from that? Furthermore, previously..."
If one merely assigns the first four of the six coarse factors to the two hindrances, why are all six defilements herein termed "afflictions" (*kleśa*)?

This is explained as follows: regarding the statement that the two hindrances arise based on the two types of grasping, the hindrance to omniscience (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) arises based upon the five mental consciousnesses (*manas*), while the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*) arises based upon the consciousness of the mental faculty (*mano-vijñāna*).
Here, however, it is the ignorance (*avidyā*) upon which the defiled mental states depend that is intended.
They are objects of knowledge (*jñeya*). Because that which relies upon the defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-citta*) constitutes the afflictions (*kleśa*), they are not the same.

One should know that if the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) are explained in terms of the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*), they are restricted; whereas this explanation of the two obstacles based on the defiled mind is comprehensive. Such is the difference between them.
△ Regarding the subsequent obstacle of ignorance (*avidyā*):
the meaning of ignorance is termed "obstruction to wisdom" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), because it can obstruct the spontaneous wisdom of worldly activity (*laukika-svayambhū-karma-jñāna*).

[Commentary] "Ignorance" refers to fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*). The phrase "can obstruct" below clarifies its meaning as an obstruction; that is, it obstructs the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).

The wisdom of measure (*pramāṇa-jñāna*) is precisely the aforementioned inconceivable activity. Because of the delusion of ignorance, there is no discrimination, which opposes this function of wisdom;
this is called "obstruction of wisdom" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). It is named after that which it obstructs. This clarifies the function of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*):
like the moon, it responds instantaneously, yet remains without intentionality toward the water; it is not like the "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*) of non-Buddhists.
[Commentary] "Without inferiority" also serves to designate the specific name of the dharma. Regarding "fundamental ignorance" (*mūla-avidyā*):

if one takes a portion from among the various consciousnesses, it also includes the branches and their offshoots; since the branches follow from the root, this designation is made. As for "that which can obstruct," etc.:
This also clarifies the definition of "obstruction. First is the explanation of the text;

following the phrase "after attaining," there is the explanation of the names of the wisdom that is obstructed, such as "omniscient wisdom" (*sarvajñā*), "conventional wisdom" (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and "expedient wisdom" (*upāyajñāna*). These arise only after one has realized *tathatā* (suchness) through fundamental wisdom (*mūlajñāna*).

It is called "subsequently attained wisdom" (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). Because it knows things according to their actual measure, it is called "wisdom that accords with the measure of reality" (*yathāvadbhāva-jñāna*).
The terms "upper" and "lower" refer to the emergence of the essence of wisdom from what obstructs it. By stating "lowered by ignorance," its obstructive characteristic is explained.

That which is named after what it obstructs is so called because it is the obstruction to wisdom; this is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive compound) analysis. This is not the same as the afflictions being the obstruction itself, which would be an analysis based on the sense of "possessing" (*dhāraṇa*). This clarifies...
[End of] Section Two: Resolving Objections. Question: This term "spontaneity" (zìrán)—how does it differ from the spontaneity of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas)?
Answer: To resolve this, [the text] explains: This mind is "without mind" yet responds to objects; its spontaneous manifestation and transformation is what is meant by spontaneity.
This is not the same as the spontaneity of the non-Buddhists who negate cause and effect. Thus, while the words are the same, the meanings are different.
△ Second, the double explanation (2). First, the inquiry; second, the explanation. First, the inquiry:
What is the meaning of this?
[Commentary] First, the question is asked: Since this ignorance causes the essence of the mind—both in its movement and stillness—to become a defiled mind, then ignorance...
This [subtle] should obstruct the wisdom of principle (li-zhi); the defiled mind is coarse and should obstruct the wisdom of cognition (liang-zhi). Why is this not so? [Commentary:

The preceding question and so forth constitute a challenge based on the distinction between the subtle and the coarse. It would simply be logical that a subtle phenomenon should obstruct a subtle phenomenon.
Coarse phenomena serve as obstacles to coarse phenomena; this alone is appropriate. Why is it not otherwise? △ Second, the explanation (in two parts):
first, the explanation of the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*); second, the explanation of the obstacle to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). First, the explanation of the obstacle of afflictions.
Because, by relying on the defiled mind, one is able to see and manifest, falsely grasping at objects; this contradicts the nature of equality.
[Commentary] "Able to see and able to manifest" refers exclusively to the latter three subtle [consciousnesses] and the former two defiled [consciousnesses].

"Falsely grasping at objects" comprehensively includes the first three defiled minds, as they all arise in dependence upon objects. "Contradicting the nature of equality" explains the establishment of obstruction.

[Commentary: Regarding these two types of defiled mind, because their activity-characteristic (*karmalakṣaṇa*) is subtle, the distinction between subject and object has not yet arisen; thus, it is difficult to establish the sense of "obstruction. However, by means of this defiled mind, there is a differentiation between subject and object that deviates from the equality of subject and object in fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*).

Consequently, it obstructs the unity of principle and wisdom (*li-zhi*). [Recorded Notes: As for the preceding two types of defiled mind, because their activity-characteristic is subtle and the subject-object distinction has not yet been divided, it is difficult to establish the meaning of "obstruction."
This contradicts what has been observed; therefore, we now specifically address the two aspects of the evolving [consciousness] and the manifesting [consciousness] to answer the previous objection.

Although this is not explicitly stated, the meaning is implicitly included, because it is said that the capacity to see arises based on the moving mind; this can be understood through the intended sense. Thus, the first three [consciousnesses] are defiled.
That is to say, the three [aspects] prior to the defilement of discerning wisdom are all *savisaya-vijñāna* (consciousness of objects);

therefore, they arise in dependence upon objects. Because these [three] involve the absence of subject and object in the wisdom of principle (*li*), while the defiled mind possesses subject and object—being diametrically opposed—the meaning of "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*) is established.
△ Second, the explanation of the obstruction to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Because all phenomena are eternally quiescent and lack any characteristic of arising, ignorance fails to realize this;
thus, through delusively opposing the nature of phenomena, one is unable to attain the various kinds of knowledge that accord with all worldly objects.
[Commentary: Regarding "the characteristic of the quiescence of phenomena" (*dharmapraśāntalakṣaṇa*): this refers to the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) that is deluded by ignorance.

"That which is contrary to the Dharma" correctly reveals that ignorance is deluded regarding the aforementioned *dharmatā*; because it fails to understand that phenomena are quiescent as they truly are, it falsely gives rise to notions of arising and ceasing, thereby being in opposition to the Dharma.
"Unable to attain" correctly explains the meaning of the obstruction to the wisdom of suchness (*yathābhūtajñāna*).
[Commentary] Regarding "the dharma-nature that is the object of delusion": this is the conventional [truth] that is itself the ultimate.
Therefore, it is eternally quiescent and without arising. Being without arising is itself the ultimate; thus, it is called "dharma-nature. The preceding text states:

"All dharmas are free from the characteristics of verbal expression," and so forth, up to "they are without change or alteration, indestructible, and are solely the one mind. The phrase "not understanding" and so forth correctly explains the contradiction.
Regarding the meaning: the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is quiescent, yet ignorance gives rise to movement. Since movement and stillness are antithetical, this constitutes a contradiction.

To correctly explain this and so forth, the *Ben-shu* states: "Because one is internally deluded regarding ultimate truth and perceives external objects through consciousness, one is unable to accord with the various cognitions regarding the sphere of 'as-it-is' (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*).
It is like a person moving their eyes, whereby heaven and earth appear to tilt and sway. Thus.
One cannot know it as it truly is. However, whereas previously the question was posed in terms of the coarse and the subtle, here it is answered comprehensively in terms of their mutual opposition.
Thus, the subsequent text states: "When ignorance is suddenly exhausted, it is called the knowledge of all modes."
*Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra-vyākhyā-pen-xi-ji*, Fascicle Six, with Phonetic Transcriptions.
*Chì* (pronounced *chì*): the appearance of a blazing fire.
*Manas* is here translated as "mind" (*yi*). It is the name of the seventh consciousness.
*Teng* (in the reading *teng-yin*) means to soar or fly.
*Huan* (in the reading *huan-yin*) means to revolve in a circle.
*Niè* (pronounced *yì*) means "rebellious"; it refers to sin and evil.
*Huàn* (pronounced *huàn*) means "to escape" or "to flee," implying a succession of turnings.
*Cán* (commonly written as *cán*) refers to the silkworm, a creature that spits out silk.
"Jiǎn" (繭) is the same as "jiǎn" (蠒); its pronunciation is jiǎn.
"Kàng" (抗) has the pronunciation kǎng; it means to oppose or diverge.
"Yǒng" (涌) has the pronunciation yǒng; it means water gushing forth.
"Mèn" (with the departing tone) means the breath is stifled and does not pass through.
"Jiāo" (rhymes with jiāo) means injury from fire.
"Huàn" (rhymes with huàn) means brilliant light.
Yì (逸): The sound is *yé*. To roam at will; to let loose. Wù (杌):
The sound is *è*. A tree stump; a tree without branches.
Wū (汙): The sound is *wū*. Same as *wū*; filth; defilement.
*Shi* (pronounced *shi*) means to bite.
*Chou* (pronounced *rou*) means dense and thick.
*Kātyāyana* is translated here as "ornamentation."
The character for "inspection" (jiǎn) is pronounced like "jian"; it means to search out.
The character for "warning" (jǐng) is pronounced like "jing"; it means to admonish and urge.
The character for "driving" (qū) is pronounced like "qu"; it means to dispatch a messenger.
The "Biography of National Preceptor Hyeon-su" was composed by Choe Ch’iwon of the Hanlin Academy.
The character *hyun* (諠) is the same as *hwan* (喧); it means clamor or noise.
The sound of *kyŏng* (傾) is pronounced *kying*; it means to sway or move.

△ Third, explaining the characteristics of arising and ceasing.

[Commentary] Regarding the characteristics of arising and ceasing: in the section on "Establishing the Proposition," it was stated that these are the characteristics of the causes and conditions for the arising and ceasing of the mind.
Within that context, the arising and ceasing of the mind and its causes and conditions have already been explained above; here, we shall now analyze the single character "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*).
However, these are characteristics of the school that maintains arising and ceasing;

therefore, they are mentioned together. The text is divided into three parts: first, restating the preceding section and indicating the number; second, interrogating, listing, and briefly revealing; third, extensively explaining their characteristics.
First, the preceding heading and enumeration are restated.
Next, regarding the analysis of the characteristics of arising and ceasing, there are two kinds.
[Commentary]: "Characteristics of arising and ceasing" restates what preceded; "there are two kinds" indicates the number.
[Commentary] First, the mind is elucidated; next, the causes and conditions are explained; subsequently, the characteristics are analyzed. Therefore, it says, "Next, the characteristics are analyzed.
To "cite what precedes" means to cite the text from the section on the "Establishment of the Thesis" (立義分).
△ Second, the interrogation, enumeration, and brief explanation.
What are the two? First, the coarse, because it is associated with the mind; second, the subtle, because it is dissociated from the mind.
[Commentary] "What is it? is the interrogative. "First, one" is the enumeration. Among the six defilements (*kleśa*), the first three are associated with the mind (*citta-samprayukta*);

their characteristics are coarse and manifest, and thus the Sūtra describes them as the arising and ceasing of marks (*nimitta*). "Second, two" refers to the latter three defilements; they are dissociated from the mind (*citta-viprayukta*).
Because they lack the coarse and manifest characteristics of mental factors, their essence is subtle and fine; thus the Sūtra describes them as...
The continuous flow of arising and ceasing.

[Commentary] As for "those with coarse and manifest characteristics": this refers to those who discriminate between defilement and purity, contemplate the three periods of time, harbor views of self and person, and in whom greed and hatred blaze intensely;
these can be distinguished by observation. Regarding the passage from the sutra: the *Laṅkāvatāra* states that there are two kinds of consciousnesses.

Arising, abiding, and ceasing refer to the "continuous flow" (*pravāha*) and the "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*). As for "characteristics," they are the manifesting essence and form (*svarūpa-lakṣaṇa*), like a root sprouting a shoot;

therefore, they belong to the coarse division. The *vṛtti-vijñāna* (active consciousness) discriminates the six sense-objects in this manner. Regarding "mindless dharmas": "mind" refers to the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) which is capable of cognition.
The single word "dharma" applies generally to both number and objects; it refers to the mental factors (*caitta*) that are the dharmas activated by the mind. These mental factors...
This refers to the *dharmas* as conditions. As understood from the preceding reflection, "flowing" (*pravāha*) refers to the continuity of seeds;
it is like level-flowing water that appears tranquil on the surface, and thus belongs to the subtle category. The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states: "The *ādāna-vijñāna* is extremely subtle;
all its seeds are like a torrential stream. The *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states: "It is a similar continuity, such that one does not perceive its absence."

This is always the case. However, the phrasing "this is associated with the mind" (*citta-samprayukta*) and so forth is not convenient for conveying the intended meaning because of the presence of the character "one" (*yi*).
This is likely due to the translators not having refined the text sufficiently. In later translations, it is simply stated that "the one" refers to the coarse [aspect], namely, the associated mind.

The second is the subtle, which refers to that which is dissociated from the mind (*citta-viprayukta*). This terminology is very convenient. If one wishes to explain it in accordance with the literal text, one may also say:
because the aspect of the object (*ālambana-nimitta*) and the aspect of cognition (*jñāna-nimitta*) are identical, it is said to be associated with the mind;
because the aspect of the object and the aspect of cognition are different, it is said to be dissociated from the mind. The explanation of the meaning is as previously considered and understood.
△ Third, the detailed explanation of their characteristics (in two parts): First, manifesting through comparison with persons; second, identifying the basis of their characteristics.
First, manifesting through comparison with persons:

Furthermore, that which is coarse among the coarse is the realm of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); that which is subtle among the coarse, as well as coarse among the subtle, is the realm of Bodhisattvas.
The realm is the subtlest of the subtle; it is the realm of the Buddhas. [Commentary]:
Regarding "the coarsest of the coarse," the first three types of defiled mind are all termed coarse. Among these, the first—the defilement associated with grasping—is further considered the coarsest.
As for "the realm of ordinary beings," those in the stage of the Three Worthies are called internal ordinary beings (*abhyantara-prthagjana*); they are able to awaken to this defilement.

Therefore, regarding those that are subtle within the coarse: among the three types of coarse defilement, the latter two—namely, the defilement associated with non-interruption (*asamuccheda-saṃprayukta-kleśa*) and the defilement associated with discriminative cognition (*vikalpa-jñāna-saṃprayukta-kleśa*)—are the slightly more subtle of the coarse. Regarding those that are coarse within the subtle:
the latter three types of defiled mind are all termed "subtle. Among these, the first two—namely, the capacity to see and the capacity to manifest—are both... [the same].
Because it is associated [with the mind], it is called "subtle. Because its form follows upon the fundamental karmic consciousness (*mūla-karma-vijñāna*), it is further described as "coarse.
That which is the object of Bodhisattvas refers to the objects of knowledge from the first through the tenth stages (*bhūmi*). That which is "the subtlest among the subtle" is the Buddha’s realm;

it is the defilement dissociated from the fundamental karmic consciousness, in which subject and object are not yet differentiated, and whose mode of activity (*ākāra*) is extremely subtle; therefore, it is realized by the Buddha alone.
[Commentary] That which is called "coarse" in both cases refers to the wisdom of discrimination (*vikalpa-jñāna*) and so forth, as these all arise dependent upon external objects.

Even more coarse are greed, hatred, views, and attachment, because the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self becomes increasingly deep. As for the "inner ordinary beings," they are in fact also within the realm of the Two Vehicles;
however, for the sake of literary convenience, they are omitted here. Regarding the "ten stages" (*daśabhūmi*) and so forth, within that...
From the first stage (*bhūmi*) to the seventh, one awakens to the subtlety within the coarse; from the eighth to the ninth, one awakens to the coarseness within the subtle.

Here, following the general sense, they are simply referred to as the Bodhisattva stages. Regarding the "fundamental" [afflictions] below, the latter three defilements are collectively termed "subtle."
Regarding the aforementioned capacity to see and manifest, this constitutes the most subtle among the subtle characteristics.
Unless one enters the stage of a Tathāgata, one cannot transcend them to perceive the nature of the mind.

△ Second, the identification of the basis for characteristics (in two parts). First, the sequential explanation of the conditions for arising; second, the reverse argument regarding the meaning of cessation.
First, the sequential explanation of the conditions for arising.
[Commentary] Although the sense of "cause" (*hetu*) is present here, it is also considered a "condition" (*pratyaya*) in relation to True Suchness (*tathatā*). Thus, from the subtle to the manifest:
This clarifies their arising; therefore, it is called "sequential exposition.
△ This section has two parts: first, the explanation of universal conditions; second, the manifestation of specific causes. First, the explanation of universal conditions.
These two types of arising and ceasing exist based upon the permeation of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsanā*).
[Commentary: Speaking generally, both the coarse and subtle consciousnesses arise based on the ground of the dwelling of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*).

This is because fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*) stirs up the three subtle states, and based upon these three subtle states, the coarse mind subsequently arises; therefore, it is due to ignorance.
Pervasive ignorance is their root.

[Commentary] Regarding "the fundamental" and so forth: it was previously stated that "due to non-awakening, three kinds of marks arise," and it was further stated that "because there are objective conditions, six kinds of marks arise again.
Although these arise in such a sequential manner, if one investigates...
Its root has ignorance as its basis.
△ Next, the specific causes are revealed:
namely, the causal basis and the conditional basis. The causal basis refers to the meaning of non-awakening; the conditional basis refers to the deluded creation of objective realms.
[Commentary]: To explain this in detail: based on the cause of ignorance, the three subtle, non-associated minds arise;
based on the condition of objective objects, the three coarse, associated minds arise.

[Commentary] The sub-commentary (*śū*) divides this into three parts. First, the text briefly explains the passage: namely, the "phrase" (*pada*) serves as the heading, while from "based on causes" (*hetu*) onwards is the explanation.

This is because each [level] individually investigates its own immediate basis; thus, it should be understood that the three subtle states arise from causes, while the three coarse states arise from conditions (*pratyaya*).
[Commentary] The text here is brief; if it were explained in full, each would have two causes. As the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* says:
"Mahāmati, the inconceivable perfuming and the inconceivable transformation are the causes of the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*).

The grasping of various objects and the perfuming of beginningless false discrimination are the causes of the discriminating consciousness of phenomena (*nirūpaṇa-vastu-vijñāna*). The explanation states: "Inconceivable perfuming" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*).
It can permeate True Suchness (*tathatā*). Because it can permeate that which is not a locus for permeation, it is called "inconceivable permeation.
Furthermore, permeation is itself non-permeation; this permeation of non-permeation is termed "inconceivable permeation.

As for "inconceivable transformation," it refers to the mind of True Suchness receiving the permeation of ignorance (*avidyā*); because it undergoes transformation despite being incapable of transformation, it is called "inconceivable transformation."
Furthermore, transformation is itself non-transformation; this transformation of non-transformation is called "inconceivable transformation.
As stated in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, that which is "stained while unstained, and unstained while stained" and is difficult to comprehend refers precisely to this inconceivability.

However, because this perfuming and transformation are extremely subtle and hidden, the manifest consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) that arises from them has a subtle mode of activity (*ākāra*); within this [manifest consciousness], there is also...

The evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) are coarse and manifest, whereas the subtle is merely termed the "manifesting consciousness" (*darśana-vijñāna*);
this is precisely this non-corresponding mind (*asaṃprayukta-citta*). Regarding "grasping various objects":

these are the various objective realms manifested by the manifesting consciousness, which can in turn stir that ocean of mind, giving rise to the waves of the various functioning consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*). Regarding "perfumed by beginningless false discrimination": this refers to...
Within that ocean of the harmonized mind, the habitual tendencies of deluded thoughts have been perfumed uninterruptedly since beginningless time;
because one has never been free from thought, these objects and thoughts perfume and stir the ocean of the mind, causing various consciousnesses to arise.

Since deluded thoughts and objects are coarse and manifest, the *vijnana* of phenomenal discrimination (*vastu-vikalpa*) that they give rise to possesses coarse and manifest modes of activity. Thus it is established.

[This is] the corresponding mind. [Commentary: Regarding this section below, there are three parts: first, citing the sūtra to provide an extensive explanation; second, indicating what is lacking and what is complete; third, the actual exposition. First, the indication of what is lacking and what is complete:

In the Treatise, the three subtle states lack conditions, while the three coarse states lack causes. In the Sūtra, however, the manifest-consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*) and the object-consciousness (*nimitta-vijñāna*) possess both causes and conditions. Therefore, this indicates [the distinction].
Each has two causes: namely, the mind dissociated from the manifest consciousness (*pratibhāsa-vijñāna*) and the mind associated with the objective consciousness (*vastu-vijñāna*).
Each has two types of causes—the cause of dependence for arising and the condition for abiding—and only then do the fruits of these two consciousnesses arise.
It may also be said that the manifest consciousness and the objective consciousness each have two kinds of causal conditions, as in *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, fascicle 2, section 2.

This directly cites the scriptural passage: "Infusion" (*vāsanā*) refers to the cause as the basis; "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) refers to the condition from which [consciousness] arises. That scripture states:

"The cause as basis refers to the beginningless habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of false conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). The condition as object refers to the objects of discrimination perceived by one's own mind.
These two are the causes of the manifesting consciousness (*nirbhāsavijñāna*), and the manifesting consciousness is the fruit of these two. Yet it is said that this is "inconceivable" (*acintya*).
As for those who deliberate: if [the mind] were exclusively subject to perfuming and transformation, it would be identical to clothing and the like;

this is conceivable and thus becomes the object of perception for ordinary people. If it were exclusively incapable of being perfumed or transformed, it would be like jade or stone; this too would be conceivable.

This would then become what is taught in the provisional teachings. Now, however, it is neither of these two; therefore, it is inconceivable. "Grasping at objects" refers to the condition (*pratyaya*);

"deluded thought" refers to the cause (*hetu*). The Tang translation states: "The phenomenal consciousness (*vṛtti-vijñāna*) takes the discrimination of objects and the habitual tendencies of beginningless conceptual proliferation as its cause.
Thus, one knows that these two are the causes of the phenomenal consciousness, and the phenomenal consciousness is [the result] of these two.

The Result. The commentary below [states]: "Three. Second, the detailed explanation of the meaning of the sutra, in two parts. First, within the subtle [level], there are two causes. Third, the primary explanation:
that is, from the very beginning, the intrinsically pure mind has never been associated with deluded defilement.
Furthermore, the dharma of ignorance is by nature illusory. Now, by means of this illusory dharma, it is able to perfume and stir the essence that is inherently quiescent;
thus, it perfumes that which is a place where perfuming cannot occur. As for "perfuming yet not perfuming," although it perfumes True Suchness (tathatā), the nature of True Suchness remains unmoved.
Moreover, the essence of this ignorance is entirely awakening (bodhi); it is of a single characteristic.

There is no difference. By what means, then, can there be that which perfumes (the perfumer) and that which is perfumed (the perfumed)? Although there is neither the perfumer nor the perfumed, phenomena nevertheless manifest clearly;
therefore, it is called "perfuming without perfuming. This refers to the stage of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Now, as for True Suchness, its meaning is that of being immutable.
Originally, it is not subject to change, yet it undergoes perfuming by ignorance (*avidyā*) and thus becomes subject to transformation. As for the characteristic of this transformation:
This refers precisely to the characteristics of karma and so forth; therefore, it is said that "that which cannot change changes. As for "change is non-change":
although movement manifests as the characteristics of consciousness, its nature is pure and undergoes no alteration.

Although its nature undergoes no alteration, the whole body appears as movement—just as water forms waves while its moist nature remains unchanged. Although the moisture does not change, the whole body becomes movement. Therefore, it is said:

This is the transformation of that which is immutable. (From the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, section two: Citing scriptural evidence. "That which is unstained" refers to what was previously described as being incapable of being perfumed and incapable of being transformed.
"That which is stained" refers to what was previously described as being capable of being perfumed and subject to transformation. However, regarding this [passage] below...
Third, the classification by connection. That which perfumes is the delusion of ignorance; that which is perfumed is the mind of *tathatā*.
Since both the mind and ignorance are devoid of form or characteristics, they are subtle and hidden.

Because the causes and conditions they give rise to are subtle and hidden, the manifested consciousness (*nirmāṇa-vijñāna*) and its modes of activity (*ākāra*) are likewise subtle. Therefore, these three types of defiled minds are all termed "subtle."
Regarding "among the subtle and coarse": if one mentions the subtle, it does not necessarily imply the coarse; however, if one mentions the coarse, its subtle counterpart must necessarily exist.
Furthermore, this manifest consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) is another name for the *ālaya-vijñāna*, which inherently contains the three characteristics (*tri-lakṣaṇa*).

"That is to say, this" concludes that [the preceding] belongs to the non-associated mind (*viprayukta-citta*) within this [category]. Regarding "taking the seeds," etc., next: the two causes within the coarse and the subtle.

First, the formal explanation: "Object" (*viṣaya*) refers to the five sensory objects; "ocean of mind" refers to the *ālaya-vijñāna*; and "waves of consciousness" refers to the *manas* and the other evolving consciousnesses. Thus, the Sūtra says:
"The winds of objects stir the ocean of mind, and various waves of consciousness arise. As stated below:

"Because there are the conditions of delusory objects and defiled dharmas, they permeate the deluded mind, causing it to give rise to attachment and the like. This is false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
Regarding "habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and so forth": these refer to the secondary ignorance (*avidyā*), which belongs to the category of that which is delusively perceived as real.

This ignorance is termed "fundamental" when it first unites with the True [Nature]; once it has reached the stage of forming consciousness (*vijñāna*), it abides within consciousness and is renamed "secondary.
Therefore, this is called the beginningless habitual tendency of deluded thought. This is the object (*viṣaya*).

Regarding the term "and so forth": internally there is ignorance, and externally there are objective realms; when causes and conditions are fully present, the *savisaya-vijnana* (consciousness of objects) arises.

From the phrase "by delusion" onwards, [the text] next concludes the classification: internal permeation refers to the lack of awakening regarding the secondary branches, while external permeation refers to the six sense-objects that are manifested.
Because the causes and conditions that give rise [to it] are already thus coarse and manifest, the resultant consciousness of phenomena (*dharmavijñāna*) is likewise clearly evident.
"Forming a correspondence" refers to the three types of corresponding minds mentioned herein.

[Commentary: In the sutra, it is intended to clarify that the manifest consciousness (*pratibhāsa-vijñāna*) arises by depending on inconceivable perfuming (*vāsana*) and abides by depending on inconceivable transformation (*pariṇāma*).
As for the objective consciousness (*vastu-vijñāna*), it arises by depending on objects and abides by depending on the ocean of mind (*citta-samudra*).

In this treatise, however, only the conditions for arising (*utpatti-pratyaya*) are discussed, while the basis for abiding is not addressed; therefore, regarding the subtle [consciousness], only non-existence (*abhāva*) is mentioned.
This clarifies the "perfuming" (*vāsanā*). Among the coarse [categories], it singles out the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). [Commentary:

Regarding the three points below the sutra passage, this is a comparative analysis of the sutras and the śāstras. First, it clarifies that the sutra is complete. As for "arising and abiding" (*utpāda-sthiti*):

that sutra states, "The various consciousnesses have two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing. Therefore, this [text] here correlates [the categories] with arising and abiding; as for ceasing, it will be clarified below by itself.
Regarding the *pravṛtti-vijñāna* (active consciousness), according to the intent of that sūtra, it should be stated: "It abides by depending on objects; it arises by depending on the ocean of mind.
Within the ocean of mind, the beginningless habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) are the cause for its arising.

From within the ocean of mind, the various active consciousnesses arise, grasping at diverse sensory objects (*viṣaya*); these constitute the conditions for its present abiding. Now, it is said that it arises by depending on objects and depends on the mind.
The phrase "attaining abiding" is an error resulting from transcription. As for the manifest consciousness (*pratibhāsa-vijñāna*):

if it lacked the fundamental non-enlightenment (*mūla-abodhi*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) as its perfuming cause, it would never arise spontaneously; nor would it arise without the objects manifested by one's own mind serving as its supporting conditions.
In the end, they do not abide of themselves; this refers to the three subtle states, which arise and abide according to the causes and conditions of delusion.
Furthermore, while True Suchness cannot be perfumed, it suddenly receives the perfuming of ignorance and thus gives rise [to phenomena].

While True Suchness does not undergo change, it transforms into various objects in accordance with conditions and thus abides. This refers to the three subtle states, which arise and abide based upon the mind of True Suchness.
As for the event-consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*): if it lacks the secondary ignorance as its perfuming cause, it does not arise spontaneously;

if it lacks the external objects of the six sense-fields as its supporting conditions, it does not abide spontaneously. Thus, these three coarse aspects arise and abide according to delusive causes and conditions.
Furthermore, within the ocean of the mind, the habit-energies of beginningless deluded thoughts perfume [the consciousness] without interruption. Therefore—
Birth occurs. The various objective realms manifested within the ocean of the mind cause it to grasp at them; thus, it abides.

These are the three gross aspects that arise and abide based on the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna). It is like waves: without water as their primary cause, they can never arise of themselves;
without wind as their auxiliary condition, they can never abide of themselves. Therefore, the waves of consciousness depend [on the fundamental consciousness].

The mind arises from water and abides by means of the wind of objects. If one were to hold that the wind is the cause for the arising of waves and the water is the condition for their abiding, this would be illogical.
One should know that it is likewise illogical to claim that for the two consciousnesses, the objective realm is the cause of arising and the mental consciousness is the condition for abiding.
To examine this in detail: what follows below clarifies the omissions in the treatise regarding the conditions for arising and the basis for abiding, according to that [text].

In the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, "basis" (*āśraya*) refers to the cause upon which [phenomena] rely; "condition" (*pratyaya*) refers to that from which they proceed. Regarding arising, abiding, and ceasing, all possess causes and conditions.

As the Sūtra states: "When the basis-cause ceases, the continuity ceases; when that from which one proceeds ceases, and when the condition ceases, the continuity ceases. Since this is the case for the causes and conditions of cessation, the causes and conditions of arising and abiding may be understood by analogy.

Now, in this commentary, the basis-cause is paired with arising because it is more convenient for the sense of being "perfumed and activated" by ignorance (*avidyā*); the condition is paired with abiding.

Because the principle of the objective realm’s reinforcement is consistent with reason, the term "conditions for arising" refers exclusively to the arising of the *ālayavijñāna* (present consciousness) based on its causes, and the abiding of the *pravṛttivijñāna* (phenomenal consciousness) following those conditions.

The phrase "not discussing dependence or abiding" means that it does not concern itself with the causal basis for the arising of the phenomenal consciousness, nor with the abiding of the present consciousness following its conditions.
Therefore, the following section concludes by establishing the permeation of ignorance.
The three subtleties depend on the cause of arising. This is because the text states: "The cause is the meaning of non-awakening.
The three gross [evolutions] depend on the condition of objective realms. This is because the text states: "The condition is the meaning of falsely constructing objective realms."
△ Second, the meaning of "contrary" (*ni*) in the term *nirodha* (cessation). [Commentary]:
Generally, when severing delusive defilements, it is logically appropriate to proceed from the coarse to the subtle. Now, this is the reverse of that; hence it is called "contrary.
This is because it is explained solely according to the underlying principle (*tattva*), rather than in relation to the treatment of persons.
△ Within this, there are two parts: first, the formal exposition; second, the resolution of doubts. First, the formal exposition:
If the cause ceases, then the condition ceases. Because the cause ceases, the dissociated mind ceases; because the condition ceases, the associated mind ceases.

[Commentary]: "If [the antidote] arises below" means that when the ignorance (*avidyā*) to be countered is extinguished, the objective realm of the manifest consciousness (*nirbhāsa-vijñāna*) produced by that ignorance is also extinguished accordingly;
this explains extinction in general. "When the cause is extinguished below" specifically clarifies extinction:

because the three subtle states arise in direct dependence on the cause of ignorance, they are also extinguished when ignorance is extinguished. "When the conditions are extinguished below" refers to the three coarse defilements...
The primary support arises dependent upon objective conditions; therefore, when the objective conditions cease, it also ceases accordingly.
This explains the meaning of the two kinds of arising and ceasing by means of the principle of beginning and end, arising and perishing, rather than in terms of momentary arising and ceasing.
[Commentary] Regarding "attaining the antidote" and so forth: ignorance serves as the cause that can produce the three subtle states. The objective realm (*viṣaya*) is one of these three;
furthermore, it can serve as a condition (*pratyaya*) to produce the six coarse states. Since the cause has already been extinguished, upon what could the condition be established?
Therefore, it ceases accordingly. The following passage, beginning with "This is based on the lower [level]," serves to eliminate ambiguity.

Fearing that there might be doubt—namely, that such arising and ceasing refers to the arising and ceasing of every single moment (*kṣaṇa*)—it now distinguishes this. Regarding the terms "beginning" and "end":

in the flow [with the current], the sixth defilement is the beginning and the first defilement is the end; in the reversal [against the current], the first defilement is the beginning and the sixth defilement is the end.

At the end, when it arises, the six defilements are in chaotic confusion, and one wanders through vast eons; at the end, when it ceases, they are all utterly severed in a single thought-moment, reaching ultimate quiescence and permanence.

Furthermore, arising and ceasing are precisely beginning and end. Thus, this refers to the birth and death of continuity and interruption throughout the course of a single lifetime, and is not the same as the birth and death that does not abide for even a single kṣaṇa or thought-moment.
△ Second, the resolution of doubts (in two parts). First, the question; second, the answer. First, the question:
It is asked, "If the mind ceases, how can it continue? If it continues, how can one speak of its ultimate cessation?"

[Commentary: If the substance of the mind were to perish when the objects of perception perish, then since the three subtle stages of ignorance have not yet been exhausted, the substance of the mind would already have vanished.
Upon what further dharma could it rely to achieve continuity? This refers to the mind associated with such doubt.

[Commentary] It was stated above that the mind of arising and ceasing arises based upon the *tathāgatagarbha*. Now it is further said that the mind ceases. If the mind were to cease, then the nature of the *garbha* would also cease.
This objection challenges the specific essence (*tathāgatagarbha*) by means of its general name (“mind”). This refers to the doubt that the substance of the corresponding mind would perish.
If that substance were to perish, one would immediately become a Buddha within the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*). Because...
Because the essence of non-mind serves as the support, the three subtleties cease. Once they have ceased, there are no longer any subtleties to be severed.
Why, then, do the three subtleties still persist now, such that one has not yet attained Buddhahood at the eighth stage?

[Commentary]: If one says that because the essence of the mind is indestructible, it causes ignorance to continue in succession—since the essence of the mind is indestructible, ignorance would then perpetually continue.
How, then, could the path of practice achieve ultimate extinction? This doubt is inconsistent with the nature of the mind.
[Commentary: Because ignorance exists in dependence upon the substance of the mind (*citta-tattva*), and since the substance of the mind is eternal, ignorance is likewise eternal.
Consequently, the three subtle states (*tri-sūkṣma*) which depend upon it cannot be extinguished; this doubt regarding the non-corresponding mind (*asamprayukta-citta*) would never be extinguished.
How, then, can it be said that one enters the Buddha-ground (*buddha-bhūmi*) and is able to ultimately extinguish these three subtle states of mind?
△ Second, the response. [Commentary]: In the response, both of the two preceding difficulties are answered.
△ The text has three parts: first, the principle (*dharma*); second, the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*); third, the application (*upanaya*). First, the principle.
Answer: That which is called "extinction" refers only to the extinction of the mind’s appearances (*citta-lakṣaṇa*), not the extinction of the mind’s essence (*citta-svabhāva*).
[Commentary: When objects (*viṣaya*) are extinguished, it is only the coarse appearances of the mind that are extinguished, not the mind’s own substance.

Furthermore, when ignorance (*avidyā*) is extinguished, it is only the subtle appearances of the mind that are extinguished, nor is the mind’s substance extinguished. This provides a general answer to both questions; the following is an analogy.

If combined, they are explained separately. [Commentary] Previously, the difficulty was raised based on the substance of the mind, namely: "When the mind ceases, its substance also ceases. This current section explains and resolves it based on the characteristics of the substance, namely:

"While the characteristics cease, the substance does not cease. Because the false characteristics are differentiated, the treatise distinguishes between the coarse and the subtle; this refers to the true mind.

There is no differentiation; therefore, it is a single essence. As the *Laṅkāvatāra* says: "The true characteristic of consciousness (the essence-characteristic, which is also the characteristic of the signless) does not perish."

It is only the characteristic of karma (the characteristic of activity, or the characteristic that can be manifested) that ceases; if the true characteristic were to cease, it would not differ from the nihilistic views of the non-Buddhists.
△ Second, the analogy:
Just as wind exists by depending on water and possesses the characteristic of movement, if the water were to cease, the characteristic of wind would be severed and have no basis for support.

Because the water does not cease, the characteristic of wind continues; it is only because the wind ceases that the characteristic of movement follows in cessation, yet this is not the case for the water itself.

"Extinction. [Commentary: "Like wind, etc. is a metaphor for the wind of ignorance. Because it relies upon the water of the mind-substance (*citta-tattva*), it possesses the characteristic of movement.
This demonstrates that ignorance, being separate from the mind-substance, cannot manifest the characteristic of movement on its own. "If the water is extinguished," and so forth, this demonstrates...
If, when objects of perception cease, the substance of the mind were also to cease, then the wind of ignorance would have nothing to stir;

consequently, the three subtle states such as karma would be severed. However, because the substance of the mind does not cease when objects cease, the three subtle states of ignorance are able to continue in succession. This is truly because when ignorance ceases, the objects [of perception]...

It ceases. It is not because the objective realm ceases that ignorance ceases. For this reason, when the objective realm ceases, the ignorance that stirs the mind continues through the three subtle phases.
This answers the first question regarding the meaning of the cessation of the corresponding mind. [The passage] beginning with "Only wind... follows below.
When ignorance is exhausted, the moving characteristics of karma and so forth also perish accordingly; it is not that the essence of the tranquil mind perishes as well.
This answers the latter question regarding the meaning of the cessation of the non-associated mind.

[Commentary] Regarding the passage "The treatise is like the wind" and below: first, this provides a general analogy for how the substance [of consciousness] is established in dependence [upon conditions]. The "fierce wind" metaphorizes the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*);

the "gentle breeze" metaphorizes the cause of ignorance (*avidyā-hetu*). The "movement of great waves" metaphorizes the three coarse defilements; the "movement of small ripples" metaphorizes the three subtle defilements.

All these are characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Water is a metaphor for the essence of the mind (*citta-tattva*), which is the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*. Regarding the mention of ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth in the commentary:

previously, it was doubted whether if the essence of the mind were extinguished, the subtle characteristics of ignorance could not continue; or if the essence of the mind were not extinguished, the subtle characteristics of ignorance would necessarily continue perpetually.
Therefore, [the text] now generally cites the mutual dependence of wind and water, which possesses the characteristic of waves.
This serves as a primary analogy to demonstrate that while the essence of the mind is indestructible, the coarse and subtle aspects of ignorance possess the characteristics of arising and ceasing.
"This shows" (referring to the following passage) clarifies the preceding point through direct affirmation; this [passage] reveals it through negative illustration.

Just as when wind leaves the sea, the appearance of waves ceases, this shows that the arising and ceasing manifested by ignorance appear in dependence upon the Truth (*tathatā*). Therefore, the previous text states: "The mind and ignorance are not mutually separable. (Treatise)

Regarding the water and so forth, there are next two distinct metaphors for the cessation of characteristics while the substance remains. First, the metaphor illustrating the meaning of the cessation of the corresponding mind has two parts.
The first is a negative demonstration (*pratiṣedha*), for which the preceding three phrases must be supplied; the meaning is very clear.

That is to say, when the condition of the violent wind ceases, the characteristic of the waves ceases accordingly, but the seawater does not cease. If the water were to cease, then even with the subtle wind, the signs would be severed and no fine ripples would exist.
Regarding the phrase "the basis" in the commentary, "this indicates," etc., it means that when the fierce wind of the objective realm ceases,
the three coarse waves of defiled mind follow suit in ceasing, yet the water of the mind's essence does not cease. If the water of the mind's essence were also made to cease,
then the subtle wind of ignorance would be unable to stir it, and the characteristics of the three subtle waves would likewise be severed and left without a basis.
The commentary explains this with two lines concerning water. Next, it provides a sequential clarification. Within the sub-commentary (*śū*), there are four parts. First, the direct explanation:

when the objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*) cease, although the associated mental characteristics (*citta-nimitta*) perish, the essence of the mind (*citta-svabhāva*) does not perish. Because it does not perish, the subtle characteristics of ignorance (*avidyā*) [persist].
Both continue in succession. This is like a fierce wind ceasing, whereby the coarse waves cease, yet the substance of the water does not cease;
thus, when a gentle breeze moves it, subtle ripples arise. "Truly, because... and so forth—this next section clarifies the underlying intent. It refers back to the previous statement:

"Because the cause ceases, the condition ceases," which does not mean that "because the condition ceases, the cause ceases. The intent is that the coarse does not encompass the subtle; even the subtle [continues].

It exists. Furthermore, since the substance of the mind does not perish, why doubt its severance? From "By this" downwards, there are three [points] which form the conclusion. This refers to the characteristics of the corresponding mind:
although they perish along with their objects, the subtle characteristics of ignorance do not perish. This answers the fourth point below. It points to the answer;
the preceding text, through reductio ad absurdum, appears to follow the nature of the doubt, restating it and then conceding it. This follows the explicit text.
This is precisely to resolve their doubts by showing the matter directly; therefore, he provides this concluding answer.

Regarding the treatise’s statement that "only wind and so forth" [cease], the subsequent analogy illustrates the meaning of the cessation of the non-associated mental factors (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*). In the commentary (*śū*), first, the text is explained: as for "ignorance and so forth,"...
This is like the cessation of subtle waves due to the cessation of a gentle breeze. As for the statement that "the mind is not stilled," it is because water does not possess the nature of motion;
thus, while the waves cease, the water does not cease. Because the mind does not possess the nature of motion, while the marks of defilement cease, its essential nature does not cease.
As stated in the preceding text: "If the wind ceases and is extinguished, the mark of motion ceases, yet the moist nature is not destroyed. This.
Answer: Next, to conclude the response, [the text] combines [the points].
Ignorance is likewise: it moves in dependence upon the substance of the mind. If the substance of the mind were to cease, then sentient beings would be cut off and non-existent.

As for the basis [of the mind], because its substance does not perish, the mind attains continuity. It is only when delusion (*moha*) ceases that the characteristics of the mind follow and cease; it is not that the wisdom of the mind (*cittajñāna*) ceases.

[Commentary] Regarding the synthesis, the sequence synthesizes the two preceding types of mind. Contemplate this according to the analogy. As for the passage "only delusion," etc., it refers to the preceding text.

Because it is contrasted with non-awakening (*abodha*), it is called awakening (*bodhi*); thus, a single consciousness possesses two meanings. Now, because it is contrasted with delusion (*moha*), it is called wisdom (*jñāna*);
thus, the one mind possesses both essence and appearance. When the appearance of non-awakening and delusion is extinguished, it becomes initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*).
Thus, original enlightenment (benjue) is not extinguished; it is non-dual and indistinguishable from initial enlightenment (shijue) returning to its source.
[Commentary] Regarding the analogy of the thinker, there are also two parts. First, the general application clarifies that the dependent and the substance are established together.

That is to say, the wind of ignorance regarding objective realms depends upon the ocean-water of the mind-substance, whereby there arise the moving marks of coarse and subtle waves of defiled mental states.
If [the text] is divided, the characteristics of extinction and the persistence of the essence are explained separately; this also consists of two parts.
First, combining the analogy and meaning of the extinction of the associated mind (*saṃprayukta-citta*). First, by way of reductio ad absurdum, it supplements the preceding three phrases, stating:

"Because the conditions of objective spheres (*ālambana*) are extinguished, the coarse characteristics of the associated mind are extinguished, but the essence of the mind is not extinguished. If the essence of the mind were extinguished, then the cause of ignorance (*avidyā*) would be severed, and yet sentient beings..."
Regarding the subtle characteristics of the mind that arises in dissociation from the life-faculty: it has no basis of support.

If it were like a fierce wind ceasing and thereby causing the seawater to cease as well, then even the subtle breeze and fine ripples would be utterly without support; how could this possibly be reasonable? O sentient beings!
This refers to the characteristics of the transformation of karma (*karma-pariṇāma-lakṣaṇa*). As stated previously: "Sentient beings revolve in dependence upon mind, thought, and consciousness.

Furthermore, "sentient beings" refers to those sentient beings who revolve in dependence upon the two aspects of the transformation of karma. (To speak precisely, there are only the two aspects of the transformation of karma;

since the objective realm is the manifestation-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and has already ceased, the mention of the "three subtle [transformations]" is a general designation. Thus, from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, all are said to be named after their reliance on the transformation of karma.

Sentient beings: now that the substance of the mind has ceased, sentient beings have no support; therefore, it is said that [the continuity] is severed. From "Because the substance... below, he next explains in accordance with the truth.
This means that because the water of the substance of the mind does not cease, the subtle waves of the fine mind—stirred by the gentle breeze of ignorance—can continue in succession.
Thus, while coarse defilements cease at this time, subtle defilements do not cease; for this reason, Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage have not yet...
"One attains Buddhahood. This answer explains the meaning of the cessation of the associated mind (*saṃprayukta-citta*), corresponding to the initial question. "Only through delusion...

and so forth constitutes the second [section], which combines the metaphor for the cessation of the dissociated mind (*viprayukta-citta*). That is to say, because the subtle wind of ignorance (*avidyā*) ceases, the wave-phenomena of the three subtle defiled minds cease accordingly;
it is not that the ocean-water body of the essence of true wisdom (*tattvajñāna-citta*) also ceases. As stated previously: "If ignorance ceases, the continuity..."

[The characteristics of karma, etc.,] then cease; yet the nature of wisdom (*jñāna*) is indestructible. Therefore, when the subtle defilements of ignorance (*avidyā*) are exhausted at the stage of Buddhahood, the essence of wisdom remains pure and is not lost.

"Delusion" (*moha*) is ignorance; it corresponds to the characteristic of movement associated with wind. "Wisdom" is the essence of awakening; it corresponds to the nature of moisture associated with water.
This response explains the meaning of the cessation of the non-corresponding mind (*viprayukta-citta*) mentioned in the subsequent question. [From the *Śāstra*].

The phrase "the aforementioned text" and so forth serves to correlate and explain the two characters *moha* (delusion) and *jñāna* (wisdom). "The aforementioned text" refers to the initial passage of the *Samsara-dvāra* (Gate of Arising and Ceasing).
The meaning of the awakening of consciousness (*vijñāna*) in the aforementioned text is precisely the essence of wisdom (*jñāna*) of the present mind;

the meaning of the non-awakening of consciousness in the aforementioned text is precisely the characteristic of delusion (*moha*) of the present mind. The reason for providing this correlation and explanation is that [it clarifies] the preceding treatise on arising...
Therefore, regarding a single consciousness, two meanings are clarified: first, awakening (*bodha*); second, non-awakening (*abodha*).

Now, in terms of extinguishing delusions and returning to the ultimate state, these two meanings must be integrated into the one mind. Thus it is said that the characteristic of the delusion of non-awakening is transformed into the essence of the wisdom of awakening.
That which constitutes initial awakening is identical to the aforementioned ultimate awakening; it is the characteristic of the purity of wisdom, wherein the Dharma emerges.

Regarding the meaning of "separating from the mirror and so forth": previously, one was deluded regarding the One Mind, thereby forming the nine appearances; now, one extinguishes the nine appearances to return to the One Mind.
There is nothing that does not flow from the Dharma-realm, and there is nothing that does not return to this Dharma-realm.

As for "returning to the source where there is no duality," the Sūtra says: "When birth and extinction have ceased, quiescent extinction manifests before one; the beginning and the fundamental are non-dual. It is only...
"The mind is present in one place.
[Commentary] Furthermore, this is a text combining the metaphor with the doctrine; it may also be explained as a comprehensive response within the doctrinal section.

The first seven phrases demonstrate that the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are established based on the substance (*dravya*) to clarify the meaning. The final three phrases clarify that while the characteristics perish, the substance remains, thereby resolving potential objections. First, the explanation:
In response to the first question, regarding the meaning of the cessation of the corresponding mind, it is said:
The wind of objective conditions depends upon the seawater of the mind’s essence, wherein there arise the three types of coarse waves of consciousness as their moving aspect.

If the seawater of the mind’s essence were to cease, then the fierce wind of objective conditions would be cut off, and the three types of coarse waves of sentient beings would have no basis for existence. However, because the seawater of the mind’s essence does not cease, the objective conditions [continue].

The waves of the mind, corresponding to the violent wind, continue in succession; however, because the violent wind—the objective conditions of the darkness of ignorance—is extinguished, the three types of coarse, defiled mental waves are extinguished accordingly, but the ocean-water of the essence of wisdom does not cease.
Next, he explains the meaning of the cessation of the non-corresponding mind in response to the subsequent question, stating:
"With ignorance as the causal wind, there are the three subtle [waves] based upon the ocean-water of the essence of the mind."

The characteristic of the waves of defiled movement is such that if the water-body of the mind were to perish, then the subtle wind of ignorance would be severed, and the wave-characteristics of the three subtleties of sentient beings would have no basis for support.
Because the water-body of the mind does not perish, the wave-characteristics of the mind continue in conjunction with the subtle wind of ignorance.
Only when the wind of the cause of ignorance—the darkness of delusion—is extinguished do the three subtleties cease.
The waves of defilement subside along with their characteristics, yet there is no cessation of the ocean-water of the mind, which is the essence of wisdom.

The commentary provides a specific explanation because it directly addresses the points raised in the questions; because it offers a profound interpretation in accordance with the meaning of the text; and because the text itself contains these distinct meanings.
Furthermore, the record provides a general explanation in accordance with the intent of the *Sūtra-ṭīkā* regarding the analogy of the Dharma, so as to make the shallow aspects easy to understand.

Because it is explained in the *Upāyikā* (Commentary), and because the text can be interpreted as providing a comprehensive answer, the reader may choose what to accept or reject according to their own judgment.
△ Second, the mutual support of the defiled and the pure.

[Commentary]: It is also said that the defiled and the pure mutually permeate (*vāsanā*) one another, giving rise to each other in an uninterrupted succession. This reveals that within the aforementioned general category, there is that which is capable of producing.
This refers to the meaning of all phenomena (*dharma*).
[Record] Regarding "mutually assisting" (*xiāngzī*): *zī* means to take up; it carries the sense of relying upon. This means that defiled phenomena and pure phenomena cannot arise by themselves;
they must mutually take up one another’s power as a condition of reliance, only then being able to arise.
Therefore, furthermore, "support" (*zī*) means the sense of mutual benefit; that is, they mutually assist one another so as to give rise to both defilement and purity.

Since the preceding section merely clarified the meaning of arising and ceasing within the respective states of defilement and purity, it did not yet extensively explain the modes of activity (*xingxiang*) by which defiled and pure phenomena arise.
Now, this is explained: the intent is to clarify that defilement and purity mutually rely upon one another and mutually assist one another.
Furthermore, they give rise to all phenomena. Just as defilement assists purity and purity relies upon defilement, then pure phenomena flow with the current, giving rise to various defiled phenomena.
When purity assists defilement and defilement relies upon purity, then defiled phenomena flow against the current, giving rise to various pure phenomena.
Although they are fundamentally opposed, they conversely become mutually compliant; thus, defiled and pure phenomena rely upon one another in alternation.
Regarding "mutual perfuming" (*xiūn*): "mutual" (*hù*) means reciprocal; "perfuming" (*xiūn*) means striking and activating, which is synonymous with "arising.

This refers to the reciprocal arising and activation that causes the defiled and pure [dharmas] to continue without interruption. Thus, while the names differ, the meaning is the same. As for "arising through mutual production," this is precisely mutual perfuming.
Regarding "without interruption," this is discussed from the perspective of a single lifetime (*yīqī*); in reality, the pure dharmas do not... [continue].
Regarding "cessation": defiled phenomena indeed have cessation. The meaning of cessation and non-cessation is as analyzed below.

As for "that which can produce" and so forth, this refers to what was stated at the beginning of the Section on Arising and Ceasing: "This consciousness has two meanings: it can encompass all phenomena and give rise to all phenomena.

The previous section has already clarified the meaning of "encompassing," which is the passage concerning the two types of awakening (*buddhi*). Here, we are specifically analyzing the meaning of "giving rise to."

[This explains] the meaning. Therefore, it is said that they mutually support one another. Question: Why is the meaning of "inclusion" (*saṃgraha*) explained first, and the meaning of "arising" (*utpāda*) explained later?
Answer: Because the meaning of inclusion is primary, it is explained first; because the meaning of arising is the cause for that inclusion, it is placed afterward.

Therefore, in the section on the establishment of the doctrine (立義分), it is said only that [the *ālayavijñāna*] "is able to encompass" (*śaknoti saṃgrahītum*), and not that it "is able to produce" (*janayati*).

(1) Alternatively, there may be the suspicion that [phenomena] arise from non-existence and are only then encompassed; the present intention clarifies that the *ālayavijñāna* has never failed to produce, nor has it ever failed to encompass.
Thus, between encompassing and producing, there is ultimately no sequence of before and after. (2) Or, it may be that the meaning of "encompassing" [is intended].

This does not limit itself to the preceding text; rather, it encompasses this single gate of arising and ceasing, wherein all defilement and purity are subsumed under the meaning of the two types of awakening, leaving nothing unexhausted (3).
The text consists of four sections: first, a general introduction by enumerating the number; second, an inquiry and listing of individual names; third, the perfuming of defilement and purity;
and fourth, the clarification of exhaustion and non-exhaustion. First, the general introduction by enumerating the number.
Furthermore, because there are four kinds of dharmas that function through the principle of perfuming (*vāsanā*), defiled and pure dharmas arise in an uninterrupted succession.
[Commentary: Because these defiled and pure dharmas mutually support one another, they arise in an uninterrupted succession.
△ Second, the interrogation and enumeration of the specific names.
What are the four? First, pure phenomena are termed *tathatā* (suchness). Second, all causes of defilement are termed ignorance (*avidyā*).
Third, the deluded mind is termed the karma-consciousness (*karmavijñāna*). Fourth, the deluded objects, namely the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).
[Commentary] “What is it? This is an interrogative inquiry. First, “one” is an enumeration. This refers to the *tathatā* (Suchness) within the gate of arising and ceasing.

Because it possesses three meanings, it is called "pure phenomena" (*śukla-dharma*). First, with respect to its essence (*svabhāva*), it is pure from the very beginning. Second, with respect to its essence and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), because of internal permeation (*paribhāvana*), it causes one to turn away from defilement and achieve initial purity.
Thus, the *Liang* translation of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "That which is able to establish [it] is called *tathatā*..."
Regarding the ten kinds of merit that are established, this refers to the ten kinds of newly arisen correct practices. Third, concerning the perfuming by function:
