For now, this section has been established provisionally by way of contrast with delusive phenomena; it must not be grasped as definitive, for it is likewise of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
△ Second, the clarification of the meaning indicated.
[Commentary] This clarifies that the aforementioned dharmas possess the functional capacity to manifest meaning. Question:

For what reason is the meaning indicated not analyzed within the Gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*), whereas it is fully analyzed as the three great meanings within the Gate of Arising and Ceasing? Answer: Because of True Suchness...

In the Gate of Non-arising (the True Suchness Gate), the essence of the Mahāyāna is revealed; subject and object are not divided, and the expression and its meaning are not distinct; therefore, they are not treated separately.
In the Gate of Arising and Ceasing, defilement and purity are not identical, and there are differences in both phenomena and their meanings; therefore, the three [aspects] are explained in full.

In the preceding "Section on Establishing the Meaning," it was stated as "revealing" within the True Suchness Gate and as "capable of revealing" within the Gate of Arising and Ceasing; the explanation of these meanings follows.
This is it. [Commentary] "The preceding dharmas" refers to the previously categorized dharmas of arising and ceasing minds.

Since the distinct modes of arising and ceasing for both defiled and pure dharmas have already been clearly explained, these dharmas of arising and ceasing consequently manifest the functional capacities of the three great natures (trisvabhāva). Therefore, now...

This refers to it. The question below is fully explained as in the "Section on Establishing the Meaning" (*Liyi fen*). Regarding "that which expresses the purport": "expression" (*quan*) means that which is able to express;

it is the explicit explanation of the meaning. As the *Shuowen jiezi* states: "Expression (*quan*) means 'to possess' (*ju*)," because it means to fully explain both phenomena (*shi*) and principle (*li*).

Now, in this single gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*), the gate is the expresser (*nengquan*) and the essence (*ti*) is the expressed (*suochuan*). Since the gate itself is designated as True Suchness, [True Suchness...]
This is precisely the intended meaning to be expressed; therefore, the gate and the essence are non-dual and without distinction.
As for the distinct meanings of the dharmas, these refer to the three great aspects of the one mind, all of which have already been explained in the "Section on Establishing the Meaning."
△ The text has two parts: first, the explanation of the two greatnesses of essence and characteristic; second, the detailed explanation of the single greatness of function.

First, the explanation of the two greatnesses of essence and characteristic (2): first, the general presentation of the names of the two greatnesses; second, the specific explanation of the meanings of the two greatnesses. First, the general presentation of the names of the two greatnesses.
Furthermore, regarding the essential nature and characteristics (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*) of True Suchness (*tathatā*):
[The *Sūtra-śāstra*] states that "essential nature and characteristics" refers to the greatness of essence (*tattva-mahattva*) and the greatness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-mahattva*).

The Section on Establishing the Meaning (*Arthavyavasthāpana*) says: "It can demonstrate the essential nature, characteristics, and functions of the Mahāyāna. It further states: "That which is called 'meaning'..."
This [subject] possesses three great meanings: essence (*tǐ*), characteristic (*xiàng*), and function (*yòng*). Therefore, this text introduces them by saying, "its own essence and characteristic.
II. Separate Explanation of the Two Great Meanings (in two parts): first, essence; second, characteristic. First, essence.
All ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas are without increase or decrease;
they are not born in the past limit and do not perish in the future limit, being ultimately eternal and constant.

[Commentary]: From "All" onwards: although people are distinguished as superior or inferior according to their respective positions, the true essence (dharmatā) follows these individuals without ever increasing or decreasing.

"Not of the prior limit" means it is eternal; the stage of ordinary beings constitutes the prior limit. "Not of the posterior limit" means it is constant; the stage of Buddhahood constitutes the posterior limit.
These three phrases all clarify the reason why there is neither increase nor decrease.
[Commentary] "All" refers to both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*). "Ordinary beings" refers to the six realms of ordinary beings, that is, all *iśvaja* (worldlings).
"Śrāvakas and below" refers to the four realms of the noble ones. This reveals the equality of *tathatā* (suchness):

from the ordinary to the noble, whether Great or Small Vehicle, whether cause or fruit, they are of one essence without difference. The delusion of ordinary beings has never diminished; the awakening of noble ones has never increased.
The same principle applies to causes and effects, whether small or large. Furthermore, when defilement arises, it does not increase; when obstructions are exhausted, it does not decrease.

Moreover, when its function is latent, it does not diminish; when its virtues are manifest, they do not increase. Nevertheless, this essence is great and pervades both the sentient and the insentient; thus the Sūtra says:
"All causes and effects, and even the finest dust motes of the world, take their substance from the mind. For now, we shall speak specifically in terms of sentient beings.

[Commentary] "Superior" (*yu*) means preeminent. This refers to the fact that while Buddhas are most superior and ordinary beings are most inferior, when compared with those in between, all may be categorized as either superior or inferior.
Regarding "the true essence and so forth": this refers to the causal nature of the inherent virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*). It is like the great void;

although there are differences between a thatched hut and a blue-tiled palace, how could the empty space within them possibly be distinct? Therefore, the *Heart Sūtra* says: "All these phenomena are empty."
Characteristics: neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing.

Regarding the phrase "identical to the stage of ordinary beings," this clarifies that the essence of this Dharma is not something that arises from non-existence within the preceding stage of ordinary beings, nor is it something that passes from existence into non-existence within the subsequent stage of Buddhahood.
Nevertheless, when discussed in its ultimate sense, the stage of ordinary beings and True Suchness are both—
There is no prior limit (*pūrvakoṭi*). This does not mean that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) themselves possess a prior limit;

rather, true nature (*tathatā*) has no prior limit, and the state of Buddhahood is likewise so. Therefore, the subsequent text states: "Because the *tathāgatagarbha* has no prior limit, the characteristic of ignorance (*avidyā*) also has no beginning.
Because the *tathāgatagarbha* has no posterior limit (*aparākoṭi*), the *nirvāṇa* realized by all Buddhas is identical to it."
If this were the case, there would be no future limit (*aparānta*). Furthermore, one may speak without reference to specific stages;
it simply means that [the cycle] is exhausted in the past, yet does not arise from a prior limit (*pūrvānta*), and is scrutinized in the future, yet does not cease into a subsequent limit.
"Limit" (*jì*) means "time. This does not mean that there is no before or after; rather, it reveals the true essence (*zhēntǐ*), which neither arises nor ceases within the limits of before and after.
In the past, during the state of delusion, its arising is not perceived, for it is truly eternal.

In the future, after the realization of awakening, its cessation is not perceived, for it is truly constant and everlasting. Furthermore, "constant" (*cháng*) and "everlasting" (*héng*) have the same meaning. (Commentary)
The specific assignments within the middle [section] are likewise merely provisional. "All manifest" means that they may neither increase nor decrease; they are not subject to arising or ceasing.

This is because they all manifest the reason for being eternally constant. Furthermore, only that which is neither born nor extinguished is without increase or decrease, being ultimately eternal and constant.
If there were arising and ceasing, there would be increase and decrease, and it would not be eternal and constant. Moreover, the phrase "eternal and constant" is...

This reveals that it is neither defiled nor pure. That is to say, while remaining within the entanglements (*saṃkleśa*), it is not defiled; yet upon emerging from the obstructions (*āvaraṇa*), it is not pure.
If it were otherwise, there would be change and transformation; how then could it be called eternal and constant? Furthermore, because it is as it was, there is no increase or decrease;
because it is true, it is neither born nor extinguished. The final phrase is a summary. Moreover, these three meanings are identical to the preceding text: "Ultimately equal, without change."
It is distinct; it cannot be destroyed. These are paired with the following in order.

△ Second, the characteristics (two parts). First, the direct manifestation of the qualities of nature; second, the further clarification through question and answer. First, the direct manifestation of the qualities of nature (two parts).

First, the manifestation of the marks of clarity; second, the manifestation of the establishment of names. First, the manifestation of the marks of clarity (three parts). First, the general [explanation]; second...
It is distinct. Regarding the three fetters: the first is general.
"From the beginning" indicates that there has been no starting point; "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva) indicates that it is not something external to the essence.
[Commentary] It is said "from the beginning" to manifest that there is no commencement. It is said "intrinsic nature" to distinguish it from being something outside the substance.
Because there is no deficiency or lack, it is called "fulfilled. Because the intention is to encompass all universally, it is called "all.
Because it refers to efficacious power and meritorious deeds, it is called "merit" (*guṇa*).
△ Second, the specific [explanation].
That is to say, as for its essential nature (*svabhāva*), it possesses the meaning of the radiance of great wisdom; the meaning of universally illuminating the *dharmadhātu*;

the meaning of true and authentic cognition; the meaning of the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-viśuddha-citta*); and the meaning of permanence, bliss, self, and purity (*nitya-sukha-ātman-śubha*). It is cool and...
Regarding the meaning of mastery over transformation: [The Commentary] states there are six points:
first, the luminous wisdom of original enlightenment; second, the manifest illumination of all phenomena by original enlightenment; third, the absence of error at the time of such illumination;
fourth, the nature being free from the defilement of afflictions; fifth, the nature’s virtues being perfectly complete; and sixth, the nature’s virtues being immutable.

[Commentary] Regarding "Great Wisdom" (*mahājñāna*) and so forth: this has both general and specific meanings. Generally, wisdom (*jñāna*) is itself discernment (*prajñā*), and light (*āloka*) is itself radiance (*prakāśa*).

Furthermore, wisdom and discernment are themselves light and radiance. Specifically, it is termed "wisdom" when designated by its meaning (*artha*), and called "light" when apprehended through its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Wisdom is the essence (*svabhāva*); discernment is the function (*vṛtti*); light is the characteristic of the essence; and radiance is... [the characteristic of the function].

This refers to its characteristic as it is actually employed. It is like a *maṇi* jewel: its substance possesses radiance; that which is self-refined is called "light" (*ābhāsa*), and that which illuminates objects is called "clarity" (*prakāśa*).
That which pervades both the ordinary and the sagely is called "great" (*mahat*). That which is manifested according to the principle is called "meaning" (*artha*).

Furthermore, the term "intrinsic substance" (*svabhāva*) is used to show that this is the characteristic of the substance itself, for there is no duality or distinction between them. The *Śāstra* states: "The wisdom-clarity of original enlightenment," thereby distinguishing it from [other forms of light].
The light of the wisdom of initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*) likewise takes only the general sense. Regarding "pervasive illumination" and so forth, this refers precisely to initial enlightenment.

There are two aspects of the *dharmadhātu*: namely, principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*). When initial enlightenment illuminates principle, it is the wisdom that accords with reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*); when initial enlightenment illuminates phenomena, it is the wisdom that discerns phenomena (*prajñapti-vyavasthāna-jñāna*).
This refers to the wisdom of knowing things as they are (*yathābhūta-jñāna*). Because it discerns both principle and phenomena with equal clarity, it is called "pervasive.

The *Śāstra* states that "original enlightenment" (*mūla-awakening*) is spoken of in terms of its essence; yet, from the perspective of the manifest illumination of that very original enlightenment, it is termed "initial awakening" (*ādi-awakening*). Such is the essence of initial awakening.

Because it is fundamentally original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya*). Regarding "truth" (*tattva*) and so forth: that which arises based on the sense faculties in the aspect of cognizing objects is termed "cognition" (*vijñāna*).

Because it cognizes reality as it is and is forever free from all faults, it is called "true. In the commentary, "non-erroneous" (*aviparyāsa*) refers to being free from the four inversions as well as other attachments and conceptualizations.
Regarding "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) and so forth: because it does not depend on other conditions, it is called "self-."
Its nature is unstained while enmeshed in bondage; therefore, it is called "pure. That which is the reality among all phenomena is what is termed "mind.

The commentary states that it is "free from defilement," meaning that its nature is fundamentally free from defilement and has been devoid of delusion since the beginning. Regarding "permanence, bliss, self, and purity": "permanence" means remaining unchanged throughout the three periods of time;
"bliss" means being unmoved by the midst of manifold sufferings; "self" means abiding within the six realms of existence [without being subject to them].
"Unrestricted and pure" means that although one passes through the nine stages of meditative transformation (*navasaṃjñā*), one remains undefiled;

these are the four virtues of *svabhāva-nirvāṇa*. Regarding "perfectly complete": although there are many virtues, they do not exceed these four, for all virtues are subsumed within these four dharmas.
"Intrinsic virtue" (*prakṛti-guṇa*) distinguishes them from "cultivated virtue" (*bhāvanā-guṇa*). "Pure and cool," etc., refers to the absence of the feverish affliction of delusion.
Therefore, it is called "cool and serene. This reveals *prajñā* (wisdom). Because there is no arising or ceasing through retribution, it is called "unchanging";
this is the *dharmakāya*. Because there is no bondage through karma, it is called "sovereign freedom"; this is *vimukti* (liberation).
Thus, by departing from the three obstacles, one accomplishes the three virtues (*triguṇa*). The commentary states "no transition," which merely cites one of the meanings among these three.
△ Third, the summary:

Because they are fully endowed with such qualities— more numerous than the sands of the Ganges— which are inseparable from, uninterrupted by, and non-different from the one inconceivable Buddha-dharma,
and because they fulfill it completely without any deficiency in meaning.

[Commentary: "Not separate" means that the sands-of-the-Ganges virtues of the nature do not depart from the true essence. "Uninterrupted" means they have continued in succession since beginningless time.

"Not different" means they share the same flavor as the essence. "Inconceivable" means that while they are not different [from the essence], they possess the significance of being as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
"Buddha-dharma" refers to that which only a Buddha has fully realized; it may also be understood as the dharmas that are to be awakened to, and so forth.
[Response: Below. If this true essence lacked the virtue of nature, the Tathāgata, upon realizing it, would not be endowed with all virtues.
Since he has realized its nature and all myriad virtues are now perfected, this verifies that True Suchness is inherently possessed [of these virtues].
[Commentary] "Exceeding the sands of the Ganges" was only briefly indicated above and could not be recorded in full; therefore, it is now summarized here to demonstrate its vast abundance.
"Not separate" means that by citing any single virtue, one fully encompasses the true nature (*tathatā*) and all virtues.
"Uninterrupted" means having no beginning and no end. "Not different" means that suchness (*tathatā*) is itself the virtues, and the virtues are themselves suchness. The above...

"Non-separation" is like a hand not being separate from the wrist, or a fruit not being separate from the tree. This is distinct from the "non-separation" of that which is not a tree [not being separate] from the ground.

This [non-separation] is non-differentiation, just as sweetness is not different from the fruit, or saltiness is not different from water (the saltiness of seawater is inherent; it is not like salt being placed into water).

To distinguish [the milk] from that which is not water, yet is not different from it (the milk within water is likewise not different). Furthermore, one distinguishes by means of four propositions: 1.
Separated yet not different, as when various vessels hold water. 2. Different yet not separated, as in the case of compounded medicinal pills. 3.
Both separated and different, as when the wind and the cattle of the Hu and the Niu do not reach one another. 4. Neither separated nor different, as in the case of...
"The fragrance and flavor of the red lotus flower" refers to that which is inconceivable: it is many meanings within a single nature, and a single nature within many meanings;
it cannot be apprehended by fixed measures, for it is where mental activity ceases and the path of language is cut off.
The commentary states, "that is not different," which means that among the three [aspects], one meaning is cited to illuminate the others by implication. As for "the Buddha-dharma":
"Buddha" means "Awakening. This clarifies that the aforementioned merits are entirely the dharma of original awakening (*prakṛti-awakening*). Thus, the *Vajra* [Sūtra] states:
"All dharmas are Buddha-dharmas. Regarding the commentary's phrase "only the Buddha," etc., the character "Buddha" is explained here in terms of initial awakening (*ādikṣaya-awakening*).
This means that the Buddha is the ultimate state of initial enlightenment (*ādikṣaya-bodhi*). "Dharma" refers to the aforementioned various merits;

because these dharmas are fully realized not at the stage of a causal practitioner but as the final consummation, they constitute the Dharma of the Buddha. As for the "dharmas that are realized," the character for "Buddha" (*buddha*) is explained in terms of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-bodhi*).

The Buddha is, in essence, the Dharma. The meaning is as explained previously. Because he transcends those sands of the Ganges, it says "even unto" (乃至). "Fulfillment" (滿足) means there is nothing lacking;
the intent is that even the principles and meanings exceeding the number of sands of the Ganges are all completely fulfilled, with nothing deficient.

In the commentary, from "If thus" (*ru ci*) onwards, the nature is revealed through cultivation; this is a negative demonstration (*pratiṣedha*). From "Since realized" (*ji zheng*) onwards, it is a positive demonstration (*anvaya*).
Commentary: It is like a jewel in the ocean that others do not know exists; once those who have traveled the sea have obtained it, how could bystanders fail to believe it?
△ Next, the establishment of the title is revealed.
It is called the *tathāgatagarbha* (Tathāgata-womb), and it is also called the *tathāgatadharmakāya* (Tathāgata-dharma-body).

[Commentary] As for the *tathāgatagarbha*, when it is in a state of concealment, it is capable of giving birth to the Tathāgata; as for the *dharmakāya*, when it is in a state of manifestation, it is the locus of reliance for all myriad virtues.

[Commentary] The *tathāgatagarbha* possesses three meanings: first, the meaning of being concealed; second, the meaning of containing; and third, the meaning of giving birth. These are explained in detail as previously stated.
Regarding the phrase "at the time of concealment" and so forth, it seems to correspond to the latter two of these meanings; because it is concealed, it is called a "garbha" (womb/store).

This refers to the Tathāgata’s intentional concealment and non-manifestation. Furthermore, it is called a "treasury" (*garbha*) because the ground of cultivation (*bhūmi*) can give rise to the merits of the ground of fruition.
Regarding the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata: if one takes the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) as the Tathāgata, then the term is explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.
If the true body (*dharmakāya*) is taken as the Tathāgata, it is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. Furthermore, this "body" (*kāya*) also possesses three meanings:

first, the sense of essence (*svabhāva*), because the self-essence of true suchness (*tathatā*) maintains itself without loss; second, the sense of basis (*āśraya*), because it serves as the support for the recompense and transformation bodies;
and third, the sense of accumulation (*caya*), because it is the gathering place of all meritorious qualities. Therefore...

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The meaning of substance (*tattva*), basis (*āśraya*), and collection (*caya*) is collectively termed 'body' (*kāya*). Regarding the phrase "manifesting time and so forth," this refers to the latter meaning.

That is to say, the myriad virtues are called "dharmas," and they rely upon the "body. Now, these virtues consist of both those acquired through cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and those inherent by nature (*prakṛti*).

If explained in terms of cultivation, they pertain to the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) and *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body), thereby fulfilling the sense of being a basis. If explained in terms of nature, this is the *dharmakāya* (dharma-body); it carries the meaning of a collection.
Furthermore, as for the meaning of its essence (*tattva*), this has already been addressed within the preceding section on essence; therefore, it is not discussed here. Question:
Since the *dharmakāya* belongs to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and is not an accumulation, why speak of "accumulation"? Answer:

Since these merits are the "many" within the "non-many," what prevents accumulation from being the accumulation of non-accumulation? All of these are explained according to their meaning, revolving perfectly without obstruction.
This is not a collection of real dharmas; there is something that can be selected [from it].

△ Second, the question-and-answer section for further clarification (in two parts): First, the objection based on doubt regarding the characteristics while clinging to the substance; second, the response clarifying that the characteristics do not contradict the substance.
First, the objection concerning the nature and characteristics of the essence:
A question is asked: "It was stated above that the essence of True Suchness (tathatā) is equal and free from all characteristics;
why, then, is it further said that this essence possesses such various kinds of meritorious qualities?"
[Commentary] "The above explains what follows" means it builds upon what precedes. In the preceding section, it was stated:

"From the very beginning, it is free from the characteristics of verbal expression, free from the characteristics of names, and free from the characteristics of mental objects; it is ultimately equal, without change or variation, and indestructible;
it is solely the one mind, and is therefore called *tathatā* (Suchness). "How so? below this initiates the objection. This refers to the aforementioned freedom from characteristics.
[The text states: "Equal. Now, to explain the distinctions of merit [is to say that] the preceding and succeeding [statements] are contradictory; where, then, lies the meaning?

Furthermore, this doubt may also be addressed by referring to the two passages on essence (*tattva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), as well as the arising of the two great [aspects of] essence and characteristics within the previous section on establishing the doctrine.
Within the essence, how can it be devoid of characteristics, without increase or decrease, and without arising or ceasing? Within the characteristics, how can they be complete...?
Virtue. Is it not the case that it exceeds the sands of the Ganges and lacks nothing?
△ Second, the answer that the characteristics do not contradict the essence (in two parts): first, clarifying that although there are distinctions, they are non-dual;
second, clarifying that although they are non-dual, there are distinctions. First, clarifying that although there are distinctions, they are non-dual.
The answer is: Although these various meanings of merit truly exist, they lack any characteristics of differentiation;

they are equal in a single flavor, being nothing other than True Suchness (tathatā). Why is this so? Because they are non-discriminative and free from the marks of discrimination, they are therefore non-dual.
[Commentary]: Although the real virtues are many, they share the single flavor of Suchness (*tathatā*). What does this mean? It asks why multiple virtues are only one.
The answer begins with "Because there is no... This explains that [Suchness] is neither the subject that discriminates nor the object that is discriminated.
"Because there is neither subject nor object.
[Commentary] In the response, there are two parts. First, the direct clarification: although the phrase "though in reality," etc., concedes the existence of subsequent differentiated characteristics.
The phrase "without equal" does not contradict the previously mentioned meaning of equality. "Equal" (等) means "uniform" (齊); it refers to the phenomena of differentiation.

"Identical" (同) means that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature and are but a single true essence. "One flavor" (一味) is clarified by analogy: like the eight qualities of water, they are of one flavor without distinction.
"One truth" (一真) is explained in terms of the Dharma: it means that both essence and appearance, in sum, are but the single truth.
As with the nature of the mind, this [passage] clarifies both the principle and the analogy. Regarding this meaning, there follow two further explanations. First, the objection is raised:
"Because it is without... and so forth. Second, the response is given: "It is not the agent," meaning there is no essence that performs the act of discerning;
"it is not the object," meaning there is no characteristic that is the object of discernment. Therefore, the preceding text states: "When the mind ceases, the manifold [phenomena]..."
The Dharma ceases. That there is neither subject nor object arises because the preceding mind and its objects have both vanished;
since essence and appearance are not distinct, differentiation is itself non-differentiation, identical to the single flavor of the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
△ Second, clarifying that although they are non-dual, there are distinctions (in two parts). First, the brief explanation; second, the detailed explanation. First, the brief explanation:
Furthermore, by what principle can one speak of distinctions? It is because they are manifested through the marks of arising and ceasing based on the *karmic consciousness*.

[Commentary] "Furthermore, below": Since they are non-dual, why speak of distinctions? "Below" refers to the fact that by relying on the characteristics of the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), the *saṃsāric* dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are presented;
conversely, this represents the pure virtues of *tathatā* (suchness) as having distinctions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
For now, citing the root of the defiled, it simply mentions "karmic consciousness" (*karma-vijñāna*).

[Commentary] The first two phrases pose a challenge. "Since they are equal" means that because both subject and object have vanished, resulting in a single essence without duality, upon what basis are the previously mentioned differentiated characteristics ultimately established for the sake of explanation?

The following two phrases provide the resolution. "Because it relies on... refers to what was stated previously: "This is the characteristic of the mind’s arising and ceasing through causes and conditions."
Because it is able to demonstrate the essence, characteristics, and functions of the Mahāyāna, that which manifests is numerous and that which is manifested is vast;

both are likened to the sands of the Ganges. To introduce the following objection: "In contrast to the *saṃkleśa*-dharmas [defiled phenomena], which are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one speaks of pure virtues [guṇas] as being as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
For what reason does the treatise mention only the karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*)? Therefore, the commentary explains: "If the root is cited, the branches manifest of themselves.
It can thus be understood that this includes all defiled phenomena as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

△ II. Extensive Explanation (2). First, the question regarding the manner of representation in relation to defiled phenomena; second, the individual presentation of those defiled phenomena in contrast [to their opposites].
First, the question regarding the manner of representation in relation to defiled phenomena.
How is this shown?
[Commentary] How is it that these characteristics of the karmic consciousness are reversed to manifest the pure virtues of True Suchness (tathatā), which exceed the sands of the Ganges?
△ Second, each of those defiled phenomena is raised to be contrasted with its counterpart.
Because all phenomena are fundamentally mind-only and truly devoid of thought, yet there is a deluded mind;

because one fails to realize this and gives rise to thoughts, perceiving various objective realms, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*). When the nature of the mind does not give rise [to thoughts], this is precisely the meaning of the radiance of great wisdom.
If the mind gives rise to views, then there is the characteristic of non-seeing; when the nature of the mind is free from views, it is the universally illuminating Dharma.

Because of the meaning of the *dhātu* (element/realm): if the mind is subject to movement, it is not true cognition; it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and is neither permanent, nor blissful, nor self, nor pure.
It is characterized by feverish affliction and decay, and thus lacks sovereignty. To this extent, it possesses meanings of false defilement exceeding those of the sands of the Ganges.
In contrast to these meanings, when the nature of the mind is unmoving, there are pure merits exceeding those of the sands of the Ganges.
This is the manifestation of the meaning of the marks of virtue. If the mind arises and perceives further dharmas as objects of recollection, then there is deficiency.
Such pure dharmas and immeasurable merits are themselves the one mind; there is nothing further to be recollected. Therefore, they are complete.
It is named the Tathāgata-garbha of the Dharma-body.
[Commentary] From "Because all... onwards, the text presents the principle that is the object of delusion.

[Record] The treatise is divided into three parts. First, it presents the essence of the principle, which is the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Its meaning is fully contained within the "Gate of True Suchness."
This answers the meaning of their non-duality. [Commentary:

"And yet," and so forth, refers to the arising of delusion based upon the True [Suchness]. This refers to the subtle and coarse defiled minds, which are the lack of awakening regarding the fundamental and the derivative.
Desiring to explain the pure, one first cites the defiled to contrast them and thereby reveal it; the subsequent phrases follow this same pattern. How is this revealed?

Yes. The subsequent passage stating "non-arising" and so forth is an elucidation of this. Since the arising of thought is precisely the ignorance of non-enlightenment (*abodha-avidyā*), its non-arising is precisely the luminous wisdom of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi-jñāna*).

[Commentary] Next, the characteristics are contrasted and revealed. This means that by contrasting the sands-of-the-Ganges of defiled phenomena characterized by arising and ceasing, the sands-of-the-Ganges of pure characteristics consisting of meritorious qualities are revealed;

this is precisely the answer to the meaning of their differentiation. Within this, there are two parts. First, the eightfold sets of meritorious characteristics are individually contrasted and paired.
First, the contrast between ignorance and wisdom: "deluded mind" refers to the aforementioned lack of accordance with reality (*ayathābhūta*).
It is known. When one is unaware and a thought arises, the preceding mind immediately moves; this is called the "phase of karma" (*karmalakṣaṇa*).
Perceiving objects is the preceding "phase of evolving-manifestation" (*pravṛtti-vijñāna-lakṣaṇa*). These three phases are none other than ignorance (*avidyā*) and the *ālayavijñāna*.

Furthermore, "perceiving various objects" has a broad meaning and also encompasses the four coarse aspects; therefore, the commentary states they are "subtle and coarse. Based on the True [Suchness], etc., birth occurs.

The characteristics of cessation are fully explained in the preceding text. As we are about to descend [to the next section], we shall interpret its meaning: because the pure cause is attained through defilement, it is necessary to ignite [the fire of wisdom].
In the *tathatā* (Suchness) gate, there is no defilement to be contrasted with; therefore, there is no sense of "manifestation. This is the gate of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*);

since defilement and purity are already distinguished therein, it is necessary to employ inversion and contrast to reveal the greatness of the characteristics. The examples for these various phrases follow the sevenfold [classification] below, etc. as appropriate.
The text is clear. What is meant by "manifesting"? This refers back to the objection. The subsequent section provides the explanation.

"The mind does not arise" means that conceptual thought (*saṃjñā*) does not arise. According to the intent of the commentary, these two phrases signify the extinction of delusion and the manifestation of the true.

The following phrases should be understood by analogy. Regarding the phrase "since [thought] arises," it is as stated previously: all sentient beings are not called awakened because they possess thought.

Thoughts continue in succession, never departing from thought. If one attains non-thought, then one knows that the characteristics of the mind are fundamentally equal, for they are one and the same awakening.
Thus, thought is non-awakening; non-thought is original awakening.
[Commentary] "If the mind is downward-looking, one does not see; this refers to false seeing that is not all-pervasive. 'Universal illumination' refers to true illumination that is perfectly bright.
[Sub-commentary] Second, regarding the contrast between limited seeing and universal illumination: "Not all-pervasive" means, for example, as when a person sees the east but does not see the west;

it is the same for near and far, internal and external, light and darkness, and so forth. As the Sūtra says: "Sentient beings look through with a penetrating vision, yet it does not exceed a mere inch. This is because they harbor [delusions].
Because it is able to see the mind, there is nothing among all objects that is not seen. As for "perfectly luminous" (yuanming), because there is no seeing, there is nothing that is not seen.
Thus, the *Zhao lun* states: "Prajñā has no cognition, yet there is nothing it does not know.
The reason the first bhūmi is named the "True Path of Seeing" (darśanamārga) is that it does not maintain the duality of subject and object.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the mind has movement": by reversing this, it is revealed that True Suchness (*tathatā*) is without movement.
[Record] 3. This contrasts false consciousness with true knowledge. That which is not true consciousness and knowledge is "movement," because it does not know things as they truly are;

therefore, it is not true. The text of the *Śū* (Commentary) is also abbreviated. If it were complete, it should say: "The movement of the mind is not true consciousness and knowledge. By reversing [this],...
This reveals that True Suchness (*tathatā*) is immovable; this is true and authentic cognition. Why? Because the mind is without movement, that which is known is real.
"Real" means being free from falsehood and delusion. Furthermore, according to the aforementioned treatise, one should supplement the text with a counter-illustration stating:
"The nature of the mind is immovable; this is true cognition. Because the treatise is concise, it only provides [the positive statement].
This is able to counteract delusion. Furthermore, from this point downward until the phrase "lack of autonomy," at the beginning of each sentence, there should be the expression "if the mind moves";
yet, at the end of each original phrase, it further states "the nature of mind is unmoving," and so forth.
These are all translated in correspondence with the respective clauses; reflect upon this section according to this pattern.

[Commentary] "Lacking intrinsic nature" clarifies that deluded defilement has no substance. Conversely, this reveals the intrinsically pure mind. [Record] 4. The correspondence between "lack of nature" and "having substance":
Deluded defilement has no substance because it arises based on the movement of the True and the Deluded; how could it have its own essence?
As for the "pure mind," because the mind is without movement, it stands independently apart from conditions. This independent essence is fundamentally non-existent.
Defilement does not arise following conditions, nor does it originate dependent upon objects; therefore, it is called the "intrinsically pure mind.
[Commentary] From "not permanent" onwards, the four inversions of delusory defilement are clarified; by reversing these, the four virtues of True Suchness (Tathatā) are revealed.
[Commentary] Five. This is the correspondence between the perverted and the truly real. Regarding the four perversions: they are impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity.

Because the mind is stirred, there arises tainted (*sāsrava*) form and mind. Since this tainted form and mind are actually not permanent and so forth, yet ordinary beings reckon them as permanent and so forth, the four perversions are established.
As for the opposite of these, because the mind is unstirred, form and mind do not arise.
Because it does not arise, it is solely the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*), which is eternally abiding, pure, sovereign, and blissful; thus, it constitutes the four virtues.

[Commentary]: Regarding "feverish affliction" (*paridāha*): the various delusions burn the mind, which is the ultimate feverish affliction; therefore, it is said that True Suchness is cool and refreshing (*śītala*).
[Commentary] Six.
The pair of "feverish affliction" (*paritāpa*) and "coolness" (*śītalatva*). As for "various delusions": because the mind is stirred, greed, anger, and other delusions arise;
since these afflictions (*kleśa*) burn fiercely, they constitute "feverish affliction. As for "coolness": because the mind is unmoved, it is precisely the Truth (*tattva*).
Suchness (tathatā) is without delusion; thus it is not afflicted by feverish distress. Since there is no feverish distress, it is called "cool and refreshing" (śītala).
[Commentary: "Decay and change" refers to the shifting and altering of false defilements; this conversely reveals that Suchness does not decay or change.
[Commentary] Seven. "The transformation of the immutable" is contrasted with "delusory defilement and change. Because the mind is in motion, the nine characteristics arise;
these nine characteristics—arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing, as well as old age, sickness, and death—constitute decay and transformation. To illustrate the opposite [of this], etc.:
Because the mind is immovable, it is suchness (*tathatā*). Within suchness, there is fundamentally no arising and ceasing, nor any transformation or alteration of the nine marks;
therefore, it is said to be "unchanging."
[Commentary: "Lacking sovereignty" means being bound by the fruits of karma; this serves to manifest the sovereignty of True Suchness (tathatā).
As stated above, it possesses the meaning of being cool, unchanging, and sovereign.
[Commentary] Eight. Regarding "bondage versus mastery" and "karmic results, etc.": because the mind is stirred, one initiates karma and undergoes retribution, falling into the five destinies;
this is called "bondage. As for "mastery of *tathatā* (suchness)": because the mind is not stirred, it is itself *tathatā*.
Within *tathatā*, there is no bondage of karma; therefore, it is called "mastery. The phrase "and so forth" mentioned above refers to...
In this section, all instances cite that which manifests delusive defilement in order to contrast it with and thereby clarify the previously mentioned pure virtues.

Because the treatise is concise, these are not listed in full; therefore, in the present commentary, I have briefly pointed out the latter three meanings. The preceding phrases may be understood by analogy.
[Commentary] "Down to 'possessing'... and so forth. Each is paired with its opposite; thus, both the defiled and the pure [dharmas] exceed the sands of the Ganges.
[Record] Next, there are two parts for the total pairing and allocation of the sands of the Ganges. First, since the dharmas exceeding the sands of the Ganges...
It cannot be described in full; hence the phrase "up to and including" (*yāvat*). "Grains of sand" and so forth refer to false defilements, which collectively represent all defiled phenomena.
In contrast to this principle, the defiled phenomena as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are established because the mind moves; when the mind does not move, all pure merits arise.

"Also exceeding the number of sands" refers to the various meanings from "the true and pure consciousness-knowledge" (*tathatā-vijñapti*) onwards, as well as all other inconceivable Buddha-dharmas beyond them.

Regarding "each one correspondingly," this clarifies the various states of defilement and purity through the alternation of the movement and non-movement of the mind-nature. Now, for the sake of brevity, [the text] uses "if the mind... [to represent this].
Mental movement comes first; the unmoving nature of the mind follows behind; and all phenomena manifested therein are subsumed in between.
Furthermore, within this [sequence], the term for "pure virtue" is missing. If one wishes to provide a specific correspondence for each element so that it may be easily understood, one should say:
"If the mind has movement, it is not true cognition; the unmoving nature of the mind is itself true cognition."
This is because one knows the meaning. Even up to the point where, if the mind has movement, there is no mastery; if the nature of the mind is without movement, then mastery is attained.
This is as previously explained in the commentary, which uses successive sections to demonstrate this through contrast.
To further provide an analogy, it should also be said: if the mind has movement, that is bondage; if the nature of the mind is without movement, that is called liberation. Thus it is.

All cases should be understood in this manner; they cannot be fully detailed here. Nevertheless, regarding the first two sections of the preceding eight pairs, each speaks of the arising of thought and the arising of views according to its own specific meaning.
Even so, these do not transcend the fundamental sense of the movement of the mind.

If one wishes to cite their respective specific meanings, such terms as "true and real cognition" (*tattvavijñapti*) also possess distinct meanings. One should say: the mind gives rise to discrimination; it is not true cognition.
"Knowing" means that when the mind is free from conceptual discrimination, it is precisely the meaning of true cognition (*vijñapti*).
Furthermore, as long as the mind gives rise to karma and its fruits, it lacks sovereignty; once the mind is freed from the bonds of karma, it attains sovereignty, and so forth.

By simply correlating the nine aspects with the eight stages in their respective order, the meaning is entirely consistent. The initial arising of thought is "karma"; the subsequent arising of views is "transformation. As for "differentiation"...

The "object-specific" [mental factors] are precisely the manifest [states], up to and including "feverish affliction. This refers to the dual characteristics of grasping at and conceptualizing names. "Decay and transformation" is precisely karma;
that is to say, if the mind gives rise to karma, there is then transition and change. The nature of the mind is separate from karma, and thus it is free from decay and transformation.
One should know that the meaning of "mind-movement" (citta-īraṇā) is general, while all others are specific. Reflect upon this according to the principle.

[Commentary: That which is deficient refers to the deluded mind’s outward thoughts; because one seeks externally, there is insufficiency. Therefore, that which is fulfilled refers to the fulfillment of the nature of pure virtue;
because there is no need for external seeking, it is complete.
[Commentary] Second: the meaning of fulfillment. As stated previously, "until it is fulfilled, there is nothing lacking";

thus, this also serves to reveal the truth by overturning deluded defilement. Regarding "deluded mind and so forth": if one perceives phenomena as existing outside the mind and gives rise to pursuit, one will ultimately never be fulfilled;
instead, there will be a sense of lack. Alternatively, it may mean that if even a single phenomenon were to exist outside the mind...
If one were to think about it, there would be some deficiency in the virtues inherent within the nature. It is like a person seeking goods from another;

one should know that what is not present in one's own home cannot be found there. As for pure virtues and the like, because the nature of the mind has no exterior, all virtues are fully complete therein.
Thus, one should forget the conceptual mind to accord with them; one must not give rise to a seeking mind to pursue them.
One should know that whatever is perceived is entirely false and illusory, because it arises from conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).

This point is intended to distinguish [this school] from the provisional teachings, which assert that the untainted merits (*anāsrava-guṇa*) of the Buddha-fruit are all produced through cultivation. In the present system of this treatise, however...

It is simply that cultivation reveals [the nature]; it is not said that cultivation produces it, because it is inherently present within the nature itself. The production of images from gold and silver can serve as a metaphor for this.
[Commentary] The phrase "named as" below concludes the title.

[Commentary] This subsequent section establishes the names by correlating both cause and effect, as previously explained. Those *saṃsāric* dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are manifested through the marks of arising and ceasing based on the *karmic consciousness*.
These *pure* virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are all manifested through their correspondence with and contrast to the *tathatā*, the *dharmakāya*, and the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Therefore, this concluding summary is provided to demonstrate that the essence and its attributes are in reality not in contradiction.
*Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra-vyākhyā-bi-shuo-ji Huìyuè*, Scroll Seven, Phonetic Glossary:
*tián* (恬) has the sound of *tián* (甜). It means serene and tranquil; it denotes stillness and peace.
*Ādāna* is translated here as "grasping and maintaining"; it is the name for the eighth consciousness.
*Bao* (in *baoyin*) means a rushing sound, like a gushing spring or a cascading waterfall.
*Zhuo* (in *zhuoyin*) means to treat jade and stone.
"Pàn" (pronounced like "bàn") means rebellion or disorder.
"Kòu" (pronounced like "kòu") means a marauder or thief.
"Língyǔ" (pronounced like "líng yǔ") refers to the prison or jail.
Xínglù (刑戮): the pronunciation is xíngliù; it means execution. Yán (妍):
the pronunciation is yán; it means beautiful. Chī (媸):
the pronunciation is chī; it means ugly.
Yù (愈): pronounced yù; to recover from illness.
Yù (諭): pronounced yù; to instruct or inform.
Zī (諮): pronounced zī; to deliberate on difficulties.
Xún (pronounced xún): to inquire. Zhēng: to ask.
Chè (pronounced chè): tracks or traces.
Chuò (pronounced chuò): to cease or rest.
*Suì* (pronounced *suì*) refers to the wood used for producing fire by friction.
*Cuō* (pronounced *cuō*) means to grind or polish; it refers to one who works with bone and horn.
"Wei Shengyuan" refers to King Ajātaśatru; this account appears in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.
The name of King Anala (Wúyànzú) appears in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
"Jì" (劑) is pronounced like "jì" (際); it means a limit or boundary.
"Gāo" (篙) is pronounced like "gāo" (高); it refers to the bamboo pole used for rowing a boat.
*Zhào* (棹) is pronounced *diào*. It refers to a vessel implement; specifically, it is the name for an oar used to propel water alongside a boat.
*Xí* (襲) is pronounced *xí*. It means to succeed or inherit.
*È* (遏) is pronounced *hé*. It means to stop or cut off.
*Kǎn* (紺): "Sweet. Refers to the colors blue and red.
*Yíng* (瑩): "To believe" and "to illuminate thoroughly. It means brilliance and purity.
*Wàn* (腕): "Graceful. Refers to the wrist.
"The wind and the horse-ox do not reach one another": the ox runs with the wind, while the horse runs against the wind;
this is a metaphor for the great distance separating north and south.

It originates from the *Zuozhuan*. "Spear and shield" (*maodun*): the pronunciation is *móudèng*. A spear (*máo*) belongs to the class of lances; a shield (*dùn*) belongs to the class of armor. Formerly, there was one who sold both implements together.
When selling a spear, one says it can pierce solid shields; when selling a shield, one says it can ward off sharp spears.
Thus, they are called "mutually contradictory" (mùdùn), used as a metaphor for self-contradiction between preceding and succeeding statements.
*Fǎng* (倣) means "to visit" and by extension, "to emulate.

△ Second: Alternative Explanations. Part One: Employing the Great [Vehicle]. (2) First: General Clarification. Second: Specific Explanation. First: General Clarification. (2) [Note: The symbols and numbering indicate the structural divisions of the original Chinese text.]
First, citing the cause in relation to the fruit; second, restating the cause to reveal the fruit. Regarding the first [citing the cause in relation to the fruit] (three parts):
first, citing the fundamental right practice; second, citing the fundamental great vow; third, citing the great skillful means. Regarding the first [citing the fundamental right practice]:
[Commentary] Right practice refers to the practices of the perfections of compassion and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding the function of True Suchness (tathatā), it is as follows: when the Buddhas and Tathāgatas were originally on the stage of the causal ground, they gave rise to great compassion.
He cultivates the various pāramitās and gathers and transforms sentient beings.
[Commentary] The first phrase cites what preceded to introduce the present topic. The section beginning with "That which is called" explains according to the meaning.
Regarding the phrase "originally in the stage of the causal ground," it refers to the various practices performed when he was a bodhisattva, for which compassion served as the foundation.
Regarding the gathering and transforming of sentient beings, there is none that does not first take benefiting others as its primary concern.
"Pāramitās" refers to using the various perfections to gather beings and bring them under one's influence, transforming them so they follow what is wholesome.

For example, one gathers the poor through giving and those who violate the precepts through upholding the ethical discipline, and so forth. Because these encompass both self-benefit and benefit for others, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: "With immeasurable wealth, [one] gathers..."
To all the poor and destitute, he upholds the precepts with purity to gather in those who violate them; with patience to harmonize his conduct, he gathers in those who harbor anger;
with great vigor, he gathers in those who are indolent; with single-minded meditative concentration, he gathers in those with distracted minds;
and with resolute wisdom, he gathers in those who lack understanding.
△ Second, raising up the original great vow and establishing the great oath:
he desires to deliver and liberate all beings, equal in number to the realm of sentient beings, and without limit as to the number of kalpas, extending to the end of the future.
[Commentary] "Desiring to deliver all" refers to the vast mind. "Without limiting the number of kalpas" refers to the long-term mind.
[Record] The "vast mind" is precisely the vow within the Four Great Vows to save boundless beings;

it is also identical to the instruction given by the Buddha in the *Vajra* [Sūtra] for those who have resolved to attain Bodhicitta to universally deliver the four modes of birth and the nine classes of beings, as explained by Maitreya.
It is also called the "vast mind" and the "long-term mind. This is consistent with what is taught in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra’s Chapter on the Vows of Samantabhadra*:
"When the realm of sentient beings is exhausted, my practice shall be exhausted; because the realm of sentient beings is inexhaustible, these vows of mine are likewise inexhaustible.
The former [passage] explains by way of spatial extent, hence it says "equal to the realm of sentient beings"; this [passage], however, explains by way of time.
This concludes the vertical discussion; hence it says, "extending to the end of the future.
△ Third, citing the Great Expedient Means.
[Commentary]: This refers to citing the great expedient means of compassion and wisdom.
Because he regards all sentient beings as his own self, yet does not grasp at the mark of a sentient being. For what reason?
It is because he knows, in accordance with reality, that all sentient beings and his own self are equal in true suchness (*tathatā*), without any distinction.

[Commentary: "As with one's own body" refers to the depth of compassion (*karuṇā*). "Not grasping at signs" refers to the depth of wisdom (*prajñā*). Taken together, these also constitute the non-perverted mind.
This may also explain the reason for the previously mentioned "long duration. The question "In what sense? probes the reason why compassion and wisdom are profound.
The passage beginning with "according to reality as it is" answers by relying on the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*) to manifest this profundity.
[Commentary] Regarding "profound compassion": it means directly perceiving sentient beings as one would one's own parents;
it is only when one perceives them as being identical to one's own body that it becomes truly profound. Regarding "profound wisdom":

because one realizes that all is but mind, one knows that all sentient beings have been devoid of inherent nature from the beginning, that they have fundamentally been without discursive thought, and that they have been in *nirvāṇa* since time immemorial, not awaiting extinction. The provisional teachings of the Lesser Vehicle cannot [attain this].
The reason they lack these characteristics is that their wisdom is shallow. Now, the Bodhisattvas of the True Teaching (Shijo) act in the opposite manner; therefore, it is said they are "deep.
Furthermore, "combined with the above" means being combined with profound compassion and being non-perverted. Sentient beings are fundamentally identical to oneself;
since they are all equally without marks (animitta), to perceive them as having distinct marks constitutes a perversion. Now, they all reverse this. As for the reason it is called "long-lasting":
This also explains the reason for the vastness [of the teaching] and the omissions in the commentary.

If one cannot realize that [the self and others] are identical and cause their characteristics to perish, how could one possibly perform such universal and eternal salvation? To inquire into the "reason why" means: [The intention is as follows:]...
For what reason does one attain [the realization] that others are like one's own body, yet not grasp at the mark of sentient beings? Regarding the phrase "based on True Suchness" (*tathatā*):
because within this gate it is revealed that all phenomena are identical to True Suchness and are all equal to Suchness, one attains the equality and non-duality of their bodies and one's own body.
How could one not feel compassion for them and desire to deliver them? Furthermore, since...
They are of one and the same reality; all are entirely without marks. Who is there to cross over? Who is there to be crossed over?

Therefore, one does not grasp at the mark of sentient beings. Furthermore, these two lines may also be used to explain the reason for the aforementioned "broad and long," and they also constitute a verse-line.
This section cites the fundamental wisdom of great skillful means (*mahopāya-jñāna*). From here downward, it investigates and explains the reason why one does not grasp at signs.
Second, it reiterates the cause to manifest the fruit:
because there exists such great wisdom of skillful means, ignorance is extinguished, and one perceives the original Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), which exists spontaneously.
The inconceivable activity and its various functions are equal to True Suchness (tathatā) and pervade all places; yet, furthermore, no characteristic of function can be apprehended therein.
Why is this? It is because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess only the body of the Dharma-body and the characteristic of wisdom, which is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Therein, there are no objects of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), and they are free from deliberate effort; they simply manifest according to the perceptions of sentient beings.
Because one gains benefit from hearing [the Dharma], it is described as "function.
[Commentary: 1. "By having... cites the preceding cause. 2. "Eliminating and extinguishing... is the fruit of self-benefit. 3. "Spontaneously... is the third [point].
This clearly reveals the function, which is the fruit of benefiting others. Within this, there are three parts: first, it clarifies that the karmic function is profoundly deep;

because it does not depend on volitional effort (*manasikāra*), it is called "spontaneous activity" (*anābhoga-karman*). As the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Like a mani-jewel or a celestial drum, they accomplish their own tasks without thought," and so forth.
Second, it reveals that the function is vast and extensive, as its operation accords with reality (*tattva*). Furthermore, third, it is the function... [text ends].

And it is eternally quiescent. Within this, first there is the direct manifestation through the phrase "Why is this so? Next is the interrogation and objection. [The text states: "The Buddhas possess the three bodies;
why then do you say they have no marks of utility? This refers to the section beginning with "As for all Buddhas," which constitutes the third part: the explanation that resolves the difficulty.

If one discards the perspective of the response to stimuli and the arousal of potential, the Tathāgata is solely the wondrous principle of fundamental wisdom, possessing no further marks of transformational response, worldly conventions, or birth-and-death.

It merely functions in accordance with conditions; yet this functioning is itself non-functioning. It is like waves being water; therefore, functioning is eternally quiescent. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"This body of mine is itself the Dharma-body," and so forth. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (She-lun) of the Liang dynasty says:

"Only Suchness and the Wisdom of Suchness remaining alone is called the Dharma-body. Regarding the phrase "merely in accordance with... [and below]: although the True Principle and the Sublime Wisdom are fundamentally...
It is eternally profound in its coming, yet it responds to conditions as they arise; thus, its utility is boundless. It is eternally active while remaining quiescent.

[Commentary] Regarding the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*), there are both general and specific explanations. As for the general explanation: skillful means is itself wisdom. Furthermore, this has two meanings.
First, it refers to the wisdom that accords with renunciation (*nairyāṇika-prajñā*), for it consists entirely of skillful means (*upāya*).

This extends from the stage of the Vajra-Interval (*vajrānantarya*) downward and is not limited to the stages prior to the [first] bhūmi; therefore, the period following the ten bhūmis is called the "fulfillment of skillful means. The *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*) also states:
"Although there are many skillful means, they are all termed wisdom that accords [with reality]. Second, this wisdom is great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

Because it is the skillful means (*upāya*). If wisdom were not the skillful means, it would not be great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), for it would fall into the trap of attachment and views (*sneha-dṛṣṭi*).

Therefore, although it was previously stated that one speaks of "sentient beings," one does not grasp at the mark of sentient beings (*sattva-nimitta*); the commentary explains this as "the depth of wisdom.

Nevertheless, there are cases where compassion arises from wisdom, for one desires to deliver others only after knowing that they are the same as oneself; or there are cases where wisdom arises from compassion.
Not knowing how to adjudicate between them, one should study both as skillful means (*upāya*) so that both explanations are understood together. As for their distinction:

realizing the truth is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*), while engaging with the conventional world is "skillful means. These are alternative names for what follows the roots [of the faculties]. This refers to severing fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*).
Seeing the Dharma-body is the achievement of wisdom (*jñāna*). The arising of inconceivable activities to transform and benefit all sentient beings is the power of skillful means (*upāya*).
Now, this [state] possesses both the universal and the particular. As for the fruit of self-benefit, it is identical to the "characteristic of pure wisdom" (*jñāna-viśuddhi-lakṣaṇa*).

The Dharma-body at the stage of fruition is precisely the original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*) within the causal state. By citing the cause to manifest the fruit, it is said that one "sees the fundamental Dharma-body."

The previous passage cited the fruit to reveal the cause, stating that one "abides in the Dharma-body" to explain original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*); these two passages mutually clarify one another.
The aspect of inconceivable activity is subtle and difficult to understand, beyond the reach of mind or words; therefore, it is said that its functional operation is profoundly deep.

It does not require first deliberating and subsequently initiating transformation. Therefore, it is said that this does not depend upon deliberate mental effort (*manasikāra*). Regarding the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other texts, they state in full:
"If the fruit of Buddhahood is manifested by non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and is free from conceptualization, how can the Buddhas perform acts of benefit for sentient beings?
[They do so] in accordance with reality, without error, and through effortless (*anābhoga*) activity. Thus, it is emphasized.
A verse says: "Just as the mani-jewel and the celestial drum accomplish their own tasks without thought, so too, without discrimination, the various deeds of a Buddha are accomplished.
This reveals that the three karmas of the Tathāgata are all performed without effort and are both inconceivable.
*Maṇi* is a Sanskrit term; here it means "free from defilement" (*vimala*) or "increasing" (*vivardhana*). It was formerly translated as "wishing-fulfilling"; this is a metaphor.
The two activities of the Tathāgata’s body and mind manifest different images according to those they encounter; this illustrates the Buddha’s bodily activity (*kāyakarman*).
When he produces various objects according to what people require, this illustrates the Buddha’s mental activity (*manaskarman*).
As for the celestial drum, it belongs to the Lord of Devas; when the armies of the asuras approach, sounds naturally issue from the drum, declaring, "The enemy!"
"Come" and "The thief has gone"—these words represent the Buddha’s verbal karma (*vākkarman*). Although these two things possess their respective functions, they lack volition;
thus, they can serve as metaphors for the Buddha’s three karmas (*trikarma*) which operate spontaneously (*anābhoga*). Regarding "accomplishing one's own task":

the manifested image and the sound each perform their function according to their specific utility to carry out the work. One may also take the jewel and the drum as examples of accomplishing one's own task, though this serves merely as a metaphor.

The body and speech are both devoid of conceptual thought; this is analogous to the mental karma (*manas-karman*). As for the functioning that accords with principle, it is because the function is identical to the essence (*tattva*);
since the essence is all-pervasive, the function is likewise all-pervasive. Because both are without spatial location, they pervade all places.

If it were otherwise, how could it be called the functioning of True Suchness (*tathatā*)? Furthermore, regarding "the characteristic of being without characteristics," there are previously no sentient beings to be transformed.
Regarding the characteristics: these are the characteristics of the unconditioned application of transformation. In relation to the preceding text, it says "furthermore" (*yòu yì*).

As for "employing eternal quiescence," this is the function of non-function; because function is itself non-function, although various bodies are manifested, one does not move from the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), and although various dharmas are taught, one eternally abides in the principle beyond words.
Regarding the three bodies within the inquiry: although the term is general...

The citation raises a question regarding the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Since the response-body is a manifestation of conditioned phenomena (*nimitta*), there are three explanations provided to resolve this. These are divided into two sections. First, it clarifies its lack of utility by means of ultimate wisdom and conventional knowledge;
thus, that which is "useful" is itself "without utility. The "Dharmakāya" refers here to the Dharmatākāya (the body of the nature of reality).
The text below states: "The Dharma-body has no such things as distinctions of self and other, nor physical characteristics. The body of the marks of wisdom is precisely the wisdom-body.
Furthermore, it says below: "The substance of form is formless; it is designated by the name 'wisdom-body. Moreover, when these two bodies are combined, they constitute the True Body."
Because principle and wisdom are non-dual, this refers to the two bodies (*kāya*) to manifest that the essence is quiescent.

Regarding "the first" and so forth, it distinguishes that the function is non-existent by means of the two truths; the intent clarifies that because this is signless (*animitta*), it is not the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Because this is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is free from purposeful activity. "Abandoning the stimulus" means not preaching in response to sentient beings.

The wondrous principle is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); fundamental wisdom is the Wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*). All that possesses form belongs to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), because it arises from the conditions of karmic resonance and stimulus.
Now, since the stimulus has been abandoned, it is said that "there is nothing further. As for the phrase "merely following," there is resonance.
This is the appropriate response. Since [the mind] arises in dependence upon conditions, and conditions lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), its functioning is eternally quiescent;

therefore, it is said to be "without function. This has two meanings. First, "without function" refers to the cause. The cause consists of compassion and wisdom (*karuṇā-prajñā*), yet there is a distinction between the immediate and the remote.
Detachment is wisdom (*jñāna*), and intimacy is compassion (*karuṇā*). Because compassion arises based on wisdom, the treatise states:
"From subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), great compassion flows forth. Without its cause, transformation will ultimately not arise, just as the two vehicles lack compassion."

Ordinary beings lack wisdom; how could there be any transformation for them? Second, regarding the statement that it is useless because it depends on conditions: this refers to those sentient beings whose faculties are matured.
If the necessary conditions are absent, even such a transformation will not arise, because there are times throughout the lands of the ten directions when no Buddha exists in the world.
Thus, these two meanings depend upon one another; only when the causes and conditions are fully present can [the result] be accomplished.

Since this belongs to the realm of causes and conditions, how could there be a "transformation-body" (nirmāṇakāya) that could be apprehended? This is like the metaphor of the waves below; therefore, the application [of the principle] follows below. "Quiescence" (*ji*) is the essence (*ti*);
thus, the *Huan-yuan guan* (Contemplation of Returning to the Source) says: "When functioning, it surges like boiling waves, operating entirely through the true essence; as for the essence..."
The mirror is still and the river is clear; as they arise in accordance with conditions, they meet in quiescence. Regarding the phrase "Nirvana" below, it cites scriptural evidence:

"This body" refers to the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body). As for the word "etc.," the full text states: "This body of mine is precisely the eternal body, the *dharmakāya*, the indestructible diamond body.
Since all three bodies possess the sense of eternity, the term "*dharmakāya*" is further employed to distinguish it [from the other two].
This is an extensive explanation. Fearing that people might not understand the characteristics of the *dharmakāya*, he therefore employs a metaphor: it is like a *vajra*, which cannot be destroyed.
"Suchness" (*tathatā*) is the *dharmakāya*; "wisdom" (*jñāna*) is the *saṃbhogakāya*. That they exist alone [as one] is because the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* are united.

The repetition of "suchness" (tathatā) indicates that there is no duality. That which is called the *dharmakāya* subsumes wisdom within suchness; this designation is established in reference to the fundamental ground.
However, while *nirvāṇa* subsumes function within the essence, the *Saṃgraha* directly reveals the true body (*bhūtakāya*). Although the terminology differs, the underlying meaning does not.
As for the phrase "merely according with," these two [terms] clarify the presence of utility by responding to the specific capacities of sentient beings.
This is truly the function of the non-functional. Although it is fundamentally lowly, the Sūtra says: "The Buddha’s true Dharma-body is like empty space;
manifesting forms in response to things is like the moon reflected in water. This is what is meant by "quiescent yet constantly functioning."
△ Second, the detailed explanation (in two parts). First, the heading and inquiry; second, the explanation of the meaning.
First, the heading and inquiry: This function is of two kinds. What are these two?
[Commentary] There are two headings. What is the inquiry? △ Second, the explanation of the meaning (in two parts):
first, the direct manifestation of the functional characteristics; second, questions and answers to dispel doubts. First, the direct manifestation of the functional characteristics (in two parts):
first, the direct manifestation of its function; second, the restatement and detailed analysis. First, the direct manifestation of its function.

(2). First, the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body); second, the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body). Regarding the first, the *nirmāṇakāya*, there are two parts: first, identifying the person by reference to consciousness; second, explaining the reason for this.
Regarding the first, identifying the person by reference to consciousness:

First: that which is perceived by the minds of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles, based on the *vikaḷpa-vastu-vijñāna* (discriminative consciousness of objects), is called the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body).

[Commentary]: First, regarding "ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles": they do not understand that all is consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) and falsely imagine the existence of external objects;

this is precisely the meaning of the *vikaḷpa-vastu-vijñāna*. When they now perceive the Buddha-body, they likewise regard it as being outside the mind, conforming to the discriminative conceptualizations of that *vastu-vijñāna*.

Therefore, it is said that one sees based on the *vikaḷpa-vastu-vijñāna* (the consciousness of differentiated phenomena). Furthermore, although such a person may be aware of the six consciousnesses, they do not know those [other] seventh and eighth consciousnesses;
thus, it is simply said that they rely on the consciousness of phenomena (*vastu-vijñāna*).

As for the designation "response body" (*nirmāṇakāya*), it is because based on this coarse consciousness and its discrimination, one perceives only the coarse marks of the response and transformation bodies, and does not perceive the subtle marks of the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*).

[Commentary] This relies on the "discriminative phrases" (*vikalpa-pada*), which refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*). Under the section "Ordinary Beings" (*pṛthagjana*), first, among humans, the mind that acts as the perceiver is raised and termed a "phrase";
next, the body that is the perceived object is raised. Alternatively, based on what follows, one may distinguish the perceiving mind and clarify the perceived object through these phrases.
In the *Śū* (the sub-commentary), under "Ordinary Beings," it is first explained that although ordinary beings and others know the seventh and eighth [consciousnesses], they merely accord with them.

Regarding the *vastu-vijñāna* (phenomenal consciousness), there are again two [aspects]. First, the general clarification of not knowing that all phenomena are merely consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*).

This refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), namely all ordinary beings from the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) and below. As for the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*), one has a refined faith in *tathatā* (suchness) and already knows that it is merely consciousness;
nevertheless, their phenomenal consciousness remains coarse, manifest, and sharp, spontaneously discriminating external phenomena. "Not knowing," etc., means that they do not...

"To know that phenomena are merely manifestations of consciousness" refers to the meaning of relying on and conforming to the *vastu-vijñāna* (the consciousness of objects). Now, following the phrase "seeing next," it specifically clarifies the ignorance regarding the Buddha-body as being merely mind.
While "phenomena" (*dharma*) encompass all realms—both defiled and pure—the Buddha belongs to the pure realm;

yet [those who do not understand] also claim he exists externally, being deluded about the fact that these are merely manifestations of mind. Furthermore, following the phrase "also can," it later clarifies that the two vehicles and others only awaken to the six [consciousnesses].

The consciousness (*vijñāna*) does not know the seventh and eighth [consciousnesses]. Because the followers of the Two Vehicles are deluded regarding the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), they previously took the phenomenal consciousness (*karmavijñāna*) as their basis;

now, they take the phenomenal consciousness as that which is awakened to. As for what is called "that which is awakened to," it merely means being able to know its existence; it does not mean awakening to its cessation.
Since they awaken only to the phenomenal consciousness, they do not rely upon the seventh or eighth. Regarding the phrase "relying on this coarse consciousness" and so forth:
It is like a bright mirror facing an object; the reflected images appear differently. How could it be that the object is ugly while the image is beautiful?
Thus, while beauty and ugliness reside in the object, the mirror has no preference for the good or the bad. It is from this that the concept of the "response body" (nirmāṇakāya) is established.
△ Second, explaining the reason for this:

Because one does not know that it is the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) that manifests, one perceives [the object] as coming from the outside and grasps at the boundaries of form; thus, one is unable to know it exhaustively.
[Commentary] This explains the reason why the aforementioned views are coarse. "Not knowing that consciousness manifests" means being deluded regarding Mind-Only.
"Grasping at the boundaries of form" means failing to realize that form is itself mind, and thus has no boundaries.
[Commentary] First, I shall briefly explain the meaning of the treatise. Those who do not penetrate [this truth] see that form arises from the mind, yet it originally has no substantial essence;
