"No, World-Honored One" (this metaphor signifies that true purity has no end). "Pūrṇa, the Tathāgata is also like this: this delusion has no origin."

The nature is ultimately empty (this combines with the beginningless delusion and defilement). Originally there was no delusion; it is as if there were delusion and awakening. When awakening realizes delusion, delusion is extinguished;
awakening does not give rise to delusion (this combines with the endless true purity). If this is so, is it not the case that both saṃsāra is without beginning and nirvāṇa is without end?
The intent of this answer is the same as the text below regarding the "treatment" [of views]. Examine this carefully. As for "the non-Buddhists and others," this refers to the Sāṃkhya...
The Master of Treatises [argues]: Since they rely on the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception to produce mundane supernormal powers, they ought to be on a false path.
They know events of eighty thousand kalpas in the past, but beyond that, they know nothing.

With the supernormal power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth, they know the passing away from here and the arising there for eighty thousand kalpas into the future, yet after that, they likewise know nothing. That which they conceive as the "primordial nature" (prakṛti) is...
It is eternal. From this, all phenomena of the world arise; because they are obscure and difficult to know, it is called "the nature of obscurity" (*tamas*).

How do they arise? It is said that from the primordial obscurity (*avyakta*), intellect (*buddhi*) arises; from intellect, the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) arises; and from the ego-sense, the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) arise.
That is to say: from the five *tanmātras* (subtle elements)—form, sound, smell, taste, and touch—the five great elements (*mahābhūtas*) arise, namely earth, water, fire, wind, and space.
From the five great elements, the eleven faculties (*indriyas*) arise: the five cognitive faculties—eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body;
the five organs of action—hands, feet, mouth, and the organs of excretion and generation; and the mind-faculty (*manas*). At that time, it is called the formation of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

They maintain that the single *puruṣa* (spiritual self) is the enjoyer; it contemplates the supreme objects, and *prakṛti* (primordial nature) undergoes transformation to produce them for the self’s enjoyment.
Because the self enjoys these, it becomes bound by the objects and fails to attain liberation. If the self does not contemplate, *prakṛti* does not transform, and the spiritual self is liberated;
this is called *nirvāṇa*. There are twenty-five principles (*tattvas*) here, with *prakṛti* as the first.

First, because it arises from the transformative [power of] the *pradhāna*. Regarding the claim that "from the *avyakta* (the unmanifest) consciousness (*buddhi*) arises, and this further produces sentient beings":

this refers to the notion that even after the *puruṣa* (the self) has attained liberation and entered *nirvāṇa*, if the self were to think again, the *avyakta* would once more transform and produce consciousness and all other dharmas, continuing in this manner without end.
This is also a [logical] fallacy; it combines with the current erroneous interpretation in concluding that things end only to begin again. Next...
This refers to the meaning of the continuous flow of existence.
△ Third, the Antidote (in two parts): First, by clarifying that the essence of phenomena is devoid of a beginning, it reveals that birth and death have no origin.

Second, by clarifying that the essence of phenomena is devoid of an end, it reveals that nirvana is inexhaustible. First, clarifying that the essence of phenomena is devoid of a beginning, it reveals...
Birth and death have no beginning.
How, then, is this countered? Because the Tathāgatagarbha has no prior limit, the characteristic of ignorance likewise has no beginning.
If it is said that beyond the three realms there are further sentient beings who first arise, this is the teaching of non-Buddhist scriptures.

[Commentary] Regarding the passage beginning with "If it is said": as the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* states, "If I were to say that outside the three realms there is a separate realm of sentient beings, this would be what is taught in the non-Buddhist *Mahābhūta Sūtra*, not the teaching of the Seven Buddhas."
[Commentary] Regarding "having no prior limit": it was stated previously that the self-substance of *tathatā* (suchness) neither increases nor decreases;

it is not born in a prior limit and does not perish in a subsequent limit. It is ultimately eternal and constant, having no beginning. This is due to four meanings: first, it is called "beginningless" based on *tathatā*.
As the preceding text states: "Based upon the *tathāgatagarbha*, there arises the mind of birth and death. Second, there are no defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*).
It begins with ignorance; therefore, it is beginningless. As the *Yingluo benye jing* states:

"Because no dharmas can arise prior to the four stages of abiding (catur-vāsa-bhūmi), it is called the stage of beginningless ignorance-abiding (*anādikālikā-avidyā-vāsa-bhūmi*). This clarifies that prior to ignorance, there is no further defiled dharma that could serve as its origin or basis;
thus, it is said to be "beginningless. Third, it has never been realized by sentient beings since time immemorial. Thus it is taught.
It is beginningless. As stated previously: "Because from the very beginning one has never been separated from thought, it is called beginningless ignorance.
Fourth, it is beginningless because it lacks substantiality. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Delusion originally has no root; its nature is ultimately empty. Question:

Since delusion arises in dependence upon the True, the True is the source of delusion. Why, then, do you say it lacks substantiality? If delusion possessed substantiality, then at the time of realizing the True, [it would still persist].

How can it be permanently stilled? Answer: Delusion falsely relies upon the True to arise; thus, the True is said to be its source. In reality, however, within the True there has never been delusion from the beginning.

It is like a second moon, which arises by relying on the original moon; one says that the original moon is the basis for the arising of the second, yet the original moon actually possesses no second disk.
This means that the second has no substantiality. Therefore, all the sūtras and śāstras state that all...
Phenomena arise from the awakened mind; it is not said that the mind gives rise to phenomena. The *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* states:
"The various illusory transformations all arise from the awakened mind, just as flowers in the sky appear from within space. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "Defilements manifest within purity."
The impure does not appear within the pure, just as clouds obscure the sky; so too the mind does not manifest [its defilements].
The afflictions of the manas and so forth defile the pure mind, just as various stains soil a clean cloth.

Just as a cloth may be freed from its grime, and as gold is extracted from ore—wherein neither the cloth nor the gold is destroyed—so too is the mind freed from its faults. Furthermore, in the past...

Fuli, the Great Master, asked: "The true nature of phenomena is fundamentally pure; from what cause do deluded thoughts arise? If delusion arises from the true, how can this delusion be stilled? If there is no beginning, there is no end; if there is an end, there must be a beginning. To have an end without a beginning—this principle has long left me in bewilderment. I pray that you will reveal its secret mystery, so that I may seek liberation from birth and death. Qingliang said: "The nature of the mind is originally tranquil and eternally still. It is like empty space, without form or characteristics.

Because sentient beings give rise to false thoughts, they fail to realize their own original nature. This is called ignorance. Ignorance gives rise to karma; karma gives rise to afflictions; and afflictions give rise to suffering. These three things—ignorance, karma, and afflictions—are the causes and conditions for the cycle of birth and death. If one wishes to transcend birth and death, one must first sever the root of ignorance.

Once ignorance is severed, karma and afflictions will naturally perish. When these three are extinguished, the ocean of suffering is exhausted. This is called Nirvana. How does one sever ignorance? One must rely on the power of wisdom. What is the power of wisdom? It is the power of the Tathāgata’s profound, subtle, and wondrous Dharma. How does one enter this Dharma? By relying on a good teacher. If one encounters a good teacher, one will hear the profound Dharma. Hearing the profound Dharma, one will awaken to the truth. Having awakened to the truth, one will attain liberation. Therefore, the Buddha taught that the Dharma-gate of the Threefold Contemplation is the most supreme and wondrous among all teachings. It is the essential path for cutting off the flow of birth and death. If you practice it with diligence, you will surely attain liberation."
National Teacher Liang replied: "When one is deluded regarding the Truth, delusive thoughts arise; when one awakens to the Truth, delusion ceases.

That which is capable of deluding is not itself the object of delusion—how could they be entirely similar? Since from the beginning there has never been awakening, it is said that delusion is without beginning.

To know that delusion is fundamentally the Truth is precisely the eternal principle. As long as the discriminating mind is not forgotten, by what means can one transcend birth and death? This clarifies everything.
This refers to the meaning that the dharma of defilement has no beginning but has an end. If one were to claim that sentient beings have a beginning, would this not be a false understanding?
Regarding the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* and others: the first fascicle of that sūtra states, "Good son, the afflictions of all sentient beings..."
The Dharma-body of the Buddhas, as well as their response-bodies and transformations, does not transcend the triple world.
Since there are no sentient beings within the triple world, what would the Buddhas have to transform? Therefore, I say that outside the triple world there exists a separate realm of sentient beings.

This is stated in the *Mahā-astu-sūtra* (The Great Existence Sūtra) of the non-Buddhists; it was not spoken by the seven Buddhas. Regarding this *Mahā-astu-sūtra*: the Vaiśeṣika masters assert six categories (*padārtha*).

First, substance (*dravya*); second, quality (*guṇa*); third, action (*karman*); fourth, great existence (*mahā-astu*); fifth, sameness-and-difference (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*); and sixth, inherence (*samavāya*).
Among these six categories, the nature of "great existence" (*mahā-astu*) refers to that which is able to exist as all phenomena. Furthermore...
Because it possesses a distinct essence that exists apart from all phenomena such as substance, quality, and action,
this single phrase "Mahāyāna" is taken and established as the title of the sūtra.
△ Second, clarifying that the essence of the Dharma is free from an end reveals that *nirvāṇa* is inexhaustible.
Furthermore, the Tathāgatagarbha has no posterior limit (*paścimakoṭi*). Since the *nirvāṇa* attained by all Buddhas corresponds to it, it likewise has no posterior limit.
[Commentary] "Having no posterior limit" refers to what was stated previously: that the nature of the mind is neither born nor extinguished.

"In accord with nirvāṇa" refers to what was stated previously: because the dharma of True Suchness (tathatā) constantly perfumes [the mind], the deluded mind is extinguished and the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) manifests;
as it gives rise to the perfuming of its functioning, there is no interruption. Thus, one knows that the Tathāgatagarbha is without beginning and without end, giving rise to [all phenomena].
Samsara depends upon it; it has no beginning but has an end. Nirvana depends upon it; it has a beginning but no end. The nature of the *tathāgatagarbha* is like space;
birth and death are like delusion; nirvana is like awakening. Furthermore, the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha* is like moisture;
birth and death are like ice; nirvana is like water. Therefore, the preceding text states: "Defiled dharmas have been continuously perfuming since beginningless time, until one attains..."
The Buddha [taught that] subsequently there is cessation; because it violates true nature, there is cessation.
Furthermore, it is said that when pure dharmas are perfumed, there is no cessation, for they persist until the end of the future; because they accord with principle, there is no cessation.
If one were to claim that *nirvāṇa* has an end, this would truly be a false and erroneous interpretation.
△ II. The Two Dharmas (three parts). First, attachment to conditions; second, attachment to characteristics; third, the antidote. Regarding the first, attachment to conditions:

for those who hold the view of a self in phenomena (*dharmātman*), because they possess the dull faculties of the two vehicles, the Tathāgata teaches them only the selflessness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*).
[Commentary]: The selflessness of persons is that which is taught in the Hīnayāna Piṭaka.
Because their faculties are not sharp, it merely distinguishes that there is no person within the aggregates, so as to lead them to realize the emptiness of persons.
△ Second, the characteristics of clinging.
Because their teaching is not ultimate, they perceive the five aggregates as phenomena subject to arising and ceasing; thus, they fear birth and death and falsely grasp at nirvana.

[Commentary] Regarding the statement that the teaching is not ultimate: it refers to the period before the teaching on the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) was expounded; this is termed the "half-syllables. Furthermore, there are several meanings:

first, regarding practice (*caryā*), one practices only for one's own benefit and is unable to benefit others; second, regarding wisdom (*jñāna*), one attains only the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

1. They do not attain the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna). 2. They abandon; they abandon only the afflictions (kleśa), but do not abandon the objects of knowledge (jñeya). 3. They realize;
they realize only the principle of the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā-tattva), but do not realize the principle of the emptiness of phenomena. 4. They attain;

they attain only nirvāṇa with remainder and nirvāṇa without remainder, but do not attain non-abiding nirvāṇa (apratisthita-nirvāṇa). For these reasons, the teaching of the emptiness of persons in the Hīnayāna is not called the full Mahāyāna.

This refers to "names. As for the statement "seeing the five aggregates and so forth": although one does not perceive the characteristic of a person within the aggregates, one still perceives the aggregates and so forth as being real dharmas.
Since one clings to these aggregate-dharmas as truly having arising and ceasing, one consequently perceives the three realms as unstable.
It is like a burning house; one seeks to escape from it as if one's head were on fire, hoping to reach the place of quiescent peace and bliss.
This is precisely the characteristic of the view of selfhood regarding phenomena (*dharmātman-dṛṣṭi*).
△ Third, the antidote. What is the antidote?
Because the nature of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) is non-arising, there is no cessation; they are primordially in *nirvāṇa*.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "the five aggregates are neither arising nor ceasing," this refers to the fact that the *dharmatā* is fundamentally empty and quiescent. As stated previously in the passage on common characteristics:
"All sentient beings are originally and eternally abiding, having entered into *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, it says below: "By means of faith in all phenomena..."
Because it has been in a state of nirvana from the very beginning; furthermore, as stated previously in the section on the Gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*):
"All phenomena have, from the very beginning, been free from the characteristics of verbal expression, names, mental objects, and conditions, being ultimately equal. It also states:
"All phenomena are the nature of reality (*bhūtatā*)," and so forth. Within the passages concerning the convergence of appearances into reality, all of these constitute the remedies.
△ Second, ultimate transcendence.

[Commentary] Previously, we provisionally relied upon the symptoms of the illness and administered medicine according to those symptoms; thus, existence was taught in contrast to emptiness, and emptiness was taught in contrast to existence, which was not yet ultimate.
Now, however, we directly refer to the true principle, disregarding both medicine and illness, and dispense with everything.
When the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases, there is the single flavor of equality; only then is it called ultimate.
This constitutes the counteractive measure that accords with the *tathatā* expressed by words, while the ultimate accords with the *tathatā* beyond words.
△ The text consists of two parts: first, clarifying the teaching by means of the Dharma; second, resolving latent doubts.
First, clarifying the teaching by means of the Dharma (2): first, a general exposition based on the Dharma; second, seeking through broad categories. First, a general exposition based on the Dharma.

Furthermore, for one who has ultimately abandoned false attachments, it should be known that defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*) and pure phenomena (*vyavadāna-dharma*) all exist in mutual dependence;
they possess no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that can be described.
[Commentary] The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "If a phenomenon is established through dependence, that phenomenon itself becomes dependent. Now, there is no dependence at all."

The same applies to the absence of accomplished dharmas and so forth; this may be understood by analogy with the preceding explanation. Whether there is mutual dependence or no mutual dependence, the essence of phenomena is inherently such;
it does not become so only after awakening.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "defilement and purity have no intrinsic characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa*)," the reason it is designated as "the defiled" is because it is established in dependence upon purity;

one should know, therefore, that the characteristic of defilement is not an intrinsic characteristic. The same applies to the characteristic of purity. Other instances—such as the existence of emptiness arising from the beginning and the end, up to the mundane and supramundane—should be understood by analogy with this.
Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "If one perceives the true nature of defilement, there is then no [defilement]."
The characteristic of purity accords with the characteristic of cessation; this is entry into the gate of non-duality. As for that which is established through mutual dependence:

if defiled phenomena are established in dependence upon purity, then pure phenomena likewise become dependent upon defilement. If this were to continue in such a cycle, it would fall into infinite regress.

[Response: It is beyond [such categories]. Regarding "that which has no causal dependence": if there were originally no defilement to serve as the cause or the dependent condition, then how could there be purity to be established?
Below the section on "mutual dependence and non-dependence," someone may ask: "These various states of defilement and purity are mutually dependent;
it is only after awakening that one attains the state where mutual dependence ceases. During the time of delusion, how can one immediately transcend such mutual dependence?"
Therefore, this commentary states: "The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is thus from the very beginning; it is not that suchness is first attained through awakening.

Since all phenomena—whether defiled or pure—are fundamentally beyond verbal expression and conceptual discrimination, they are ultimately equal. Why, then, would one need to wait for awakening before they become non-existent?
As the treatise itself explains below.
△ Second, citing broad categories for inquiry:
Therefore, all dharmas, from the very beginning, are neither form nor mind, neither wisdom nor consciousness, neither existent nor non-existent;
they are ultimately inexpressible in their characteristics.
[Commentary: "Not consciousness" reveals that it is not mind (*citta*). "Neither existent nor non-existent" reveals that it is not form (*rūpa*).

[Sub-commentary: The phrase "not form" provides a general and concise indication. That which lacks cognition is called form; that which possesses cognition is called mind. "Not consciousness," etc., [follows].
To explain this further: non-discrimination is called *jñāna* (wisdom), while discrimination is called *vijñāna* (consciousness).

That which can be characterized is called "existence" (*bhava*), and that which is not so is called "non-existence" (*abhava*). These terms encompass all relative phenomena of both the mundane and supramundane worlds.

Yet, why does [the text] state that they are all "not"? Because every phenomenon is itself the ultimate reality (*tathatā*) and transcends all opposition; therefore, all phenomena are non-existent. Thus...
In the previous [section] on the transcendence of antidotes, both the remedial factors and the remediable phenomena—namely, emptiness and existence—were likewise not established.
In the former case, medicine was used to treat a disease; here, both medicine and disease are dispensed with. Through this, the ultimate meaning of transcendence is clearly revealed.

This is the ultimate statement; it serves as a conclusion. Fearing that those who hear this might mistake it for meaninglessness, thereby falling into the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*), or that they might emerge from non-existence only to enter into existence, thus falling into the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*), the conclusion is now stated:
"Ultimately, it is ineffable. This has two meanings. First, regarding phenomena (*dharma*): it does not mean that the essence of phenomena cannot be categorized as form, mind, and so forth.

First, regarding characteristics: it is because all other characteristics—such as those of annihilationism and eternalism, identity and difference, ordinary beings and sages, cause and effect, birth-and-death and nirvana—are ultimately inexpressible.
Second, regarding time: this clarifies that the characteristics of form, mind, and so forth are not only inexpressible for the present moment;
from the past through to the end of the future, they are ultimately inexpressible as well. Thus.

The previous section on the Gate of True Suchness (Tathatā) stated that all phenomena have, from the very beginning, been free from the characteristics of verbal expression and free from the characteristics of names and so forth.
Now, these characteristics being exhausted, they return to Suchness and merge with the fundamental substance; this is entry into the Gate of True Suchness.
△ Second, resolving doubts through reconciliation (three parts): First, directly reconciling the latent doubts; second, determining the Sage’s intent;
third, resolving it by means of a counter-argument. First, directly reconciling the latent doubts.
[Commentary] This refers to reconciling the Buddha’s intent to resolve doubts and difficulties. These doubts are not explicitly stated; there is only the text of the resolution.
Because they remain suppressed and do not manifest, they are termed "suppressed" (fu).
As for the existence of verbal expressions, one should know that these are the Tathāgata’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), employing provisional speech to guide sentient beings.
[Commentary] A doubt arises: "O Noble One, since you have realized that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature and possess an ineffable character, how can there be such [expressions]?"
Because there are various forms of verbal expression, the external objection is restated as follows: "Yet there is verbal expression. The subsequent passage provides the explanation:

"One should know that this is the Tathāgata’s skillful means; he provisionally employs verbal expression to guide the ears of sentient beings. This explanatory text directly addresses the anticipated objection:
by using provisional words to skillfully lead others, his intention does not reside in the words themselves.
[Commentary] Regarding "separation from nature": because its fundamental nature (*prakṛti*) does not exist. Since its fundamental nature is non-existent, what characteristics could there be?
This is as stated in the preceding passage concerning that which is neither form nor mind and so forth. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Whatever has characteristics is entirely false and illusory."
"Various forms of verbal expression" refers to the preceding passage that elucidates the true meaning.
"Provisional words," and so forth, are like using a raft to cross a river; the intention does not lie in the raft itself.

Because the sentient beings of this land all enter samādhi through hearing, reflection, and cultivation, it is necessary to employ sound as a Buddha-work. As the Sūtra says: "The true essence of the teaching in this region..."
"Purity lies in hearing and listening. If one wishes to attain samādhi, one must truly enter through hearing. It is further said:
'Dhāraṇī is without words, yet the Buddha has taught it by means of words.'"
△ Second, clarifying the definitive intention of the Sage.
Its underlying purpose is entirely to eliminate conceptualization and return to True Suchness (tathatā).

[Commentary] As for the Sage’s use of provisional verbal expressions to guide others, his intent is to cause them to abandon the aforementioned erroneous attachments to conceptualizations such as existence and non-existence.
It returns solely to True Suchness (*tathatā*). Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* says: "One must not grasp at the meaning according to the words. Why?

Because the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is free from words. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "When recollection, conceptualization, and contemplation have been eliminated..."
When all linguistic conventions are extinguished, such a venerable and sublime person is then able to perceive Prajñā.
(3) This is further explained by way of contrast:
because recollecting all phenomena causes the mind to arise and cease, one does not enter into true wisdom.

[Commentary: Regarding "causing the mind to arise and perish": the mind encompasses both the true and the false; one should reflect that this distinction merely depends on the difference between the substratum (the holder) and its activity (the function).
"True wisdom" is none other than original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*), while "being able to enter" refers to initial enlightenment (*ādi-awakening*).

That those from the tenth stage downward are unable to enter is because they still possess discursive thought. As stated previously: "All sentient beings are not called 'awakened,' because from the very beginning..."

Coming and going, moment by moment, they arise and perish, never departing from thought. By contrast, this reveals that when one does not direct the mind toward any phenomena, the mind is thus, quiescent, and immovable.
Therefore, the preceding text states: "If one can contemplate the mind as being without thought, one immediately attains entry into the gate of True Suchness (Tathatā)."
It further states: "Because one has distanced oneself from even subtle thoughts, one attains the vision of the mind-nature; this mind is then eternally abiding, which is called ultimate awakening.
△ Third, the characteristics of the various paths of practice and advancement.
[Commentary] Although the correct meaning has already been clarified and erroneous attachments have been eliminated, we shall now discuss directly the views and understandings.

While there may be no partiality or bias, one is still far from fully conversant with the stages of generating the aspiration for enlightenment, seeking it, practicing, and realizing it. If one merely stops here and does not advance, [the goal will not be attained].
If that is so, what is the purpose of prior understanding? Understanding without practice is like a lamp in the wind; it illuminates objects but does not clarify them.
It is also like having eyes but no feet—how could one reach the destination ahead? If one were to advance [without such understanding], where would one go?

Therefore, this analytical discernment is intended to bring about knowledge, and once knowledge is attained, to encourage progress. Thus, one avoids the faults of presumptuous arrogance toward those of superior capacity, as well as self-deprecation and retreat.
Thus it is. From this point downward, the meaning of the "Vehicle" (*yāna*) established in the "Section on Establishing the Meaning" is explained.
The text consists of two parts: first, stating the intent and explaining the name; second, opening the chapters and explaining the characteristics. First, stating the intent and explaining the name.
[Commentary] "Indicating the intent" means to set forth the intention of generating the resolve to advance toward the Buddha-way.
"Explaining the names" means to interpret the designations for the gates that characterize the aspects of advancing toward the Way. Both refer to all the subsequent passages.
Furthermore, the character "yi" (intended) may be an error; it should read "biaomen" (marking the gate). This refers to the initial sentence, which cites and marks the general gate.
"Shiming" (explaining the name) refers to the subsequent text, which explains the meaning of its name.

Regarding the characteristics of the stages of progress on the path: this refers to the path realized by all Buddhas, which has the sense of being that toward which all Bodhisattvas direct their minds, practice, and progress.
[Commentary: The "phrases on the Buddhas" cite the path of awakening toward which they proceed; "Bodhisattvas and others" manifest the causal practices by which they proceed.

Since it is intended to clarify that the types of bodhisattvas who resolve their minds to proceed toward the path realized by the Buddhas differ, it is called "the analysis of the characteristics of the paths of proceeding."
[Commentary] "The path of awakening" refers to the fruit of *bodhi* that is realized. Because the fruit of Buddhahood is perfectly pervasive and unobstructed, it is called a "path.

"Generating the mind" refers to generating the three types of resolve. "Cultivation" refers to the practice of the various *pāramitās* for the benefit of self and others, beginning from the stage of faith (*śraddhā*) and continuing until the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
Since each of these practices is able to lead toward higher stages, they are so designated. "Desire" [refers to the aspiration for enlightenment].

Regarding the phrase "clarifying, etc.," this generally summarizes the intended meaning. "Clarifying" (ming) refers to discernment (fenbie). The phrase "different types" explains the single character "characteristic" (xiang);
that is, the resolve for awakening (cittotpāda) and the practice (pratipatti) each have their own differences, and thus they are called "characteristics.

For example, regarding the resolve for awakening, there are horizontally [distinguished] categories of true (such as the resolve arising from the perfection of faith) and false (such as the resolve imitated from others); and vertically [distinguished] categories of shallow (the resolve arising from the perfection of faith) and deep (the resolve arising from realization and understanding).
Because the practice of generating the mind (*cittotpāda*) applies to both the profound and the shallow, its nature can be understood through its practice.

△ Second, opening the chapters to explain the characteristics (in three parts): first, stating the number; second, interrogating and listing; third, discerning the characteristics. First, stating the number.
Briefly stated, there are three types of generating the mind (*cittotpāda*).

[Commentary: Regarding these three types of generating the mind, the meaning has both general and specific aspects. Generally, they are collectively termed "generating and proceeding" (*utpāda-prasthāna*);

thus, the heading states "generating the mind," because it carries the sense of practicing and proceeding toward the goal. Specifically, the first two are "initiating" and "arising," while the latter one is "opening."
It is "aroused. Furthermore, the mind is that which is aroused; the person and bodhi are that which arouse it. This means that the person can initiate it, while bodhi can induce it.
That is to say, this person has internal permeation as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and roots of goodness as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

Bodhi is the object of focus (*ālambana*). Through these various conditions, one gives rise to the mind; this is termed "arousing the mind" (*cittotpāda*) by taking the subject as it relates to the object.

Furthermore, according to the respective stages, there are distinct meanings of that which initiates and that which is initiated toward [enlightenment], which shall be analyzed in the relevant passages.
△ Second, the inquiry and enumeration:
What are the three? First, the resolve through the accomplishment of faith; second, the resolve through the stage of practice and understanding; third, the resolve through realization.

[Commentary: "Faith" refers to the fulfillment of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) and the entry into the first stage of the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*), the Stage of Initial Resolve (*prathama-cittotpāda-vihāra*).

"Understanding and Practice" refers to the stage of the ten practices (*daśa-carita*), wherein one is able to understand the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) and practice the ten perfections (*daśa-pāramitā*) in accordance with them;

when these practices have become fully matured, one generates the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-citta*) and enters the stage of the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*). "Realization" refers to the stages from the first ground (*bhūmi*) upward, up to the tenth ground.
The first two are the semblance resolve (*pratirūpa-cittotpāda*); the latter one is the true resolve (*bhūta-cittotpāda*).
[Commentary] "How so? is a question. First, "one" is a listing. Regarding "the ten faiths," etc.:

this means that those at the stage of the fulfillment of the ten faiths are the agents who can generate [the resolve], while the three minds beginning with "directly" (*ṛju*) are what is generated. Furthermore, the fulfillment of the ten faiths is that which can approach [the goal].

The stage of the ten abidings (*daśabhūmi*) is that which is to be reached. The entry and exit of these two stages occur simultaneously; the meaning is as previously explained. Regarding the understanding of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), it is stated below:
"Because one knows that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is without stinginess or greed, up to being without ignorance (*avidyā*)," and so forth. This is what is meant by "knowing."

This is precisely the explanation. Regarding "practicing the ten perfections in accordance [with their nature]": this refers to the subsequent explanation of practicing the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) in accordance with its nature, up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and so forth.
The relationship between the agent of practice and the object of practice can be understood by analogy with what precedes. As for "the first stage" (*bhūmi*) and so forth:

This explains the meanings of the subject and object of the process of advancement from the second bhūmi up to the fruit of Buddhahood. Regarding the first two [stages], they are distinguished as inferior;
those that are "similar" are called "similar awakening" because they involve conceptual thought (*vikalpa*). As for the "real":

Because one has attained non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), one realizes awakening according to one's capacity; since this generally refers to the realization of principle, it is termed "ultimate reality" (*tattva*).

Among these three [types of mind], the first encompasses the stages of faith (*śraddhā*) and abiding (*vihāra*); the second encompasses the stages of practice (*caryā*) and approach (*pratipatti*); and the last encompasses the stages of the grounds (*bhūmi*) and fruition (*phala*).
These three types of mind are entirely sufficient for all stages of practice, from cause to fruit.

△ III. Discerning the Characteristics (three parts). First, the arousal of the mind through the accomplishment of faith; second, the arousal of the mind through the stage of practice and understanding; third, the arousal of the mind through realization.
Regarding the first, the arousal of the mind through the accomplishment of faith (three parts): first, the practice for accomplishing faith; second, the characteristics of the arousal of the mind.
III. The Benefit of Arousing the Mind. First, the practice for accomplishing faith.
[Commentary] This clarifies the practice for the accomplishment of the mind of faith.
△ The middle section has two parts: first, the question; second, the answer. First, the question.

Regarding those who have achieved faith and resolve their aspiration: upon what kind of person does it depend? What kind of practice must they cultivate to achieve the perfection of faith and become capable of generating the aspiration?
[Commentary] The first phrase asks about the practitioner capable of cultivation; the second phrase asks about the practice to be cultivated; "achieve" and below refer to the result.
3. Question on the Practice that Accomplishes the Capacity for Arousing [the Mind].

[Commentary]: What kind of person? Regarding what stage of a person is the meaning of "arousing the mind" explained? What kind of practice? By practicing what kind of practice does one attain the arousal of the mind?
According to the intent of the answer below, it refers to a person at the stage of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) who cultivates faith and diligence.

By practicing the ten kinds of wholesome deeds, such as mindfulness (*smṛti*), for the full duration of ten thousand *kalpas*, one reaches the tenth stage, the "mind of perfected faith" (*śraddhā-paripūrṇa-citta*), at which point one is able to give rise [to the bodhicitta].
Therefore, it is said that one is "capable of giving rise" to it.
△ Next, the answer follows.
[Commentary]: Because the preceding faith was fulfilled, there is progress; because the subsequent faith is not yet established, there is regression.
[Record]: This clarifies that within this response, there are the meanings of two sections: the former and the latter.

△ The text consists of two parts: first, the direct answer to the preceding question; second, the demonstration of superiority by means of the inferior. First, the direct answer to the preceding question (2):

first, the answers to the three questions; second, the conclusion establishing the stage. First, the answers to the three questions (3): 1. Answering regarding the practitioner who is able to cultivate;
2. Answering regarding the practice that is cultivated; 3. Answering regarding the attainment of the practice’s completion and its capacity for manifestation. First, answering... [the practitioner].
The practitioner refers to those who rely on the indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*) of sentient beings. [Commentary:
There are many ways to distinguish the three groups (*tri-rāśi*); however, in this present text, the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*) of the bodhisattva are directly elucidated.

Those mentioned above are definitively non-retrogressive and are termed the *samyaktva-niyata-rāśi* (the group of those fixed in correctness). Those who have not yet entered the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) and do not believe in cause and effect are termed the *mithyātva-niyata-rāśi* (the group of those fixed in error).
Between these two categories are those at the stage of the ten faiths, who seek the great fruit but whose minds are not yet resolved.

Advancing at times and retreating at others; as stated in the *Benye jing* (Sutra on Fundamental Actions), Bodhisattvas of the ten stages of faith are like hairs in the air and are termed the "indeterminate assembly.
Now, based on such a person, their practice is elucidated.
[Commentary] "Many gates" refers to the distinctions between the Hīnayāna and the provisional versus the ultimate, as already seen in the preceding introductory discussion (*xuántán*).
Among these three [approaches], we now take the teaching of reality (*shíjiào*) to clarify the meaning of the three aggregates (*sāṃghātika*), as analyzed in the sub-commentary (*shū*).
△ Second, the answer concerning the practices to be cultivated:

Because of the power of the roots of goodness resulting from habitual perfuming, one believes in the retribution of karma and is able to give rise to the ten wholesome actions. One comes to loathe the suffering of birth and death and desires to seek unsurpassed bodhi.
Thus, one encounters various Buddhas, personally receives their teachings and makes offerings to them, and cultivates the practice of faith.

[Commentary: Regarding "there is the power of perfuming," this refers to the power of hearing-perfuming (*śrutavāsanā*), the internal perfuming power of original enlightenment (*prakṛtistha-gotra*), and the power of various roots of goodness from previous lives.
Because of these, one is able to believe in karmic retribution, abandon evil, and follow good; this constitutes the portion of merit (*puṇyabhāga*).

The section beginning with "disgusted with birth-and-death" constitutes the portions of goodness conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣya*) and liberation (*mokṣabhāga*). All that precedes [this] is...

Discriminating the causes of practice. "Being able to encounter a Buddha" and below clarify the conditions for cultivation. This means that based on these causes and conditions, one cultivates ten kinds of practices of faith.

[Commentary] Regarding "believing in the retribution of karma": karma encompasses both good and evil; its fruits encompass both pleasure and suffering. Because the fruit can recompense the cause, [one must believe in it].
This is called "retribution" (*vipāka*); this is stated in general terms and does not refer to the specific and the universal. Regarding the "ten wholesome acts" (*daśa-kuśala*):

these refer to the ten [precepts] beginning with non-killing, and do not mean the ten kinds of faith. If one refers to the ten [faculties] beginning with faith, they will be correlated later in the text.

As for "having the lower," it refers to the permeation by hearing (*śruta-vāsanā*), which encompasses both the teacher's instruction and internal permeation, as well as the essence and characteristics. Regarding "wholesome roots": if one follows the past, they still arise from permeation.
It is accomplished through power. Looking back at the present, it is provisionally termed "past wholesome [roots]. In terms of its causal basis, it is therefore called a "root.

Regarding the passage "capable of believing in the lower [stages]" and so forth, this refers to the meaning of the characteristics of cessation and quiescence. Although there was previously wholesome [karma], because it was only recently perfumed, the wholesome roots were subtle and inferior;
they merely formed the seeds but were not yet able to give rise to faith or the diligent pursuit of various practices. Now, through repeated cultivation...

Through the perfuming [of seeds] and the concurrent power of these three factors, [the fruit] is able to arise. Thus, the roots of goodness were that which was accomplished in the past, and they are now that which brings about the arising.
This is precisely analogous to the parable in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* concerning the tying of the jewel and the untying of the jewel. This is the portion on merit.

"Portion" (bhāga) means "cause. These ten wholesome actions initially constitute worldly, out-flowing merit (*sāsrava-puṇya*) and ultimately constitute supramundane, non-out-flowing merit (*anāsrava-puṇya*);
therefore, they are also a portion within the category of merit. This is because merit is immeasurable.
This is also the measure of merit (*puṇya*). It is revealed as being distinct from wisdom (*prajñā*). Regarding "disgust for birth-and-death" (*saṃsāra*) and so forth:
because one's faith and understanding gradually increase, one is able to know that the three realms (*tridhātu*) are unstable, like a burning house; therefore, one feels disgust toward them.
Knowing that Bodhi and the fruit of Buddhahood are the ultimate coolness, one seeks them. The factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) and so forth are all as previously described.

It is said: these two divisions, together with the aforementioned division of merit, culminate in the attainment of the fruit; they correspond respectively to the three virtues of wisdom (*jñāna*), abandonment (*prahāṇa*), and grace (*anugraha*).
As for the cause of practice, it consists of the matters of delight and aversion; when the emotions are stirred within, practice arises therefrom.

Therefore, it is called the "cause of practice" (*caryā-hetu*). Question: Since cultivating the causes of the ten wholesome paths is already itself a practice, why is it designated as the "cause of practice"?
Answer: It is because, in view of subsequent supramundane practice, worldly goodness serves as its cause.

This means that mundane, out-flowing (*sāsrava*) practice acts as the cause for supramundane, non-out-flowing (*anāsrava*) practice. Question: One feels weary of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and seeks enlightenment (*bodhi*).

"Is this not, then, the practice for transcending the world? The answer is: "Although one possesses this mind, the actual deed has not yet been performed. This can be seen by reflecting upon the words regarding 'weariness with desire.

Furthermore, this seeking through weariness is merely a mundane goodness (*dharma-kuśala*); it has not yet corresponded with contemplation of the principle (*tattva-darśana*) and thus is not called 'correct practice' (*samyak-caryā*).
Nevertheless, according to this text, one is still performing preparatory means (*upāya*) prior to the stage of faith (*śraddhā*), having not yet entered the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*)."
If those who give rise to a mind of weariness with the world and seek to practice goodness were already persons of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), how could they be so?

Therefore, the Commentary states that "the above all distinguish the causes of practice"; this is precisely that meaning. What follows next—practicing the faith—is only then the proper stage of the Ten Faiths.
As for "meeting the Buddha," the Buddha here refers to his position; he must be the Response Body (*nirmāṇakāya*), appearing therein according to the capacities of beings.
Manifestation is not fixed to a single type; that is to say, it may take the form of parents, relatives, and so forth, as already explained previously.
The present mention of "the Buddha" alone refers to the primary case. Alternatively, it may be stated by way of a specific example for those who are to be liberated through the form of a Buddha.
"To draw near, serve, provide for, and support" means that one may also personally receive [the teachings]. This refers to personally receiving and inheriting the Buddha’s instructions.
Since he has manifested his body, one will certainly hear the essentials of the Dharma; having heard the Dharma, one gives rise to understanding and practices with faith.
Regarding "the conditions for practice," this refers specifically to the various auxiliary conditions within the process of perfuming (*vāsanā*). As for "in terms of equality," it is because...
It was stated previously that [an undertaking] is accomplished only when causes and conditions are fully present; therefore, nothing may be lacking.
The ten levels of faith consist of: faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, giving, precept-keeping, protection, relinquishment, and aspiration.

Within this stage, one fully gives rise to the four kinds of faith, practices the five kinds of sublime conduct, and cultivates the samādhi of *tathatā* (suchness), gradually entering and deepening it until—
Matured; thus one becomes capable of entering the first stage (*bhūmi*).
△ Third, the answer concerning the completion of practice and the capacity for generating the resolve (*cittotpāda*):
After ten thousand *kalpas*, because the faith-mind (*śraddhā-citta*) has been perfected, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas instruct and cause one to generate the resolve, or else by means of the Great...

Because of compassion, one is able to generate the aspiration [for enlightenment] by oneself; or, because the True Dharma is about to perish, one is able to generate the aspiration by oneself due to the causal conditions of protecting the Dharma.

[Commentary: From "Throughout kalpas" onwards is the first section, clarifying the accomplishment of practice. From "The Buddhas" onwards is the second section, which, regarding superior conditions, clearly explains the generation of the aspiration.
This refers to the initial aspiration of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Although there are many superior conditions, three types are briefly cited.

Among these, the first is through the power of others (*parāśraya*), while the latter two are through one's own power (*svāśraya*). Alternatively, these may correspond to the three subsequent minds mentioned below; that is, by following the teachings, one attains the straightforward mind (*ṛjukacitta*).
Because of protecting the Dharma, one attains the profound mind (*adhyāśaya*); the rest is the same as this.
[Commentary] Regarding the "ten thousand kalpas," there are four permutations based on the sharpness or dullness of the faculties: 1. those with sharp faculties who are not diligent; 2.
those with sharp faculties who are diligent—the number of kalpas for these two cannot be fixed; 3. those with dull faculties who are diligent.
The maximum duration is ten thousand kalpas. Fourth, those who are dull-witted and lack diligence are like those who are impoverished yet refuse to study;
how could it be appropriate to discuss their duration in terms of kalpas? In this treatise, the third category is taken as the standard; therefore, it says "ten thousand kalpas."
Therefore, the *Benye jing* (Sutra on Original Karma) states: "This Bodhisattva Xinxiang practiced the ten precepts for ten thousand kalpas;
he shall emerge from the ten stages of faith and enter the stage of the first abode (*prathama-vihāra*). Furthermore, that same sutra says:

"If one cultivates the ten wholesome dharmas for one, two, or three kalpas, one may still regress or emerge [from them]. If one encounters a virtuous friend and is able to believe in the Buddha-dharma, then for one, two..."

"Kalpas. Regarding "entering the stage of abiding and practicing until completion," the *Ben-shu* (Original Commentary) states: "When the time is fulfilled and the practice is completed; that is, ten thousand kalpas.

'Practice' refers to the fulfillment of the ten stages of faith, reaching up to the 'mind of emergence. As for 'Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,' these are the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas encountered previously.
Since this section instructs one to resolve the mind [of enlightenment], it refers to the Buddhas encountered while still in the stage of faith."

These are either transformative or retributive. As for superior conditions, these are the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; the suffering of sentient beings and the extinction of the True Dharma are all superior conditions.
Since the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others have already bestowed their instructions and exhortations, how could one not resolve to generate the aspiration for enlightenment?
When we encounter those of slight wisdom or meager merit and offer them some counsel, they still manage to generate the aspiration; how much more so in the case of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas?

"Has the Buddha personally bestowed his teachings upon me? Or rather, does he contemplate all sentient beings as no different from himself, seeing that they merely suffer in vain through saṃsāra due to delusion regarding the truth and attachment to the false?
For this reason, he gives rise to great compassion, desiring to deliver them all. Yet, feeling ashamed of my own limited power, I see that my actions fall short of my aspirations;
therefore, I shall first resolve to seek the fruit of Buddhahood, so that once I have perfected its divine functions, [I may fulfill that vow]."

Thus, one is capable of providing rescue and relief. Accordingly, the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states: "Seeing sentient beings who are solitary and without companions, one gives rise to a heart of compassion.
This is like a person who sees the people utterly exhausted by heavy taxes and manifold corvée labor, where just laws are not implemented and they know not to whom to appeal;
reflecting that he himself lacks the power to rectify the situation, he therefore advances in virtue and cultivates his practice, seeking recommendation and advancement.
He served his office, striving to remove the grievances of the people so that there would be no resentment between superiors and subordinates, thereby bringing about good governance.

Seeing that the Buddha-dharma was nearing extinction and sentient beings were without refuge, he sought to protect and uphold it; yet, as his power in the Way was meager, he resolved to practice cultivation in the hope of attaining realization.

Only by exerting his strength and capacity could he truly uplift the tradition. Now, to speak of the Dharma, it must comprise the teaching (*śāsana*), the principle (*yukti*), and the practice (*pratipatti*).

Regarding the fruit: that which is currently said to have "perished" refers only to its extinction within the context of the four [categories]. In terms of teaching and practice, it has perished; however, in terms of principle and the fruit, it has not perished. As for the extinction of the teaching:
since the Buddha’s establishment of the teachings was intended for their propagation, if they are neglected and no longer practiced, this constitutes the meaning of "extinction.
It does not necessarily mean being reduced to ashes like the First Emperor’s books or burned up like the lion’s [prey], but rather, as stated in the preface, the sinking of the palm-leaf manuscripts.

This is the meaning [of protecting the Dharma]. As for the extinction of practice, it is because there is no one to cultivate it. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The extinction of the Dharma refers to the extinction of its cultivation.

What we now protect and uphold consists solely of the cultivation of the teachings and practices—namely, transcribing, reading, reciting, explaining according to the parts, and exhorting later students so that the lamp may be passed from one to another, shining on and on without end. This is what it means to protect the teaching. If...

To discipline oneself in cultivation and progress, and to exhort those with whom one has a karmic connection so that the seed of the Buddha is not severed—this is the practice of protection (*ārakṣā*).

Furthermore, if one examines it in detail, both the principle (*li*) and the fruit (*guo*) also possess the sense of cessation; however, they cease in mutual dependence upon the aforementioned teachings and practices.
Due to the absence of non-informative action (*avijñapti*), there is no practice; due to the absence of practice, there is no realization; and due to the absence of realization, there is no fruit.

Although these four are all termed "cessation" (*nirodha*), their meanings of cessation differ: teaching and practice involve only the cessation through abandonment; the principle-dharma involves only the cessation through concealment;

and the fruit, in terms of its nature and characteristics, encompasses both meanings. Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states that there are two kinds of causes and conditions that bring about [this state].
The True Dharma shall abide for a long time. First, there are bhikṣus within who uphold the precepts; second, there are donors without who possess sincere faith.
Furthermore, it is said that when the final extinction of Śākyamuni’s bequeathed Dharma approaches, it is not because the bhikṣus lack offerings that the Buddha-dharma perishes;
rather, it is because the four requisites are so abundant that arrogance and indulgence arise in their hearts, allowing the celestial Māras to gain an opportunity.
Then, the Dharma of Śākyamuni will perish forever from this point on. If one were to resolve their mind to seek the fruit of Buddhahood, it would not be through the mere observance of precepts alone;
thus, there would be no way for his Buddha-dharma to cease. In the present treatise, the word "perhaps" (*huò*) carries the sense of uncertainty;
among the three aforementioned [conditions], by following any one of them, one is able to resolve their mind. Regarding the phrase "superior conditions" below, however, this—
Bodhisattvas have practiced for ten thousand kalpas; their capacity is not shallow. As for the conditions that prompt their advancement, how could they be limited to these three alone?
Therefore, I now cite them briefly. Within the practices of the two benefits (self and others), the conditions are immeasurable and cannot be recorded in full;
thus, it is said to be "brief. Among these, the lower [category] corresponds to self and others: the mind arises from being taught by others, giving rise to one's own mind. Second.

Because they are not the same. Furthermore, the following sections may be correlated with the minds that are generated. Regarding the "direct mind" (*ṛju-citta*): it is stated below, "First is the direct mind, because one correctly contemplates the dharma of *tathatā* (suchness).
Having received the personal instruction, one is thus able to generate the mind and correctly contemplate *tathatā*.

Being free from all sinking, agitation, and every form of crookedness, it is called "direct. Regarding the "profound mind" (*gambhīra-citta*): it is for the purpose of wishing to protect the Dharma. Thus it is said.
One must give rise to the resolve. By fully cultivating the myriad practices and perfecting all merits, one immediately accomplishes this mind.
Other instances of "that which is the same as this" refer to the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-citta*); this may be seen from the text itself.
△ Second, the conclusion of the stage:
Thus, those who have accomplished faith and attained the arousal of the mind enter the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and shall never again fall back;
they are said to dwell within the lineage of the Tathāgata, being in accord with the true cause.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "such as these," there are two points below. First, "non-retrogression" reveals that there is no falling back to lower stages;

this refers to entering the stage of the Initial Resolve within the Ten Abidings, wherein one does not fall into the realms of ordinary beings or the Lesser Vehicle. Second, "abiding in the lineage" clarifies that there is attainment on higher levels;
this refers to abiding in the stage of the Nature of Cultivation, where one practices in accordance with the cause of internal permeation. Therefore, it is called "correct."
Cause. Furthermore, from this stage onward, one is certain to attain the fruit; therefore, it is called the "True Cause" (*samyag-hetu*), because there is no further falling back or loss.

[Commentary] Regarding "not falling into the stages of ordinary beings or the Lesser Vehicle," the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that one causes the protection of two practices, namely, the protection against afflictions (*kleśa*).
Regarding the practices: if a beginner hears the censure of the practices of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), they may fall back into the practices of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*);

if they hear the rebuke of the practices of the Two Vehicles, they may instead enter into the practices of ordinary beings. Thus, they are unwilling to practice the Middle Way. Now, having attained the fulfillment of faith, they do not fall into such errors.
As for the nature of the stage of cultivation (*śikṣamāṇa-gotra*), according to the *Benye jing* (Sutra on Original Karma), it proceeds from cause to fruit.

These are subsumed into six types of nature: namely, the nature of the seeds of practice in the ten abodes; the nature of the seeds of conduct in the ten practices; the nature of the seeds of the path in the ten transferences;
the noble nature of the ten stages; the nature of equal enlightenment; and the nature of wondrous enlightenment. The present case refers to the first.

Regarding "conforming to internal perfuming," it means that [the mind] accords with the essence and characteristics of True Suchness (Tathatā). This distinguishes it from the non-conceptual mind of the [ten] stages and above.
This is because they are in accord with principle; thus, it is called "conformity" (*saṃprayoga*). Now, prior to this stage, one merely accords with [the path], and thus it is called "conformity.

Because one has not yet attained non-conceptual cognition, yet is certain to attain the fruit—due to abiding in the direct cause for the fruit of Buddhahood—it is said that this Bodhisattva has entered the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*). This is because...
The Buddha is in accord with the true cause. Having conformed to that cause, one will certainly attain the fruit;
therefore, it is said that one "plants within the lineage of the Tathāgata. This refers precisely to the cause.
△ Second, elevating the inferior to manifest the superior.
[Commentary: "Superior" refers to advancing as before; "inferior" refers to retreating as here. △ The text has two parts:
first, clarifying the characteristics of subtle inferiority; second, concluding with the formation of retrogression and loss. First, clarifying the characteristics of subtle inferiority.
(2). First, the power of internal causes is weak; second, the power of external conditions is inferior. Regarding the first, the weakness of internal causes:
if there are sentient beings whose roots of goodness are meager and whose afflictions have been deep-seated for a long time, even though they encounter a Buddha...
They may also receive offerings; however, they plant the seeds for rebirth as humans or devas, or they plant the seeds for the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha).
Even if there are those who seek the Mahāyāna, their faculties are not fixed, such that they may advance or retreat.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "If there are... and so forth, there are two parts below this. First, "afflictions are thick" refers to the heaviness of delusion. Second, "even though they encounter...
and so forth refers to the meagerness of merit. Within this, there are three points: first, "humans and devas" refers to seeking erroneously; second, "the two vehicles" refers to seeking differently;
third, "advancing and retreating" refers to being hesitant regarding the Mahāyāna.
[Commentary] "Those with meager roots of goodness" refers to those whose faculties are inferior; this is because they were unable to cultivate many seeds of goodness in their past lives.

"Those with heavy afflictions" refers to those for whom greed and hatred burn intensely and cannot be restrained. "Those who encounter a Buddha" includes those who, even after his parinirvāṇa, behold the physical image of the Buddha and are able to offer worship.
"Those who seek erroneously" refers to those who delight in practicing the five precepts and ten wholesome paths, yet merely hope for [rebirth as] a human being.
The fruit of heavenly rebirth. Both humans and devas do not escape birth and death; yet they seek what ought to be loathed. Therefore, it is called "inverted.
Speaking of the cause by way of the fruit, the Treatise calls it the "seed. Those who seek differently are those who fear birth and death.

They take the noble truths as their object of contemplation and seek the fruits of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). Although they transcend the triple world, they have not yet reached the ultimate;

they do not travel the same path as the Buddhas of the three periods of time, and for this reason they are said to be "different. Their advancement and retreat, and so forth, are distinguished in the treatise below.

These three all clarify the characteristics of meager and inferior virtue and conduct. This is entirely because their roots of goodness and the foundation of their merit are not profound or substantial.
△ Second, the power of external conditions is inferior. There are those who,
having made offerings to the Buddhas for less than ten thousand kalpas, encounter the necessary conditions therein and likewise give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment—
namely, giving rise to that mind upon seeing the physical marks of a Buddha, or giving rise to that mind because of making offerings to the Sangha, or...
Because of those of the Two Vehicles, they are taught to resolve their minds [for enlightenment], or they follow others in resolving their minds.

[Commentary]: There are some who perform offerings and so forth; below this, there are two points. First, they have not yet passed through ten thousand kalpas, meaning their period of practice is not yet complete.
Second, they may also arise when encountering conditions, yet these conditions are not sufficient to sustain them. Within this, there are four types: first, seeing the Buddha through form;

second, making offerings to the Sangha while abiding in signs; third, generating the aspiration for enlightenment following inferior teachings; and fourth, emulating the tracks of others. These are not the mind of compassion and wisdom of a bodhisattva;
therefore, they are prone to falling back and losing [the resolve].
[Commentary]: From this point, there are some who make offerings [to Buddhas] until they eventually fall to the stages of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

All of these are signs of the progress and regression of those seeking the Mahāyāna. As for the phrase "whose time is not yet full," this is because it is spoken in reference to those of dull faculties who possess diligence.
Those who see by means of form and seek by means of sound walk upon a deviant path and cannot perceive the Tathāgata.

Therefore, it was said previously that because they do not know that the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are manifesting, they perceive [the Buddha] as coming from the outside and grasp at the boundaries of forms;

or, those who dwell upon signs while making offerings to such things as the sculpted or painted images of the Tathāgata are unable to penetrate the emptiness of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala-śūnyatā*).
This refers to practicing giving without abiding. As for those who follow inferior teachings, this differs from the previous case of generating the seeds of the two vehicles;
in the former, the cause was inferior, whereas here, the conditions are inferior. As for those who study the traces of others, they merely follow after them without any independent discernment.
By imitating the external traces of others while failing to reflect upon their own minds, they see others retreat and consequently retreat themselves. Or...
"When the mind grows weary, one withdraws of one's own accord. These words serve as a concluding distinction, for compassion and wisdom constitute the very essence of the bodhicitta.
Now, when a practitioner of the Mahāyāna first generates the bodhicitta, they must first possess wisdom:

they must realize that true nature is inherently present and that ignorance is fundamentally empty. They seek to sever this fundamentally empty ignorance and seek to realize this inherently present true nature. Next, one must...

It is endowed with compassion. It continues until the end of the future, delivering the realms of sentient beings; thereafter, by means of vows, it is firmly constrained so that one does not momentarily abandon them and no fatigue is incurred.
Because these three are complete, this alone constitutes the true initial practice of the Mahāyāna.

Since it is not like those [other practices], it is said to be "not" [so]. However, the term "arousing the mind" (*cittotpāda*) used here refers, for the time being, to the initial stage of the level of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*).
The initial arousal of the aspiration for the Way is not the same as the arousal of the mind upon reaching the stage of "entry and abiding" through the fulfillment of faith;
it is like those practitioners today who have merely begun to arouse Mahayana faith. This refers to one who is still at the very beginning of the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*).
△ Second, the conclusion on retrogression:
Such productions of the resolve as these are all indeterminate; encountering adverse conditions, they may suddenly regress and fall to the stage of the two vehicles.

[Commentary] The passage beginning with "In this way, etc. first concludes the preceding section on the inferiority of the mind. The section beginning with "Encountering adverse conditions" next clarifies the actual process of falling back and degenerating.

"Adverse conditions" refers to the five desires (*pañca-kāma-guṇa*) and the two vehicles (*dvi-yāna*). "Falling back and losing" means losing the bodhicitta that was generated, failing to enter the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*), and regressing to the level of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

This occurs because the five desires serve as the adverse conditions. Regarding "falling into the stage of the two vehicles": [this refers to those who, due to such conditions, deviate toward the paths of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas].
This is because the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) serve as adverse conditions. A sutra states:
"Of hundreds of thousands of millions of people who resolve upon bodhicitta, perhaps only one or two will reach the fruit of Buddhahood; the rest all fall into the two vehicles. It further states:

"When Bodhisattvas resolve upon the Great Mind, it is like fish eggs or mango blossoms—these three things are abundant at the time of the cause, yet those that attain the fruit are extremely few. However, this [preceding passage]...

Subsequently, when comparing the superior and the inferior, there are seven points for each. First, regarding the seven points of the inferior: 1. Inferiority of rank and position: the initial stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*).
2. Inferiority of internal permeation: lacking power. 3. Inferiority of roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*):

being extremely slight. 4. Inferiority of temporal limit: not having passed through ten thousand kalpas. 5. Inferiority of external conditions: perceiving the Buddha through physical forms (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*). 6. Inferiority in initiating practice: [the level of] humans and devas (*manuṣya-deva*).
The two vehicles are ultimately inferior in seven respects; they regress and enter the stage of ordinary persons and the Lesser Vehicle. As for the seven matters in which [the Bodhisattva] excels:

first, excellence in rank and position, having perfected the stage of the ten faiths; second, excellence in internal permeation, possessing great power; third, excellence in roots of goodness, having long planted the foundations of virtue; fourth...
Fifth, superiority in duration: it lasts for ten thousand kalpas. Sixth, superiority in external conditions: encountering a Buddha and receiving his teachings.

Seventh, superiority in the arousal of practice: possessing direct and profound compassion and so forth. Eighth, superiority in the ultimate goal: attaining right concentration without regression. Such are the distinctions between superior and inferior; advancement and retreat should accordingly follow these principles.

Phonetic Glossary:
*Pāramitā*— this is translated as "reaching the other shore."
*Fèi* (沸): The sound of boiling; it describes the appearance of a spring gushing forth.
*Kiè* (愜): Pronounced *qiè*; it means to satisfy the mind or to find contentment.
*Vairocana*: This is translated as "Pervading All Places. It is a name for the Buddha.
"Tiwei" (提謂) is translated as "hugu" (胡瓜, melon); it is the name of a wealthy elder.
"Tan" (炭) is pronounced like "tan" (歎); it refers to burnt wood that has not yet become ash.
"Vipaśyin" (毗婆尸) is translated as "Victorious Vision" (勝觀).
Śikhin means "Fire" in this language;
Kāśyapa means "Drinker of Light";
Maitreya means "The Benevolent One."
"Hu" (怙) is pronounced as "wu" (悟). It means to rely upon or depend on.
Jambudvīpa (閻浮提) is translated here as "Superior Gold.
"Chao" (麨) is pronounced as "chao" (炒); it refers to parched rice or wheat, and to the crumbs of dried rice.
*Mùyuàn* (Deer Park) refers to a park for raising deer.
*Qū* (袪) has the pronunciation *qù*; it means to wave or brush away.
*Pǒ* (叵) has the pronunciation *pō*; it means "not possible" or "cannot."
*Ōu* (pronounced *ōu*) refers to bubbles floating on water.
*Yǔn* (pronounced *yǔn*) means to perish or vanish.
*Jiǎndú* refers to writing tablets; in antiquity there was no paper, so when there were matters to record, they were written upon these tablets.
*Quán* (pronounced *gān*): to stop; to change; to transform.
*Jiǒng* (pronounced *qióng*): the wooden bolt of a door.
*Chì* (pronounced *chī*): to reject; to repudiate.
Pūrṇa is here translated as Mǎncí (Full Compassion).
"Měng" (懵) has the phonetic value of "méng" (蒙), meaning "obscured" or "dull-witted.

*Xiǔ* (pronounced *xù*) means to encourage and exhort.
*Zhěng* (pronounced *zhěng*) means to assist, rescue, extricate, and save.
*Fù* (pronounced *fù*) refers to taxes and levies.
*Sù* (訴): the sound *sù*; to inform; to litigate. *Mò* (瘼):
the sound *mò*; illness. *Wēijìn* (煨燼):
the sounds *wēi* and *jìn*; embers in a basin.
*Tiāo* (with the fourth tone): to sway, to move, to scatter, to be disordered.
*Hē*: pronounced as *hē*, to revile and rebuke.
*Yóu-yù*: pronounced as *yóu-yù*; the name of a beast whose nature is characterized by much doubt and hesitation.
*Xiào* (斆) means "to emulate" (*xiào*). *Fǎ* (法) also means "to emulate.
*Āmra* is translated here as "difficult to distinguish"; it is the name of the king's tree.
*Lán* (音藍) means "decay" or "withering."

△ Second, the characteristics of the arousal of the mind (in three parts): First, citing the chapter to pose the question; second, indicating the headings, listing them, and providing the explanation;
third, resolving doubts through questions and answers. First, citing the chapter to pose the question.
Furthermore, regarding those who have achieved faith and give rise to the resolve [for awakening]:
what kind of mind do they generate? [Commentary] The phrase "furthermore" introduces the chapter. The phrase "what kind of mind" poses the question.

What has been explained previously consists only of the causes and conditions for generating [the resolve]; it was not yet known what the characteristics of the mind thus generated would be. Therefore, this inquiry is raised.
...Thus. △ Second, the heading, inquiry, enumeration, and explanation.
Briefly stated, there are three kinds. What are the three? First, the direct mind (*ṛju-citta*), because it correctly contemplates the dharma of *tathatā*. Second, ...

The profound mind (*adhyāśaya*), because it delights in practicing all virtuous deeds. Third, the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-citta*), because it desires to uproot the suffering of all sentient beings.

[Commentary] "Three kinds" indicates the categories. "What are they? asks for the enumeration. First, "the straightforward mind" (*ṛju-citta*) refers to that which is directed toward the principle (*tattva*).

Because there are no divergent paths, these constitute the foundation of the two types of practice. The profound mind (*adhyāśaya*) is the perfection of all virtues and the turning toward the source of the mind;
it is the foundation of the practice for one's own benefit (*svārtha*). Great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is the extensive uprooting of the suffering of sentient beings to enable them to attain Bodhi;

it is the foundation of the practice for the benefit of others (*parārtha*). Although sublime practices are vast, they are subsumed within these three; therefore, it is stated that this is a brief [explanation].

This explains the three [aspects]. Because these are precisely the three clusters of precepts (trisaṃvarāḥ), and because the three virtues and the three bodies (trikāya) are all accomplished through them, they are also identical to those three dedications (pariṇāmanā).
That is to say: the first is directed toward the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), the next toward enlightenment (bodhi), and the last toward sentient beings;
each of these should be explained in accordance with its respective correspondence.

[Commentary] Regarding "directing oneself toward the principle" and so forth: the wondrous principle of *tathatā* (suchness) is in its essence free from all marks of extremes and perversity—such as existence and non-existence, unity and difference, ordinary person and sage, or defilement and purity.
If one wishes to approach it, one must necessarily possess right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).

Right mindfulness is precisely right wisdom (*samyak-prajñā*), and right wisdom is itself the straightforward mind (*ṛju-citta*). This is because the principle has no differentiation; therefore, the mind that directs itself toward it must necessarily be straightforward. Thus it is said.
The *Zancha jing* (Sūtra on the Divination of the Auspicious and Inauspicious) states that true suchness (*tathatā*) can bring about the practitioner’s mind of straightforwardness (*ṛjukacitta*).

Just as the nature of a snake’s movement is crooked, yet it becomes straight when entering a tube, so too is the mind regulated by samādhi. Herein, right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*) is precisely the samādhi of true suchness.
Regarding the "two practices as the root": this straightforward mind universally serves as the foundation for the two practices. Below—
The two minds serve as the fundamental basis for the two types of practice. That which universally serves as the basis for these two practices is the mindfulness of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
It is endowed with untainted merit (*anāsrava-guṇa*), and all sentient beings equally possess this nature; thus, they shall all become Buddhas.

Because one knows it is endowed with such merit, one is able to initiate practice for one's own benefit (*svārtha-caryā*); because one knows that their nature is identical, one is able to initiate practice for the benefit of others (*parārtha-caryā*).
