(The Foundation of the Practice): Furthermore, by recollecting that *tathatā* (suchness) is neither born in the past nor extinguished in the future, one is able to bring the two practices to ultimate completion without weariness (the foundation of the non-interruption of practice).

Moreover, by knowing that this nature is beyond verbal expression and conceptualization, and is ultimately equal, one is able to cause the two practices to be free from signs and become the cause for the untainted (*anāsrava*) (the foundation of the correspondence of practice). Thus, this one...
The mind serves as the root for both. Regarding "delightful accumulation" and so forth: "delight" (*ruci*) refers to aspiration; it denotes focused determination.
From this, one knows that "liking" (*priya*) is not equal to "delight," and that "liking" is not equal to "delight."
One who is fully endowed with the myriad virtues cultivates all the practices of the six perfections.

Each of these cultivated practices serves as an antidote to delusion and defilement, thereby manifesting the *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges-sand) merits inherent in the nature. For example, through wisdom, one overturns and destroys ignorance.

This reveals and establishes the meaning of the great wisdom-light of the ultimate nature (*dharmatā*), and so forth. Thus, one knows that cultivation is undertaken precisely to manifest these virtues;

therefore, cultivation is explained here by way of what is accomplished. Based on this, it is not only called the "profound mind" (*gambhīra-citta*), but may also be called the "vast mind" (*vipula-citta*), because all myriad practices are cultivated simultaneously (vastness) and because they all penetrate the source of the mind (profundity). This is now indicated.
Because it is vertical, it is called "profound mind" (*gambhīra-citta*); because it is explained as horizontal, it is said to be "all.
The intent is that these two phrases manifest one another. The commentary (*śāstra*) also incorporates these two meanings.

If there is profundity without breadth (the single practice of penetrating principle), or if there is breadth without profundity (practicing many worldly virtues), neither constitutes the practice of the Mahāyāna. Now, this [text] clarifies both together. Because...
This constitutes the great practice of a bodhisattva. Regarding the basis of self-benefiting practice: it is because of the profound aspiration and joyful resolve.
If one does not aspire and take joy in it, how could one possibly carry out such practice? Therefore, this is the foundation. "Desiring to uproot" and so forth: "desire" (欲) refers to hope;
it has the same meaning as the character for "joy" (樂) and can be used interchangeably with it. "Extensively uprooting the suffering of beings" refers to the vast mind. [The three realms...]
To universally deliver all beings without distinction between enemy and kin is the foremost intention for causing them to attain *bodhi*.

This is because such a resolve transcends the realms of humans and devas, as well as those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). If it were otherwise, how could it be called "great compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*)?

Indeed, while the extraction of sentient beings from suffering is precisely great compassion, causing them to attain *bodhi* is great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), for *bodhi* is the fruit of bliss, and loving-kindness is that which can bestow bliss.
Therefore, this treatise mentions only great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) for uprooting suffering; it must necessarily imply great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) for bestowing happiness.

Thus, the commentary explains them together. Without this mind, how could one deliver and liberate others? Hence, they are called the "basis of practice. From the phrase "wondrous practice" (*miao xing*) below, the concise is shown to encompass the extensive.
Although there are three textual categories, their meaning embraces all things. They unite the practice of principle and phenomena, benefiting both self and others.
There is nothing that is not encompassed. From "By this" onwards, [the text] correctly correlates [these] with the various practices. Regarding the three clusters of precepts (*tri-śīla-saṃgraha*):

the "direct mind" (*ṛju-citta*) encompasses the *saṃvara-śīla*, because by being rightly mindful of true suchness (*tathatā*), one is free from all transgressions. The "profound mind" (*gambhīra-citta*) encompasses the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*.

Compassion (*karuṇā*) is the precept that gathers sentient beings. As for the three virtues: the straightforward mind (*ṛjukatā-citta*) accomplishes the virtue of severance (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), which is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);

the profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*) accomplishes the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*), which is Prajñā; and compassion accomplishes the virtue of grace (*anuśaṃsā-guṇa*), which is Liberation (*vimukti*).

The three bodies (*trikāya*) correspond respectively to the Dharma, Enjoyment, and Transformation bodies. "That person" refers to one who has resolved their mind through the perfection of faith. [They] turn back toward themselves...

One's own mind is directed toward three points; therefore, it is called "dedication" (*pariṇāmanā*). "The limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*) refers to *tathatā* (suchness), because it is the true limit of reality.
"Enlightenment" (*bodhi*) is so called because all virtuous practices take great wisdom as their foremost principle. Sentient beings can understand this.
Based on this, among the three [types of dedication], the first is practice free from signs (*animitta*), while the latter two are practices that follow signs (*sanimitta*).

Practice. The aspect of detachment is the general; the aspects of following [phenomena] are the particular. Although explained sequentially, practice is simultaneous, because the former one encompasses the latter two.
Thus, although one contemplates emptiness, the myriad practices remain distinct; yet the latter two are identical to the former.

Although one engages with existence, the single truth remains quiescent. If either of these aspects were lacking, it would result in the empty cessation of the Two Vehicles or the tainted existence of ordinary beings;
only when the initial and final states mutually support one another does it constitute the sublime practice of the Middle Way of the Mahāyāna.

For this reason, although all practices are numerous, they are entirely subsumed within these three. Furthermore, there are other triads, such as the Three Jewels, the three types of Bodhi, and the three types of Nirvāṇa.
All three dharmas should be applied in this manner. Therefore, Vimalakīrti taught these as the practices for the Pure Land.
The Sūtra says: "The straightforward mind is the bodhisattva’s pure land; when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings who are free from flattery will come to be born in that land.
The profound mind is the bodhisattva’s pure land; when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, those endowed with perfected merit [will come to be born in that land]."
Sentient beings come to be born in that land because the four immeasurable minds are the bodhisattva’s pure land.
When the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings who have accomplished loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity come to be born in that land.
△ Section Three: Questions and Answers to Remove Doubts (2). Part One: The Question; Part Two: The Answer. First, the Question:

It was stated above that the Dharma-realm has but one characteristic and the Buddha-body is non-dual. For what reason, then, do we not simply contemplate True Suchness alone, but must further rely upon the cultivation of various virtuous practices?

[Commentary] The above explains what follows below, citing what was previously stated as the fundamental tenet of the meaning. That is, it refers to what was said before: "As for the meaning of 'awakening' (bodhi), it means that the substance of the mind is free from thought.
This characteristic of being free from thought is equal to the realm of empty space; there is nowhere it does not pervade. It is the single characteristic of the dharma-realm," and so forth.
Furthermore, this is explained in detail within the Gate of True Suchness (tathatā-mukha) and within the substance and characteristics of True Suchness itself. Why is it explained below?

This constitutes a formal objection. The intention is as follows: if the *tathatā* (suchness) of sentient beings is identical to the body of the Buddha, then by merely contemplating *tathatā*, one can attain the Way;
what need is there to further cultivate various practices? This implies that one should simply employ a direct mind (*ṛju-citta*).
It is not appropriate to further discuss the latter two [points].
△ Second, the response (in two parts): first, the direct answer to the question; second, the re-explanation of the skillful means.
First, the direct answer to the question (in two parts): first, the analogy; second, the application. First, the analogy.
The answer is: For example, it is like a great maṇi jewel whose essential nature is luminous and pure, yet which is defiled by the impurities of ore.
Even if a person contemplates its precious nature, they will never attain its purity unless they employ various skillful means to grind and polish it.

[Commentary]: The essential nature and characteristics of a mani jewel are originally luminous and pure. Now, however, it is defiled by impurities; although its fundamental substance is pure, its appearance is not.
Therefore, it must be purified.
△ II. The Second Conjunction (3). First, the direct conjunction; second, the detailed explanation; third, the accord with reality. First, the direct conjunction:
Thus, the *tathatā* of sentient beings is by nature empty and pure, yet it possesses the defilements of immeasurable afflictions (*kleśa*).
If a person, although mindful of True Suchness (tathatā), does not cultivate it through various skillful means, they will likewise fail to attain purity.
[Commentary] True Suchness is the dharma of the mind, comparable to a mani jewel; yet, when it is referred to as "sentient beings," this refers to True Suchness that is entangled in defilements.
It is distinguished from the pure True Suchness of the Buddhas, which is free from such entanglements. It is like the union of emptiness and purity with luminous clarity.

"Clarity" (*ming*) refers to the illumination of wisdom; "purity" (*jing*) refers to emptiness and stillness. As for the term "essential nature" (*tixing*), it refers to the original nature’s clarity and purity, distinguishing it from the clarity and purity that results from the removal of defilements.

"Afflictions" (*fan-nao*) correspond to ore and impurities. "The person" refers to one who has attained faith and initiated the mind [of enlightenment], corresponding to the person who perceives the jewel.
"Cultivation through perfuming" (*xunxiu*) corresponds to polishing and refining; it means the internal arising of the habitual tendencies of weariness with suffering and the seeking of liberation.

The power of causes is like that [jewel] being carved and polished by hand; the power of conditions, such as hearing and cultivation under the guidance of a teacher, is like that [jewel] being scrubbed and ground with sand and stones.
Thus it is said there are "various skillful means. Furthermore, there is no one who is inherently pure, for one cannot attain a stainless purity.
Although the jewel, when combined with dust and defilement, is fundamentally empty and quiescent in its essence, it nevertheless appears to exist in its phenomenal aspects.
Regarding "dust and toil" (*kleśa*): if one does not initiate the practice of antidotes, there is no way to become equal to the Buddhas.
Thus we know that while the Buddha and sentient beings are identical in essence, they differ in their characteristics. The characteristic of sentient beings is the blazing of the six defilements;

the characteristic of the Buddhas is the universal assembly of all virtues. Their difference is as vast as that between heaven and earth—how could they be treated as the same? Therefore, the three types of awakening were previously explained.

Regarding the five stages of awakening (*pañca-bodhi*): as for awakening, their nature is identical; as for the three [stages] and five [levels], their positions are distinct. Since their nature is identical, there is no need for cultivation; since their positions are distinct, they must be severed and realized.

Furthermore, the Tiantai Perfect Teaching fully elucidates the six levels of "immediacy" (*liu-ji*). Because they are immediate, True Suchness (*tathatā*) is equal; because they are six, the practices and positions are fundamentally distinct.
How could this be the same as dark realization, which is merely the principle? Therefore, one should advance in practice to eliminate defilements and delusions.
If one merely practices mindfulness, one will not avoid sinking into emptiness. Only when calm abiding and insight are mutually required does one truly possess the Buddha-dharma;
the analogy of eyes and feet should be reflected upon accordingly.
△ Next is the detailed explanation.
Because defilements are immeasurable and pervade all phenomena, one cultivates all virtuous practices as their antidote.
[Commentary] This explains the reason why one must cultivate a multitude of practices.
[Commentary] An objection is raised: Since the precious nature of True Suchness (tathatā) is singular and unique, why must it be cultivated through manifold practices?

To this, the following explanation is given: Since beginningless time, sentient beings have turned their backs on awakening and conformed to the sensory dusts (rajas), giving rise to immeasurable afflictions (kleśa) and defiled dharmas, such as greed and hatred, toward all phenomena including form and sound.
Now that they have realized these faults and calamities, they practice cultivation.
Regarding the antidotes: since the defilements to be countered are numerous, how could the wholesome qualities that serve as their antidotes be singular?
It is just as when there are many illnesses, the medicines are not of a single kind; therefore, one cultivates all practices. The *Vajracchedikā* also says:
"By means of non-self and non-person, cultivating all wholesome dharmas, one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," and so forth.
△ Subsequently, it accords with the True [Suchness].
If a person practices all wholesome dharmas, they naturally accord with and return to the Dharma of True Suchness.
[Commentary]: Because all virtuous practices externally oppose false defilement and internally accord with True Suchness.
[Commentary] An objection is raised: "Immeasurable virtuous practices were originally intended as remedies for immeasurable defilements and afflictions;
how can they be in accord with the single essence-nature of True Suchness (tathatā)? Therefore, this explanation states: "Since all unwholesome practices contradict the True Principle..."

All wholesome practices naturally accord with the Truth. Furthermore, by means of various remedial wholesome practices, one eliminates defilements, thereby enabling the single jewel of True Suchness (tathatā) to attain clarity and purity. Regarding "external opposition" and so forth:

for example, when practicing generosity, it externally opposes stinginess and greed while internally accords with non-stinginess; this continues up to wisdom, which externally opposes ignorance while internally [accords with non-ignorance].
This follows the principle of the essence of clarity, and so forth.
△ Second, the re-explanation of skillful means.
[Commentary] The previous response to the question stated: "Without cultivation through skillful means, one will ultimately never attain purity. Therefore, it is now explained once more.

This is the practice of skillful means. Previously, one merely gave rise to the aspiration but had not yet carried out the actual deeds; what is now being explained is precisely that which is to be practiced.
Thus, the former constitutes the mind that initiates, while this constitutes the conduct that is initiated. Therefore, the previous commentary marked it thus.

All these are said to be the basis of practice. One should know that the preceding passage merely revealed the characteristics of generating the resolve (*cittotpāda*), whereas this clarifies the characteristics of cultivation (*pratipatti*).
The text has two parts: first, the heading and inquiry; second, the detailed explanation. First, the heading and inquiry:
Briefly stated, there are four kinds of skillful means (*upāya*).
What are the four? [Commentary: "There are four" indicates the number; "what are they? poses the inquiry.
[Commentary] Regarding "expedient means" (*upāya*): in general discussion, there are four types. First, the expedient means of advancement; second, the expedient means of skillful artifice;
third, the expedient means of cultivation; and fourth, the expedient means of integration. This passage properly corresponds to the first and third, while also encompassing the second and fourth.
△ Second, the detailed explanation. [Commentary]:

Each of the four gates has three parts: first, the designation of the name; second, the explanation of its characteristics; third, the clarification of its intent. These may be understood from the text as they appear.
Now, the text of these four gates is divided into three parts: the first concerns the path of non-abiding; the next two concern practice for one's own benefit;
and the last concerns practice for the benefit of others.
[Commentary] The text is divided into three parts; these correspond, respectively, to the practices arising from the first three minds. Reflect upon this in relation to the text.
Furthermore, this represents the profound and subtle meaning of the treatise as categorized by the author of the sub-commentary (*śāstravṛtti*).
△ First, the path of non-abiding.
[Commentary] "The path of non-abiding" possesses two meanings. First, "not" (bu) means "non-existent" (wu). "Path" (dao) refers to the cause.
Because it is a causal practice that is without abiding, the Original Commentary states: "the practice of non-abiding. Second, "path" refers to the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Because this nature is fundamentally without abiding, these two meanings must be combined to reveal it; only then will one accord with the intent of the treatise.
This is because since nature is fundamentally without abiding, one follows it by means of practice that is itself without abiding.
First is the practice of the fundamental skillful means: that is, contemplating that all phenomena are by nature unarisen and free from deluded views, thereby not dwelling in birth and death;
and contemplating that all phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions, such that the fruits of karma are never lost, thereby giving rise to great compassion.
They cultivate all manner of merit and virtue to gather and transform sentient beings, yet they do not abide in nirvana, because they accord with the non-abiding nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
[Commentary: Not abiding in saṃsāra is wisdom; not abiding in nirvana is compassion.
[Commentary] First, "lower" refers to the preliminary designation of the title and the expedient means of practice;

because it is the root, it serves as the foundation for the two subsequent types of beneficial conduct. That is to say, regarding "contemplating the lower": next, the characteristics of the meaning are shown.
"The nature is non-arising" means that all phenomena have been eternally quiescent from the very beginning. "Not abiding in birth-and-death" means that if one were to abide...

Birth and death involve revolving without rest. Since it is said that one must depart from deluded views, one should know that "not abiding" refers to practicing the cultivation of *śamatha* (calm abiding) based on the meaning of the unchanging nature of *tathatā* (suchness).
The Commentary states: "If a wise person perceives that all phenomena have arising and ceasing, they immediately become an ordinary person with deluded consciousness;
this is abiding in birth and death. One should know that the opposite of this is what should be called [the state of a wise person]."
Regarding "Wisdom" and "causes and conditions": if defiled causes and conditions conjoin, then the bitter fruits of evil karma are not lost;
if pure causes and conditions conjoin, then the pleasant fruits of virtuous causes are not lost.

Thus, the defiled and evil [realms] pertain only to the three miserable paths, whereas the pure and virtuous [states] extend to humans, devas, the two vehicles, and the Buddha-way. As for "arousing great compassion," once one has seen...
Through the convergence of causes and conditions, the retributions of good and evil arise; thus, one may overturn delusion to achieve awakening and transform from an ordinary being into a sage.

Thereupon, great compassion arises, and one desires to deliver all beings. Regarding those who cultivate merit and so forth: they fully practice generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom to gather in sentient beings.
That is to say, generosity gathers in the poor, while maintaining ethical discipline gathers in those who violate precepts, and so on. By means of these five...
This is because it is a gateway to merit. This constitutes cultivating merit for the sake of transforming sentient beings;

one benefits oneself by means of benefiting others. Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "The realm of sentient beings is the pure land of the bodhisattva," and so forth. As for "not abiding":

if one were to abide in nirvana, one would be exclusively in a state of quiescence. Since it is said that one transforms sentient beings while cultivating merit, one should know [that this is not mere quiescence].
"Not abiding" refers to the practice of contemplative cultivation according to the principle of True Suchness (tathatā) following conditions. The subsequent passage clarifies the reason for this:
because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is fundamentally not existent, one does not now abide in saṃsāra; because it is fundamentally not non-existent, one does not now abide in nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, because its nature is immutable, one does not abide in saṃsāra; because it follows conditions, one [does not abide in nirvāṇa].
Abiding in nirvāṇa—indeed, all dualistic dharmas such as the ordinary and the sage, annihilation and permanence, or unity and difference—cannot be fully described.

Only by departing from these two extremes can one be said to accord with the nature (*dharmatā*). Now, through *śamatha* that is simultaneous with *vipaśyanā*, one accords with the non-arising nature of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharmatā*), which serves as the foundation for the practice of great wisdom that does not abide in saṃsāra.
Through *vipaśyanā* that is simultaneous with *śamatha*, one accords with conditions (*pratyaya*).
The arising of the *dharmatā* serves as the basis for the practice of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) that does not abide in *nirvāṇa*.

Furthermore, wisdom that is identical to compassion serves as the basis for the practice of self-benefit, while compassion that is identical to wisdom serves as the basis for the practice of benefiting others.

Moreover, this single passage is first termed "stopping through the non-arising of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva-anutpāda-śamatha*), secondly termed "stopping through the non-forfeiture of causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya-avaiparītya-śamatha*), and finally termed "stopping through the non-abiding of *dharmatā*" (*dharmatā-apratiṣṭhita-śamatha*).
Cease. Furthermore, the first may be called the contemplation of non-abiding in saṃsāra; the second, the contemplation of non-abiding in nirvāṇa;

and the last, the contemplation that accords with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). Taken as a whole, the first may be termed the great wisdom of śamatha and vipaśyanā that is free from false views.
It may be called the *śamatha-vipaśyanā* of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Next, it may be called the *śamatha-vipaśyanā* of Great Compassion for gathering and transforming sentient beings.
Or it may be called the *śamatha-vipaśyanā* of arising and ceasing. Finally, it may be called the *śamatha-vipaśyanā* of accord with non-abiding equality.

Or it may be called the *śamatha-vipaśyanā* of the one mind. If these are correlated with the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, the first is the *śamatha-vipaśyanā* of the empty *tathāgatagarbha*-mind; the next is...
First is the śamatha and vipaśyanā of the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*-mind; next is the śamatha and vipaśyanā of both empty and non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*-minds.
Furthermore, this is correlated with the *Awakening of Faith Sūtra*: the first is *śamatha*, the second is *samādhi*, and the last is *dhyāna*.

Furthermore, this is identical in meaning to the Tiantai school’s doctrine of the threefold contemplation within a single mind (*yixin san guan*). That is to say: contemplating that phenomena are unborn is the contemplation of emptiness (*kong guan*), which contemplates the ultimate truth (*zhendi*).

Contemplating the harmonious conjunction of causes and conditions is the contemplation of the provisional (*jia guan*), which contemplates the conventional truth (*suditi*). To accord with the nature of phenomena (*faxing*)...

This is precisely the Middle Way. It contemplates the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), wherein the three are one and the one is three; they are neither vertical nor horizontal, nor are they separate or distinct.
When observed with true insight, all things are thus. For this reason, it is called the root of practice.
△ Next, the two types of practice for one’s own benefit (2). First, the virtue of abandonment; second, the virtue of wisdom. Regarding the first, the virtue of abandonment:
there are two aspects. First is the skillful means of cessation, namely, shame (*hrī*), dread of blame (*apatrāpya*), and repentance (*pratikramaṇa*).
These can cease all unwholesome dharmas so that they do not increase, because they accord with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) and are free from all faults.
[Commentary] "That which can stop" refers to diligently severing the two kinds of evil; this is the gate of stopping and maintaining (*zhi-chí*).
[Record] Regarding the phrase "the two," etc.: first, it indicates the name. "Diligently severing the two evils" means that for evil already arisen, one severs it so that it does not continue;
for evil not yet arisen, one severs it so that it does not arise. It is called "stopping and maintaining" because it is discussed in relation to unwholesome dharmas.

"Cessation" (*śamatha*) is termed "maintaining," while "activity" (*pravṛtti*) is termed "transgression. This is the formal explanation of the meaning. Regarding "shame" (*hrī*) and "modesty" (*apatrāpya*):

these are two of the eleven wholesome mental factors. "Shame" refers to the predominance of self-respect; it is the honoring of what is noble and good, the feeling of shame regarding faults and transgressions, and the cessation of all unwholesome conduct.

"Modesty" refers to the predominance of the dread of blame; it is the revulsion toward and rejection of violence and evil, the feeling of shame regarding faults and transgressions, and the cessation of all [unwholesome conduct].
"Evil karma. "Repentance" (huìguò) is the Chinese translation for the Sanskrit term *kṣamā*, which means "repentance.

This refers to confessing past transgressions and reforming the past while cultivating the future. Among these, the six characters meaning "to be able to cease all unwholesome dharmas" apply to both those [transgressions] already committed and those not yet committed;
the others are restricted to those already committed. Since all such evils are ceased, it is said "all. This explains that which has already arisen.
Evil, having been prevented from increasing, will naturally not arise in that which has not yet been produced. The reason for this is explained below.
Since the nature is fundamentally free from transgression, the arising of transgression constitutes a violation; now that it has been ceased, one must accordingly accord with principle.

When transgressions are exhausted and the nature is manifested, it is called the *dharmakāya*. The *dharmakāya* is precisely the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*); therefore, it is designated by this name here.
Section.
△ Second, the virtue of wisdom.
Third, the skillful means for initiating and increasing roots of goodness, namely: diligently making offerings to and prostrating before the Triple Gem, and offering praise.
Through rejoicing and entreating all Buddhas, and by virtue of a heart of profound sincerity born from love and reverence for the Triple Gem, one’s faith increases;
thus, one is able to aspire to the unsurpassed Way. Furthermore, through the protection of the power of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, one is able to eliminate karmic obstructions.
The roots of goodness do not regress, because they accord with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and are free from the obstruction of delusion.

[Commentary: "Initiation" refers to the diligent cultivation of the two types of goodness; it constitutes the gateway of practice and maintenance. "Diligent offerings and so forth" refer to cultivation in relation to conditions.
"Because of affection," and so on, distinguishes the benefits of cultivation. Regarding the four permutations of affection and respect: first, there is affection without respect.
1. Like a mother toward her child: [this is] respect without affection. 2. Like a servant toward his master: [this is] respect without affection. 3.
Like a practitioner toward the Triple Gem: [this is] both respect and affection. 4. Like an enemy: [this is] neither respect nor affection.
[Commentary] "Three" and below: first, the names are indicated. Regarding "diligently cultivating the two kinds of goodness":
one cultivates existing goodness so that it increases, and one cultivates unarisen goodness so that it arises; hence the phrase "arousing and increasing. This indicates these two meanings.
Regarding "performing and maintaining": this is discussed in terms of wholesome dharmas. To perform [wholesome acts] is called "maintaining," while to cease [them] is called "transgressing.

The following section correctly demonstrates the meaning. Regarding "making offerings," there are three kinds: namely, material wealth, the Dharma, and contemplative practice. Regarding "prostrating,"...
The Tripitaka Master Paramārtha says there are seven kinds of prostration: 1. Prostration of ego-conceit (*asmimāna*). 2. Prostration of chanting and responding.

These two are not in accordance with proper ritual. 3. Prostration of reverence. Reverence arises from the mind and is expressed through body and speech; the five wheels (the five points of the body) touch the ground. 4. Prostration of signlessness (*animitta*).

One enters deeply into the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), transcending the characteristics of subject and object. 5. Prostration of manifesting function. One contemplates that one’s own body is identical to the Buddha.
1. The Universal Contemplation: Like an illusion or a shadow, universally directing body and mind to pay homage to all. Six: Internal Contemplation Homage:
Paying homage only to the true Buddha of the Dharma-body within one's own body, without taking other Buddhas as objects. Seven: Reality-mark Homage:

Whether internal or external, whether ordinary beings or Buddhas, they share the same reality-mark (*dharmatā*). To perceive a Buddha as an object of homage is itself a false view; one should contemplate the body...
The true mark (*dharmatā*). Contemplating the Buddha is likewise so; this is what is called "equal prostration and reverence. Thus, the verse of Mañjuśrī says:

"Because it is neither born nor extinguished, I pay homage to that which has nothing to be observed. According to the *Dharmodgataparipṛcchā-buddhadharma-pūjā-vidhi-sūtra*, there are eight stages in total:
first, making offerings; second, praising; third, prostrating to the Buddha; fourth, repentance; fifth, requesting [the turning of the wheel]; sixth...
Rejoicing; seventh, dedication; eighth, making vows. Within these eight, the "right intention" (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) is the actual act of bowing to the Buddha;

the remaining seven are all the causal conditions for bowing to the Buddha. That is to say, offering and praising are the manifestations of bowing to the Buddha; repentance, exhortation, and rejoicing are the intentions behind bowing to the Buddha.
The [first] seven collectively dedicate the merit of bowing and so forth toward the three objects; the eighth describes the intent of the mind.
Aspiration. Now, each of these eight practices is capable of removing specific obstacles: making offerings removes the obstacle of stinginess and greed, resulting in great wealth;
praising [the Buddha] removes the obstacle of harsh speech, resulting in unimpeded eloquence; prostrating to the Buddha removes the obstacle of pride, resulting in a noble and honorable body;

repentance removes the three obstacles of karma, afflictions, and retribution (as well as the four obstacles including views), resulting in the perfection of both the primary and secondary environments; requesting [the turning of the wheel of Dharma and remaining in the world]...
Eliminating the disparagement of the Dharma, one attains great learning and wisdom. Rejoicing in others' merit eliminates jealousy, whereby one gains a vast retinue.
Dedication eliminates narrow-mindedness, whereby one achieves expansive goodness. Making vows eliminates despondency, whereby one maintains all practices.
Within this present text, these five dharmas are fully present: there is repentance at the beginning and making vows at the end; however, dedication is absent, its presence being implied.
This is also stated in the text. Regarding "cultivation through conditions": this refers to cultivating the practice of entering and abiding by means of the Three Jewels as supreme conditions.
There are two benefits. First, if one is respectful, the Path increases. The four phrases concerning "affectionate respect" can be understood accordingly.

If we follow the teachings of Confucianism, a mother is the object of affection alone, a ruler is the object of respect alone, and a father possesses both affection and respect. Therefore, the *Xiaojing* says: "One relies on the service rendered to one's father to serve one's mother."
Affection is the same; by relying on the service due to one's father, one serves the ruler, and thus reverence is the same.
Therefore, the mother takes her affection and the ruler takes his reverence, while the father is the one who possesses both. However, this is spoken of in terms of the majority of cases.

Now, by offering the mind with which one serves one’s father to the Triple Gem, one combines both love and reverence; that which is "pure and profound" (chún hòu) means to treat it with gravity (thickly).
The mind being free from confusion (purity). There are also four permutations: first, pure but not profound, meaning sincere for only a short time;
second, profound but not pure, meaning long-standing yet turbid and mixed; third, both, meaning remaining without discord until death; fourth, neither.
They do not coexist; that is to say, there is suddenly no thought of devotion. Now, the third [case] is taken. Regarding "the increase of faith" and so forth:

this refers to migrating from the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) into right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*). Furthermore, regarding the subsequent passage on "protection": at the lower level, karma is extinguished;

at the upper level, there is the power of internal causal cultivation. This, then, is the power of external conditions through protection. It may also be said that the former is named the benefit of generating wisdom, while this is named the extinction [of afflictions].
Regarding "obstructing benefit" and "dissolving karma," etc.: as previously assigned, the preceding acts of prostration, praise, and so forth are each capable of removing obstructions;

furthermore, they can accomplish virtue, as explained in the fourth section below. To clarify this meaning according to the sequence below: by nature, one is originally free from the obstruction of delusion;
now, by cultivating wisdom to sever these obstructions, is this not in accord with one's nature? When this practice is perfected, it is...
This reveals the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*). Since the Reward Body is itself the virtue of wisdom (*jñānaguṇa*), this serves as the heading for the section.
△ The latter one concerns the practice of benefiting others.
Fourth is the skillful means of great, impartial vows; that is to say, the making of vows to continue until the end of the future, transforming and delivering all beings.
Sentient beings, without exception, are all led to the ultimate nirvana without remainder. This is because they accord with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), which is uninterrupted;
for the nature of phenomena is vast, pervading all sentient beings, equal and non-dual, and because it does not conceive of "self" or "other," it is ultimately quiescent.
[Commentary]: "Exhausting the future" refers to the long-term mind. "Delivering all beings" refers to the vast mind. "Causing them to reach the ultimate" refers to the supreme mind.
The first [section] following this explicitly reveals compliance with the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena). The second [section] following the *dharmatā* clarifies the arousal of the great vow;
it is also the constant mind.
[Commentary] "Four" below indicates the title. "The object" below explains the characteristics. *Prasthāna* (setting forth) refers to the exertion and application of the mind;
*praṇidhāna* (vow) refers to the longing and aspiration. There are four types [of vows]; because they involve binding the mind, they are called *praṇidhāna*. This present one is one among those four.

The remaining three vows have already appeared in the preceding text, namely: the vow of skillful means for cessation (*śamatha*), and the vows for eliminating obstacles and for detachment (*vairāgya*).
Delusion: this is the vow to sever infinite afflictions. The skillful means for initiating and increasing roots of goodness:
this is the vow to study immeasurable Dharma-gates. Practicing these two dharmas is entirely for the sake of Bodhi; this is the vow to realize the unsurpassed Buddha-way.
As for the "long-term mind," it takes the total liberation of all beings as its deadline, without limiting itself to a specific number of kalpas; therefore, it continues until the very end.
"Limitless" means that the vast mind makes no discrimination, for it seeks to deliver all beings of the four modes of birth and nine categories of existence.
"Supreme" means that it transcends the realms of humans, devas, and the two vehicles, enabling them to attain the bliss of unsurpassed quiescence (*nirvāṇa*).
The phrase "accordingly" clarifies the intent; it explains the reasons for the preceding three types of minds. The first two phrases explain [the first mind].
The "long-term mind" refers to the fact that the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) is eternally abiding, without beginning or end;

therefore, one now delivers sentient beings until the end of the future, following along with them without weariness or fatigue. The commentary (*śūtra*) text is easy to understand. The three phrases following "the nature of phenomena" explain the "vast mind":
because its nature is all-pervasive, equal, and non-dual, one now transforms and delivers beings without making any discriminations.
This means to rescue and deliver impartially while remaining in accordance with [the nature of reality]. The latter two phrases are not considered here. This explains the first mind:

because its nature is fundamentally free from the discrimination of self and other, it is eternally quiescent. Therefore, now, through transformation, one causes all beings to reach the ultimate nirvana of extinction;
this is to accord with that nature. The subsequent two sections of the text merely first indicate the dharma-nature, and then...
The reason for forming a concluding phrase at the end of each section, rather than marking the conclusion with every instance of terms such as "conformity" (*anuloma*),

is the skillful abbreviation of the translator. Furthermore, regarding the term "eternal mind" (*nitya-citta*), the intent is to clarify that because this [mind] possesses the quality of ultimate quiescence (*atyanta-śānti*),
it is called "eternal."
△ 3. The Benefit of Arousing the Mind.
[Commentary] To clarify the benefit of arousing the mind: because one practices various sublime deeds following the initial arousal of the mind, one attains entry into the first stage (*bhūmi*).
This refers to perceiving the Dharmakāya and giving rise to its functioning for the benefit of others.
△ Within this, there are four sections: first, manifesting supreme virtues; second, clarifying subtle faults; third, accommodating provisional teachings; and fourth, praising actual practice.
First, manifesting supreme virtues.
Because the bodhisattva has generated this mind, he attains a partial vision of the Dharmakāya.

By virtue of seeing the Dharmakāya, he is able to manifest eight modes of appearance according to his power of aspiration for the benefit of sentient beings; that is to say: descending from Tuṣita Heaven, entering the womb, and so forth.
[Dwelling in the womb], emerging from the womb, leaving home, attaining the Way, turning the wheel of Dharma, and entering Nirvana.

[Commentary]: Because Bodhisattvas of the Ten Understandings perceive this through the gate of analogical contemplation, it is called "partial. Alternatively, it may be seen through the emptiness of persons.
As for the eight kinds of benefits, one is able to perform these deeds within the stage of Initial Resolve (Prathamacittotpāda-vihāra).
[Commentary] Regarding the "one who observes by comparison": because they have attained mastery over the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), they possess a vision that is analogous to it;

however, as this is not yet a direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) regarding the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), it is termed "partial. Alternatively, [the text continues]: if one relies on the emptiness of persons, this is indeed already realized;
yet, because the emptiness of phenomena has not been attained, it is called "partial. This refers to the vision based on the emptiness of persons. The former was...
This is the correct interpretation. This is explained here by way of comprehensive clarification.

One who performs these deeds while in the Stage of Generating the Mind (Cittotpāda-vihāra) is able, through the power of their compassion and vows, to manifest the eight phases of attaining enlightenment (*aṣṭābhisambodhi*) to benefit and bring joy to sentient beings, just like the transformative activities of Śākyamuni today.
This is as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Furthermore, within this text, there is a distinction between self-benefit and benefiting others; one should examine this in detail.

Regarding "seeing": if explained in terms of the mutual relationship between the preceding and succeeding stages, one gives rise to the profound mind (*adhyāśaya*) by means of protecting the Dharma, practices the path of self-benefit, and attains the vision of the Dharmakāya.
By means of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), one gives rise to the mind of great compassion, practices the path of benefiting others, and benefits sentient beings through the eight manifestations.
By means of the teachings of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one gives rise to the straightforward mind (*ṛjukacitta*), practices the non-abiding path, and manifests the vision of the Dharmakāya.
There are eight kinds; these are benefits accorded in accordance with their vows.
△ Second, clarifying minor transgressions:
although these are bodhisattvas, they are not yet named "Dharmakāya," because throughout immeasurable past lives they have possessed out-flowing (sāsrava) karma.

They have not yet attained definitive resolution; they experience a slight degree of suffering corresponding to whatever state arises, yet they are not bound by karma, because they possess the sovereign power of their great vows.

[Commentary] "Not yet named as having attained the Dharma-body" means they differ from those on the stages above the ground (*bhūmi*). Because they have not yet realized the Truth, they see only a small portion [of reality] by relying solely on the power of faith.
The passage beginning with "Because of their past... explains the reason for this difference. Furthermore, "not bound by karma" means they differ from ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Regarding their retribution, Bodhisattvas possess mastery over its duration; it does not arise from delusions or karma. This is because they possess mastery over their great vows.
They retain their delusions in order to benefit sentient beings, by the power of their compassionate vows.

[Commentary] "Not yet having realized" and so forth means that they merely correspond to inferential contemplation; because they have not yet abandoned conceptual discrimination, this explains the reason why.
This clarifies that the causes of worldly karma created in previous lives encompass both the wholesome and the unwholesome;

thus, past karma does not perish. Regarding "subtle suffering," there are two meanings: first, the suffering of conditioned change (*pariṇāma-duḥkha*); second, the suffering of segmented existence (*bheda-duḥkha*) that follows from karma.
Because they have attained mastery and are not like ordinary beings, it is called "subtle. As for "long or short" and so forth, this refers to conditioned change.
Their bodies are sustained by the power of their vows and wisdom, which have no fixed limit. They are able to transform coarse bodies into subtle forms and change short lifespans into long ones;

thus they are said to be "sovereign. Regarding the phrase "retaining afflictions," because they possess great vows, they retain afflictions without severing them to moisten rebirth and receive retribution;
because they possess great wisdom, they are able to exercise sovereignty over the length of their lives according to their will.
They are not defiled by delusions; thus they are not the same as ordinary beings who are driven by afflictions and unable to sever them.

This state is therefore not yet called the Dharma-body, and for this reason it differs from the stages above the ground (bhūmi). Because it is below those [stages], it is distinct from them. Furthermore, because it is not bound by karma, it differs from ordinary beings.
Because it is above [the stage of] below, it is distinct from them. Since it is superior to the sages above and different from the ranks of ordinary beings below, it is so.
Regarding the stage of the worthy (ārya):
△ Third, the provisional teaching.

As stated in the sūtras, there are instances where it is said that some may fall back and descend into the evil realms; this is not an actual falling back, but is merely for the sake of the beginners.
Regarding the bodhisattva who has not yet entered the stages (*bhūmi*) but is indolent: [this teaching] is intended to inspire them with courage. [Commentary:
"As in the Sūtra" and so forth constitutes the first point, citing the scriptural authority. "It is not its reality" and so forth constitutes the second point, providing the explanation.
Both passages are clear in the text. As stated in the *Sragdharā-mūla-karma-sūtra*: "Prior to the seventh stage, it is called the stage of regression."
If one does not encounter a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), then even after one *kalpa* up to ten *kalpas*, one may regress from the bodhicitta.
For example, the Devaputra Viśuddhanetra, Prince Dharmatāra, Śāriputra, and others each entered the sixth stage;

however, due to encountering the conditions of evil associates (*pāpamitra*) during that interval, they regressed and fell into the unwholesome destinies of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), as explained at length.

The current explanation of this meaning is a provisional teaching (*upāya-vacana*), not a statement of actual regression. It is merely intended to terrify those who have newly entered [the path], so that they may not become arrogant.

[Commentary] Regarding "regression prior to the seventh stage": it is only at the seventh stage that it is called the "Stage of Non-regression" (*avaivartika-bhūmi*). (However, in that sutra, it only mentions Viśuddhanetra and others, each...)

Upon reaching the sixth stage (*vihāra*), one may regress due to encountering evil associates (*pāpamitra*); however, the specific causes, conditions, and modes of such an encounter have not been detailed here and shall be examined later before proceeding. The *Śāstra* states that "not having entered the true position" (*samyaktvaniyāma*) encompasses two meanings:
first, not yet having entered the first stage; second, not yet having reached the seventh stage, which is the stage of non-regression through the correct cause.
Therefore, it is termed the "true position. The former meaning is considered the primary one.
△ Fourth, praising the practice of realization:
Furthermore, after this bodhisattva has once generated the mind of enlightenment, they remain far removed from cowardice and ultimately never fear falling into the stages of the two vehicles.

Even if one hears that nirvana is attained only after enduring diligent practice and difficult austerities for immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) eons, one does not become timid or weak;
for through faith, one knows that all phenomena have been in a state of nirvana from the very beginning.

[Commentary: Furthermore, "below" [in the text] refers to the first point: not being attached to what is inferior. "If one hears" [the teaching] below refers to the second point: not being intimidated by what is superior.
"Because of faith" explains the reason why one is not intimidated. This clarifies that the passage from that sutra is provisional (*upāya*) and not ultimate (*paramārtha*).
[Commentary] "Not longing for what is below" means that one does not give rise to attachment toward the fruits of retribution of the two vehicles or ordinary beings.

"If one hears [the teaching]" and so forth refers to what is said in the *Lotus Sūtra*: "The Buddha-way is long and distant; only after enduring diligent suffering for a long time can it be accomplished."

Regarding "not being timid toward what is above": it means that one possesses a mind of diligent vigor toward bodhi and nirvāṇa, because one does not give rise to fear while practicing various ascetic disciplines.
To explain the reason for this, it also explains the reason for the previous lack of attachment:

because one knows that self-nature nirvāṇa is ultimately not something obtained from the outside, its realization depends on oneself whether sooner or later; why then fixate on the duration of kalpas? Therefore, even if one hears of this sūtra for kalpas...
One attains the state described as "nirvāṇa through diligent effort" without any fear or trepidation. This means that because one is not afraid of what is above, one does not cling to what is below.

Therefore, in this commentary, I have merely explained the reason for this lack of fear. Furthermore, by virtue of faith, one knows that the self-nature of all beings—both oneself and others—is nirvāṇa;
thus, even while remaining within saṃsāra, one is constantly in a state of cessation. For this reason...
All sentient beings who aspire to seek the Buddha-way extensively cultivate merit and virtue; though they do not delight in existence (*bhava*), they likewise do not fall into emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Therefore, upon hearing words that describe the realm of birth and death as being full of suffering and difficult to transform, they feel no timidity or weakness.
This means they have no attachment to what is below, and thus no fear regarding what is above. Consequently, they are able to simultaneously resolve the aforementioned lack of attachment.

It is for this reason. Within these two passages, there are both expressions of fearlessness. However, the fearlessness mentioned previously is compassion (*karuṇā*), because one does not dread that sentient beings are difficult to transform.
The fearlessness mentioned later is wisdom (*prajñā*), because one does not fear that the Buddha-way is difficult to accomplish.
This is because, as stated below, this [passage] uses the former to refute the latter; it clarifies the ultimate reality (*bhūta-artha*) rather than being a provisional teaching (*upāya-deśanā*).
In the Stage of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*), there is already no falling back; how much less so upon entering the sixth stage—how could there be any regression? II.
Resolving Conduct and Generating the Mind (*adhimukti-caryā-cittotpāda*) (in two parts): A. General Statement Praising its Excellence. B. Manifesting its Excellent Characteristics.
A. General Statement Praising its Excellence.
It should be known that the "arousing of the mind through the stage of practice and understanding" (*adhimukti-caryā-prasthāna*) is even more superior.

[Commentary: In the preceding stage, one enters into understanding (*adhimukti*) upon the fulfillment of faith; now, with the fulfillment of this practice, one enters into the stage of "heading toward" (*pratipannaka*). This is because the arousal of the mind is even deeper.

[Commentary] "Now, from 'this' onwards" refers to abiding in practice; having perfected the stages of practice, one gives rise to profound understanding and conduct and enters the stage of the ten practices of dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*).
Because this is not the same as the preceding stage of faith (*śraddhā*), it is said to be "superior."
△ Second, revealing its superior characteristics (in two parts): first, superiority in time; second, superiority in practice. Regarding superiority in time:
because this bodhisattva, from the time of initial right faith until the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa is about to be completed, [is thus distinguished].
[Commentary]: "The completion of one kalpa" refers to its proximity to the first bhūmi. [Record]:

"Proximity to the first bhūmi" means that from the first stage (prathama-vihāra) up to the first bhūmi constitutes one asaṃkhyeya-kalpa; the present stage is the ten stages of dedication (daśa-pariṇāmanā).
It is proximate to the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), for it is adjacent to the ultimate truth (*tattva*).
△ Second, the excellence of practice (in two parts): first, the general; second, the specific. First, the general:
within the dharma of *tathatā*, profound understanding manifests, and that which is cultivated is free from marks (*animitta*).

[Commentary] "Deep understanding" refers to *prajñā* (wisdom). "Transcending characteristics" refers to *caryā* (practice). Throughout the following sections on the six *pāramitās*, both of these are elucidated.

[Sub-commentary] Because this understanding penetrates thoroughly to the *tathatā* (suchness), it is called "deep understanding. Because it is distinct, clear, and manifest, with no further obscurity, it is called "manifest before one.

Furthermore, it is called "deep" because it surpasses what precedes it, and it is called "understanding" because it differs from what follows. Regarding "transcending characteristics in practice": [this refers to] the *tathatā*.
Just as there is no mark (*animitta*), because it accords with *tathatā*, each and every practice that is cultivated is markless.

For example, as it is said: "One gives alms without dwelling on form; one gives alms without dwelling on sound, fragrance, and so forth. All such practices are likewise thus; therefore, it is said that "what is cultivated is free from marks.
These two [points] refer to the stage of understanding and practice (*adhimukti-caryā*).
△ Next, the specific [explanation]:
Because one knows that the essence of the dharma-nature is devoid of stinginess and greed, one practices the *dāna-pāramitā* in accordance with it.
Because one knows that the dharma-nature is unstained and free from the faults of the five desires, one practices the *śīla-pāramitā* in accordance with it. Because one knows the dharma-nature...
There is no suffering, because one is free from anger and affliction; thus, one practices the *kṣānti-pāramitā* in accordance with reality.

Because one knows that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is devoid of the characteristics of body and mind, one is free from indolence; thus, one practices the *vīrya-pāramitā* in accordance with reality.

Because one knows that the nature of phenomena is eternally concentrated and its essence is without distraction, one practices the *dhyāna-pāramitā* in accordance with reality. Because one knows the essence of the nature of phenomena...
"Clear," because it is free from ignorance; thus one practices in accordance with the *prajñāpāramitā*.

[Commentary] The passage beginning "By knowing the nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā*) reveals that the aforementioned profound understanding is manifest. "Practicing in accordance with *dāna*" (generosity) reveals that the practice described above is free from signs (*animitta*).
The same applies to each of the following five perfections, meaning they are free from the signs of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*) and so forth.

From the stage of the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) onward, because the bodhisattva has attained the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), they are able to accord with the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and cultivate the practices such as the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).

This is precisely the practice of understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*) upon which the initial resolve (*cittotpāda*) depends. Since defilements and obstructions deviate from reality, one cultivates practices that eliminate these obstructions in order to accord with Suchness (*tathatā*).
[Commentary] Regarding "one who is without stinginess or greed": "Stinginess" (*mātsarya*) refers to being parsimonious with one's own possessions and refusing to give them to others.

"Greed" (*lobha*) refers to desiring the wealth of others in order to take it for oneself. Knowing that within the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), these things do not fundamentally exist, is what the Sub-commentary calls "understanding.
As for *dānapāramitā*: *Dāna* is fully called *dānā*, which here means "giving" (*śī*). *Pāramitā* here means...
To reach the other shore. The other shore is precisely *nirvāṇa*. *Nirvāṇa* is precisely the principle of *tathatā* (suchness).
Now, practicing giving while detached from signs corresponds with this principle; this is the meaning of reaching the other shore. The rest should be understood by analogy.
Thus, withholding oneself to bestow upon others is what is called "giving" (*dāna*). It merely accords with non-avarice; by this, it also accords with non-greed.

The meaning is as follows: Why is this? If one gives even one’s own possessions to others, it goes without saying that one should certainly not take the possessions of others; this is an illustration from the profound to the shallow.
This refers to "separation from the lower," which clarifies the characteristics of what is to be abandoned—the three wheels, namely: the giver, the recipient, and the object given.

To realize these three characteristics, their substance cannot be apprehended; therefore, they are called "detached" (*viveka*). If one can indeed detach from these characteristics, then the cause becomes untainted (*anāsrava*), and the fruit realizes *bodhi*.
Because it possesses the sense of "revolving," it is called a "wheel" (*cakra*). Furthermore, because it can crush and grind all afflictions and obstacles, it possesses the sense of "crushing";
thus it is designated as a "wheel. The passage beginning with "By means of the ten... explains the reason for this detachment from characteristics.
Regarding "attaining the emptiness of dharmas": this refers merely to entering deeply into this contemplation, yet it is not yet its realization.

However, this is explained according to the path of teaching (*śāsana-mārga*). If spoken of in terms of actual reality, one is able to enter deeply even within the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), as in the following passage on the mind of faith.
Cultivating the samādhi of true suchness—is this not precisely the emptiness of dharmas? Regarding the "understanding and practice" upon which one relies:

"understanding" refers to the ten abodes (*bhūmi*), and "practice" refers to the ten practices (*caryā*). Thus, the ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*) are the dependent, while the abodes and practices are the basis of dependence.

Furthermore, the abodes and practices are that which gives rise [to the transferences], while the ten transferences are that which is given rise to; for it is by relying on this understanding and practice that the mind of transference is generated. This is because...

Below the section on "Defilements" (*mala*), this explains the reason for conforming to reality (*tattva*). It means that stinginess and the like are hindrances (*āvaraṇa*) that are constantly contrary to its nature.

Since the nature is fundamentally free from stinginess and the like, it is never conjoined with hindrances; therefore, by practicing acts such as giving, one externally opposes hindrances such as stinginess and greed, while internally conforming to the nature that is free from stinginess and the like.
As for the "five desires" (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*), they refer to the five sense objects: form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch.
These five [desires] cause sentient beings to give rise to longing;

therefore, it was stated previously that because there are conditions consisting of delusive objects and defiled dharmas, they permeate the deluded mind, causing it to harbor attachment and create various karmas, thereby undergoing all manner of suffering of body and mind.
Furthermore, the *Anityatā-sūtra* says: "Constantly seeking the realm of desire, one does not practice the good."

Regarding "affairs" (*vastu*): because desire arises toward objects, it is called a "transgression. A transgression is itself defilement; one should know that within the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), this defilement is fundamentally non-existent.
As for *śī* (the first syllable of *śīla*): in full, it is *śīla*, which here means "precept" (*jie*). "Precept" refers to preventing what is wrong and ceasing evil;

that is, it is the departure from the transgressions of the five desires. Regarding "hatred and affliction": because one gives rise to anger due to being provoked by others, or likewise [due to other causes].
Affliction gives rise to anger; because of anger, there is burning distress, and this burning distress is itself suffering.
One knows that by nature this suffering is fundamentally non-existent. *Kṣānti* (羼提) means "patience" (忍辱). To endure the conditions of insult is to depart from anger and affliction.

Regarding "laziness and so forth": it is due to grasping at body and mind that laziness is produced. Now, since the nature is pure and one perceives neither body nor mind, for whom would there be laziness? Therefore...

"Vīrya" means "detachment. *Vīrya* here means "diligence. "Diligence" (*jing*) refers to being pure and refined, with a single mind free from distraction. "Diligence" (*jin*) refers to advancing forward, being courageous and non-retrogressive;
it is thus detachment from indolence and constant stability. This is explained in terms of manifesting the essence, which is non-distraction.
Speaking in terms of being free from faults: *dhyāna* (禪) is fully termed *dhyāna*, which here means "meditative concentration" (*靜慮*).

This is the concentration of wisdom; concentration is non-distraction. Regarding "being free from ignorance and so forth": within the luminosity of original enlightenment (*本覺*), there is fundamentally no lack of enlightenment. Thus, it is *prajñā* (般若).
This is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*). Wisdom is itself clarity; clarity is the departure from ignorance (*avidyā*).

Because it is the wisdom inherent in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), this [sixth stage] and the fifth [stage] constitute the intrinsic nature of concentration and wisdom. Fundamentally, they are a single dharma; they are distinguished only in terms of their essence and function.
However, according to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Bodhisattvas of the ten stages practice the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) in successive order.

The practitioner, having realized the truth, practices according to reality as it is. Within this context, the six perfections constitute practice in accordance with that realization, differing in their degrees of depth.
Furthermore, while these [six perfections] accord with the nature of reality, they are gradual cultivation;

whereas that [practice of the dharma-realm], which is "one practice encompassing all practices," is perfect cultivation. Thus, there is a distinction between the partial and the perfect, which should be examined in detail.

△ III. Realization of the Arising of the Mind (three parts). First, clarifying the essence of the arising mind; second, clarifying the characteristics of the arising mind; third, clarifying the merit of its fulfillment.
First, clarifying the essence of the arising mind (three parts): first, indicating the basis of the stages; second, clarifying the essence of the practice;
third, clarifying the superior function. First, indicating the basis of the stages.
[Commentary] Regarding "the basis of the stages" (*bhūmi-āśraya*): As the text states, "What realm is realized? It is *tathatā* (suchness).
This means that *tathatā* is the objective sphere upon which the ten stages depend. Now, as for the term "stages" (*bhūmi*), it is established by way of metaphor;
it is used to illustrate how true wisdom can give rise to the noble dharmas. Here, however, we refer to *tathatā* as the support of that wisdom; therefore, it is called the "basis of the stages."
Regarding the "realization-awakening" (pramiti-citta): from the Stage of Pure Mind (śuddhacittabhūmi) up to the Ultimate Stage of the Bodhisattva (bodhisattvanisthābhūmi), what realm is realized?

It is called *tathatā* (suchness). [Commentary] The phrase "realization" introduces the section. From the following, the characteristics are distinguished. First, there is the inquiry; the phrase "it is called" follows. Second, there is the explanatory response, namely:

Although these Bodhisattvas of the ten stages differ in the degree to which they have severed hindrances and in the depth and breadth of their practices according to their respective positions, each one realizes the same object of realization: true suchness (*tathatā*).
There is only a distinction in the fullness of this realization, but no difference in its essential nature. Therefore, true suchness is universally designated as the realized object.

This is the realm (*dhātu*). In the "Ten Stages" chapter (*Daśabhūmika-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, it is likewise explained in this way. Thus, the verse defining its essential nature (*svabhāva*) therein says:
"The path of the Great Sage Tathāgata is subtle and difficult to comprehend; it is beyond thought and free from all thoughts, and cannot be found even if one seeks to see it."
△ Second, clarifying the essence of practice.
[Commentary] The essence of practice is the fundamental [wisdom].
[Record] "Fundamental" refers to the fundamental wisdom that realizes the principle of the ultimate truth; this is the true path of vision (*darśana-mārga*).

Because it relies upon the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), they are said to be its objects; yet for this realized one, there are no objects—only the wisdom of *tathatā* (suchness) is called the *dharmakāya*.
[Commentary: "Object" refers to the manifesting consciousness (*pratibhāsa-vijñāna*), for it necessarily arises based upon the evolving aspect (*vivarta-lakṣaṇa*).
As for these [terms], at the time when fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) directly realizes reality, there is in fact neither subject nor object; how, then, could it be said that there is an "object"?

Here, we are merely speaking in reference to the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), wherein because the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) has not yet been exhausted, the evolving and manifesting aspects still persist. It is on the basis of this consciousness that [the term "object"] is provisionally explained.
Within the state of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), there is necessarily the true suchness (*tathatā*) as the object of realization.

Because the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) reflexively takes that direct realization as its object, there likewise appears a semblance of an object; thus it is said that "transformed consciousnesses appear. However, in actual direct realization, subject and object are equal.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "because it relies upon," etc.: First, a question is raised: Since True Suchness (tathatā) is free from the characteristics of mental objects, and since its realization is free from subject and object, why is it said that True Suchness serves as an objective sphere (*viṣaya*)?
Therefore, this is explained: That which necessarily arises by relying on the aspect of transformation is precisely this evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).
When considered in relation to the place where the manifest object appears, it is termed the "manifesting consciousness" (*darśana-vijñāna*); ultimately, it has no separate substance.

However, according to the sequence, it is explained in terms of meaning that they are mutually dependent. This means that based on the mind that is able to perceive, there arises the object that is perceived.

Thus, the preceding treatise states: "Because one relies on the perceiving subject, the objective realm falsely appears. When primordial wisdom (*jñāna*) realizes this, wisdom merges with principle and the mind unites with the spirit;
it is a single mark and a single flavor, equal and perfectly equal. In reality, there is no distinction between subject and object.

Therefore, the verse says: "When, with respect to an object of cognition, wisdom perceives nothing at all, at that time one abides in consciousness-only (vijñapti-mātra), because one is free from the characteristics of the two grasps.
Now, the following section provides a further explanation regarding the intent behind stating that [objects] exist based on the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛtti-vijñāna). This has two meanings.

First, concerning Bodhisattvas who have not yet abandoned the karmic consciousness (ālaya-vijñāna), they still possess the aspects of the perceiver and the perceived when entering meditative observation.

Although it is associated with non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and does not differentiate between subject and object, upon emerging from meditative absorption, it is associated with this consciousness (*vijñāna*).

With reference to this consciousness, it is said that what was previously realized serves as its objective domain. Second, with reference to subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*): [it is said that]...

Within the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*), one repeatedly contemplates the Truth (*tattva*) as the object of cognition, whereby a mental image arises. At the time of actual realization, it is said that "Truth" is the object;

however, this is merely a semblance of an object and does not mean it exists substantially. Nevertheless, it does not arise apart from the manifestation of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).

Therefore, in the Commentary, both [the preceding and subsequent wisdoms] are designated within the context of subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), as the karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*) has not yet been exhausted. However, when explaining the characteristics [of the Path of Vision], the discussion is restricted solely to the karmic consciousness.
The explanation of the meaning is not yet exhaustive; therefore, it is said that "the evolving consciousness and the manifesting consciousness still persist," and so forth. This is the first meaning.

Following the phrase "by means of the subsequently attained [wisdom]," the second meaning is set forth. Someone might ask: "I have already heard your instruction regarding the fact that the karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*) as described above is not yet exhausted.

But within the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), how is discrimination performed? To answer this, he provides the following explanation, intending to clarify the fundamental reality.
At the time of realization, it is simply the true path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) of the one mind, devoid of the characteristics of subject and object as distinct entities.
However, within subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), the perceiving mind turns back to take that which was realized as its object.
Because this perceiving mind exists, there arises an image of *tathatā* before the mind as its objective sphere. Although this image is not real, it nevertheless resembles the reality itself.

According to this principle alone, it is said that within subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), the objective realm is designated based upon the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).
It is like a person drinking water: at the very moment of drinking, one cannot describe its coldness or warmth; only after having drunk can one describe it.
Although the actual substance of the water is not grasped at the time of description, the water as it is described still resembles what was actually drunk.
It is like water and its wetness; yet, in reality, they are equal. Suchness (*tathatā*) is that which is realized, and wisdom (*jñāna*) is that which realizes.

When subject and object are non-dual, it is only then called the *dharmakāya*. Since the *dharmakāya* is fundamentally endowed with both principle and wisdom, and since principle and wisdom are fundamentally non-dual, this constitutes abiding in the principle of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*) and being free from the marks of the grasped and the grasper.
△ The Superior Function of the Three Clarities.
[Commentary] "Superior function" refers to the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
[Record] "Subsequently attained" means that through provisional wisdom one penetrates the conventional world, emerging from the realm of phenomena to transform sentient beings.
△ The text consists of four parts: first, the virtue of being the preeminent leader in gathering the Dharma; second, the virtue of extending or abbreviating [the teaching] according to faculties;

third, the virtue of practice being non-different in reality; fourth, the virtue of distinct practices responding to capacities. First, the virtue of being the preeminent leader in gathering the Dharma.

In a single thought-moment, this bodhisattva is able to reach all worlds throughout the ten directions without exception, making offerings to all Buddhas and requesting them to turn the wheel of Dharma,
solely for the purpose of guiding and benefiting sentient beings, without relying on words and letters.

[Commentary]: Below this, there are two parts. First, "Offerings, etc.," which correctly clarifies the method of invitation. Second, "Solely for the sake of, etc.," which reveals the intent of the invitation.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "in a single thought-moment reaching worlds without remainder": according to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, a Bodhisattva of the first stage (*bhūmi*) can reach a hundred Buddha-worlds;
one of the second stage, a thousand Buddha-worlds; and so on, up to the tenth stage, where they can reach unspeakably unspeakable *asaṃkhyeya* worlds.
This is because their capacities differ according to their respective stages, being superior or inferior. Now, in this [context]:
In this text, the intention is to provide a general discussion of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*); therefore, the phrase "without remainder" (*anavaśeṣa*) is used to encompass them all.

Regarding those who request the Dharma: in various worlds and within various assemblies, they exert themselves as leaders, acting as guides for the multitude to request the Buddha to preach the Dharma.
As for the intent of such a request, the newly translated treatise states: "It is solely for the sake of sentient beings that one acts for their benefit."
Furthermore, it is not for the sake of seeking to hear or receive beautiful words and phrases that one requests the preaching of the Dharma.

Truly, it lies in the meaning and intent of what is revealed, cultivated, and realized, so that the assembled multitude may grasp it upon hearing, contemplate it, and put it into practice, while also hoping to extend these benefits progressively to all sentient beings at a distance.
How could it be merely a matter of listening to words in vain? It is just as in the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* regarding the twelve bodhisattvas...
Sā. Each extended a question, all saying: "We pray that [the Buddha] will do so for this assembly, and for the sake of those in the final age," and so forth.
△ Second, the virtue of extending or shortening [the teaching] according to faculties:
He may manifest the transcendence of stages and the swift attainment of perfect enlightenment for the sake of sentient beings who are timid; or he may say, "I, regarding the [unconditioned]..."

After immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, he shall attain the path of Buddhahood. For the sake of sentient beings who are indolent and lax, he is able to manifest such countless skillful means that are inconceivable.

[Commentary: "Or below" refers to the first [point], which is concise. Within this, first the function is presented; "below" subsequently clarifies the underlying meaning. "Or it is said below" [refers to the following].

2. "Extended" (*yán*) means "also first. It raises the application [of the term] below, while subsequently revealing its intended meaning. "Able to show" below constitutes the third section, which is the conclusion. [Commentary]:
"Brief" refers to a class of sentient beings whose faculties and dispositions are timid and weak; when they hear it said that the Buddha-way is long and distant...
Having endured diligent suffering for a long time, one may finally achieve success; yet, they instead give rise to despondency and refuse to cultivate further progress.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva manifests for these sentient beings a transcendence of the stages and positions, realizing the fruit of Buddhahood without passing through the full number of kalpas.

This is intended to cause them to emulate [the Buddhas], to resolve their minds toward enlightenment, and to advance toward it—just as Śākyamuni attained perfect awakening after six years of practice.
